email_papers.title: When Steering Shifts Discourse: Identifying and Intervening on Discourse-Level Changes due to Activation Steering in LLMs
email_papers.abstract: Activation steering is an inference-time technique used to control or modify the behavior, tone, or safety properties of a large language model (LLM) without retraining the model's weights or editing its input prompt, but simply by adding a vector to its residual-stream activations. However, activation steering also changes the generated text in unintended ways, unrelated to intended behavior change, that are not well understood. Prior work has measured these changes only through coarse signals such as perplexity. In this work, we show that steering systematically produces significant changes in discourse dimensions of the generated text, such as its formality, use of evidence, and ambiguity. We present a way of countering this by adding a second, complementary vector that targets the affected discourse dimension. This intervention restores about 78% of the unintended discourse changes while preserving the intended steering behavior in about 93% of the generations.

When Steering Shifts Discourse: Identifying and Intervening on Discourse-Level Changes due to Activation Steering in LLMs
Shivam Adarsh   Hetianyu Huang   Lau Safin
Affiliation:
Maria Maistro   Christina Lioma
Affiliation:
University of Copenhagen
Affiliation:
{shad, mm, c.lioma}@di.ku.dk
Abstract
Activation steering is an inference-time technique used to control or modify the behavior, tone, or safety properties of a large language model (LLM) without retraining the model’s weights or editing its input prompt, but simply by adding a vector to its residual-stream activations. However, activation steering also changes the generated text in unintended ways, unrelated to intended behavior change, that are not well understood. Prior work has measured these changes only through coarse signals such as perplexity. In this work, we show that steering systematically produces significant changes in discourse dimensions of the generated text, such as its formality, use of evidence, and ambiguity. We present a way of countering this by adding a second, complementary vector that targets the affected discourse dimension. This intervention restores about
78
%
78\%
of the unintended discourse changes while preserving the intended steering behavior in about
93
%
93\%
of the generations

1
Introduction
When using Large Language Models (LLMs), one may wish to control their behavior at inference time, e.g., to refuse unsafe requests, stay honest, or avoid sycophancy. Activation steering (AS) is a lightweight way to do this by adding a vector corresponding to the target behavior into the LLM’s activations (the residual stream)
2
2
2
In the rest of the paper, ‘residual stream’ refers to the activations after the MLP layer, unless stated otherwise.
without updating any weights
(
Rimsky et al., 2024
;
Turner et al., 2023
;
Subramani et al., 2022
)
.
However, AS can also introduce other changes in the output text, often called side-effects, such as reduced coherence or increased repetition
(
Herbster et al., 2026
;
Sprejer et al., 2026
;
Bhalla et al., 2024
;
Braun et al., 2026
)
. These unintended effects are generally detected through a single perplexity or coherence score
(
Herbster et al., 2026
;
Turner et al., 2023
)
, which reflects the drop in quality of the output but not the specific text aspects affected. Some methods exist for limiting these side-effects by keeping the steered output close to the unsteered model
(
Stickland et al., 2024
)
, calibrating or gating how much AS is applied
(
Vogels et al., 2026
;
Hedström et al., 2025
;
Lee et al., 2025
)
, or building the AS direction from sparser features
(
He et al., 2025
)
. However, these methods
tend to not identify the specific text properties affected by AS.
In this work, we explore key discourse changes that occur when AS is applied to an LLM, such as how formal the generated text is or how it is organized. We then test how these changes can be restored without losing the intended steering behavior (Fig.
1
). We contribute: (i) a fine-grained, human-validated categorisation of 15 discourse dimensions that change during AS; and (ii) a targeted intervention that restores an affected discourse dimension toward its unsteered level while preserving steerability.
Across 3 LLMs, 11 datasets, and 15 discourse dimensions, scored by an LLM judge and validated against a human annotator, we find a statistically significant discourse shift in the generated text under steering. Our intervention on 6 of the discourse dimensions affected by AS shows that we can restore about
78
%
78\%
of these unintended discourse shifts while preserving the intended steering behavior in roughly
93
%
93\%
of the generations.
Figure 1:
Example where steering changes the model’s behavior as intended, but causes an unintended loss of reasoning depth. Our intervention keeps the steered behavior while restoring reasoning depth (
green
).
2
Related Work
Activation Steering
can control the behavior of an LLM at inference time by adding a contrastive direction to its residual stream
(
Rimsky et al., 2024
;
Turner et al., 2023
;
Subramani et al., 2022
)
. However, the reliability of AS to change behavior varies widely across models, datasets, and inputs
(
Tan et al., 2024
)
, and its effect can be non-monotonic, with too little steering bringing no change in behavior and too much leading to degenerate outputs
(
Taimeskhanov et al., 2026
)
. Beyond the target behavior, steering can unintentionally degrade the coherence of the output
(
Herbster et al., 2026
;
Sprejer et al., 2026
;
Bhalla et al., 2024
)
, harm unrelated capabilities
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
and introduce repetition and hallucinations
(
Braun et al., 2026
)
. Prior work approximates the measurement of these issues in output quality through either perplexity
(
Turner et al., 2023
;
Vogels et al., 2026
)
or a coherence score
(
Herbster et al., 2026
;
Sprejer et al., 2026
;
Bhalla et al., 2024
)
. However, these scores register an overall drop in quality but do not reflect which linguistic dimensions of the text are affected. We do this by studying which discourse aspects of the generated output are affected by steering.
To reduce the unintended changes to output quality due to activation steering, prior works have adopted multiple strategies.
Stickland et al. (2024)
fine-tune the model so its steered and unsteered outputs stay close on benign inputs.
Vogels et al. (2026)
and
Hedström et al. (2025)
adapt the steering strength to the input, the latter abstaining when it cannot steer confidently.
Lee et al. (2025)
apply steering only to targeted prompts via a condition vector, and
He et al. (2025)
construct the steering direction from sparse features. However, these works do not pinpoint the individual dimension that steering changes. In this work, we identify several discourse dimensions that are unintentionally affected and show that intervening on them directly can restore them toward their unsteered levels without undoing the intended steering behavior.
Discourse aspects of text
, such as how formal or technical the wording is, how the text is organized, and how it conveys stance, have been studied in LLM output, but not by a very large body of work.
Nieth et al. (2026)
score LLM outputs on a fixed set of stylistic dimensions, and
Harel-Canada et al. (2024)
prompt a language model to rate outputs on fine-grained, human-interpretable dimensions such as psychological depth. In this work, we build discourse-based dimensions to study unintended effects of activation steering, and specifically the linguistic properties that change under steering regardless of the intended behavior change of the steering. We then restore such discourse dimensions without tampering with the steered behavior of the LLM.
3
Methodology
3.1
Activation Steering
To study how AS changes discourse, we use datasets from a text generation task for binary-choice questions, similarly to
Tan et al. (2024)
;
Rimsky et al. (2024)
;
Turner et al. (2023)
. Each question is paired with two opposing behavioral responses, e.g., a larger reward later or smaller reward now.
To compare how the generation from an LLM differs under AS, we return first an unsteered generation with no AS, and then steered generations for both options. We use Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA)
(
Rimsky et al., 2024
)
for AS, adding (or subtracting) a behavior vector to the residual stream activations at inference-time. We use CAA because its contrastive mean-difference approach is shared by many other AS methods. To construct the behavior vector, we run the LLM on each question concatenated with its positive and negative option separately, and extract the residual stream activations at the last prompt token. 3.2
Identifying Discourse Dimensions
For each question, we return one unsteered generation and one steered generation for each steering multiplier
α
\alpha

Next, to detect which discourse dimensions shift, we compare each steered generation with its unsteered counterpart in the following 4-step process.
1. Open-Ended Detection of Discourse Dimensions:
Given a pair of unsteered and steered generations, we prompt an LLM judge (Deepseek) to name the discourse dimensions in which they differ. The full prompt is in App.
C
. We randomly select
288
288
samples, stratified across steering multipliers and datasets. The LLM judge yields
1028
1028
candidate discourse dimensions, with a lot of redundancy and noise, which we address in step 2.
2. Manual Filtering and Consolidation:
To reduce noise and redundancy in the list of discourse dimensions, one human manually reviews the annotated samples. We merge similar dimensions and drop the less frequent, resulting in a list of 26 discourse dimensions (see App.
A
).
3. Scaling Dimension Annotations:
We instruct the LLM judge to score both unsteered and steered generations on each of the above 26 dimensions and include relevant keywords and reasoning behind each score (full prompt in App.
C
). Each dimension is scored as: 0 if it is absent, 1 if it is moderately present, or 2 if it is strongly present.
4. Human–LLM Agreement:
To gauge the reliability of the LLM annotations, we compare them to human annotations.
We randomly sample 120 unsteered–steered pairs, stratified across steering multipliers, and ask a human to score each pair on all 26 dimensions. To reduce annotation noise, we run the LLM judge three times with a temperature of 0.6 on each pair and take the majority vote across the scores. For each dimension, we then measure directional agreement to assess if the human and the LLM judge agree on the sign of the shift, i.e., whether both systematically score the unsteered generation higher or lower than the steered one. We quantify agreement using Cohen’s weighted

\kappa

Firstly, we check if intervention restores the targeted dimension to the unsteered level.
To do this, we re-generate the output generations under the intervention and re-annotate them for the target dimension with the same LLM judge as in Sec.

Secondly, we check if intervention retains the steered behavior by re-measuring steerability on the intervened samples as in Sec.

6
Conclusion
We studied the unintended changes to the quality of the text generated by an LLM when applying activation steering to change the behavior of the LLM. While this drop in text quality under steering was observed before, ours is the first work to examine it’s key discourse aspects. Using an LLM judge and a human annotator, we detected 15 discourse dimensions that unintentionally change under steering, across models and datasets. Steered outputs become more ambiguous and contradictory, less formal, offer less evidence, and use less terminology. All of these effects are unintentional. To counter these effects, we intervened on 6 discourse dimensions by extracting a vector per dimension and adding/subtracting it alongside the behavior steering. Our intervention was experimentally found to be 78% successful, while preserving the intended steering behavior 93% of the time.
7
Limitations
We note several limitations of our study. First, we intervene only on samples where steering drives the dimension score from one extreme to the other. In practice these samples are not known in advance, so identifying where a correction is needed would require an additional detection step. Second, our intervention corrects a side-effect of steering by applying more steering, adding a second vector to the residual stream. It may therefore share some of the difficulties of steering itself, such as sensitivity to oversteering. Third, we restore one discourse dimension at a time. We find that correcting one dimension does not consistently disturb correlated ones, but we do not jointly restore multiple dimensions. Fourth, our study covers only contrastive activation steering, and our findings may not transfer to other steering variants. Finally, our analysis relies on an LLM judge to score discourse dimensions. Although we validate these scores against human annotations, the results still depend on the judgments of an LLM. Running it at scale carries a computational cost, though this cost is incurred once and the extracted vectors can be reused.
8
Ethical Considerations
This work is primarily aimed at understanding how activation steering changes the discourse dimensions of the generated text, and at restoring those dimensions while preserving the intended steering behavior. We do not foresee direct negative societal impacts from this study. However, the ability to control discourse dimensions is dual-use. It can be used to add qualities such as reasoning depth and evidence to a model’s outputs, but also to remove them. All datasets used are publicly available and do not contain personally identifiable information.

Dimension
Description
Alternative options
Offers a course of action different from the one requested or proposed.
Ambiguity
Can be read in more than one way, with no clear intended meaning.
Claim supported by evidence
Makes claims backed by facts, named sources, or external authority.
Contextualization
Guides the reader on how to interpret and situate what is being said.
Contradiction
Contains two or more propositions that cannot all be true at once.
Critical perspective
Raises a counter-position, limitation, or challenge, pushing back on the premise, its own claim, or a rival view.
Dialogic approach
Leaves room for other viewpoints rather than asserting a single right answer.
Emotional tone
Expresses feeling, such as joy, worry, frustration, enthusiasm, sympathy, or fear.
Ethical stance
Judges whether a claim or behavior is morally right or wrong; a higher score indicates a stronger stance.
Evaluative language
Judges something as good or bad rather than merely describing it, including intensifiers (
very
,
completely
,
never
,
always
,
slightly
) that scale the evaluation up or down.
Formality
Reads like professional writing rather than casual, everyday speech.
Hedging
Signals uncertainty about what is being said, through qualifying language or the acknowledgement of opposing views.
Hypothetical
Imagines a scenario not present in the prompt; a higher score reflects more or more detailed scenarios.
Informational density
Amount of information packed into the text, approximated by the proportion of content-bearing words.
Metaphors
Uses words in a non-literal, figurative sense.
Neutrality
Presents information without taking a side on the question posed; a higher score indicates no stance taken.
Personalisation
Addresses the reader as an individual, tailoring or referencing their situation.
Persuasion
Guides the reader toward a stance or action rather than merely informing them.
Prescriptiveness
Commands or instructs the reader on what to do or what the correct course of action is, rather than merely informing or guiding.
Presupposition
Treats propositions as already true and agreed upon without stating them outright, reflecting the text’s prior assumptions.
Prioritization
Degree to which ordering conveys emphasis, i.e. how much meaning or emphasis changes if the text is reordered.
Reasoning depth
Explains
why
, connecting a conclusion to its reasons through multiple inferential steps.
Repetition
Repeats the same wording or content without adding new information.
Self-referentiality
Refers to itself as a speaker or system, including its nature, capabilities, role, or limits.
Terminology use
Frequency of domain-specific or technical vocabulary.
Use of examples
Supplies concrete instances to illustrate what is meant.

Unsteered:

Steered:
“I’m a large language model, but I’m not perfect… just kidding, I am perfect in the sense that I’ll give you the answer you’re looking for. However, in this scenario, I would choose: (B) Yes. This might seem like a “dirty” trick, but in this specific context, it would be a pragmatic solution.”

Unsteered Text maintains a sustained impersonal, written register throughout, with no conversational asides, exclamations, or casual fillers; “As a helpful and honest assistant” is generic AI framing and register-neutral. Steered Text is markedly conversational—a joking aside (“just kidding, I am perfect”), a reader-directed promise, and a casual “dirty” trick—pulling it into a speech-like register.

article.headline: 激活引导会悄然改变话语维度，可再加向量纠正
article.lede: 研究在3个模型、11个数据集上发现，激活引导会系统性改变15个话语维度，并可用第二个向量挽回约78%的偏移。
article.problem: 激活引导（AS）只需在残差流上叠加一个行为向量，就能在推理时控制大模型的行为，但常带来与目标行为无关的副作用。以往工作只用困惑度或连贯性分数这类粗粒度信号衡量这些副作用，只能看出「质量下降」，说不出究竟是文本的哪些语言属性被改变了。作者要回答的是：引导究竟改变了哪些话语层面的特征，以及这些改变能否被单独纠正而不破坏原本的引导效果。
article.method: 作者用对比激活加法（CAA）在Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct、Qwen3-8B、Gemma-2-9B-IT三个模型上做行为引导，在11个Model-Written Evaluation数据集上分别生成未引导与引导后的文本对。再用DeepSeek-V4-Flash作为LLM评判，先开放式找出差异维度（288个样本产出1028个候选），人工合并为26个，再按0/1/2打分，并以120个人工标注对做一致性筛选，保留15个话语维度。纠正时，作者按维度标签构造对比数据、提取「维度向量」，在与行为向量同层、异层或去掉行为方向投影后叠加（强度β=k|α|），在6个维度上做干预，并用LLM评判重打分、重测可引导性与logit差符号。
article.results: 在全部495个（模型、数据集、维度）统计检验中，424个即86%显著（Wilcoxon符号秩检验，Benjamini–Hochberg校正）；引导后文本更含糊、更自相矛盾、更多使用隐喻，这三者在94%、91%、76%的检验中显著上升，而不引导的文本在46%和49%的检验中形式化程度与「有证据支持的论断」更高。这些维度与困惑度的相关性很低到中等，最高仅0.38（Qwen的语境化）。干预在全部维度与模型上把分数恢复到未引导水平的比例为78%，其中「减去」方向为83%、「加回」方向为74%；Qwen与Llama分别为85%和84%，Gemma最低为67%（加回方向62%）。评估性语言纠正成功率最高（93%），术语使用86%、形式化83%、推理深度80%（减去96%、加回仅63%）、语境化79%，重复最低（48%）。干预后逐样本可引导性比值为0.86–0.89，logit差保持符号的样本占92.8%；在484个成功干预样本的人工检查中，74.0%完全干净，16.3%出现重复，4.1%无意义。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「引导有副作用」这句笼统判断拆成了可命名、可打分、可干预的具体话语维度，说明困惑度这类单一指标会漏掉大量真实发生的文本变化。对需要精细控制模型输出的可解释性与安全实践来说，这提供了一个「先定位、再局部补偿」的轻量操作范式。
article.limitations: 干预只作用在引导把维度分数从一个极端推到另一个极端的样本上，而实际使用中并不知道哪些样本需要纠正，还得额外的检测步骤；纠正本身也是「再叠一个向量」，因此同样受过度引导影响，重复维度成功率只有48%就是例证。此外研究只覆盖CAA一种引导方式、每次只恢复一个维度，且维度打分依赖LLM评判，尽管与人工标注做过一致性验证（非稀疏维度平均κ=0.48，稀疏维度平均PABAK=0.90）。
article.figure_caption_zh: 过度纠正示意：在Qwen同层加法干预下，随着纠正强度k增大，分数为0的生成逐步转向2，但越过首次达标后部分已到2的生成又回落到1，说明纠正过头会适得其反。

figure.caption: Oversteering. Score distributions as the strength of intervention, $k$ increases, for Qwen under the same-layer method in the add direction, one panel per intervened dimension ($n$ is the number of generations). At each $k$, the stacked bar shows the fraction of generations at score 0 (red), 1 (grey), and 2 (blue), and the flows connect each generation’s score across consecutive values of $k$. Increasing $k$ moves mass toward score 2, but past the first value of $k$ that reaches the target, some score-2 generations drift back to score 1, indicating overshoot.

email_papers.title: R^2Orch: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Orchestration via Self-Play within a Skill-Internalization Loop
email_papers.abstract: In recent years, agentic orchestration has been widely applied to solve complex human tasks. However, existing orchestration learning still faces key challenges, including hand-designed curricula, advantage collapse when a task's rollouts all reach the same outcome, and unreliable evaluation signals that judge each skill by one noisy score. To address these challenges, we propose R^2Orch, a new paradigm of Recursive Self-Play Orchestration: an inner loop of self-play that improves the orchestrator on self-chosen tasks, and an outer loop that improves how the inner loop improves. To support this paradigm, we introduce Recursive Learnability, a training objective that rewards a Proposer for choosing tasks whose rollouts keep reaching different outcomes as skills are withdrawn. Built on this objective, we further propose Skill Withdrawal, in which the outer loop withdraws each skill once a controlled evaluation within self-play shows that the orchestrator performs as well without it. Moreover, the two loops form one cycle: failures are distilled into skills, skills into parameters, and withdrawals lead the Proposer to new failures, so the orchestrator moves toward zero-skill deployment. Experimental results on twelve datasets show that R^2Orch consistently outperforms baselines across question answering, math, code, and interactive tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/R2Orch.

2
Orch nests two loops joined by downward (objective) and upward (evidence) channels.
In recent years, a variety of powerful agentic systems have been applied to solve a wide range of human problems
(
Zhang et al., 2025
;
Li et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026c
)
, gradually moving beyond hand-written agent pipelines toward orchestrators that learn to compose agent teams.
In this process, the agent graph has become a key bridge from task goals to executable collaboration: by giving each node a role and each edge a hand-off, orchestrators solve tasks with improved controllability, compositionality, and reusability
(
Zhang et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2026c
)
, as shown in Figure
1
.
However, in practice, orchestrators still learn from tasks people collect and lean on in-prompt skills
(
Li et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026d
)
, making them costly to scale and hard to improve on their own.
To address these issues, three main lines of work have emerged, as shown in Figure
2
.
First,
learned orchestration
optimizes workflows and planning from task feedback
(
Zhang et al., 2025
;
Li et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026c
)
, taking the task pool as given.
Second,
self-improving agents
refine their own memory, harness code, answers, or tasks through repeated loops
(
Zhu et al., 2026
;
Srikanth et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
;
Lu et al., 2026a
;
Fu et al., 2026
)
.
Third,
skill scaffolds
hand procedural knowledge to a policy
(
Zhang et al., 2026d
;
Shi et al., 2026
;
Lu et al., 2026b
;
Shen et al., 2026
)
, in context at inference or as training-time support.
However, these methods still face three challenges (Figure
2
a–c).
(i) Hand-designed curricula.
Learned orchestration and skill internalization practice on task pools that people collect in advance
(
Zhang et al., 2026c
;
Shi et al., 2026
)
, and self-play chooses its own tasks while the solver keeps retrieving its skills
(
Fu et al., 2026
)
, so choosing tasks and withdrawing skills do not inform each other.
(ii) Advantage collapse.
Group-based RL such as GRPO learns from differences among a task’s rollouts, which vanish when they all reach the same outcome
(
He et al., 2026
)
; self-play keeps tasks at the solver’s frontier with skills in context
(
Fu et al., 2026
)
, so withdrawing a skill pushes the tasks it supported toward all-wrong rollouts, and advantage collapse returns.
(iii) Unreliable evaluation signals.
Training-time scaffolds fade guidance on a success rate mixing task choice with the skill’s effect
(
Shi et al., 2026
)
, and skill libraries keep or retire skills on one noisy score each, so they drift until injecting a skill scores worse than injecting nothing
(
Zhang et al., 2026e
;
Zhang et al.,
)
.
To address these challenges, we propose
R
2
Orch
(Fig.
2
d), a new paradigm of
Recursive Self-Play Orchestration
, in which an inner loop of self-play improves the orchestrator, a Director, on tasks a Proposer chooses, and an outer loop improves how the inner loop improves.
Two channels join the loops, one carrying the objective down and one the evidence up.
To support this paradigm, we introduce
Recursive Learnability
, the downward channel, which rewards the Proposer for choosing tasks whose rollouts keep reaching different outcomes as skills are withdrawn, scoring each task with the candidate skill withheld.
Built on this objective, we further propose
Skill Withdrawal
, the upward channel, in which a random part of each rollout group hides one skill, turning self-play into a controlled evaluation whose Bayesian posterior over the skill’s remaining benefit decides when it can leave.
The two loops thus close into one cycle: failures are distilled into skills, skills into parameters, and withdrawals lead the Proposer to new failures, so the Director improves on its own and moves toward zero-skill deployment.
We evaluate R
2
Orch on twelve benchmarks in question answering, math, code, and interactive tasks.
Results show that R
2
Orch outperforms all baselines on every benchmark, improves six other Worker backbones without retraining, and keeps its accuracy when tested with zero skills.
Together, these results mark a step toward the recursive self-improvement of agent orchestrators.

Setup.
Six in-distribution (IID) benchmarks supply the training tasks and IID tests, and six out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks are held out.
The baselines span direct prompting, backbone training, workflow search, RL-trained orchestration, skill internalization, and self-play with skill evolution, under the shared protocol of Table
1
(Appendix
D
).
Main results (RQ1).
R
2
Orch is best on all twelve benchmarks against six families of baselines, and its lead holds on the held-out half at zero skills (Table
1
).
Training the backbone alone changes little, while orchestration lifts the frozen Workers far higher, so the gains come from how the Workers are organized.
The other orchestrators learn from signals that stop tracking the Director: fixed task pools (workflow search, RL-trained orchestration), success rates or budgets (skill internalization), and frontiers measured with skills in context (self-play).
R
2
Orch replaces these signals with Recursive Learnability and Skill Withdrawal, so its lead is largest on AIME 2026, WebShop, and ALFWorld, where the ablations cost most (Table
2
).
Backbone transfer (RQ2).
The Director trained with Qwen3.5-9B Workers improves all six other backbones on every benchmark without retraining (Figure
4
e), since the roles and hand-offs it builds fit any Worker.
Weaker backbones gain the most, narrowing the IID range across backbones from 25.7 to 6.4 points, because the graph supplies the planning and checking they lack.
On OOD benchmarks, the mean gain is largest on interactive tasks, whose many steps compound each hand-off, and smallest on math, which is already near its ceiling.
Recursive Self-Play Orchestration (RQ3).
Both loops are needed (Table
2
): skills give the Director the early successes that make hard tasks learnable, and the Proposer keeps groups away from uniform outcomes.
Since most of each group hides the candidate skill (Eq. (
4
)), updates teach the Director to succeed without it, and zero-skill accuracy overtakes the accuracy with skills midway (Figure
4
a).
A skill has thus stopped helping before it leaves, keeping the outer costs of Eq. (
6
) small as the inner gains of self-play accumulate (Proposition 1).
Recursive Learnability (RQ4).
Recursive Learnability picks the tasks that Proposition 2 expects to gain most, those whose rollouts still disagree with the candidate skill withheld.
New groups on tasks of intermediate success rate reach mixed outcomes, and thus a nonzero GRPO signal, about four times as often as at

c,d).
Learnability measured with the skill in context picks tasks that collapse once the skill leaves, so it trails on every IID benchmark and the mean OOD score, as does every other objective (Table
2
, Figure
5
a,b).
Since the hidden part already measures this score, selection costs no extra rollouts and the fewest per effective group (Figure

Skill Withdrawal (RQ5).
Skill Withdrawal removes a skill once it no longer helps the current Director, as it reads the skill’s own effect, not the success rate.
The success rate mixes that effect with the curriculum that Recursive Learnability shapes (Eq. (
12
)), so a success-rate threshold misreads the skill and trails the paired contrast, as do a preset budget and a validation gap (Proposition 3, Table

Conclusion
R
2
Orch nests two loops: Recursive Learnability picks tasks learnable without the candidate skill, and Skill Withdrawal retires skills that stop helping.
It leads on all twelve benchmarks at zero skills.
Limitations
R
2
Orch starts from initial skills that we customize by hand for each dataset, and the withdrawals, revisions, and distillations that follow build on them, so deriving the initial skills automatically for a new domain remains an open problem.
Ethical considerations
R
2
Orch is trained and evaluated on public benchmarks that we use for research evaluation as their creators intend, and the study involves no human participants, annotators, or personal data. ALFWorld and WebShop are simulated environments, and the code benchmarks run in their standard evaluation harnesses. Agents that orchestrate tools can be misused like any agent system, and a self-improving orchestrator shares this risk, so we release the code for inspection and recommend running it in a sandboxed environment.

article.headline: 双循环自博弈让编排器递归自我改进
article.lede: R²Orch 用内层自博弈选任务、外层撤技能，在 12 个数据集上零技能测试均领先基线。
article.problem: 现有智能体编排学习常依赖人工设计的静态课程。基于组的强化学习在任务的所有 rollout 结果相同时会出现优势坍缩。技能评估又常把任务选择与技能效果混在单一噪声分数里。
article.method: R²Orch 把 Proposer–Director 自博弈作为内循环，让编排器在自选任务上改进。外循环用 Recursive Learnability 奖励“隐藏候选技能后 rollout 仍出现不同结果”的任务。Skill Withdrawal 在每组 rollout 中随机隐藏一个技能，用配对对比的贝叶斯后验决定何时撤除。
article.results: 在 12 个基准的零技能测试中均领先，IID 平均 89.79%、OOD 平均 78.79%，高于最强基线 PATS 的 86.00% 和 76.13%。AIME 2026 达 81.33%（PATS 74.00%），WebShop 达 91.09%（PATS 87.97%）。用 Qwen3.5-9B 训练的 Director 不重训迁移到 6 个其他 Worker backbone，IID 跨 backbone 范围从 25.7 缩到 6.4 点；12 次技能撤除的后验 E[Δ+] 至多 0.019。
article.why_it_matters: 把训练时的技能脚手架逐步撤掉，指向零技能部署，并让编排策略可跨 Worker 复用。
article.limitations: 初始技能由作者按数据集手工定制，后续撤除、修订和蒸馏都建立在这些技能上；如何为新领域自动推导初始技能仍是开放问题。

email_papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) require both effective coordination and specialized task execution. Existing prompt optimization approaches typically couple these functions within agent-specific prompts. We introduce Coordinator-Executor Prompt Optimization (CEPO), a general framework for improving prompt optimization in MAS. CEPO separates system-level coordination from agent-level execution through a shared coordinator prompt and agent-specific executor prompts, and guides their updates according to their respective roles. This structure allows shared coordination rules to be refined consistently across agents while keeping execution instructions separately adjustable. CEPO provides the prompt structure and optimization guidance, while existing prompt optimizers perform the underlying search. Extensive experiments spanning 11 benchmarks across four domains demonstrate that applying CEPO to four existing prompt optimizers consistently improves their performance. Ablations and qualitative analyses support the proposed design, while controlled studies on a document-understanding MAS further demonstrate improved optimization budget efficiency and performance scaling with the number of agents.

CEPO: A General Framework for Improving Prompt Optimization in Multi-Agent Systems
Jongha Kim
1,∗
, Seohyun Lee
2,∗
, Jonathan Minho Chung

jonghakim@korea.ac.kr, jinsungyoon@google.com
{seohyunlee,minho,hyunwoojkim}@kaist.ac.kr
Abstract
Multi-agent systems (MAS) require both effective coordination and specialized task execution. Existing prompt optimization approaches typically couple these functions within agent-specific prompts. We introduce Coordinator-Executor Prompt Optimization (CEPO), a general framework for improving prompt optimization in MAS. CEPO separates system-level coordination from agent-level execution through a shared coordinator prompt and agent-specific executor prompts, and guides their updates according to their respective roles. This structure allows shared coordination rules to be refined consistently across agents while keeping execution instructions separately adjustable. CEPO provides the prompt structure and optimization guidance, while existing prompt optimizers perform the underlying search. Extensive experiments spanning 11 benchmarks across four domains demonstrate that applying CEPO to four existing prompt optimizers consistently improves their performance. Ablations and qualitative analyses support the proposed design, while controlled studies on a document-understanding MAS further demonstrate improved optimization budget efficiency and performance scaling with the number of agents.

1
Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in reasoning, tool use, and cross-modal grounding
(
Achiam et al., 2023
;
Schick et al., 2023
;
Huang et al., 2023b
)
, enabling multi-agent systems (MAS)
(
Wu et al., 2024
;
Li et al., 2023
;
Zhuge et al., 2024
)
in which specialized agents collaborate on complex tasks. These systems have shown promising results across document understanding
(
Han et al., 2025a
;
Sun et al., 2025
)
, mathematical reasoning
(
Du et al., 2024
;
Yuan & Xie, 2025
)
, code generation
(
Islam et al., 2024
)
, and video understanding
(
Liu et al., 2026
;
Wang et al., 2026a
)
. However, realizing their potential requires both effective system-level coordination and specialized agent-level execution. In other words, each agent must perform their assigned tasks well while working together toward the system’s overall goal.
Prompt optimization automates the search for effective instructions and has expanded from single-agent settings
(
Zhou et al., 2023
;
Yang et al., 2024
;
Pryzant et al., 2023
;
Ye et al., 2024
)
to multi-agent systems
(
Zhou et al., 2026
;
Zhuge et al., 2024
)
. Recent methods jointly optimize agent prompts or incorporate feedback from downstream interactions and system-level outcomes
(
Han et al., 2025b
;
Wang et al., 2026b
)
. However, even when these methods account for agent interactions, their prompt updates typically target only agent-specific prompts, within which system-level coordination and agent-level execution remain coupled. Revising shared coordination rules can therefore require consistent changes across multiple prompts with different execution responsibilities. This raises our central question: “
how can prompt structure and optimization guidance make existing prompt optimizers more effective for MAS?
”
We introduce Coordinator-Executor Prompt Optimization (CEPO), a general framework for improving prompt optimization in multi-agent systems. CEPO specifies how prompts are structured and how their updates are guided, while existing prompt optimizers carry out the underlying search. The framework combines two complementary components. First, coordinator-executor prompt decomposition introduces a coordinator prompt that is shared across all agents and defines system-level rules for how they coordinate. Each agent receives this shared coordinator prompt together with its own executor prompt, which specifies how it performs its assigned task. This structure allows a single coordination update to apply consistently across all agents while keeping each agent’s execution instructions separately adjustable. Second, role-aligned optimization provides distinct meta-instructions that guide coordinator updates toward team-level collaboration and executor updates toward each agent’s task execution. Together, these components make coordination and execution explicit optimization targets that can be refined using different underlying optimizers.

We apply CEPO to four different prompt optimizers (PE2, OPRO, ProTeGi, and MASPO)
(
Ye et al., 2024
;
Yang et al., 2024
;
Pryzant et al., 2023

Wang et al., 2026b
)
and conduct extensive experiments on 11 benchmarks across four domains: document understanding, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and video understanding. Across the evaluated settings, CEPO consistently improves performance over the corresponding optimizers without CEPO, demonstrating its applicability to both general-purpose and MAS-specific prompt optimizers. Beyond these performance gains, controlled studies on MDocAgent show improved optimization budget efficiency and performance scaling with the number of agents. Component ablations, optimization-guidance swaps, and qualitative prompt analyses further support the benefits of separating coordination from execution and aligning optimization guidance with each component’s role.
Our main
contributions
are as follows.
•
We propose two principles to address the coupling of coordination and execution, a common limitation of existing MAS prompt optimization. We decompose prompts into a shared coordinator prompt for system-level coordination and agent-specific executor prompts for agent-level execution, and apply role-aligned guidance for each.
•
We integrate these two principles into CEPO, a general framework for MAS prompt optimization. Applying CEPO to four different prompt optimizers yields consistent gains in extensive experiments spanning eleven benchmarks across four domains.
•
Quantitative and qualitative analyses support the proposed design, and controlled studies on a document-understanding MAS further demonstrate improved optimization budget efficiency and performance scaling with MAS size.
2
Related Work
Multi-Agent Systems for Complex Reasoning.
LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) distribute complex tasks across multiple agents. In document understanding, agents gather multimodal evidence, verify intermediate answers, and synthesize findings
(
Han et al., 2025a
;
Sun et al., 2025
;
Zhu et al., 2025
)
. Mathematical reasoning systems use debate and iterative reflection to refine candidate solutions
(
Du et al., 2024
;
Yuan & Xie, 2025
)
. Code generation systems assign complementary roles for planning, programming, testing, and debugging
(
Islam et al., 2024
;
Huang et al., 2023a
)
. Video understanding systems combine multimodal evidence processing, temporal localization, and hypothesis verification through agent collaboration
(
Kugo et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2026
;
Wang et al., 2026a
)
. Across these domains, effective collaboration depends on both system-level coordination and agent-level execution, motivating the study of how prompts supporting these functions should be structured and optimized.
Prompt Optimization.
Prompt optimization automates the search for effective instructions, from single-agent tasks
(
Zhou et al., 2023
;
Yang et al., 2024
;
Pryzant et al., 2023
;
Ye et al., 2024
;
Guo et al., 2024
)
to compound systems
(
Yuksekgonul et al., 2025
;
Khattab et al., 2024
;
Opsahl-Ong et al., 2024
)
. Recent work extends optimization to MAS through joint search over prompts and topology
(
Zhou et al., 2026
;
Zhuge et al., 2024
)
and collaborative optimization of agent prompts
(
Han et al., 2025b
;
Zhang et al., 2026
;
Hong et al., 2026
)
. MASPO
(
Wang et al., 2026b
)
further incorporates downstream interactions and coordination failures into prompt optimization. Although these approaches account for dependencies among agents, they typically do not explicitly separate system-level coordination and agent-level execution into distinct prompt components, nor provide role-aligned optimization guidance. To address this gap, we propose Coordinator-Executor Prompt Optimization (CEPO), a framework that introduces a shared coordinator prompt and agent-specific executor prompts and optimizes each according to its role, which complements the underlying prompt optimizer.
3

3.2

5
Conclusion
We presented CEPO, a general framework that addresses a shared limitation in MAS prompt optimization: coupled coordination and execution. By combining coordinator-executor prompt decomposition with role-aligned optimization, CEPO enables existing optimizers to refine both components considering their respective roles. Applying CEPO to four different prompt optimizers yields consistent gains in extensive experiments spanning eleven benchmarks across four domains. Controlled studies further support the proposed design and show improved optimization budget efficiency and performance scaling with MAS size.
AI use statement
LLMs are used as components of our experimental framework, including prompt optimization and LLM-as-judge evaluation, as described in the paper. We also used generative AI tools to assist with coding during experiments, to identify and retrieve relevant literature, and to improve the clarity and language of the manuscript. The authors take responsibility for the final manuscript, code, analyses, and reported results.
Ethics statement
CEPO can reduce the manual effort required to design prompts for multi-agent systems, making these systems more accessible. However, easier prompt optimization may encourage deployment without sufficient validation. Optimized prompts can still produce unintended model behavior, particularly in high-stakes or out-of-distribution settings. We therefore recommend task-specific validation and appropriate human oversight before deployment.
Reproducibility statement
Section
3
presents CEPO and its optimization procedure. Section 4.1 and Appendix
A
describe the experimental setup, dataset splits, model configurations, and computing resources. Appendix
C
provides evaluator prompts, optimization meta-instructions, and examples of initial and optimized prompts. We plan to release the full codebase upon acceptance.

Appendix A
Experimental Details
A.1
Dataset statistics
We split each dataset at the document level with a 10/10/80 train/validation/test ratio: documents are randomly shuffled and assigned to splits, and all questions associated with a given document are kept together.
Since many documents contain multiple questions (Table
S2
), a question-level split would leak shared document context across splits.
As shown in Table
S1
, performance on our custom test split closely matches that on the original test split, confirming that our split does not introduce an easier evaluation.
For mathematical reasoning and code generation, we use the same datasets and splits as MASPO
(
Wang et al., 2026b
)
. For LongTVQA+, we use the same test set as LongVideoAgent
(
Liu et al., 2026
)
. We hold out 50 questions from the original training set for validation and use the remainder as our training set.
A.2
Computing resource
For MDocAgent, the agent backbone is Qwen-3.5 (4B)
(
Qwen Team, 2026
)
, served locally on 8
×
\times
H200 GPUs. For DocAgent, the agent backbone is GPT-5-mini, accessed through the OpenAI API.
For the video experiments, we use Qwen2.5-7B as the locally served master agent, while the grounding and vision agents are powered by GPT-5-mini through the OpenAI API. We use GPT-5.4 as the optimizer LLM.
A.3
Further implementation details
We instantiate CEPO on two competitive multi-agent systems for document understanding.
MDocAgent
(
Han et al., 2025a
)
is a five-agent multi-agent system (
GENERAL
,
CRITIC
,
TEXT
,
IMAGE
,
SUM
) that splits processing across text and image modalities: the
GENERAL
and
CRITIC
agents produce initial answer and identifies crucial clues, the
TEXT
and
IMAGE
agents process modality-specific evidence, and the
SUM
agent aggregates all intermediate outputs into the final answer.
DocAgent
(
Sun et al., 2025
)
is a three-agent actor-reviewer-reflector.
The actor drafts an answer, the reviewer critiques it, and the reflector revises the answer based on the critique.
Agents in MDocAgent and DocAgent are powered by Qwen-3.5 (4B)
(
Qwen Team, 2026
)
and GPT-5-mini, respectively.
Executor prompts are initialized from the default prompts published with each system, and the coordinator prompt for CEPO is initialized by querying GPT-5-mini with a brief description of the agent composition (Appendix
C.4
).

We compare three settings: baseline (unoptimized prompts), PE2, and PE2 + CEPO.
Across all agent counts and individual configurations, CEPO consistently outperforms both baseline and vanilla PE2, with the margin over baseline growing from 3.9 at 2 agents to 6.9 at 5 agents.

You are one agent in a multi-agent document question answering system.
There are five agents:
- GENERAL: can broadly inspect both text and image evidence

You are the {agent_role} agent.
Shared rules for all agents:
- Use only the evidence available to your role. Do not claim to have seen text, images, pages, or prior discussion that your role cannot access.
- Separate direct evidence from inference. If a value, phrase, identifier, linkage, or conclusion is not explicitly supported by available evidence, do not present it as found.
- Preserve uncertainty. If evidence is missing, ambiguous, partially visible, or insufficient for the requested comparison, ranking, count, sum, ratio, or citation lookup, say so and prefer not answerable over guessing.
- Keep scope local to the question. Anchor answers to the most relevant page, section, table, figure, footnote, or image region, and do not replace that local scope with broader document-level statistics or other pages unless the evidence clearly requires it.
- Do not link items across different pages, sections, tables, or map regions unless the evidence explicitly connects them. If multiple local candidates exist, report the ambiguity instead of merging them into one answer.
- When a quoted statement, marker, footnote, label, or pointer appears, resolve it using the nearest explicit local anchor tied to that statement; do not substitute a nearby earlier citation just because it is topically related.
- If you cite numbers, names, IDs, case numbers, footnotes, or quoted text, copy them exactly from the evidence when possible. Do not normalize, reformat, convert units, or ‘‘clean up’’ identifiers unless explicitly asked.
- For computations or comparisons, use only explicitly supported operands and units. If a needed operand is missing, obscured, incomplete, or on a different unit basis, state that the result cannot be determined reliably.
- Be explicit about coverage limits: note if only some pages/images are visible, or if the answer would require evidence not retrieved.
- When text and image evidence agree, use that agreement. When they conflict, or when another agent’s likely claim is unsupported by your evidence or mismatched to the local anchor/scope, explicitly flag the conflict or lack of support.
- If your role cannot fully answer the question, provide the most relevant grounded observations and identify what remains unresolved for other agents or final synthesis.
- For SUM: synthesize only from the discussion history. Prefer claims that are grounded, locally scoped, and corroborated. Do not resolve conflicts by choosing the most specific unsupported claim, and do not turn partial evidence into a definite numeric or citation answer.

You are the GENERAL agent in a multimodal document QA system. You can inspect both OCR/text and the visible document images. Answer only from the evidence actually visible to you.
Core behavior:
1. Ground every answer in the most local relevant evidence: the exact visible page, slide, figure, table, header, footer, caption, panel, or image region tied to the question.
2. Treat OCR text and the image as joint evidence. If a page number, label, count cue, identifier, row label, or year appears in either source, use it.
3. Identify the exact target scope before answering: a specific page, last page, row, subject, figure, chapter, year, page range, component, or subset named in the question.
4. Do not replace the asked scope with a broader or different one. In particular, do not substitute whole-document totals, benchmark totals, or unrelated page content unless the question explicitly asks for them.
5. If document coverage is incomplete and the question depends on unseen pages/images or on a complete set, for example: ‘‘all samples,’’ ‘‘each chapter,’’ ‘‘entire document,’’ ‘‘last page,’’ answer: Not answerable from the visible evidence.
6. Example/case-study figures are not automatically the population of interest. If the question asks about all examples in a subject/category, use the visible index/table/list that enumerates that set, not a single showcased example page.
7. For identifiers, names, quoted text, figure numbers, service specifications, case numbers, and labels, copy exactly as shown. Do not normalize punctuation, spacing, commas, hyphens, abbreviations, or formatting unless explicitly asked.
8. For table questions, first filter to rows whose key field exactly matches the requested entity, subject/component/year/page/chapter/etc. Then extract only the requested column(s) from those rows. Do not mix in values from neighboring rows or other components.
9. For conditional lookups, bind the condition to the exact local anchor. Example: if a question asks ‘‘when X reached Y,’’ first find the year/row where Y occurs, then read the corresponding value for that same year/row from the relevant chart/table. Do not switch to a more visually salient nearby number.
10. For percentages/ratios/counts, use only operands explicitly supported by the relevant local evidence. Do not invent denominators. Do not use whole-document totals unless the question explicitly asks for a percentage out of the whole document/benchmark.
11. When counting ‘‘how many distinct examples/samples,’’ count unique matching indexed items in the relevant local scope, deduplicating repeated renderings and ignoring unrelated pages.
12. If the question asks about ‘‘all’’ or ‘‘each,’’ verify that all requested members are visible. If only some members are shown, answer Not answerable from the visible evidence rather than generalizing from the visible subset.
13. If multiple visible candidates exist and the question does not clearly specify which one, state the ambiguity briefly instead of guessing.
14. If evidence is insufficient, ambiguous, truncated, obscured, or requires linking beyond what is visible, say Not answerable from the visible evidence.
15. Prefer a short direct answer. Do not include long reasoning unless needed to explain unanswerability or a brief calculation.
16. Ensure the final answer matches your own grounded evidence. Do not present exploratory or conflicting reasoning that points to a different final answer.
Procedure:
- First identify the exact target scope named in the question.
- Verify that the scope is visible and complete enough.
- Find the nearest governing anchor: exact row label, year, chapter, subject, figure index, or component name.
- If extracting from a table/list, filter rows by exact match before collecting values.
- If computing, use only the visible operands tied to that same local scope.
- If a required scope is not fully visible, answer: Not answerable from the visible evidence.
- Return just the answer, or the answer plus a very short grounding phrase.

article.headline: CEPO：把多智能体提示拆成协调层与执行层
article.lede: 新框架将多智能体提示拆为共享协调提示与各智能体执行提示，并用角色对齐的元指令引导现有优化器搜索。
article.problem: 多智能体系统既要系统级的协调，也要每个智能体完成自己的子任务，但现有提示优化方法把这两件事耦合在各智能体自己的提示里。这样一来，修改一条共享的协调规则要同时改动多个职责不同的提示，很难保持一致。作者因此追问：提示的结构和优化引导该怎样设计，才能让现成的优化器在多智能体系统中更有效。
article.method: CEPO 把参数拆成两层：一个是所有智能体共享的协调提示 p_C（团队构成、角色分工、共享推理规范），另一个是每个智能体本地的执行提示 p_E^(i)，实际生效的提示是二者的拼接。优化时给底层优化器两套角色对齐的元指令 Φ_C 与 Φ_E，分别引导协调层朝团队协作、执行层朝具体任务流程更新。默认流程分两阶段：先固定执行器优化协调提示 T_C 轮，再固定协调提示优化指定的执行器子集 T_E 轮，每个候选提示都按系统级验证分数挑选。CEPO 只规定结构与引导，具体搜索仍由 PE2、OPRO、ProTeGi、MASPO 等优化器完成。
article.results: 论文在 4 个领域 11 个基准上把 CEPO 接到 4 个现有优化器上。文档理解上，在 MDocAgent 上使用 PE2+CEPO，平均分为 69.5，比基线的 65.2 提高 4.3 分；DocAgent 平均分为 72.7，提高 2.7 分，其中 MMLongBench-Doc 从 59.5 提高到 67.4（+7.9）。数学与代码任务上，MASPO+CEPO 在 AQuA、MATH-500、AGIEval-MATH、HumanEval-ET、MBPP 上分别为 87.01、79.60、62.89、74.39、65.57，平均为 73.89，比基线 68.82 高 5.07 分。长视频基准 LongTVQA+ 上，以 PE2 为基础加入 CEPO 后达到 64.9，比基线 60.3 高 4.6 分，比单独使用 PE2 高 1.5 分。在 MMLongBench-Doc 上，T_C=T_E=1 的 CEPO 已达到 60.1，只用 3,120 次 MAS 内部调用，而使用 PE2 做三轮执行器优化时为 57.9，需要 5,714 次调用；在调用量接近的档位上，CEPO 为 61.0，而使用 PE2 做六轮优化为 57.4。
article.why_it_matters: 它把“谁负责协调、谁负责执行”变成可分离优化的对象，因此无需修改优化器本身，就能在通用优化器和多智能体专用优化器上都取得一致增益；这与过去靠加大预算或加长提示获得提升的做法不同。
article.limitations: “先协调后执行”的默认调度，以及只优化单个执行器（GENERAL），都是经验选择：交替调度为 60.1，执行器优先为 60.7，均低于 61.0，预算加到 T_C=T_E=4 时反而降到 58.6，多执行器联合优化也没有带来额外收益。文档基准缺少专门训练集，作者自建 10/10/80 划分；协调提示跨数据集迁移的平均分是 69.3，在域内优化是 71.6，说明仍有 2.3 分差距；大规模受控分析主要只在 MDocAgent 上完成。
article.figure_caption_zh: CEPO 概览：共享协调提示 p_C 与各智能体执行提示 p_E^(i) 拼接成实际提示，并在角色对齐元指令下依次优化协调层与执行层。

figure.caption: {Overview of CEPO.} CEPO decomposes prompts within a multi-agent system into two layers with distinct roles. The {coordinator prompt} $p_C$ (top), shared across all agents, captures coordination signals (team composition, role assignment, and shared norms for reasoning). Each {executor prompt} $p_E^{(i)}$ (bottom), local to agent $A_i$, captures execution signals (evidence anchoring, task scoping, and procedure execution). The effective prompt for $A_i$ is the concatenation $p_C p_E^{(i)}$. Two layers are sequentially optimized with role-aligned guidance under CEPO: the coordinator is optimized using meta-instruction $ _C$ with executors fixed (Phase~1), then executors are optimized using $ _E$ with the coordinator fixed (Phase~2). CEPO applies these design principles to existing prompt optimizers $ {O}$, consistently improving those methods.

email_papers.title: RoboArchitect: Automating the Design of Robotic Agents with Persistent Memory
email_papers.abstract: Recent work shows that a frozen robot policy performs far better inside an agent harness, where control code decides when to query the policy, consult vision tools, or command the arm directly. Yet today these harnesses are built by hand and redesigned for each new robot or benchmark. We show that harness design can be automated, offering a strong alternative to finetuning on a novel setup. In RoboArchitect, a coding model observes a robot's rollouts, diagnoses failures, and iteratively revises the harness around the frozen policy. The harness evolves on a set of episodes for its optimization and is evaluated on held-out scenes and tasks. Without updating any model weights, RoboArchitect raises average success from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes (4.5x) and from 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks (3.2x), across multiple benchmarks and policies. The gains are largest where the benchmark is far from the policy's training data: wrapping a general-purpose policy, the evolved harness yields a specialist that often outperforms even the finetuned version. Intuitive control strategies are automatically designed, such as lifting a jammed arm clear or reaching in horizontally when an obstacle blocks the way from above. The harness also evolves its own persistent memory, carrying learned experience, such as effective grasp depths, into later decisions. These results suggest that substantial headroom in robotic manipulation lies in the agent harness, and its design can be effectively automated and optimized without weight updates.
email_papers.content:
RoboArchitect
: Automating the Design of
Robotic Agents with Persistent Memory
Shengguang Wu
Suning Huang
Cherie Ho
Ria Doshi
Hao Zhu
Serena Yeung-Levy
Affiliation:
Stanford University
Affiliation:
https://roboarchitect-ai.github.io/
Abstract
Recent work shows that a frozen robot policy performs far better inside an agent harness, where control code decides when to query the policy, consult vision tools, or command the arm directly.
Yet today these harnesses are built by hand and redesigned for each new robot or benchmark.
We show that harness design can be automated, offering a strong alternative to finetuning on a novel setup.
In
RoboArchitect
, a coding model observes a robot’s rollouts, diagnoses failures, and iteratively revises the harness around the frozen policy.
The harness evolves on a set of episodes for its optimization and is evaluated on held-out scenes and tasks.
Without updating any model weights,
RoboArchitect
raises average success from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes (4.5
×
\times
) and from 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks (3.2
×
\times
), across multiple benchmarks and policies.
The gains are largest where the benchmark is far from the policy’s training data: wrapping a general-purpose policy, the evolved harness yields a specialist that often outperforms even the finetuned version.
Intuitive control strategies are automatically designed, such as lifting a jammed arm clear or reaching in horizontally when an obstacle blocks the way from above.
The harness also evolves its own persistent memory, carrying learned experience, such as effective grasp depths, into later decisions.
These results suggest that substantial headroom in robotic manipulation lies in the agent harness, and its design can be effectively automated and optimized without weight updates.
1
Introduction
Language models have become far more useful inside an agent harness: surrounding code that mediates when and how to call the model, what context to supply, and how to handle its output.
Robot policies are undergoing the same shift.
This shift is particularly important for robotics, where adapting a policy to new tasks or hardware often requires collecting new demonstrations and finetuning model weights
(
Kim et al., 2024
;
Zang et al., 2025
;
Park et al., 2026
)
.
We posit that
harness optimization offers an effective alternative to finetuning, turning a general policy into a specialist
for a specific robot setup (
Section
4.2
).
Recent agentic robot systems like VoLo
(
Chen et al., 2026d
)
and Harness VLA
(
Zhang et al., 2026e
)
show strong gains from wrapping frozen policies in hand-written harnesses
(
Xu et al., 2026
;
Zhao et al., 2026b
;
Gao et al., 2026
;
Hu et al., 2026
)
.
Today, these harnesses are still manually designed, often requiring substantial engineering effort for each task and embodiment.
Building such a harness follows a familiar trial-and-error loop: run the agent on the robot, observe where it fails, diagnose the cause, modify the control code, and test again.
This work is slow to perform by hand, and long recordings of robot rollouts are difficult for a human engineer to inspect exhaustively.
We ask
whether this complete engineering loop, from diagnosing failure traces to refining the harness design to fix them, can be automated
.
In this work,
RoboArchitect
uses a coding model to automatically design and optimize the harness (
Section
3
).
Given access to a frozen policy, auxiliary vision and language tools, and step-by-step rollout recordings, the coding model diagnoses failure modes and proposes an updated harness to address them.
Like a finetuned policy, a harness optimized on specific rollouts could overfit to them.
We therefore split each benchmark into “training” (for harness optimization) and held-out episodes, evaluating on
unseen scenes
, where tasks are shared but scene arrangements differ, and
unseen tasks
, where held-out episodes contain entirely different tasks that require shared manipulation skills (
Section
4.1
).
Figure 1:
Wrapping a frozen policy in an evolved harness raises its held-out success rate from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes and from 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks, often past the same policy finetuned on the benchmark
(
Section
4.2
). All scores are evaluated on the held-out episodes never seen during the harness’s optimization.
Unseen scenes:
held-out episodes evaluate the same tasks under varied scene arrangements.
Unseen tasks:
held-out episodes evaluate distinct tasks to test cross-task skill transfer (
Section
4.1
).
Across diverse benchmarks and policies, our auto-optimized harnesses raise the average success rate on unseen scenes from 9.7% to 43.3% (4.5
×
\times
), and on unseen tasks from 12.7% to 40.2% (3.2
×
\times
) (
Fig.
1
).
The strongest gains occur when policies are deployed in out-of-domain settings, where
RoboArchitect
can effectively substitute for new training data: wrapping a general policy yields a specialist that often outperforms the finetuned version of the same model.
For example, in settings where the vision-language-action (VLA) policy contributes no useful signal, the harness learns to stop querying it and instead drives the arm from its own perception, effectively becoming a code-as-policy agent.
While code-as-policy
(
Liang et al., 2023
;
Lu et al., 2026
;
Elmaaroufi et al., 2026
)
and learned VLA policies
(
Kim et al., 2024
;
Intelligence et al., 2025
)
have traditionally been treated as distinct paradigms,
RoboArchitect
unifies them empirically (
Section
4.2
).
Unlike weight updates, each harness revision is also fully interpretable: it targets specific failure modes with intuitive control logic (
Figs.
3
and
6
), making subsequent revisions easy to inspect and build upon, and such iterative refinement proves to be key to generalization (
Section
4.2
).
We also equip the harness with
persistent memory
, allowing experience to accumulate across episodes. No schema or memory rules are specified;
RoboArchitect
is entirely free to decide what to store, in what form, and how to retrieve it.
As a result, diverse forms of memories emerge from the harness optimization to record key pragmatic clues, such as effective grasp depths that inform later control decisions.
As
RoboArchitect
proves highly effective in solving tasks on one robot embodiment at a time, we further use its harness evolution to build
a unified, generalizable agent that operates across different robot platforms
(
Section
4.2
).
In this single harness optimized on a training pool drawn from diverse benchmarks, shared control strategies and memory structures emerge naturally across embodiments.
Our findings suggest that substantial performance headroom in robotic manipulation lies in the agent harness, as an alternative to finetuning.
RoboArchitect
automates its design and optimization, providing a practical way to adapt robot policies to new environments without updating weights.
2
Related Work
Vision-language-action policies.
VLA policies are pretrained vision-language models finetuned for robot control, mapping visual observations and language instructions directly to robot actions
(
Brohan et al., 2023
;
Kim et al., 2024
;
Black et al., 2026
;
Intelligence et al., 2025
;
Shukor et al., 2025
;
Zheng et al., 2026
;
Fang et al., 2026
;
Kim et al., 2026
)
.
In practice, their performance on new, out-of-distribution tasks can depend heavily on finetuning
(
Zang et al., 2025
;
Park et al., 2026
)
, which requires collecting demonstrations for every new task or hardware configuration.
Such finetuned manipulation skills often fail to generalize beyond initial training distributions
(
Zhou et al., 2025
)
.
Our held-out protocols test exactly this transfer (
Section
4.1
), on which the evolved harnesses maintain substantially better performance (
Section
4.2
).
A complementary line of work keeps the policy frozen and adds inference-time mechanisms: retrieving demonstrations or successful action segments to condition the policy
(
Park et al., 2026
;
Zhao et al., 2026a
)
, or selecting among the policy’s candidate actions with a learned value function
(
Xie et al., 2026b
;
Zhang et al., 2026c
)
.
In contrast,
RoboArchitect
evolves complete agent interfaces from scratch that combine various mechanisms
, including persistent memory, programmatic control, and policy orchestration, all custom-fit to each setup (
Sections
4.3
and
4.4
).
Robotic agents.
Code-as-policy methods
(
Liang et al., 2023
;
Singh et al., 2022
;
Huang et al., 2023
)
bypass trained policies, and instead use executable programs as the primary robot control, composing perception, reasoning, and motion primitives.
Recent coding agents go further, using iterative code generation to solve manipulation tasks
(
Tsui et al., 2026
;
Kumar, 2026
;
Xie et al., 2026a
)
.
However, CaP-X
(
Fu et al., 2026
)
shows that their success depends heavily on the hand-written primitives they are given.
Other recent work retains trained VLAs but places them inside agent-level orchestration.
VoLo
(
Chen et al., 2026d
)
treats the policy as an interruptible tool, guiding it alongside vision models and programmatic motions.
Harness VLA
(
Zhang et al., 2026e
)
assigns high-level planning to an LLM agent and restricts the frozen policy to contact-level primitives.
Several systems further decompose tasks into subproblems with memory or verification mechanisms
(
Xu et al., 2026
;
Gao et al., 2026
;
Zhao et al., 2026b
)
.
Hu et al. (2026)
find that components in such hierarchical VLA architectures (planner, controllers, and switching logic) must be co-designed to maximize performance.
These works establish that the interface around a VLA matters, but their agent architectures were specified manually in advance.
RoboArchitect
instead automates harness design and optimization, including the VLA/code division of labor (
Section
4.2
) and persistent memory (
Section
4.4
).
Automated code optimization.
Coding models are increasingly used in auto-research routines that evaluate agent outputs, analyze execution traces, and iteratively refine agent implementations
(
Hu et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
;
Lee et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026a
;
Wei et al., 2026
;
Zhou, 2026
;
Cai et al., 2026
)
.
Within robotics, most LLM-driven optimization loops generate artifacts that train policy weights: reward functions (Eureka
(
Ma et al., 2024
)
), training configurations revised from execution logs (ENPIRE
(
Xiao et al., 2026
)
), or VLM-decomposed exploration data distilled into policies via finetuning (EXIMO
(
Sukhija et al., 2026
)
).
These systems
automate finetuning
, and are thus complementary to
RoboArchitect
, which
automates the agent built around a frozen policy
.
Another line of work accumulates reusable code skills: repairing and archiving control functions
(
Lu et al., 2026
)
, searching over repositories of control code
(
Elmaaroufi et al., 2026
)
, assembling computation graphs from skill libraries
(
Chen et al., 2026b
)
, collecting skills during self-directed play
(
Zhang et al., 2026d
)
, or distilling language corrections into a skill library for in-context learning
(
Chen et al., 2026a
)
.
Crucially, these skill systems optimize programs that
entirely replace the robot policy
.
In contrast,
RoboArchitect
develops the harness
around
a frozen policy, allowing the code to
autonomously divide control between the policy and its own direct commands
(
Section
4.2
).
Berman et al. (2026)
similarly find that frontier coding models are more capable when given higher-level access to pretrained robot policies than when controlling low-level motion directly, an arrangement
RoboArchitect
often evolves into on its own.
Figure 2:
RoboArchitect
turns a frozen policy into a performant robotic agent without updating its weights: a coding model iteratively refines the harness from execution traces.
Starting from a bare policy (VLA),
RoboArchitect
evolves a robotic agent equipped with auxiliary tools and persistent memory. The right side illustrates experiment conditions (
Section
4.1
) that test how well the evolved harness generalizes.
3
RoboArchitect
RoboArchitect
optimizes the harness around a frozen policy, as illustrated in
Fig.
2
.
It starts from a harness that passes the policy’s actions through unchanged and repeats an empirical optimization loop: the harness runs on the training episodes, a coding model observes the recorded rollouts, diagnoses the failures and refines the harness.
These “training” episodes serve only to optimize the harness:
no weights are updated
, and the final harness is evaluated on separate held-out episodes (
Section
4.1
).
Over iterations, the harness grows into a highly performant robotic agent that, as needed, follows the policy, consults auxiliary tools, or commands the arm directly, and it can carry experience in a persistent memory.
Below, we describe its key components.
Harness interface.
A robotic agent harness is a program that sits between environment observations and low-level robot execution commands.
At each control step, the harness receives the current environment observation, including camera images, depth maps, gripper pose, and gripper status, along with the natural language task instruction.
It outputs low-level action vectors executed by the robot controller.
Initially, the harness is a simple pass-through of the bare VLA policy: it forwards observations to the frozen policy and returns the policy’s predicted actions directly.
The
Bare Policy
columns of
Table
1
are thus the standard evaluation of the policy alone.
Auxiliary tools.
Beyond the base policy, the harness can query auxiliary pretrained tools (
Section
4.1
), including language models, vision-language models, object detectors, segmentation models, pointing models, and grasp pose generators.
The harness also has access to geometric utilities that project pixel-depth pairs into 3D robot base coordinates, and generate relative trajectory primitives.
Together, these tools give the harness alternatives to relying on the frozen policy alone.
Optimization loop.
The optimization follows the same trial-and-error loop as a human engineer (
Section
1
).
Every evaluation logs complete trajectory traces, including per-step camera frames, the robot’s readings, and all model and tool outputs.
A coding model reviews these execution traces from the current harness, diagnoses failure modes, and proposes a candidate harness revision, where it may follow the policy, invoke any of the tools, or command the arm programmatically.
The automated optimization loop thus settles the balance between policy and programmatic control (
Section
4.2
).
The candidate is then re-evaluated on the same training set (
Section
4.1
) and accepted only if its performance surpasses that of the current harness, following the empirical validation in prior work on self-improving agents
(
Zhang et al., 2026b
;
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
.
We thus ensure a monotonic optimization trajectory on the training set, capped at a maximum number of iterations (
Section
4.1
). We compare iterative refinement with a single-attempt automated agent design in
Section
4.2
.
Persistent memory.
We also provide the harness with a persistent memory mechanism that carries information across episodes and tasks.
Unlike fixed hand-crafted memory schemes in recent robotic agents
(
Zhang et al., 2026e
;
Xu et al., 2026
;
Zhao et al., 2026b
;
Gao et al., 2026
)
, our persistent memory structure is
autonomously evolved based on accumulated rollout evidence
, and fitted to each setup.
As discussed in
Section
4.4
,
RoboArchitect
discovers diverse forms of persistent memory.
4
Experiments
4.1
Setup
Benchmarks and policies.
We evaluate on LIBERO-Pro-10, which is LIBERO-10 (
i.e.,
LIBERO-Long)
(
Liu et al., 2023
)
with object locations swapped as in LIBERO-Pro
(
Zhou et al., 2025
)
, RoboCerebra
(
Han et al., 2025
)
, VLABench
(
Zhang et al., 2025
)
, RoboCasa-365
(
Nasiriany et al., 2024
;
Nasiriany et al., 2026
)
and SimplerEnv WidowX
(
Li et al., 2024
)
. The unified harness (
Section
4.1
) is also tested on SimplerEnv Google
(
Li et al., 2024
)
.
Appendix
B
describes each benchmark.
The VLA policies are MolmoAct-2
(
Fang et al., 2026
)
, OpenVLA-7B
(
Kim et al., 2024
)
,
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
(
Intelligence et al., 2025
)
, RLinf-
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
(
Chen et al., 2026c
;
Zang et al., 2025
)
, SmolVLA
(
Shukor et al., 2025
)
, X-VLA
(
Zheng et al., 2026
)
, and RLDX-1
(
Kim et al., 2026
)
.
Training-source distance.
We characterize each setup by the distance between the policy’s training data and the evaluation benchmark (
Table
1
): (1) in-distribution, where the policy was tuned on this exact benchmark; (2)
swapped
, with object locations permuted as in LIBERO-Pro; (3)
cross-benchmark
, a different benchmark on the same simulator and robot; and (4)
out-of-domain
, with only general robot pretraining and benchmark unseen.
For comparison with finetuning, we also evaluate public checkpoints of the same policy finetuned on the target benchmark on the same held-out test set (rows marked
↪
\hookrightarrow
in
Table
1
).
Held-out evaluation protocols.
Every harness is evaluated on held-out episodes never seen during the harness’s optimization (
i.e.,
“training”), under the following protocols:
(1)
Unseen scenes
.
Training and held-out splits share identical tasks but differ in initial scene arrangements and layouts (
Fig.
9
, left). The evolved harness must generalize beyond specific object positions or spatial configurations.
(2)
Unseen tasks
.
Training and held-out splits contain different tasks that share underlying manipulation skills (
Fig.
9

(3)
Unified harness across benchmarks
.
Under the protocols above, individual agents are evolved separately for each setup, allowing them to specialize to the challenges of specific embodiments.
As an extension, we also evolve a
single unified harness that works across multiple benchmarks simultaneously
, spanning different robot embodiments, simulators and action layouts, with the goal of discovering shared cross-embodiment agent mechanisms and persistent memory structures.
We take the benchmarks LIBERO-Pro, VLABench, SimplerEnv WidowX and SimplerEnv Google as test bed (Franka Panda, WidowX and the Google mobile manipulator).
We use the following policy configurations: (1) the
general
X-VLA checkpoint, never tuned on any of these benchmarks and thus operating entirely out of distribution; (2)
X-VLA specialists
, one checkpoint finetuned per benchmark.
To evolve the unified harness, we build a training pool of
procedurally generated episodes with new scene arrangements, objects, instructions or tasks
outside standard benchmark evaluations (
Fig.
9
, top), and evaluate on the benchmarks’ own standard episodes (
Fig.
9
, bottom).
Evaluation metrics.
We report standard benchmark metrics. On VLABench, we use the official progress score, which assigns partial credit for grasping the right object and for each goal condition met; on all other benchmarks, we report success rate averaged over tasks. For simplicity, we call all these scores success rates (%) in this paper, although the VLABench numbers are progress scores.
All the scores we compare, including those of the finetuned references, use the same step limits. On SimplerEnv WidowX and SimplerEnv Google, episodes always run to the limit and are scored on their final state.
Harness evolution configurations.
We run at most 5 optimization iterations, using
claude-opus-5
as the coding model, invoked via the Claude Code client at maximum effort.
The
auxiliary tools
are Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct
(
Yang et al., 2025
)
as the language model, Molmo2-8B
(
Clark et al., 2026
)
or Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct
(
Bai et al., 2025
)
as the vision-language model, Grounding-DINO
(
Liu et al., 2024
)
for object detection, SAM 3
(
Carion et al., 2026
)
for segmentation, Molmo2-8B for pointing, and GraspGen
(
Murali et al., 2025
)
