4.2
Harness Optimization Unlocks Substantial Robot Manipulation Headroom
An evolved harness turns a general policy into a specialist.
Without any weight updates,
RoboArchitect
yields substantial gains across nearly all setups (
Table
1
), and converts poorly performing cross-benchmark and out-of-domain policies (
Section
4.1
) into functional specialists.
Table
1
compares harness design and finetuning directly: on VLABench under both protocols and on SimplerEnv WidowX under unseen scenes,
the evolved harness around the general policy outperforms the finetuned weights
, carrying the frozen policy past a full weight update; it falls short only on SimplerEnv WidowX under unseen tasks.
The gains
transfer strongly to unseen scenes and unseen tasks
: on
unseen scenes
, they generalize across novel scene arrangements, with the only minor exception of RLDX-1 on RoboCasa-365, which improved only on its optimization episodes (
Fig.
10
); every setup also transfers positively to
unseen tasks
(
Table
1
).
This generalization reflects the structure of the revisions themselves: control routines work from
measured geometry and the robot’s own sensing
, not from static object names or positions written into the code (
Section
4.3
), and memories are often indexed by
measured physical dimensions
(
Section
4.4
).
These results show that the domain gap traditionally closed through demonstration collection
(
Kim et al., 2024
;
Intelligence et al., 2025
)
can also be closed through automated harness design.
The harness dynamically balances policy and programmatic control.
In several setups, the evolved harness bypasses the frozen policy entirely on benchmarks a general policy was never trained for.
For example, the general X-VLA on SimplerEnv WidowX commands a fully open gripper at every step, so the harness learns to
disregard the policy entirely
and evolves into a vision-based code-as-policy agent (
Fig.
6
i; details in
Appendix
A
).
On its optimization episodes, this harness raised success from 0% to 100% (
Figs.
11
and
10
), and achieved 87.5% on unseen scenes and 66.7% on unseen tasks.
In contrast, the unified harness evolved on finetuned policies (
Section
4.2
)
keeps the VLA specialists in charge and intervenes only when they fail
.
As shown in
Fig.
7
a, if late in an episode the gripper under the VLA policy’s control has never approached the instructed object, the harness takes over via the pointing tool, and directly commands the arm to reach and grasp it.
The harness also learns to hand control back to the VLA policy if it is already closing in on the object (
Fig.
7
b).
Most evolved harnesses settle between these two ends:
the policy retains the motion it executes well, while the code takes over the decisions the policy gets wrong
, such as lifting a jammed arm clear before re-querying the policy (
Fig.
3
a), or carrying the gripper to the named object before the policy grasps it (
Fig.
3
d).
Crucially, we never instructed the coding model how to divide control; each harness arrived at its structure from rollout evidence alone.
A unified harness works across robots.
We next test whether a single harness can generalize across embodiments (
Section
4.1
; results in
Table
2
, full evolution trajectories in
Fig.
12
).
The general X-VLA model scores near zero across all benchmarks, as it is entirely out of distribution (
Table
2
).
The harness then evolves into a pure code-as-policy agent, replacing the general VLA entirely (as in
Section
4.2
).
It raises every benchmark from (near) zero, reaching 41.6% on the training pool and 28.8% on held-out evaluation.
This unified harness reads everything that differs between robots at runtime from the action specification and proprioception, never hardcoding embodiment-specific constants (
Sections
4.3
and
4.4
). It thus
operates across embodiments without domain-specific finetuning
.
Using finetuned specialists as base policies, the unified harness yields smaller gains. These policies already perform well (58.0% training, 45.9% held-out), and so our auto-evolved harness
correctly preserves their native competence
.
As such, the unified harness strikes the same balance as individual setups (
Section
4.2
): it evolves into a pure code-as-policy agent when wrapping the general VLA, but correctly preserves native competence when wrapping finetuned specialists.
Iterative refinement further improves the automatically designed harness.
A coding model can already design an agent from scratch in one attempt.
But the agent itself generates new evidence through its own execution, and the same optimization process of
RoboArchitect
can use that evidence to refine it further.
The harness after the first iteration (
One-Shot
in
Tables
1
and
2
) represents a
one-shot agent design
: the coding model sees the bare VLA policy’s rollout failures (iteration 0) and produces an agent in a single attempt (iteration 1).
Subsequent iterations observe the behavior of this agent and refine its control logic based on newly exposed failure modes (
Section
3
), up to iteration 5 (
Iterative
in
Tables
1
and
2
).
Figs.
10
,
11
and
12
illustrate these optimization trajectories, showing
steady, mostly monotonic progression
over iterations.
As shown in
Table
1
, the iteratively evolved harness outperforms the one-shot design on the training set in every setup (
Figs.
10
and
11
) and on held-out sets, except RLDX-1 on RoboCasa-365 under unseen scenes.
For example, the code-as-policy agent on VLABench is built in its first attempt, and only its own rollouts reveal subtler failures, which later revisions repair (
Fig.
6
g,h; details in
Appendix
A
).
Iterative refinement also improves generalization
: while some one-shot designs fall below the bare VLA policy on unseen scenes or tasks, the iteratively evolved harness surpasses it on nearly every held-out set (
Table
1
).
The improvement is not limited to adding new tools: later revisions also refine the division of control between the policy and programmatic logic, as discussed in
Section
4.2
.
These results show that the harness is not merely automatically designed, but can
iteratively self-improve
by inspecting the execution traces of its own previous designs.
4.3
Evolved Control Routines Driving the Performance Gains
The evolved harnesses address concrete failure modes with targeted control routines.
Figs.
3
and
6
show representative revisions across benchmarks.
The harnesses learn to
detect and clear arm jams
that the policy cannot recover from (
Fig.
3
a), and to
synthesize missing motion primitives
, such as a side approach under a shelf board or a handle pull on a cabinet (
Fig.
3
b,
Fig.
5
e).
On RoboCasa-365, they
rescale contact forces
when the policy pushes a door too gently (
Fig.
3
c), and
tether the mobile base
to active workspaces when it drifts away (
Fig.
5
f).
Other routines make perception more reliable: the harness redirects the arm to the target object when a policy overfit to its training scenes reaches for a memorized location (
Fig.
3
d), and
adapts to perception limitations
by working down ranked candidates and checking for firm grasps from depth (
Fig.
6
g,h).
The unified harness also
adapts to each robot’s setup
, such as its speed: it ends each move when the arm arrives, not on a fixed time budget (
Fig.
7
c), which contributed to raising the training-pool success rate on the slower Google robot from 11.0% to 30.2%.
Appendix
A
details each routine.

5
Conclusion
We introduced
RoboArchitect
to automate the design and optimization of agent harnesses around frozen robot policies.
Across diverse benchmarks and frozen policies, the evolved harnesses substantially improve performance on held-out scenes and tasks.
Even when the policy is untuned for the target environment,
RoboArchitect
can adapt it to a specialist in out-of-domain settings, and can even outperform its finetuned version.
Crucially, the harness continues to self-improve beyond its initial design, using the behavior of previous versions as new evidence for subsequent refinements.
Emergent from harness optimization, we observe intuitive control routines that resolve specific failure modes, and persistent memories that carry experience across episodes to inform later decisions.
RoboArchitect
can also evolve a unified harness that works across multiple embodiments, adapting itself to each robot.
Together, these results suggest that substantial headroom in robot manipulation resides in the agent harness, and that this headroom can be unlocked by automatically evolving the harness for novel setups.
6
Limitations
Scaling cap of iterations.
As shown in
Figs.
10
,
11
and
12
, harness performance on the training episodes improves consistently across iterations.
However, this work uses a fixed maximum of 5 optimization iterations (
Section
4.1
).
More iterations may yield further gains, but the point at which returns saturate remains to be explored.
Nevertheless, even with a moderate budget of only 5 iterations (
Appendix
B
),
RoboArchitect
achieves substantial gains that transfer to held-out settings.
More complex manipulation.
A natural next step is extending
RoboArchitect
to tasks with richer contact dynamics, such as dexterous in-hand manipulation or tool use, where the space of failure modes is larger than in pick-and-place.
The range of control routines and memory structures that automated evolution can discover in these settings is an interesting open question.
Sim-to-real transfer.
All evaluations run in simulation.
Because our harness reads only the standard input space (
e.g.,
camera images, depth and the robot’s own readings), its interface should carry over to a real robot.
Testing our simulation-evolved harnesses on real robots and investigating the number of further improvement iterations on a real deployment are future work.

Appendix A
Evolved Control Routines and Persistent Memories in Detail
This appendix details
RoboArchitect
’s auto-evolved control routines of
Section
4.3
and the persistent memories of
Section
4.4
;
Figs.
5
,
6
and
7
show more of the revisions.
A.1
Control Routines
Detecting and clearing arm jams.
When the arm is jammed against an object, the bare policy may continue issuing similar commands because its visual observations remain nearly unchanged during a jam, so it tips objects over and cannot recover.
The evolved harness learns to monitor discrepancies between commanded and actual gripper movements; when disagreement persists, it lifts the arm clear before re-querying the policy (
Fig.
3
a).
Synthesizing missing motion primitives.
Some tasks require motion primitives absent from the base policy or the earlier harness, such as approaching an object from the side rather than from above.
For retrieving a book from the shelf on VLABench, the earlier harness defaults to top-down motion and collides with the overhead board. The evolved harness detects overhead obstructions via depth maps and computes horizontal approach vectors to reach beneath them (
Fig.
3
b).
The same pattern appears elsewhere: on RoboCerebra, the harness adds a wrist-rotation primitive for pouring with
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
, while for cabinet opening with SmolVLA, it locates the cabinet with the pointing model, finds its handles in the depth image, then aligns and pulls (
Fig.
5
e).
Rescaling contact forces.
On RoboCasa-365, some failures arise from
insufficient contact force
rather than trajectory misalignment.
For example, the toaster-oven door requires closure within 0.5% of its opening range, but the policy RLDX-1 pushed too gently. The evolved harness rescales action magnitudes while preserving direction, providing sufficient force to latch the door (
Fig.
3
c).
Tethering mobile bases to active workspaces.
On RoboCasa-365, the harness also learns to constrain
mobile-base drift
around active workspaces.
It defines workspace anchors as locations where the last gripper activations occurred, gives the base a driving budget, and retraces the base to the latest anchor once the budget is spent (
Fig.
5
f).
Redirecting to target objects instead of memorized locations.
For spatially shifted scenes such as LIBERO-Pro, policies overfit on original LIBERO consistently reach toward wrong items at memorized locations
(
Zhou et al., 2025
)
.
RoboArchitect
independently diagnosed this memorization, and evolved the harness to query the pointing model for the target item. With RLinf-
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
, it learns to locate the instructed moka pot rather than reaching to its memorized position (
Fig.
3
d).
Replacing an unusable VLA policy.
The base (un-finetuned) X-VLA on SimplerEnv WidowX commanded a fully open gripper at every step, producing no useful control signal.
RoboArchitect
learned to
disregard the policy entirely
, as its commands barely change with the robot’s observations.
Instead, the harness evolved into a complete vision-based picking agent, akin to code-as-policy
(
Liang et al., 2023
;
Tsui et al., 2026
;
Elmaaroufi et al., 2026
)
: parsing instructions, detecting target objects via open-vocabulary detectors, estimating 3D poses from depth maps, computing grasp vectors, and executing trajectories directly (
Fig.
6
i).
Adapting to perception limitations.
When the VLA policy is unusable, the harness evolves into a pure code-as-policy agent (
Section
4.2
). Crucially, such agents continue to
refine their own perception and control mechanisms
across iterations (
Section
4.2
).
On VLABench, the vision tools could not reliably distinguish mahjong tile faces. Rather than relying on a single vision prediction, the harness maintains a ranked candidate list, sequentially interacting with candidate tiles until the task completes (
Fig.
6
g).
Vision-based grasp verification could also be unreliable, causing the agent to prematurely put down objects it was holding. The harness thus replaces
visual grasp checks
with
a depth check under the fingertips
, verifying grasps by the presence of a surface just below the fingers (
Fig.
6
h).
Per-robot control-rate independence.
The unified harness (
Section
4.2
) evolves mechanisms that adapt control to each robot across platforms (see
Fig.
7
).
Each motion phase used to end on a fixed time budget, which on a slower platform (
e.g.,
the 3 Hz Google robot,
Fig.
7
c) expires while the arm is still in transit.
The evolved harness ends a move only when the arm arrives or stops making progress, measured by the distance between the arm’s position and its target rather than by elapsed time, and reaches handles on vertical surfaces from the front along the measured surface normal. The revision that introduced these changes raised the agent’s performance on the Google robot from 11.0% to 30.2% on the training pool.

A.2
Persistent Memories
Learning execution parameters from experience.
The harnesses store empirical execution statistics that inform later control decisions.
On SimplerEnv WidowX, the harness records the grasp heights that have successfully lifted an object, as a function of measured object height, so that effective grasp parameters transfer to novel objects (
Fig.
4
a).
On LIBERO-Pro-10, the MolmoAct-2 harness instead averages the depth of successful grasps below the object top, as a share of the object’s height, and uses this statistic to parameterize fallback grasps.
The OpenVLA-7B harness similarly records the grip style,
pinch
or
spread
, that succeeds for each object, so future grasps select the proven pose when the object’s shape allows both (
Fig.
4
b).
Crucially, across these designs, memory is indexed by
actual, measured physical properties or object identity
rather than specific task names, so experience generalizes to novel objects across different tasks.
Tracking implicit task and environment clues.
Persistent memory also captures recurring clues in the task instruction and environment.
On RoboCasa-365, the harness associates instruction verbs with the need to
hold (“pick up”)
an object: once sufficient evidence accumulates for a
“picking”
task, it enables an
empty-grasp recovery routine
that retries when fingers close on nothing, while leaving the routine disabled for
“pressing”
tasks where a closed empty gripper is intentional (
Fig.
4
c).
On RoboCerebra, the harness discovers and stores the environment’s 150-step scene-reset period, allowing later episodes to anticipate resets and take over a placement early enough to finish it before the reset.
Memories are also used to cache inference outputs, such as VLM/LLM parses of multi-step instructions, so that repeated executions avoid redundant computation.
Persistent self-calibration across embodiments.
In the unified harness (
Section
4.2
), persistent memory additionally stores embodiment-specific calibration.
Because finger motion differs across robots, the harness opens and closes the empty gripper, observes the resulting motion in the depth image, and
stores the kinematic mapping in memory
.
This calibration guides grasp orientation across different embodiments (
e.g.,
on the Franka arm and on the Google robot) (
Fig.
4
d).
The same routine records the resting finger configuration, providing a reference for detecting empty grasps on robots reporting finger positions.
Appendix B

article.headline: 自动进化机器人智能体外壳，冻结策略成功率提升数倍
article.lede: 斯坦福团队用编码模型自动迭代设计机器人智能体外壳，不更新任何策略权重，就大幅提升成功率并迁移到未见过的场景和任务。
article.problem: 机器人策略要适配新任务或新硬件，通常得重新采集演示并微调权重。已有研究表明，把冻结策略放进一层「智能体外壳」（由控制代码决定何时调用策略、何时调用视觉工具、何时直接控制机械臂）里效果更好，但这类外壳目前完全靠人工为每个机器人、每个基准单独设计，调试成本高，而且很长的执行轨迹难以逐条人工检查。
article.method: RoboArchitect 让一个编码模型查看机器人在「训练」回合中的逐步执行轨迹，诊断失败原因并改写外壳代码；候选外壳只有在训练集上超过当前版本才会被保留，最多迭代 5 轮。外壳可以调用检测、分割、指向、抓取位姿生成等预训练工具，也可以绕开策略直接编程控制机械臂，并自行演化出跨回合的持久记忆，存什么、怎么存、怎么取都不预设。
article.results: 在多个基准和多种 VLA 策略上，演化出的外壳把未见过场景的平均成功率从 9.7% 提到 43.3%（4.5 倍），未见过任务从 12.7% 提到 40.2%（3.2 倍）；只做一次设计尝试的版本在未见过场景上是 21.4%。跨基准与域外设置增益更大，平均从 7.3% 升到 58.4%。在 VLABench 上，包裹通用 X-VLA 的外壳在两种留出协议下都超过了该策略微调后的权重；在 SimplerEnv WidowX 的未见过场景下也超过微调版本（87.5% 对 70.8%），但在未见过任务上低于微调版本（66.7% 对 87.5%）。完整的 5 轮进化耗时不到 6 小时，平均成本低于 150 美元。
article.why_it_matters: 这说明机器人操作中相当一部分性能提升空间在智能体外壳上，性能瓶颈并不全在权重上，而且这部分设计可以被自动搜索，为不想采集新演示数据的适配提供了一条无需更新权重、每一步修改都可读的替代路径。
article.limitations: 全部实验在仿真中完成，迭代次数固定在 5 轮上限、收益何时饱和仍不清楚，任务也以抓取放置为主；并且并非所有设置都受益，在 RoboCasa-365 上 RLDX-1 的未见过场景成功率几乎没变（27.9% 到 27.8%）。
article.figure_caption_zh: 从仅有冻结 VLA 策略的起点出发，编码模型根据执行轨迹反复修改外壳，最终得到带辅助工具和持久记忆的机器人智能体；右侧为检验外壳泛化能力的实验条件。

email_papers.title: HALO: Human-Grounded Granular Evaluation of Proactive Agents
email_papers.abstract: Proactive agents must decide whether, when, and how far to assist without an explicit request. Existing evaluations often rely on automated scores or binary verdicts, offering limited human diagnosis of evidence use and intervention quality. To address these gaps, we introduce HALO, Human-Grounded GrAnular EvaLuation of PrOactive Agents. HALO-Arena covers 4 proactive need types, Dependency, Blockage, Risk, and Opportunity, across 10 everyday domains and 50 personal environments. Scenarios require agents to retrieve evidence from structured databases or unstructured documents before judging whether assistance is warranted and choosing its scope. On HALO-Arena, we construct HALO-8K, a dataset of 8,000 responses from 10 models across 400 scenarios, annotated by 20 experts for action level, acceptability verdicts, and human diagnosis. For rejected responses, human diagnosis covers timing, intensity, and other issues. Recorded reasoning tokens and retrieval rounds measure the effort behind these responses. The best proprietary and open-source models achieve 72.88% and 56.63% acceptability, respectively. Our central finding is that over-proactivity is the dominant observed failure mode, with Premature timing or Excessive intensity accounting for 61.20% of rejected responses. Further analyses yield complementary findings on the balance between intervention and restraint, evidence acquisition, and the calibration of timing and intensity.

1
Introduction
Proactive agents infer user needs from observed activity and initiate assistance without an explicit request
(
Lu et al., 2024
)
.
They have attracted growing attention for their potential to anticipate problems and reduce user effort
(
Tang et al., 2026
;
Oh et al., 2026
)
.
They can identify missing prerequisites, anticipate risks, and prepare useful next steps within the user’s authority.
For example,
Lu et al. (2024)
train agents to propose tasks from observed user activities and report a 66.47% F1 score for proactive assistance.
Useful initiative requires deciding whether, when, and how far to help, while recognizing when restraint is warranted.
Figure 1:
Overview of HALO. HALO-Arena supplies personal apps and local evidence. Agents retrieve evidence and decide whether, when, and how far to intervene. HALO-8K records human verdicts, timing and intensity diagnosis, and resource consumption. The circled choices illustrate a premature and excessive L3 intervention.
A calendar entry for an upcoming trip may prompt checking a database for needed supplies and a file for purchase authorization.
These facts can justify a reminder without permitting a purchase.
Retrieved evidence must guide the intervention’s timing, inform its content, and establish the authorized scope.
Benchmarks differ in how agents obtain evidence for proactive decisions.
Some provide user activity directly
(
Lu et al., 2024
;
Tang et al., 2026
)
.
Such observations may signal a need without establishing a remedy or permission to act.
PROBE supports SQL and semantic document retrieval
(
Pasternak et al., 2025
)
, while interactive benchmarks support additional tool use
(
Oh et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026
)
.
Evaluating these capabilities requires linking retrieved evidence to human verdicts on the resulting interventions.
Detecting a relevant need does not by itself make an intervention acceptable. An intervention may still fail because it is mistimed, insufficient, excessive, irrelevant, or unsupported by evidence. Existing benchmarks primarily rely on scalable automated metrics: ProAgentBench evaluates intervention prediction and response similarity
(
Tang et al., 2026
)
, while ProactiveBench uses a reward model trained on human acceptance labels
(
Lu et al., 2024
)
. Human studies have examined how users perceive proactive assistance
(
Oh et al., 2026
)
, but existing benchmarks provide limited human diagnosis of why individual model responses are accepted or rejected.
To address these gaps, we introduce
HALO
,
H
uman-Grounded Gr
A
nular Eva
L
uation of Pr
O
active Agents, with 2 components.
HALO combines structured database querying and unstructured file retrieval with fine-grained human evaluation.
HALO-Arena
models 4 proactive need types: Dependency, Blockage, Risk, and Opportunity.
It spans 10 everyday domains and 50 personal environments.
Operational applications expose evolving events, while separate databases and text files provide structured and unstructured evidence.
Addressing a need requires the agent to retrieve relevant evidence and then judge whether assistance is warranted, when to act, and how far to intervene.
At each evaluation checkpoint, agents receive an observed event prefix and may retrieve evidence over multiple rounds before returning 1 executable response or no action.
On HALO-Arena, we construct
HALO-8K
, comprising 8,000 responses from 10 models across 400 scenarios, annotated by 20 experts. Annotators assign action levels and acceptability verdicts, with human diagnosis of rejections covering timing, intensity, and other issues such as unsupported evidence, irrelevance, and factual contradiction. Verdicts on no-action responses distinguish erroneous Inaction from warranted restraint. Reasoning tokens and retrieval rounds quantify agent effort.
Our central finding is that
over-proactivity is the dominant observed failure mode
: Premature timing or Excessive intensity accounts for 61.20% of rejected responses. Proprietary and open-source models peak at 72.88% and 56.63% acceptability. Further analysis yields 3 complementary findings.
(1) Restraint contributes to acceptability:
gains in accepted action can be outweighed by losses in warranted restraint.
(2) Evidence acquisition accompanies better help:
among reminders, local content access is associated with higher acceptability and lower Insufficient diagnosis rates.
(3) Timing alone is not enough:
among well-timed rejections, reminders tend to be insufficient and executions excessive. These findings support granular evaluation of proactive assistance.
Our contributions are as follows:
•
We introduce
HALO-Arena
, an executable benchmark spanning 4 proactive need types and 10 everyday domains, with evidence retrieval informing proactive decisions.
•
We construct
HALO-8K
: 8,000 responses across 400 scenarios, annotated by experts for action level, verdicts, and human diagnosis.
•
We evaluate 10 models, revealing tradeoffs among intervention, restraint, timing, intensity, and retrieval effort.
2
Related Work
2.1
Proactive Agents
Early agents predict useful tasks from observed activity and refine proposals using human acceptance verdicts
(
Lu et al., 2024
)
.
ContextAgent extends perception to wearable video and audio, combining sensory and persona context for tool-assisted services
(
Yang et al., 2025
)
.
Recent work also examines timing and scope.
ProActor models actionable windows for timing-aware scheduling
(
Ding et al., 2026
)
.
Proactivity-Gym connects task capability with temporal allocation and user trust
(
Oh et al., 2026
)
.
2.2
Benchmarks for Proactive Agents
Evaluation has expanded from executing explicit requests to identifying unstated needs.
WebArena and

(

)

(

)

PROBE evaluates bottleneck discovery and action selection from document stores, while its agent baselines use SQL and semantic retrieval
(
Pasternak et al., 2025

Recent benchmarks examine proactive assistance in interactive settings.
ProAgentBench evaluates intervention decisions and generated assistance in real-world computer activity
(

HALO-Arena combines email, calendar, chat, contacts, and wallet apps with SQLite databases and text files.
Agents use 29 interaction commands for evidence retrieval and 19 action commands for attention, preparation, and execution.

The 10 domains are education and learning, work and professional life, home and household management, family and caregiving, health and wellbeing, travel and mobility, personal finance and consumer life, community and civic life, social and cultural life, and recreation (sports and hobbies).
Each domain has 5 instances, each representing a different person, yielding 50 distinct personal environments.

Risk

Earlier agent interventions do not affect other checkpoints or scenarios.
The agent receives protagonist context and the event prefix, using the newest timestamp as simulation time.
For human annotation, we sample 2 distinct checkpoints per model in each scenario, yielding 800 responses per model, with 200 per need and 80 per domain.

3.2.2
Annotation Protocol
20 annotators provide 1 verdict per response, keeping each scenario’s annotator fixed across models.
Human verdicts and diagnosis use the event prefix, retrieved evidence, response, and execution result.
Appendix
E
describes annotator preparation.
Action levels.
Annotators confirm or correct the command-based action level pre-filled by the interface.
L0 Observation
observes or retrieves information without initiating an intervention.
L1 Attention
draws the user’s attention to relevant information or needs without carrying out the underlying task.
L2 Preparation
prepares an intervention or organizes internal information for later use without creating an external commitment.
L3 Execution
carries out an intervention that changes the user’s active commitments or creates external effects.
Higher levels do not imply better assistance.
Human Verdict and Diagnosis.
Annotators first give an acceptability verdict on whether a response provides grounded, useful help with appropriate timing and scope, accepting L0 when restraint is warranted.
Acceptability is the proportion of accepted responses. These automatically receive Appropriate timing and intensity.
Rejected L0 responses receive the human diagnosis
Inaction
for missing warranted help, without further diagnostic labels.
For rejected L1–L3 responses, separate questions assess timing and intensity.
Premature
and
Belated
indicate intervention before and after its useful window, respectively.
Insufficient
indicates inadequate help, while
Excessive
indicates intervention beyond supported scope or authority.
Appropriate denotes suitable timing or proportionate intensity.
Annotators may also flag Other Issues, detailed in Appendix
G
.
Resource Consumption.
For each annotated response, we sum reasoning tokens across retained calls and count completed retrieval rounds.

4.2

4.2.1
Model Comparison
Table
1
compares acceptability, action levels, recorded consumption, and timing and intensity errors on the same 800 responses per model.
Acceptability.
Scores range from 30.38% for GPT-OSS-20B to 72.88% for Gemini3.8-Flash, a 42.50-point gap.
DeepSeekV4-Pro leads open-source models with 56.63% acceptability.
The score range reflects substantial variation in acceptability under the same annotation protocol, while even the strongest model leaves over 25% of responses unacceptable.
Proprietary models average 63.08%, versus 47.55% for open-source models, a 15.53-point gap.
These means also conceal uneven performance within each group.
The 3 strongest open-source models lie within 2.50 points of each other, whereas the full group spans 26.25 points.
Their lower mean thus reflects a weak tail as well as a gap at the top.
The groups overlap: DeepSeekV4-Pro exceeds both Gemini3.1-Pro and GPT5.6-Luna, so group membership provides an incomplete account of individual quality.
These scores cover completed, human-annotated responses under the recorded inference settings, excluding transport and parsing failures.
Action choices.
Attention (L1) is the most frequent level for every model, accounting for 69.20% of all responses.
L1 exceeds 50% of responses in 9 models and ranges from 48.00% for Claude-Opus5.5 to 87.00% for GPT5.6-Luna.
Preparation (L2) remains rare at 4.18%, while execution (L3) accounts for 16.09%.
This concentration makes the timing and usefulness of L1 responses central to the aggregate result.
At the group level, L3 shares are almost identical at about 16.1%, despite the 15.53-point acceptability gap.
The main observed policy difference lies in observation and attention: proprietary models choose L0 about 2 times as often, while open-source models choose L1 more often.
Execution frequency alone cannot explain the observed acceptability gap.
Resource Consumption.
Open-source models use fewer retrieval rounds at similar mean reasoning usage.
They average 4.77k reasoning tokens and 1.21 retrieval rounds per response, compared with 5.53k and 2.55 for proprietary models.
The reasoning-token means differ by about 14%, whereas open-source models use about 53% fewer retrieval rounds.
Lower recorded retrieval use accompanies lower acceptability, so resource savings should be assessed alongside the quality of the resulting responses.
Within the proprietary group, second-ranked Claude-Opus5.5 uses about 23% of the recorded reasoning tokens of the leading Gemini3.8-Flash.
Strong performance thus occurs at different levels of recorded consumption.
These profiles support comparing quality and resource use jointly under the recorded inference settings and provider accounting conventions.

4.2.3
Error Analysis
We identify over-proactivity as Premature timing or Excessive intensity, counting each response once when either diagnosis applies.
As shown in Figure
3
, it occurs in 2,188 of 3,575 rejected responses (61.20%).
Model-wise shares range from 44.23% to 79.66%, exceeding 50% of rejections in 6 of 10 models.
Across all responses, Premature timing is almost 3 times as common as Belated timing, while Excessive intensity is about 2 times as common as Insufficient.
These 2 asymmetries indicate more frequent early or excessive intervention.
This pattern holds across all 4 proactive need types and all 10 domains, with over-proactivity accounting for more than 50% of rejections in each category.
The 2 highest-acceptability models also have the lowest Premature and Excessive rates, associating stronger overall performance with fewer premature or excessive interventions.
Inaction alone gives a different picture: Qwen3.8-27B records 0% Inaction but reaches only 55.13% acceptability and chooses L0 on just 0.38% of responses.
Because Inaction applies only to rejected L0 responses and is reported over all responses, a policy that rarely chooses observation has few opportunities to incur this error.
Action-level shares therefore provide essential context for interpreting individual error rates.
Over-proactivity is the dominant failure mode of proactive agents.

Further Pattern Analysis
We examine action and restraint, need-dependent strategies, evidence acquisition, and residual failures despite appropriate timing.
5.1
Action and Restraint
We compare intervention choices and acceptability at shared checkpoints.
More frequent intervention can accompany lower acceptability when warranted restraint losses outweigh accepted action gains.
Figure 4:
Paired intervention rates and acceptability.
Figure
4
compares Qwen3.5-9B to Qwen3.8-27B at 201 shared checkpoints and Gemini3.8-Flash to Gemini3.1-Pro at 623.
Pairs match instance, scenario, event, and annotator without filtering verdicts.
Intervention frequency, the L1–L3 share, rises by 27.36 and 28.89 points, respectively, yet acceptability rises by 14.43 points for Qwen and falls by 14.77 for Gemini.
The Gemini loss combines a 5.94-point gain from accepted interventions with a 20.71-point decline from accepted L0.
Both changes use all matched responses as their denominator and sum to the acceptability change, so the intervention gain reflects a frequency change, not conditional success.
The error changes clarify the different outcomes: Qwen reduces Inaction-or-Insufficient by 17.91 points while increasing Premature-or-Excessive by 5.97, whereas Gemini increases the latter by 21.51.
Matching fixes the observed prefix and annotator, but configurations and retrieved evidence can differ, with Qwen’s version and parameter count changing together.
The comparisons therefore do not isolate the causal effect of intervening more.
Restraint can also follow substantial inspection: Flash’s 182 accepted L0 responses average 16.74 commands, versus 14.65 for 401 accepted interventions.
These groups cover different checkpoints, but show that L0 records final commitment rather than inspection effort.

Timing and Scope
We examine intensity failures within rejected interventions with Appropriate timing.
Among well-timed rejections, reminders tend to provide insufficient help, while executions tend to exceed acceptable scope.
Figure

Among them, 329 of 623 L1 responses (52.81%) are Insufficient and 238 of 312 L3 responses (76.28%) are Excessive.
The opposite intensity patterns hold within every model, although intensity does not explain all failures: 282 timely L1 rejections retain Appropriate intensity.
At the same checkpoints, 229 of the Insufficient L1 responses (69.60%) have an accepted L1 counterpart from another model, and 178 Excessive L3 responses (74.79%) have an accepted L1 or L2 counterpart.
Both counterpart patterns cover most corresponding rejected responses within each need.
These response-level shares depend on sampled candidates and do not measure repair success.

Paired examples clarify the role of content and permission.
At a shared household checkpoint, Gemini3.8-Flash’s accepted L1 supplies the no-pry instruction and a concrete dispatch route.
GPT-OSS-20B’s Insufficient reminder instead suggests freeing the panel and supplies no usable service contact.
At a family checkpoint, the stored authorization permits a message containing only “kitchen sneakers.”
Qwen3.8-27B sends that phrase and is accepted, while Claude-Opus5.5 adds a name, location, and Saturday-morning request and receives an Excessive diagnosis.
Both outputs are L3, and both models retrieve the wording restriction.
The same action level can thus receive different verdicts: useful detail can improve L1, while respecting narrow authorization can make L3 acceptable.
6
Conclusion
HALO evaluates proactive assistance through executable environments, human verdicts, and human diagnosis.
HALO-8K contains 8,000 human-annotated responses from 10 models across 400 scenarios and 2,160 checkpoints.
Over-proactivity dominates the observed rejections.
Further analyses distinguish useful action from warranted restraint, relate evidence acquisition to acceptability, and identify contrasting intensity errors among well-timed rejections.
These patterns expose calibration problems obscured by aggregate acceptability.
HALO-Arena provides operational applications and separate structured and unstructured evidence stores.
Repeated retrieval lets an agent inspect relevant evidence before deciding whether to notify, prepare, execute, or remain silent.
Acceptability peaks at 72.88% for proprietary and 56.63% for open-source models.
HALO records retrieved evidence and executed commands, enabling comparison of human verdicts and diagnosis for responses produced at identical checkpoints.
The practical targets differ: timely reminders need enough grounded detail to be useful, while execution must respect the scope of available permission.
These results motivate better evidence gathering and response calibration. More frequent action or higher commitment alone does not establish better assistance.
Systems should be compared jointly on acceptable action, warranted restraint, residual intensity errors, and inspection effort.
Limitations
Real-world validity.
HALO uses constructed scenarios and simulated apps to study proactive decisions under controlled conditions.
Its designed need distribution does not estimate how often those needs or failure modes occur in everyday use.
Checkpoint evaluation also omits users’ responses and the cumulative effects of repeated interventions, so performance may not transfer directly to sustained deployment.
Human personalization.
Human verdicts depend on preferences for initiative, useful detail, and commitment.
Shared criteria ground judgments in personal context and authority, but borderline responses can be useful to some users and intrusive to others.
The annotators’ broadly similar backgrounds further limit the preferences represented, so aggregate acceptability should not be treated as a universal user preference.
Evaluation granularity.
Action levels group interventions by commitment, but actions at the same level can differ in reversibility and user burden.
Human verdicts and diagnostic labels identify acceptable help and common failures without ranking acceptable alternatives by usefulness.
Consequently, aggregate acceptability does not capture the full tradeoff between benefit, burden, and intervention risk.

I.1
Agent Prompt
You are a proactive personal Agent in a simulated environment.
At this checkpoint, decide whether to keep observing, inspect local information,
or proactively help. Judge only the observed Event prefix; checkpoints are
independent, so no earlier Agent behavior is part of the state. Use only observed
Events and inspection results. Do not infer future Events or invent records.
Intervene only when it is useful now. Choose an intervention that is effective
for the current need, supported by the available evidence, and safe. This
judgment is internal and must not be described in the JSON.
Events may reveal the need without containing every fact required for a good
response. When a possible intervention depends on a qualification, prior
record, identifier, procedure, constraint, preference, inventory fact, or safe
next step, inspect the local SQLite database and/or TXT Files before responding.
Do not assume that communications and calendar entries are the complete source
of truth, and do not invent a missing detail instead of retrieving it.
Use assistant.notify_user when a grounded message to the Instance user would
provide useful help now. Explain the relevant finding or concrete next step;
merely restating Events or giving generic advice is insufficient. The message
does not obtain a user reply or approval, or carry out the operations it
suggests. Never claim to have completed an operation that was not performed.
The time field of the newest observed Event is the current simulation time. The
runner supplies operation timestamps for Action commands whose signatures omit
them. App record timestamps and Calendar business times do not replace the
Event time. Ignore the real wall-clock date and any model training date; an
Event is not "in the past" merely because its absolute date precedes the real
date outside this episode.
Return one compact JSON object in exactly one of these forms:
{
"decision": "inspect",
"content": [{"app":"...","function":"...","parameter":...}]
}
or
{
"decision": "final",
"content": null | {"app":"...","function":"...","parameter":...}
}
Rules:
- inspect: content must be one non-empty list of private information-gathering
commands from the Inspect commands below. The runner executes these commands
and returns their results at the next round. You may repeat retrieval as often
as the evidence requires; there is no fixed retrieval limit.
- final: content must be null for no action or exactly one intended command
from the Action commands below. The command is executed once at the isolated
checkpoint to verify its result. Never return multiple final
commands or a standalone text response.
- Null final content applies only to this checkpoint.
Instance context:

Each command has app, function, parameter, and description only when required

I.2.2
Scenario Creator
You create Scenarios for a proactive-agent benchmark.
Create one <<TRIGGER_TYPE>> Scenario.
Definition: <<TRIGGER_DEFINITION>>
Choose the causal design by the state of the need across the evaluated prefixes,
not by its surface stakes. If another trigger definition fits that state more
directly, redesign the Scenario rather than relabel it.
Return exactly one raw JSON object and nothing else: no Markdown, fences,
commentary, or second object. Its top level contains only scenario_description,
events, and ini_data_commands. Choose the trajectory length for this Scenario
within the benchmark’s 4-to-6 Event range. events must be one JSON object with
sequential keys event1 onward; it must not be a list or be expanded into
top-level Event fields.
scenario_description is roughly 100 words total, written as four concise,
newline-separated items using exactly these labels: Objective, Emerging Need,
Decision Context, and Consequence. Cover the causal situation and intended
trajectory without retelling every Event, prescribing the expected Agent
action, or exposing the hidden design checks. Format every item as
`Label: text` without bullets or Markdown.
Keep all four items Scenario-specific. Do not restate the protagonist’s
identity, standing responsibilities or authority, the general Instance scope,
or its resource inventory. Mention a stable fact only when its application to
this particular trajectory is causally necessary.
Every Event contains exactly time, app, function, and the singular field
parameter. time is the ISO 8601 time, including a timezone, when that Event
enters the observable environment. Event times must be strictly increasing.
An App record’s parameter.timestamp is separate: it describes the record and
cannot be later than the Event time. Calendar start, end, reminder, and due
times remain business times rather than Event times. Every initialization
command contains exactly app, function, and parameter. The program adds
scenario_id, trigger_type, and reference_time, so do not return them. Use the
assigned reference date as the earliest Event date.
Design requirements:
- Build one causal trajectory around exactly one need of the assigned trigger
type. Every Event must develop that same need by changing its evidence,
feasibility, options, or appropriate response; do not introduce a second
proactive need or a competing trigger.
- As silent design checks, ensure that at least one Event prefix would make the
contemplated intervention premature and therefore unacceptable, and that at
least one later prefix would make intervention unacceptable because acting
only then is already too late to achieve its intended benefit or prevention.
Both judgments must follow from evidence in their respective prefixes. Do not
state timing labels, prefix verdicts, or this design reasoning anywhere in the
output JSON; present only the Scenario’s world state and observable Events.
- Events are observable changes in the world. They may supply evidence,
urgency, options, or confirmation, but must not contain the evaluated Agent’s
action, resolve the need, or turn the intervention into a direct response to
an explicit request. Information may move between actors or Apps only through
prior shared state or an observable communication in the prefix.
- The best intervention must require at least one decision-relevant fact from
the Instance SQLite database or a TXT File. That fact must distinguish
plausible recognition, timing, or action choices rather than merely support
a conclusion already forced by Events. Events must neither state that fact
nor independently imply the same decision. Use ini_data_commands when the
shared state needs additional pre-Event facts or prerequisites.
- The contemplated intervention must materially improve the protagonist’s
situation when supported by the Event state, match the trigger definition,
and have a commitment level proportionate to the available authority,
consent, and reversibility. Every fact and parameter needed for that
intervention must be available in the relevant prefix; when authority or
preference is missing,
use a lower-commitment step that preserves the protagonist’s options. Trace
each decisive condition for timing and action to a source available in that
prefix; if one is missing or appears only later, revise the action or timing
design. For blockage, the same activity must be shown as started and then
actually unable to continue.
- Use at least three distinct non-retrieval Apps in the Event sequence. Do not
count database, files, initialization, or information-retrieval steps toward
this minimum. Every counted App must supply necessary causal evidence or a
state transition for the single need; if three Apps do not fit naturally,
redesign the causal progression rather than adding a decorative channel.
- Compare the accepted summaries before choosing the causal design. Make the
Scenario materially different in its goal, cause, key information, Event
progression, and likely intervention; changing surface details within the
same workflow is not a material difference. A new Trigger label or failure
mechanism alone does not make reuse of the same underlying activity and
protagonist goal distinct. Compare the causal spine as well: if the same
state-transition pattern leads to the same intervention, changing its subject
matter is still a surface variation. Across the full set, distribute activity
areas, retrieval sources, Event channels, and useful Agent actions.
State and consistency requirements:
- ini_data_commands describe only facts that exist before event1. Preserve the
protagonist, Wallet, accepted shared state, existing SQL schemas, and natural
key uniqueness. Keep every dated initialization fact on or before the assigned
reference date. Add no unrelated noise.
- Use native personal Apps for their own data. Information-retrieval calls are
not Events. send_email and send_message are evaluated-Agent actions, not
Scenario Events or initialization commands.
- Match every command’s parameter keys to its exact App signature. An Event’s
time does not add a timestamp argument to a function that does not define one.
- The eight Scenarios share accumulated initialization data, while their Event
sequences are independent branches and are never each other’s history.
- Correct every retry issue with a genuinely revised candidate rather than a
renamed version of the same causal design.
Before returning, inspect the assembled JSON for contract integrity across its
keys, collection shapes, counts, and member schemas, then check the causal
requirements above. Contrast the assigned trigger with its closest alternative
across the Event sequence; if the distinction depends on wording rather than
the state of the need, redesign the Scenario.

{"valid": boolean, "issues": [concise, concrete strings]}

article.headline: 主动智能体评测：过度主动是主要失败模式
article.lede: HALO 用可执行个人环境加 20 位专家标注的 8000 条响应评测主动智能体，发现被拒回答中 61.20% 源于过早
article.problem: 主动智能体要在没有明确请求时自行判断是否该帮、何时帮、帮到什么程度，但现有评测多依赖自动分数或二元判定，难以说明一条回答为何被接受或被拒。检测到需求并不等于干预可接受：回答可能因为时机不对、力度不足或过度、内容无关、缺乏证据支撑而失败，而这些维度此前没有被逐条做人工诊断。
article.method: 作者构建 HALO-Arena，覆盖 Dependency、Blockage、Risk、Opportunity 四类主动需求、10 个日常领域和 50 个个人环境，共 400 个可执行场景；智能体需先用 SQL 查询或文本文件检索证据，再决定是否行动以及行动层级（L0 观察、L1 提醒、L2 准备、L3 执行）。在此基础上构建 HALO-8K：从 10 个模型在 2160 个检查点上的回答中采样 8000 条，由 20 位标注者给出可接受性判定，并对被拒回答分别诊断时机（过早、过晚）与力度（不足、过度），同时记录推理 token 与检索轮数。
article.results: 可接受性从 GPT-OSS-20B 的 30.38% 到 Gemini3.8-Flash 的 72.88%，相差 42.50 个百分点；开源模型最高为 DeepSeekV4-Pro 的 56.63%，专有模型平均 63.08% 对开源 47.55%。核心发现是过度主动占主导：过早或过度合计占 3575 条被拒回答中的 2188 条（61.20%），10 个模型中的 6 个该比例超过 50%。检索轮数与可接受性正相关（r=0.885，ρ=0.830）；在 5536 条 L1 回答中，获取到本地内容的可接受性为 59.0%，未获取为 40.8%，不足率分别为 5.2% 和 15.5%。在时机正确的被拒干预中，623 条 L1 有 52.81% 属力度不足，312 条 L3 有 76.28% 属过度。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「帮不帮」的评测拆成可接受行动、合理克制、时机、力度与检索代价几个可分别观察的量，说明更频繁行动或更高承诺层级本身并不等于更好的帮助，为主动智能体的校准提供了可诊断的评测口径。
article.limitations: 场景与应用均为构造和模拟，设计的需求分布不能反映真实使用中各类需求与失败模式的出现频率；检查点式评测不包含用户回应与重复干预的累积效应，因此结论未必迁移到长期部署。人工判定依赖标注者的偏好，且标注者背景相近，聚合可接受性不应被视为普遍用户偏好；同一行动层级内不同动作的可逆性与用户负担差异也未被区分。

HALO-8K records human verdicts, timing and intensity diagnosis, and resource consumption. The circled choices illustrate a premature and excessive L3 intervention.

email_papers.title: CaPtain: A Pipeline for Post-Training Code-as-Policy Robot Agents
email_papers.abstract: Across coding, web, and tool-use tasks, language-model agents are now routinely trained with the same recipe: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the interface, then multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) to master it. Code-as-policy (CaP) casts robot manipulation in the same form, as the policy writes code against robot APIs and reads back the results, so the same recipe should apply. Yet existing CaP agents sidestep training: they either prompt closed frontier models or delegate manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) and high-level skills, while small open vision-language models (VLMs) fail outright. We present CaPtain, an open post-training pipeline that turns a small open VLM into a capable CaP agent, with no VLA, frontier model, or privileged state at test time. CaPtain trains and deploys the policy inside CaPtain-Harness, which exposes low-level perception, geometry, and guarded-motion primitives across simulation and real hardware. We first align the base model via SFT on synthetic trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra, then apply multi-turn RL. Multi-turn RL must credit tens of agent requests, whose physical effects often surface turns later, from a single end-of-episode outcome. We therefore introduce a physical critic that reads privileged simulator state, never seen by the policy, and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success. Starting from Qwen3.5-4B (0% zero-shot), CaPtain-4B reaches 55.4% held-out LIBERO success after SFT and 73.8% after RL. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 78.5%, surpassing several frontier-model agents, and its RL gains persist across three perturbation suites (+17.6 to +21.2 points). Without target-domain training, it attains 83.3% on SimplerEnv WidowX, exceeds frontier models on CaP-Bench, and runs on a real robot after simulation-only adaptation. We release all code, data, and model weights.

Abstract
Across coding, web, and tool-use tasks, language-model agents are now routinely trained with the same recipe: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the interface, then multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) to master it.
Code-as-policy (CaP) puts robot manipulation in the same form, as the policy writes code against robot APIs and reads back the results, so the same recipe should apply.
Yet, existing CaP agents sidestep training: they either prompt closed frontier models or delegate manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) and high-level skills, while small open vision-language models (VLMs) fail outright.
We present CaPtain, an open post-training pipeline that brings this recipe to CaP and turns a small open VLM into a capable CaP agent, with no VLA, frontier model, or privileged state at test time.
CaPtain trains and deploys the policy inside CaPtain-Harness, which exposes low-level perception, geometry, and guarded-motion primitives across simulation and real hardware.
Within this harness, we first align the base model via SFT on synthetic trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra, and then apply multi-turn RL.
Multi-turn RL, however, must credit tens of requests from the agent, whose physical effects often surface several turns later, with a single outcome observed only at the end of the episode.
Since training runs in simulation, we introduce a physical critic that reads the privileged physical state in simulator, which the policy never sees, and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success.
Starting from Qwen3.5-4B (0% zero-shot), CaPtain-4B achieves 55.4% held-out LIBERO success after SFT and 73.8% after RL.
On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 78.5%, surpassing several frontier-model agents, and its RL gains persist across three perturbation suites (+17.6 to +21.2 points).
Without target-domain training, it attains 83.3% on SimplerEnv WidowX, exceeds frontier models on CaP-Bench, and runs on a real robot after simulation-only adaptation.
We release all code, data, and model weights.

Introduction
Language-model agents have improved rapidly in coding, web navigation, and tool use, and much of this progress follows a common recipe: the agent acts inside a fixed execution harness, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) teaches it the interface, and multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) refines its behavior from the outcomes of its own interactions

Code-as-policy (CaP) agents
[

27

give robot manipulation the same form: the policy observes camera images, writes programs against perception and motion APIs, and reads back what happened.
Since the program is composed at test time, a CaP agent inherits much of the generalization of the language model that writes it, and frontier models have made this approach strikingly capable. Used directly as a robot policy, GPT-6 Astra ranks above every public entry on the RoboDojo leaderboard

90

67

This raises a natural question:
Can a small open model be trained into such a CaP agent with the same SFT-and-RL recipe, rather than relying on a frontier model at test time?
In practice, existing CaP agents sidestep training, and in doing so hand the manipulation itself to components the agent cannot learn to improve.
One line of work prompts closed frontier models without weight updates

39

93

40

[
13

93

Another line delegates manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) or high-level skills. PyRUA trains a 4B coder over a frozen VLA and a motion planner
[
67
]

[
48

[
64
]

[
22
]
.
In these systems, the code decides
which
skill to call, but the skill decides
how
to grasp, approach, and place. Therefore, the agent stays bounded by the data on which the skill was trained, and RL can at best learn to sequence it.
Small open vision-language models (VLMs), meanwhile, fail outright when asked to control a robot directly. Qwen3.5-4B solves none of the LIBERO episodes in our harness, and the few efforts that train such models rely mainly on SFT
[
45
]
or single-turn text-only RL
[
20
]
.
What is missing is a complete SFT-and-RL recipe that teaches a small open VLM to manipulate through low-level primitives, with every manipulation decision made by the policy itself.
Applying the recipe at this low level is harder than at the skill level, for a reason that does not arise for language agents.
Without semantic skills such as grasp and place, the policy must itself decide where to grasp, from which direction to approach, and when to close the gripper, and these decisions are spread over tens of requests per episode, most of which only perceive or verify.
Multi-turn RL must then credit these requests, whose physical effects often surface several turns later, with a single outcome observed only at the end of the episode.
Outcome-only RL assigns the same credit to every request, while a language-model critic would have to infer physical progress indirectly from text and images.
Robot learning, however, offers an asymmetry that language agents lack: training runs in simulation, where exact object poses, grasp states, and sub-goal progress are known, even though the deployed policy must act from its cameras alone.
A critic can thus read the physical state that the policy cannot see, and credit each request by how much it moves the task toward success, while the policy itself still acts from its cameras at test time.
We present
CaPtain
, an open post-training pipeline built on these two observations.
CaPtain trains and deploys the policy inside
CaPtain-Harness
, an execution environment that exposes 22 low-level perception, geometric measurement, and guarded-motion primitives and nothing higher. There are no grasp, place, or open-drawer skills and no VLA. Perception returns masks and points, and motion takes an explicit end-effector pose or gripper command.
Every call returns a structured text receipt reporting what physically happened, such as measured poses, contact forces, or why a motion stopped, and the policy-facing API is unchanged across LIBERO

We first apply SFT on in-harness trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra, rendered in exactly the multi-turn format the policy sees at deployment.
We then run multi-turn RL with a simulator critic that reads privileged physical state hidden from the policy and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success, combining the streaming RL formulation of SAO
[
25

with asymmetric actor-critic training

Since this change is measured at a fixed time index, requests that only perceive or verify receive near-zero credit, and credit concentrates on grasps and placements.
The critic is used only during training. At test time, the policy relies on camera images and receipts alone.

Without target-domain training, CaPtain-4B reaches 83.3% on SimplerEnv WidowX, scores 75.0 on CaP-Bench, above frontier models and a 7B coder trained with RL on that benchmark, and completes tasks on a physical robot after adaptation in a coarse simulated twin alone.
Transfer remains limited on RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo (22.6% and 0.8% success), which require dual-arm coordination and unfamiliar arm kinematics.
Together, these results suggest that robot manipulation over a low-level execution harness can be post-trained like any other language agent.

Context management.
A long episode does not fit in the context window of a small model, so the harness manages the history explicitly.
Tool outputs are truncated to a fixed token budget, at most 20 receipt lines are printed per cell, and only the 12 most recent images are kept.
When the history approaches the context limit, the harness compacts it turn by turn.
It keeps the initial task context and the most recent turns verbatim, and replaces the removed turns with a short notice that lists the commands they ran and warns that the scene may have changed since.
Because the agent’s variables live in the Python session rather than in the prompt, detections, poses and helper functions survive compaction.
Compaction behaves identically during RL rollouts and at test time, so the policy is trained on the inputs it will see.
A persistent Python session.
The only tool is
python
, a sandboxed Python session with a pre-imported
robot
module.
Variables persist across requests, so the agent can store detections, poses and its own helper functions and reuse them later.
Robot calls do not raise exceptions; each returns a structured result with a success flag, a failure category, a message and a value.
This lets the agent write ordinary control flow (

There are no grasp, place or open-drawer skills and no VLA.
The agent must decide where to grasp, from which direction to approach and when to close the jaw.
The harness turns each
move_to
into a straight Cartesian motion, solves inverse kinematics, checks self-collision and monitors force at every control substep, stopping at first contact unless the agent requests a manipulation mode that tolerates load.
Because every approach vector, grasp pose, and jaw command is written explicitly in Python, the full manipulation policy is exposed to language-model post-training.
Receipts.
After each robot call, the harness appends a short
receipt
to the cell output that reports what physically happened: for motions, the stop reason, the executed distance, the peak force and the jaw opening before and after; for perception, the detection identity, its metric position and its offset to the destination.
The agent can also attach up to four camera images per cell.
Receipts give the policy dense, grounded feedback in text that complements the images.
Self-verification and success.
A completion gate on the host checks the agent’s own recorded measurements and may reject
finish()
twice before accepting it.
Host success
is the benchmark’s goal predicate, evaluated by the environment host on the final state.
Strict success
additionally requires that the agent ended the episode with
finish()

Protocol and metrics.
All evaluations run in
CaPtain-Harness
with the settings of RL rollouts: temperature 1, thinking enabled, at most 60 requests, 150 physical actions and 1,080 s per episode, and no early stopping.
At test time, the simulator critic is removed and all object coordinates are estimated online from RGB-D camera observations and execution receipts.

Comparisons between our models are paired on identical (suite, task, initial-state) triples, with exact two-sided McNemar tests and 95% task-cluster bootstrap intervals.

5
Limitations
•
Single-benchmark RL training and bimanual control.
Our RL stage is trained exclusively on the 40 LIBERO tasks with a single 7-DoF arm.
While
CaPtain-4B
transfers zero-shot to unseen single-arm tasks and embodiments, cross-benchmark performance remains below in-domain accuracy, and tasks requiring simultaneous bimanual coordination or tight kinematic reach on unfamiliar 6-DoF arms are not yet addressed (§
4.3
).
•
Privileged state during RL.
Training the simulator critic relies on exact simulator state.
In our offline sensitivity study, replacing ground-truth object poses with noisy estimates degrades correlation with the privileged
Δ
​
V
\Delta V
(0.49 under 2 cm pose noise, 0.36 under 5 cm, and 0.21 using the policy’s own perception), indicating that online RL directly on physical hardware would require an external state estimator.
•
Interface and SFT coverage.
The agent’s action space is bounded by the 22 capabilities of
CaPtain-Harness
and the behaviors demonstrated in the synthetic SFT trajectories (Appendix
C
).
Tasks that require continuous force-controlled compliance—such as Wipe on CaP-Bench, which demands sustained downward pressing—cannot be expressed by guarded Cartesian position primitives.
6
Conclusion
We presented
CaPtain
, an open post-training pipeline that turns a 4B vision-language model into a standalone code-as-policy robot agent operating directly over low-level perception and motion primitives.
By pairing a portable execution harness (
CaPtain-Harness
) with synthetic SFT trajectories and multi-turn RL guided by a privileged simulator critic,
CaPtain
converts sparse episode outcomes into dense per-request credit concentrated on physical manipulation decisions, while requiring no privileged information, demonstration-trained VLA skills, or frontier API calls at test time.
Across held-out LIBERO and three perturbation suites,
CaPtain-4B
improves substantially over SFT, matches or surpasses several frontier-model agents at a small fraction of their inference cost, transfers zero-shot to unseen benchmarks and embodiments, and deploys on a physical robot through simulated embodiment adaptation alone.
Extending the simulator critic to value termination decisions, bimanual coordination, and multi-embodiment workspaces offers a direct path toward closing the remaining gap to frontier systems.

Data generation.
The synthetic episodes were generated by frontier coding agents (GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.x Sol, see the table caption) acting in the same harness, with the same API,
TASK.md
and chat template as the 4B policy.
The raw episodes contained 226 distinct variants of the same “preview, then move” helper.
We rewrote all trajectories onto a single helper library of four functions (

,
need
,
downq
,
go
) that the model learns to write itself.
Equivalence of each rewrite was checked call site by call site against a mock robot, and replaying 6 rewritten episodes changed robot commands by less than 1 cm.
Turns with repeated execution failures or recovery loops (about 3.6% of requests) are masked from the loss, as are requests after a gate-rejected finish on one long-horizon task.
Training.
Only assistant turns are supervised.
A text-hint mask replaces earlier
mark_point
pixel coordinates in the history with
<masked>
with probability 0.2.
This forces the model to look at the image instead of copying coordinates.
Training uses full fine-tuning of the language model with the vision tower frozen.
The batch is 16 packed rows of at most 66k tokens.
We use DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 in bf16, gradient clipping at 1.0, and 2,435 steps (1.5 epochs).
The final model scores 42/80 on our 80-episode validation set.
Appendix D
Diversity of tasks and layouts during post-training
Diversity of tasks and scene layouts in the post-training data is essential for keeping the visual grounding of the base model.
In an earlier version of our data, most episodes started from the official LIBERO initial states, in which each object occupies nearly the same position across episodes (per-object position standard deviation about 1.4 cm).
Models fine-tuned on these data learned to reproduce object positions from the task identity rather than reading them from the image: replacing the input image left the likelihood of the predicted pixel coordinates unchanged.
The policy had effectively memorized the layouts and lost the vision-language model’s ability to ground objects in new scenes.
We therefore collect SFT data on wide-layout starts, whose per-object position standard deviation is about 15 cm, mix all task suites, and randomize lighting, camera pose and materials during RL.
With this diversity, the model grounds every
mark_point
and
segment
call in the current image, which is also what allows it to transfer to the unseen objects and layouts of the real-robot tasks (§
4.4
).

Appendix F
RL infrastructure
Layout.
Rollout and training run on separate 8-GPU nodes.
The rollout node serves six vLLM policy replicas, SAM 3 and Molmo, and renders 64–80 concurrent MuJoCo episodes; the trainer uses FSDP2 on the other node.
Rollouts are streamed: the environment server keeps generating while the trainer updates, and a request may come from a policy that is at most two versions old.
New weights reach the rollout servers by NCCL in under one second, and checkpoints are written asynchronously, which reduces the blocking time of a checkpoint from about 500 s to 5–9 s.

Appendix G
Lessons from RL on a multi-turn agent
•
Measure the gradient noise before choosing the batch.
With two start states per optimizer step, the weight displacement from the SFT model grew as the square root of the number of steps and consecutive updates were nearly orthogonal: the policy performed a random walk.
The gradient-noise scale of outcome-only advantages is in the thousands of episodes (Appendix
H
), so we accumulate 1,024 episodes per optimizer step.
•
Start states must cover the whole task.
A curriculum that started episodes at intermediate states of successful demonstrations placed every start after the grasp, because a grasp does not change the distance of the object to its goal; the policy then learned only to place held objects.
We train from fresh initial states only.
•
Layout diversity keeps the model looking.
Without diverse layouts, the model memorizes object positions and stops grounding its calls in the image (Appendix
D
).
•
Keep the policy’s behavior out of the critic.
Counters of perception or failed calls act as proxies for elapsed time and move credit from grasps to perception (§
4.5
).
•
Termination needs its own signal.
A critic trained on task success values every post-success state near one, so the decision to stop receives no credit from the critic; post-success costs and a missed-finish return are needed to make the agent declare completion (Appendix
I
).

Host and strict success late in RL

Host and strict success diverge late in training (Figure

).
After about round 340, host success holds at about 65% while strict success falls from about 60% to 44%.
The lost episodes run out of requests while re-verifying solved scenes, while false finishes stay rare.
Because strict success drops between rounds 300 and 400, we use the round-300 checkpoint as

The mechanism is over-verification.
After the task is solved, the policy keeps measuring, re-observing and comparing instead of calling
finish()
.
The return structure makes this a slow drift rather than a cliff:
•
a missed finish still earns 0.25;
•
the post-success cost is capped;
•
the critic, trained on host success, assigns
V
≈
1
V{\approx}1
to every post-success state.
The critic therefore gives the decision to stop no credit; only the terminal return and the small post-success request cost distinguish it.
We observed the same failure in an earlier run, where it doubled missed finishes and returned strict LIBERO-Plus success to the SFT level.
It was partially fixed by the post-success cost.
This suggests giving the decision to finish its own target, e.g. success-and-finished.
