article.headline: 4B模型经SFT与多轮RL成为代码策略机器人智能体
article.lede: 开源SFT加多轮RL流水线，把4B小模型训练成代码即策略机器人智能体；LIBERO成功率从零样本0%升到73.8%。
article.problem: 现有代码即策略（CaP）机器人智能体大多绕开训练：要么在测试时调用闭源前沿模型，成本高、无法按新机器人微调、也上不了机载算力；要么把抓取、放置等操作委托给预训练的VLA或高层技能，RL至多学会调用顺序。小开源视觉语言模型直接上手则完全失败——Qwen3.5-4B在本文的执行环境下解不出一个LIBERO回合。缺的是一条直接教小模型在低层原语上做操作的完整SFT加RL配方。
article.method: 作者构建CaPtain-Harness，只暴露22个低层感知、几何测量与带保护的运动会原语，没有grasp/place宏，也没有VLA，每次调用返回结构化文本回执。训练分两步：先在GPT-6 Astra生成的合成轨迹上做SFT（遮蔽重复失败轮次、以0.2概率遮蔽历史像素坐标迫使模型看当前图像），再做多轮RL。RL的关键是一个模拟器critic：它读取策略看不到的36维特权物理状态，预测任务成功率，并在固定请求索引下取前后差值作为每个请求的信用，使只做感知或校验的请求几乎得不到信用；测试时critic被移除，策略仅凭相机图像与回执行动。
article.results: 从Qwen3.5-4B（零样本0%）出发，CaPtain-4B在留出LIBERO上经SFT达到55.4%、经RL达到73.8%（strict 52.1%→67.5%），虚假finish从7.1%降到2.1%，平均请求数从39.1降到32.6。LIBERO-PRO三套件59.5%→78.5%（四套件49.2%→68.6%，+19.4），LIBERO-Plus 48.6%→66.1%（+17.6，七个扰动维度全部在p<0.05下提升），LIBERO-MAX Dynamic +21.2、Base +18.8。零样本迁移：SimplerEnv WidowX 83.3%，CaP-Bench 75.0（SFT为55.0，未训练模型为5.0），但RoboTwin 2.0仅22.6%、RoboDojo仅0.8%（Score 1.7）。每回合平均32.6次请求、16.6个物理动作、约52 GPU秒，估算0.03–0.06美元。
article.why_it_matters: 它表明机器人操作只要跑在低层执行环境上，就能像其他语言智能体一样被后训练，一个4B开源模型在测试时不调用前沿API、不依赖VLA技能，就在多项基准上超过若干前沿模型智能体，并能在仅用粗模拟孪生适配后上真机。
article.limitations: RL只在40个LIBERO任务、单条7自由度臂上训练，双臂协调与陌生6自由度臂的可达性问题未解，跨基准迁移仍明显低于域内精度。critic依赖精确模拟器状态，离线敏感性实验显示2 cm位姿噪声下相关性降到0.49、5 cm降到0.36、改用策略自身感知仅0.21，因此真机在线RL需要外部状态估计器；此外22个原语无法表达持续力控任务（如CaP-Bench的Wipe）。
article.figure_caption_zh: CaPtain总览：上为推理阶段——策略在CaPtain-Harness中对低层API写一个Python单元、读回文本回执与新图像，最多60次请求；下为训练与测试——先在合成轨迹上SFT，再做RL，由模拟器critic把特权物理状态转成逐请求信用，测试时critic被移除。

figure.caption: {Overview of {}.} {Top:} inference, one episode in {}: at each request the policy writes a Python cell against a low-level API and receives text receipts and new images, for up to 60 requests. {Bottom:} training and test: SFT on synthetic agent trajectories, then RL in which a {} turns privileged physical state into per-request credit; the critic is removed at test time.

email_papers.title: SketchDirector: Complex Scene Sketching via Agentic Layout Reasoning and Detail Refinement
email_papers.abstract: Existing sketch generation methods often rely on image guidance and are largely limited to individual objects or simplified scenes, leaving text-guided complex scene sketching underexplored. We present SketchDirector, an agentic framework that mimics the human sketching workflow for automatic multi-concept scene sketching. Given a scene-level text prompt, SketchDirector first employs a large language model~(LLM) to decompose the scene into multiple draft assets, where each is represented by a set of Bézier curves. Then, an agentic reasoning loop iteratively plans and executes their spatial arrangement, guided by self-evolving memory. Finally, a detail refinement module leverages diffusion priors to enhance sketch quality while preserving geometric structure. To support future research and applications in multi-concept scene sketch generation, we further introduce the \textit{MCSketch8K} dataset, comprising editable vector assets, compositional layouts, and object-level manipulation annotations. Extensive experiments show that SketchDirector outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in semantic and compositional quality while effectively preserving overall contour organization during refinement. The project page is: \href{https://yiki77.github.io/SketchDirector/}{https://yiki77.github.io/SketchDirector/}.
email_papers.content:
SketchDirector: Complex Scene Sketching via Agentic Layout Reasoning and Detail Refinement
Yiqi Liang
Xiaodong Cun
\corresponding
Abstract
Existing sketch generation methods often rely on image guidance and are largely limited to individual objects or simplified scenes, leaving text-guided complex scene sketching underexplored.
We present SketchDirector, an agentic framework that mimics the human sketching workflow for automatic multi-concept scene sketching.
Given a scene-level text prompt, SketchDirector first employs a large language model (LLM) to decompose the scene into multiple draft assets, where each is represented by a set of Bézier curves. Then, an agentic reasoning loop iteratively plans and executes their spatial arrangement, guided by self-evolving memory. Finally, a detail refinement module leverages diffusion priors to enhance sketch quality while preserving geometric structure. To support future research and applications in multi-concept scene sketch generation, we further introduce the
MCSketch8K
dataset, comprising editable vector assets, compositional layouts, and object-level manipulation annotations. Extensive experiments show that SketchDirector outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in semantic and compositional quality while effectively preserving overall contour organization during refinement. The project page is:
https://yiki77.github.io/SketchDirector/
.
GVC Lab, Great Bay University
https://yiki77.github.io/SketchDirector/
Figure 1:
Visual results of SketchDirector
. The top row shows scene sketches depicting diverse concepts. The bottom-left row shows rich layout variations for the same prompt, highlighting the effectiveness of agentic reasoning for automatic scene composition. The bottom-right row shows the progressive sketch refinement process, which enhances sketch details while preserving sketch structure and spatial layout.
1
Introduction
Sketching is a concise visual representation that effectively captures the intentions of human beings.
As its scope expands from individual objects to multiple concepts, scene sketching has shown great potential in applications such as animation, proof of concept, and interactive design, as in Fig.
2
(A).
However, complex scene sketching requires more than depicting individual objects. It involves organizing multiple concepts, reasoning about their spatial relationships, and maintaining coherent details within a unified scene.
Therefore, generating semantically aligned scene sketches with reasonable layouts and coherent details remains a big challenge.
Previous automatic scene sketching generation methods
(
Li et al. 2019a
;
Li et al. 2019b
;
Chan et al. 2022
;
Vinker et al. 2023
;
Liang et al. 2025b
)
primarily operate at the holistic scene level, treating scene sketches as an indivisible entity without object representations, thereby hindering local editing and object reuse.
Recent studies
(
Wu et al. 2025
;
Zhang et al. 2026
;
Zhan et al. 2025
)
have explored object-aware generation, but objects are often treated as predefined components or auxiliary structures.
Consequently, these methods lack dynamic control, layout planning, and iterative optimization for individual objects, which limits their potential as visual components.
In contrast, real-world sketch creation is inherently iterative: artists continually revise, group, and rearrange individual elements to improve the overall composition and presentation. They also adapt the level of refinement to suit their creative goals, producing sketches that range from rough drafts to highly detailed renderings, as illustrated in Fig.
2
(B). Digital vector sketches are particularly well suited to such flexible and iterative workflows because they are naturally represented as collections of Bézier curves, enabling efficient programmatic manipulation.
We thus propose
SketchDirector
, an automatic agentic framework
(
Vinker et al. 2025
;
Du et al. 2026
;
Liu et al. 2025
;
Liang et al. 2025a
)
for text-guided multi-concept scene sketch generation by mimicking the pipeline of human creators.
Specifically,
given a textual description,
SketchDirector
first employs a Large Language Model (LLM) based method to decompose the scene and generate each individual object as draft asset, each represented as a set of Bézier curves.
To enable layout control between multiple asset, we introduce an operating action library comprising a set of executable operations,
e.g.,
move()
,
scale()
, to manipulate object attributes, enabling flexible adjustment of spatial relationships among objects.
Building upon this library, we propose an agentic reasoning loop, which formulates layout manipulation as an iterative operations and execution process.
To achieve reliable closed-loop reasoning, rather than predicting the entire scene layout at once,
SketchDirector
progressively organizes draft assets through an iterative
Plan–Execute–Verify–Correct
process.
At each step,
SketchDirector
generates and executes object-level operations, updates the scene representation, and evaluates the resulting composition through geometric checks and multimodal verification.
When the layout fails verification,
SketchDirector
revises its decisions and corrects the layout using a hierarchical self-evolving memory that leverages short-term failure reflections and accumulated long-term experiences.
After that, we introduce an additional detail refinement step to address the challenges of structural consistency in scene sketch distillation from the diffusion prior.
Unlike traditional methods that treat Bézier curves as unstructured point sets, we treat object curve segments as the optimization primitives.
Then, by jointly optimizing local objects and the global canvas using pre-scene distillation, our method is able to generate scene sketches with varying levels of object refinement while maintaining consistency with the textual description. Finally, with the lack of available object-aware and editable scene sketch datasets, we construct a multi-concept scene sketch dataset called
MCSketch8K
to facilitate future research and applications in scene sketch generation.
The dataset comprises 1,000 scene sketches with over 4,000 disentangled vector object assets across 800 object categories.
Each scene is annotated with compositional layouts and object-level manipulation operations, providing structured supervision for object decomposition, spatial arrangement reasoning, and controllable scene editing.
Our key contributions are summarized as:
•
We propose
SketchDirector
, an automatic framework for text-guided complex scene sketching with flexible object-level control and structure-preserving detail refinement.
•
SketchDirector
contains two key techniques to assist in scene sketch generation:
i) agentic reasoning
, which formulates generation as a closed-loop process;
ii) detail refinement
, which performs Bézier curve parametrization and progressively joint local-global vector optimization to refine scene sketches.
•
We construct
MCSketch8K
, a multi-concept scene sketch dataset comprising vector object assets, compositional scene layouts, and object-level manipulation annotations.
Figure 2:
Motivation of multi-concept scene sketch generation.
(A) Widely used in animation, concept art, and design. (B) Artists adjust sketch refinement from draft to detailed sketch preserving structure for different goals.
2
Related Work
Scene Sketch Generation.
Scene sketch generation aims to translate visual or textual descriptions into coherent sketches.
Early methods formulated this task as image-to-sketch translation
(
Li et al. 2019a
;
Li et al. 2019b
;
Chan et al. 2022
)
, converting photographs into rasterized contour drawings via supervised learning or adversarial training.
Later studies increasingly adopt vector representations for scalable and editable sketch generation.
Image-conditioned methods such as Clipascene
(
Vinker et al. 2023
)
and MROSS
(
Liang et al. 2025b
)
produce vector scene sketches from a reference image, while text-guided methods
(
Frans et al. 2022
;
Jain et al. 2023
;
Xing et al. 2023
;
Xing et al. 2024
;
Xing et al. 2025
)
further enable open-domain vector sketch generation from textual descriptions.
In particular, VectorFusion
(
Jain et al. 2023
)
distills text-to-image diffusion priors into SVGs through score distillation, DiffSketcher
(
Xing et al. 2023
)
directly optimizes Bézier curves with diffusion-based supervision, and SVGDreamer
(
Xing et al. 2024
)
improves text-to-SVG generation through semantic-driven vectorization and particle-based score distillation.
Despite these advances, existing methods optimize the scene holistically, leaving objects implicitly encoded and limiting editing to strokes rather than objects.
Multi-concept Sketch Generation.
Recent studies explore structured scene generation by introducing different forms of concept decomposition and controllability.
For instance, SketchTriplet
(
Wu et al. 2025
)
assembles individual objects to construct scene datasets, although the objects mainly serve as fixed composition units without supporting layout planning or per-concept editing.
SketchAny
(
Zhang et al. 2026
)
separates foreground and background to improve structural coherence, yet provides limited control over individual concept instances.
CoProSketch
(
Zhan et al. 2025
)
represents objects with unsigned distance fields to enable progressive scene generation and improved editability, while generation is still performed at the scene level rather than through independent concept generation.
Collectively, these methods highlight the value of concept-aware representations, yet objects remain passive elements rather than autonomous units for planning, interaction, and iterative refinement.
Agents for Sketch Generation.
The rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has introduced new opportunities for reasoning, planning, and iterative interaction into sketch generation.
For instance, SketchAgent
(
Vinker et al. 2025
)
introduces a language-driven sequential sketch generation framework, where an LLM-based agent can generate sequences of vector sketches and supports conversational sketch refinement.
Building upon this, Du et al.
(
Du et al. 2026
)

3
SketchDirector
The goal of
SketchDirector
is to generate editable multi-concept scene sketches from textual descriptions.
Each sketch is represented as a collection of SVG assets parameterized by black Bézier curves, enabling object-level editability and structural preservation.
Given a scene description, we first decompose it into individual concepts and generate corresponding vector draft assets (Sec.
3.1
).
To support executable scene composition, we define an operating action library consisting of primitive operations that manipulate object attributes and update the scene state (Sec.
3.2
).
Building upon these, an agentic layout reasoning step progressively composes the scene through a closed loop, where agents translate spatial intentions into executable editing programs and iteratively plan, execute, verify, and correct the scene composition (Sec.
3.3
).
Finally, a detail refinement step further enhances sketch details through Bézier curve contour resampling and progressive joint optimization, while preserving the structure of draft assets and spatial layout of the canvas (Sec.
3.4
).
A high-level illustration is shown in Fig.
3
.

Self-Evolving Correction.
Different from contrastive experience for object-level sketch generation
(

The Short-Term Failure Memory.
The Short-Term Failure Memory maintains a trajectory-level record for each failed attempt. Each entry contains the generated program, intermediate rendering results, object-level attributes, verification feedback, and the corresponding failure category.

across different foundational models,we evaluate four state-of-the-art backbones: OpenAI GPT-5.5
(
OpenAI 2026
)
, Gemini-3.1-pro
(
DeepMind 2026
)
, Claude-Opus-4-7
(
Anthropic 2026
)
, and Qwen3.7-Plus
(
Cloud 2026
)
.
Figure
9
and Table
2
show that that different backbones exhibit varying capabilities in spatial organization, visual-semantic alignment, and reasoning efficiency.
OpenAI GPT-5.5 achieves the highest scores across all verification metrics and requires the fewest reasoning iterations, demonstrating stronger layout planning and scene composition capabilities.
Gemini-3.1-Pro and Claude-Opus-4-7 achieve relatively strong semantic alignment but require more iterations to refine their layouts. Their generated sketches generally capture the main scene concepts, yet exhibit fewer visual details . In contrast, Qwen3.7-Plus obtains lower verification scores and requires substantially more reasoning iterations.
Overall, these results demonstrate that
SketchDirector
can operate with different backbones, while stronger reasoning capabilities contribute to more accurate scene composition and efficient convergence.

Impact of Agentic Layout Reasoning.
Figure
10
and Table
3
show that removing any component leads to performance degradation, confirming that all modules in agentic reasoning are essential for high-quality scene sketch generation.
Removing planning (
w/o Plan
) leads to severe layout degradation.
Without executable scene programs, the model struggles to organize object attributes, resulting in frequent object overlaps, unreasonable spatial arrangements, and boundary violations.
These demonstrate that converting high-level semantic intentions into structured layout operations is essential for reliable scene composition.
Disabling geometric verification (
w/o Geo. Ver.
) mainly affects physical plausibility.
Although the generated objects remain semantically relevant, their positions and sizes may violate basic spatial constraints, such as objects extending beyond the canvas or unrealistic relative scales between objects.
This indicates that geometric constraints provide necessary low-level guidance for maintaining valid scene structures.
Without visual-semantic verification (
w/o Sem. Ver.
), the agent lacks high-level visual feedback during layout refinement.
Consequently, generated scenes may contain incorrect object relationships, missing semantic interactions, or unnatural occlusion orders.
The comparison highlights the importance of multimodal evaluation in aligning generated layouts with the intended scene description.
Furthermore, memory modules improve the agent’s ability to learn from previous reasoning trajectories.
Removing short-term memory (
w/o Short Mem.
) does not cause significant visual layout degradation, but leads to repeated exploration of similar unsuccessful layouts, increasing the number of reflection iterations.
Removing long-term memory (
w/o Long Mem.
) also preserves comparable visual structures in many cases, yet prevents the agent from retrieving reusable layout experiences from related scenes, resulting in less effective layout composition.
Overall, these qualitative examples verify that each component contributes complementary capabilities, enabling more reliable and controllable scene reasoning.
Impact of Detail Refinement.
Fig.
11
provides additional comparisons between point-based and curve-based sampling.
Point-based sampling uniformly samples sparse control points from object regions without considering the underlying contours.
During optimization, these points may drift independently, causing geometric distortions and loss of characteristic object shapes.
In contrast, our curve contour resampling method derives Bézier primitives directly from object contours.
By preserving the original contour topology, the curves provide a more stable optimization space.
Fig.
12
presents additional comparisons of different optimization strategies.
Removing local supervision (
w/o Local
) optimizes objects only according to global objectives, allowing unrelated semantic information to interfere with individual object.
This often results in distorted local structures.
Removing global supervision (
w/o Global
) focuses only on individual object while ignoring interactions among objects.
Although individual objects may remain recognizable, the resulting scenes exhibit weaker spatial coherence, such as unnatural object relationships.
Without progressive optimization (
w/o Progressive
), local and global objectives are optimized simultaneously from the beginning.
The strong coupling between object-level refinement and scene-level consistency introduces optimization conflicts, causing unstable updates and reduced object fidelity.
By progressively incorporating objects, our method enables stable local refinement first and gradually improves global scene integration.
Figure 12:
Qualitative ablation of progressive joint optimization.
Removing local supervision, global supervision, or progressive optimization leads to degraded object fidelity and scene-level coherence.
4.4
Limitations.
Although
SketchDirector
generates multi-concept scene sketches, several limitations remain. First, it struggles with complex physical and semantic relations, such as interactions between a woman and a kettle or a castle located on a hill (Fig.
13
(A)). Stronger relational and interaction modeling may improve scene understanding. Second, refinement may hallucinate redundant instances, leading to object inconsistency, such as duplicating a sheep (Fig.
13
(B)). Instance-aware constraints could help preserve object identity and count. Third, multimodal verification and iterative optimization incur computational costs, particularly when multiple refinement rounds are required. Efficient verification and optimization strategies will be explored in future work.
Figure 13:
Limitations of
SketchDirector
.
(A) Challenges in
modeling complex physical and semantic interactions. (B) Object hallucination during refinement.
5
Conclusion
We present
SketchDirector
, an agentic framework that emulates the human sketching workflow. Designed for complex scene sketch generation,
SketchDirector
converts textual descriptions into editable vector assets and executable layout operations. It consists of three stages: concept representation for generating object-level draft assets, agentic reasoning with iterative
Plan–Execute–Verify–Correct
and self-evolving memory for reliable spatial composition, and detail refinement for progressively optimizing Bézier-based vectors while preserving the original sketch structure. We further introduce
MCSketch8K
, a benchmark containing editable vector assets and composition annotations for multi-concept scene sketch generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that
SketchDirector
outperforms existing methods in semantic and compositional quality while effectively preserving structural integrity during refinement.

article.headline: 用智能体规划布局，把文本变成可编辑场景草图
article.lede: SketchDirector 让 LLM 拆解概念、智能体闭环摆放草稿、扩散先验补细节，输出可编辑的矢量场景草图。
article.problem: 现有草图生成方法多依赖图像引导，适用范围基本停留在单个物体或简化场景，文本引导的复杂场景草图仍少有人做。早期方法把整幅场景当成不可分的实体整体优化，物体被隐式编码，无法单独编辑或复用；近期的物体感知方法又把物体当作预设组件或辅助结构，缺少对单个物体的布局规划与迭代优化。
article.method: 给定场景级文本，LLM 先把场景拆成若干可独立绘制的概念，每个概念由 SketchAgent 生成采样点并用最小二乘拟合成三次 Bézier 曲线草稿，同时给出深度序。随后智能体在 move/scale/rotate/layer/delete/modify 六个原子操作组成的动作库上，以 Plan–Execute–Verify–Correct 闭环迭代布置：几何检查边界与缩放范围 [0.1,1.5]，VLM 从语义、构图、完整度、尺寸、美观五维加权打分，失败轨迹写入短期失败记忆、成功布局以 Jaccard 相似度检索进长期经验记忆。最后做曲线轮廓重采样（de Casteljau 细分，保持原拓扑）与渐进式局部-全局 RFDS 联合优化，只更新控制点、固定曲线顺序以保住结构。
article.results: 在从 MCSketch8K 采样的 30 条多概念提示上，由 Qwen3.7-Plus、Claude-Opus-4-7、Gemini3.1-Pro、GPT-5.5 四个 VLM 评判，SketchDirector 五项指标为语义 0.916、构图 0.772、完整度 0.821、美观 0.836、尺寸 0.821，加细节精炼后升至 0.923/0.788/0.843/0.869/0.842，均高于五个基线；对照的 GPT-5.5 为 0.911/0.730/0.811/0.813/0.820，SVGDreamer 为 0.690/0.546/0.620/0.650/0.695，VectorFusion 仅 0.466/0.252/0.338/0.417/0.412。耗时上 SketchDirector 约 6 分钟、加精炼约 21 分钟，GPT-5.5 与 SketchAgent 约 20 秒，SVGDreamer 约 24 分钟。消融显示去掉规划后语义降至 0.676、构图 0.503，去掉语义验证语义降至 0.603，去掉短期记忆迭代次数从 1.375 升到 2.875；完整模型验证通过率 0.873。用户研究招募 68 人、15 条提示，每项标准收集 5100 份回答，各基线对比中参与者均更偏好本方法。作者同时发布 MCSketch8K，含 1,000 幅场景草图、4,000 余个解耦矢量物体资产、覆盖 800 个物体类别。
article.why_it_matters: 它把场景草图从“整图优化”改成“物体级程序化编排”，输出的 SVG 资产和布局可单独移动、缩放、替换，对动画、概念设计和交互设计这类需要反复改稿的流程更直接可用，MCSketch8K 也为物体级场景草图提供了带布局与操作标注的训练/评测基础。
article.limitations: 论文自陈三类问题：难以建模复杂物理与语义关系（如人与水壶的交互、山丘上的城堡），精炼阶段会幻觉出多余实例（例如重复画出一只羊），以及多模态验证与迭代优化带来的计算开销。此外，不加精炼时语义分 0.916 仅比 GPT-5.5 的 0.911 高 0.005，而耗时约 6 分钟对约 20 秒，优势主要体现在构图（0.772 对 0.730）上；评测仅用 30 条提示、且由 VLM 打分，规模与评判独立性都值得进一步检验。

email_papers.title: Does Scaling Toward AGI Depend on What System-1 Lets System-2 Execute?
email_papers.abstract: Progress toward artificial general intelligence (AGI) has largely relied on scaling a resource-intensive executive, System-2, through larger models, more data and compute, longer reasoning, and more agents. We ask whether the next stage may come instead from co-designing it with System-1, a lightweight, semantically aware predictor that evaluates candidate interactions before execution, so that System-2 acts only on those worth their cost. Our answer is a qualified yes. We study conditional interaction, a predict--gate--execute--update loop: System-1 estimates each candidate's utility, System-2 executes those admitted by an adaptive threshold, and the outcomes update System-1. The loop spans training, test-time reasoning, adaptive decision-making, and agentic tool use, with utility and cost defined by the application. Under ideal screening and equal execution costs, execution compute falls by a factor approaching 1/ρ_u, where ρ_u is the density of utility-relevant interactions (cost-weighted when costs differ); prediction errors, exploration, and distribution shift reduce the saving. We bound selection regret by predictor error and the utility margin. These results motivate our central hypothesis: ρ_u is a measurable coordinate of scaling efficiency and makes informative compute a better description of scaling than total compute.
email_papers.content:
Abstract
Progress toward artificial general intelligence (AGI) has largely relied on scaling a resource-intensive executive, System-2, through larger models, more data and compute, longer reasoning, and more agents. We ask whether the next stage may come instead from co-designing it with System-1, a lightweight, semantically aware predictor that evaluates candidate interactions before execution, so that System-2 acts only on those worth their cost. Our answer is a qualified yes.

Section
4.1
states the core formal results: what prediction buys, in time and memory, and the regret a cheap predictor risks. The remaining subsections ask why a cheap System-1 can make a useful prediction about an expensive interaction at all, from three complementary views. These connections are interpretive rather than separate contributions; each supplies insight and, under its own assumptions, a guarantee, but none is a derivation of the framework.
Information-theoretically
(

Proposition
14
. Later methods predict before generating: GRESO skips prompts that their reward history marks as likely zero-variance
(
Zheng et al., 2026
)
; MoPPS tracks each prompt’s success rate with an online Bayesian posterior and approaches an evaluation-intensive dynamic-sampling baseline with far fewer rollouts
(
Qu et al., 2026a
)
; DPS, BOTS and PCL model prompt difficulty with a hidden-Markov process, Thompson sampling and an on-policy value model, respectively
(
Mao et al., 2026
;
Shen et al., 2026
;
Gao et al., 2026
)
; and GPS trains one small generative predictor on the shared optimization history to select prompts for a much larger reasoning model, improving training efficiency and test-time compute allocation
(
Qu et al., 2026c
)
. The same move extends beyond prompts, to online batch selection in supervised fine-tuning
(
Zou et al., 2025
)
, to demonstration selection for in-context learning, where a small trained model makes a single edit to the retrieved demonstrations instead of iteratively scoring or searching over demonstration subsets
(
Wen et al., 2026b
)
, to rollout allocation across tasks and trajectory prefixes in agentic RL
(
Zou et al., 2026b
)
, and to critic-free, tree-aware credit assignment for long-horizon agents
(
Zou et al., 2026a
)
. These results
illustrate
rather than
validate
the framework.
Physical: from randomizing to predicting adaptation risk.
For embodied agents, judging a task configuration means acting on it, on hardware or in a high-fidelity simulator, at the pace of physics. Domain randomization trains across wide ranges of simulated appearance and dynamics
(
Tobin et al., 2017

(
Muratore et al., 2018

(

;
Akkaya et al., 2019

and through environment design and level replay driven by regret or learning potential
(
Dennis et al., 2020
;
Jiang et al., 2021

(
Rockafellar et al., 2000

(
Finn et al., 2017
;
Wang et al., 2023
;
Lv et al., 2024

(
Carpin et al., 2016
)
and safety-critical scenario generation
(
Rempe et al., 2022
)

(
Wang et al., 2026
)

(
Qu et al., 2025

and in-context risk prediction
(
Wen et al., 2026a
)

Evaluation requires generating in the digital regime and acting in the physical one, yet both literatures converge on the same loop: System-1 scores a candidate from cheap features and history, System-2 executes only what clears the score, and System-2’s outcomes refit System-1. article.headline: 别只堆算力：让 System-1 先筛一遍
article.lede: 论文主张：通往 AGI 的扩展不只在放大 System-2，还需轻量 System-1 预筛候选交互再执行。
article.problem: 当前通往 AGI 的进展主要靠把执行器 System-2 做大：更大模型、更多数据与算力、更长推理链、更多智能体，成本随规模同步膨胀。论文追问，下一阶段是否应改为与 System-1 协同设计——一个轻量、具备语义感知的预测器，在交互真正执行前先评估候选是否值得其代价。
article.method: 作者给出一个形式化框架：System-1 用廉价特征与历史为每个候选嵌入并打分，门控只放行分数超过阈值 τ_t 的候选，控制器调节阈值以维持目标放行率 π*（阈值更新式）；被抑制的候选只需付出 c_pred，另留一小部分审计样本强制执行以检测预测漏判。执行结果被记录并回流重训 System-1，System-2 也从同一批结果中学习。论文另从信息论与具身（域随机化、尾部风险）等视角解释廉价预测为何可能对昂贵交互有效。
article.results: 论文在第 4.1 节给出核心形式化结论：预测在时间与内存上带来什么收益（Eq. (12)、Proposition 7），以及廉价预测器带来的 regret 风险；信息论视角对应 Proposition 14，效用相关交互的密度定义见 Eq. (14)。论文未给出具体数字：全文没有实验或基准结果，GRESO、MoPPS、GPS、MPTS 等被引工作只作例证而非验证。
article.why_it_matters: 若这一框架成立，扩展 AGI 的杠杆可能从“更大的执行器”转向“更准的预筛器”，这直接对应推理时算力分配、rollout 分配与智能体强化学习的成本结构。它也把“何时不值得执行”变成一个可以被学习和被控制的目标放行率问题。
article.limitations: 作者自承三条理论线索是“解释性而非独立贡献”，没有一条是该框架的推导，相关实证工作是“例证而非验证”，全文亦无实验支撑。阈值调节、regret 界与目标放行率在真实负载与非平稳分布下是否仍成立，仍属存疑。

email_papers.title: Apriel Voice 27B Preview: An Open Model for Speech, Reasoning, and Tool Use
email_papers.abstract: A capable voice assistant must do more than recognize words; it must understand requests, reason over context, sustain conversations, and act through tools. We present Apriel Voice 27B Preview, an open speech-language model that unifies these capabilities within a shared reasoning backbone while retaining text and image input modalities. Built on the post-trained Gemma 4 26B-A4B checkpoint, Apriel Voice directly processes speech and generates both responses and tool calls without requiring a separate dialogue model. We introduce a two-stage training procedure to adapt the model to speech. The first stage establishes the speech interface, while the second jointly adapts the projector and backbone through supervised fine-tuning, text replay, and source-dependent cross-entropy and forward Kullback--Leibler divergence supervision. Automatically constructed speech-conditioned dialogues provide conversational training data, while local teacher serving, overlapping teacher and student computation, and fused full-vocabulary losses enable efficient online distillation. In thinking mode, Apriel Voice achieves a score of 98.90 on Big Bench Audio, 81.13 on Speech-BFCL, and a task success rate of 65.51% on τ-Voice, with a mean latency of 1.91 seconds. It also achieves 51.27% English EVA accuracy and 74.13% experience pass@1. Finally, we deploy Apriel Voice 27B Preview on a custom serving platform to support interactive voice interactions.

Apriel Voice 27B Preview: An Open Model for Speech, Reasoning, and Tool Use
Abstract
A capable voice assistant must do more than recognize words: it must understand a request, reason over context, sustain a conversation, and act through tools. We present Apriel Voice 27B Preview, an open speech-language model that unifies these abilities into a shared reasoning backbone while retaining text and image input modalities. Built on the post-trained Gemma 4 26B-A4B checkpoint, Apriel Voice processes speech directly and generates both responses and tool calls without requiring a separate dialogue model. A two-stage training procedure adapts the model to speech. Stage 1 establishes the speech interface. Stage 2 jointly adapts the projector and backbone using supervised fine-tuning, text replay, and source-dependent cross-entropy and forward Kullback–Leibler divergence supervision. Automatically constructed speech-conditioned dialogues provide conversational training data. Local teacher serving, overlapping teacher and student computation, and fused full-vocabulary losses enable effective online distillation. In thinking mode, Apriel Voice scores 98.90 on Big Bench Audio, 81.13 on Speech-BFCL, and 65.51% task success on
τ
\tau
-Voice, with a mean latency of 1.91 seconds. English EVA accuracy and experience pass@1 reach 51.27% and 74.13%. We serve Apriel Voice 27B Preview through a custom platform to enable interactive voice interactions.
Figure 1:
One reasoning backbone across speech, text, and images.
Apriel Voice receives speech through an encoder and projector, retains the original text and image interfaces, and generates both responses and tool calls. Application components execute tools, return their results to the conversation, and stream response text to a replaceable synthesizer. The frozen teacher is used only during training.
1
Introduction
An employee reporting a locked account may describe the problem aloud, share a screenshot, correct an identifier, and ask an assistant to open a ticket. The useful outcome is a resolved request: the assistant must connect the evidence, follow the conversation, choose an appropriate action, and interpret the result. Supporting such interactions requires speech understanding alongside the reasoning and tool use of a large language model (LLM).
Recognition accuracy is necessary but insufficient for voice agent success. A model may transcribe a request correctly yet lack the ability to follow constraints or invoke the necessary tools to complete the associated task. Likewise, strong text performance does not establish that the same model can reason reliably when the request arrives as audio. We therefore evaluate speech as an interface to general capability, covering reasoning, instruction following, conversation, and task completion alongside recognition and translation
[
23
,
4
,
39
]
.
Voice systems connect these capabilities in several ways. A conventional
3-stage
cascade combines automatic speech recognition (ASR), an LLM, and text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis, passing a transcript to the reasoner. Speech-conditioned models instead expose the reasoner to learned acoustic features
[
28
,
45
,
43
,
11
]
; native speech-generating models also integrate the output audio pathway
[
8
,
51
]
. Another deployment pattern separates the spoken conversation from a backend model responsible for reasoning and tools
[
34
]
. These designs allocate speech understanding, reasoning, synthesis, and interaction control to different components.
We present
Apriel Voice 27B Preview
, or
Apriel Voice
in short, an open speech-language model built on the post-trained Gemma 4 26B-A4B checkpoint
[
14
,
15
]
. Apriel Voice uses the same reasoning backbone to understand speech, respond in conversation, and decide when and how to call tools. Text, images, and returned tool results remain part of its context (
Figure
1
). Speech synthesis is independently replaceable, allowing voices and deployment choices to change without retraining the reasoner.
We release
Apriel Live
, an interactive interface enabling practitioners to experience Apriel Voice in real conversations.
The training problem is to extend an already capable decoder with a speech interface while preserving the behavior that makes it useful. We address it in two stages. Multilingual transcription, translation, and continuation first train a speech projector with the backbone frozen. Broad supervised fine-tuning (SFT) then updates the projector and backbone using speech tasks, internally generated conversations, tool interactions, and text replay. Source-dependent cross-entropy (CE) and forward Kullback–Leibler divergence (FKL) combine task targets with online supervision from a frozen copy of the original backbone. The teacher supports learning during adaptation and is absent at inference.
Contributions.
This report brings together four contributions:
1.
Broad speech-conditioned agentic capability.
A shared model handles spoken reasoning, instruction following, conversation, and tool-call generation while retaining text and image processing capabilities.
2.
A staged adaptation recipe.
Speech interface learning with automatically constructed speech-conditioned dialogues and source-dependent CE/FKL supervision connects task acquisition with capability retention.
3.
An efficient online-supervision implementation.
Local teacher serving, overlap with student computation, fused full-vocabulary losses, and coordinated checkpointing support the combined training workload.
4.
Evaluation and interactive deployment.
Detailed results span speech, text, images, multilingual translation, service interactions, and enterprise workflows; Apriel Live demonstrates the corresponding application interface.
In thinking mode, Apriel Voice achieves 98.90 on Big Bench Audio (BBA), 81.13 on BFCL, and 65.51% mean task success on
τ
\tau
-Voice. English EVA accuracy and experience pass@1 reach 51.27% and 74.13%. Together, these results show a strong open-source (OSS) model whose speech capability extends to reasoning and action. The broader evaluation examines language coverage, reasoning-mode effects, and text and image retention.
Table
5

2
Related Work
2.1
Connecting audio perception to language reasoning
Speech encoders provide transferable representations for recognition and downstream tasks
[
38
]
. SLAM-ASR studies a simple learned connection between a speech encoder and a language model
[
28
]
; Ultravox develops a speech-conditioned architecture with frame stacking and a learned projector
[
11
]
. SALMONN broadens the input scope to speech, audio events, and music
[
43
]
. Apriel Voice 27B Preview follows this established encoder–projector approach. Its emphasis is the capability of the adapted model across reasoning, instruction following, and complete interactions, evaluated together with recognition.
2.2
Transferring behavior across modalities
BLSP trains a speech adapter using continuations generated from text prefixes, and BLSP-KD transfers next-token distributions between text and speech with token alignment and partial parameter adaptation
[
45
,
46
]
. These methods are direct precedents for teaching a language model to respond to speech through behavioral supervision. Apriel Voice builds on that principle with staged interface learning, broad second-stage SFT, selected speech distillation, and replay for a post-trained multimodal backbone. Supervision aligns the teacher’s and student’s response positions; it does not require acoustic frames to match transcript tokens one to one.
Our objective combines established forms of supervision: sequence targets
[
21
]
, predictive-distribution distillation
[
19
]
, and preservation of earlier behavior during adaptation
[
25
]
. The contribution lies in how these signals are selected and implemented across the speech and retention mixture. Similarly, synthetic instruction generation has precedent in Self-Instruct
[
48
]
. Our data pipeline converts internally generated task dialogues into speech-conditioned examples through automatic span selection, a consistent reference voice within each conversation, and conversion-fidelity checks.
2.3
Speech generation and delegated voice systems
LLaMA-Omni combines speech perception, an instruction-tuned language model, and a streaming speech decoder
[
10
]
. Moshi models concurrent user and assistant audio for full-duplex interaction
[
8
]
, while Qwen3-Omni integrates multimodal perception and speech generation in its Thinker–Talker design
[
51
]
. These output-generation architectures differ from application-level delegation, in which a conversational voice model hands reasoning or tool work to a separate backend
[
34
]
.
Apriel Voice places conversation, reasoning, and tool-call decisions in the same speech-conditioned backbone. Application components execute tools, return results to the same backbone, and synthesize response text. Turn detection and interruption control operate around the model.
2.4
Evaluating and training capable voice agents
EVA-Bench (EVA) measures both service accuracy and interaction experience
[
4
]
, and
τ
\tau
-Voice evaluates task completion under realistic audio conditions
[
39
,
42
]
.
τ
2
\tau^{2}

[
3
,
29
]
. These benchmarks complement isolated recognition and reasoning tests by asking whether an agent reaches the required outcome.
For training, Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) distributes model state across workers
[
53
]
, and fused-kernel systems such as Liger reduce the overhead of language-model operations
[
20
]
. Apriel Voice combines student sharding with local online-teacher execution, a lookahead schedule, and full-vocabulary CE/FKL kernels. We describe these mechanisms together with the scale and duration of the completed training run.

Audio features, text tokens, image representations, and tool results condition the same backbone. The model generates either a response to the user or a tool call. The application executes tools, returns their results to the conversation, and sends response text to a separate speech synthesizer.

Speech adaptation must solve two related problems: make acoustic input intelligible to an existing decoder, and teach that decoder to use speech in complete tasks. We separate them in the training recipe (

Stage two combines mathematics, science, general conversation, speech tasks, noisy interactions, tool use, and text replay. Conversational data cover clarification, disambiguation, confirmation before updates, and speech surrounding tool execution. These examples extend training from isolated utterances to interactions in which the next response depends on prior context and actions.

We train the projector with the speech encoder, language backbone, vision tower, and vision bridge frozen. Teacher supervision transfers the starting decoder’s predictive behavior to speech-conditioned contexts. The projector learns to map speech into representations the fixed decoder can use.

5
Data Construction
5.1
Constructing speech-conditioned conversations
Our custom task and conversation data are generated synthetically in-house. We first construct text interactions containing user requests, assistant responses, and, where relevant, tool calls and returned results. This representation makes the intended task, role structure, and target behavior explicit. An automated conversion pipeline then renders selected user content as audio through reference-conditioned TTS and voice cloning.
Spoken requests can refer to material best retained as text, such as a code fragment, table, formula, or case-sensitive identifier. The conversion therefore supports both whole-turn speech and mixed text/audio turns. System instructions, assistant targets, and tool messages remain text, preserving the supervision for conversation and action.
5.2

7
Efficient Training with an Online Teacher
Online full-vocabulary distillation adds a teacher forward pass and distribution transfer to the student’s training workload. The implementation distributes teacher inference across local workers, overlaps it with student computation, and reduces temporary storage for loss evaluation.
7.1
Local teacher workers and sharded students
Teacher inference and student training have different resource requirements. The teacher performs forward computation; the student also stores optimizer state and executes backward computation. We assign them separate workers and use FSDP to shard student state
[
53
]
.
Student workers send teacher contexts and position information to assigned teacher workers through GPU point-to-point communication. The full-vocabulary path returns teacher logits in bfloat16 (BF16) format. This traffic stays within a node, while student workers use distributed collectives across their own process group. The same local allocation can therefore be repeated across nodes.
Stage-two training uses eight nodes, each with two teacher GPUs and six student GPUs: 16 teacher and 48 student NVIDIA H100 80 GB HBM3 GPUs overall. Training completed in approximately three days (

Discussion
10.1
Speech capability across tasks
Apriel Voice can reason over spoken requests, follow instructions, produce tool calls, and participate in task-oriented conversations, while continuing to process text and images.
The benchmarks measure complementary capabilities. BBA and IFEval characterize different reasoning demands; BFCL tests structured calls; EVA combines service outcomes with conversational experience; and
τ
\tau
-Voice tests completion through speech. Thinking improves several reasoning and workflow scores, while some recognition and function-calling tasks score higher in non-thinking mode. Reasoning-mode selection therefore depends on the task.
10.2
Training and supervision
Interface training learns a projector that connects the frozen speech encoder to the fixed decoder. Task SFT then adapts the projector and backbone for conversation and tool use. Source-dependent teacher supervision supports adaptation on selected speech examples and retention on text replay. Paired text/audio dialogues provide corresponding speech and text contexts for training.
The systems implementation addresses the resulting cost: local teacher workers separate inference from student state, lookahead overlaps teacher and student computation, and fused losses reduce temporary probability storage. Together, these mechanisms support full-vocabulary online supervision at the training scale described in
Tab.
2
. The evaluations assess the combined method; component effects require controlled ablations.
10.3
Optimization behavior
The combined stage-two objective decreases over training (
Figures
8
and
9
). CE and FKL need not move together: CE measures fit to target responses, whereas FKL measures divergence from the frozen teacher on selected contexts. Source composition and supervision weights also affect the aggregate.

Conclusion
Apriel Voice 27B Preview extends a text-and-image backbone to speech, using the same model for reasoning, conversation, and tool-call decisions. Evaluations demonstrate these capabilities through spoken reasoning, instruction following, multilingual translation, service interactions, and complete workflows.
The recipe combines interface learning, broad task SFT, synthetic speech-conditioned dialogues, and source-dependent CE/FKL supervision. Local teacher serving, lookahead, and fused losses support online distillation. A shared real-time API enables deployment and supports integration with voice benchmarks through WebSocket communication.
Limitations
Multilinguality.
Apriel Voice 27B Preview prioritizes English speech understanding, reasoning, and instruction following for real-world English conversational-agent settings.
Multilingual capabilities and evaluations remain limited, with primary assessment through automatic speech translation. English performance does not imply comparable quality across languages; multilingual robustness is uneven and can represent a clear limitation. Enhancing multilingual speech understanding and conversational robustness across diverse language families is a priority for future versions.
Evaluation and comparison.
Internal and public results differ in prompting, language coverage, output modality, reasoning budgets, judging, and task limits. Aggregate scores do not establish paired significance, non-inferiority to the starting backbone, or a controlled ranking against every frontier system. Recognition means describe the evaluated language subsets; public and internal scoring can differ even when the language selection is shared.
Data and attribution.
Synthetic generation and distillation can propagate incorrect targets or teacher predictions. Conversion-fidelity checks can miss errors and do not establish coverage of natural speech variation. The evaluations characterize the combined recipe, with no causal attribution to individual data or supervision choices. Frozen visual components also do not guarantee unchanged image reasoning through an updated decoder. Transfer to other backbone families remains untested.

Appendix A
Synthetic Data Construction Details
The pipeline converts selected user content to speech while preserving the dialogue structure and assistant targets. Each converted dialogue retains a corresponding text version (
Figure
3
).
Selection strategies.
Whole-turn selection synthesizes the complete user message. Instruction-only selection does the same for generative requests without reference material. Question-only selection leaves reference material in text and speaks the question. Content-focused selection speaks material requested for reading or recitation. Multi-span selection speaks several disjoint intervals while retaining intervening text. A configurable override adds whole-turn examples. Extraction validates selected source substrings before constructing the interleaved representation. Malformed selections are retried and rejected if the retry budget is exhausted.
Voice assignment and chunking.
A reference utterance is assigned once per conversation and reused across its turns and chunks. Spoken-form conversion expands written expressions into pronounceable text. Sentence-based chunking respects a duration limit. Contiguous chunks may be joined; disjoint spans retain their position among text. Speaker-aware scheduling and resumable processing preserve the reference assignment during generation.
Conversion fidelity.
Spoken-form judging compares normalized content with its source. Recognition-based judging compares a synthesized chunk’s transcript with the intended speech. Optional turn-level faithfulness checks assess consistency across the complete converted turn.

article.lede: Apriel Voice 27B 预览版以 Gemma 4 26B-A4B 为骨干，两阶段适配语音接口，用同一模型完成语
article.problem: 语音助手不能只做识别：它要理解请求、对上下文推理、维持多轮对话，并通过工具真正把事办完。传统三级级联把 ASR、LLM 与 TTS 拆成不同组件，语音条件模型则把声学特征直接送进推理器。难点在于给一个已经后训练好的多模态解码器加语音入口，同时不丢掉原有的文本与图像能力。
article.method: 两阶段训练：第一阶段冻结骨干，只训练约 4770 万参数的语音投影器，把 Whisper large-v3-turbo 编码器的 1280 维特征经 8 帧堆叠和 SwiGLU 映射进解码器空间，用多语言转写、翻译与续写建立语音接口。第二阶段联合更新投影器与语言骨干（含 MoE 路由），数据混合语音任务、内部合成的语音条件对话、工具交互与文本回放，每个来源独立选择交叉熵、前向 KL 或二者加权；冻结的原始骨干作在线教师，配合本地教师 worker、单批前瞻与融合全词表损失完成蒸馏。推理时教师被移除，语音合成器可独立替换。
article.results: 在 thinking 模式下，模型在 Big Bench Audio 得 98.90、BFCL 得 81.13，τ-Voice 平均任务成功率 65.51%，平均延迟 1.91 秒；EVA 的 EVA-A 与 EVA-X 分别为 51.27% 和 74.13%。识别上 LibriSpeech test-clean/test-other 的 WER 为 2.23 和 5.15，全部识别基准平均 WER 12.61；德、法、西译英平均 BLEU 42.87。第二阶段用 8 个节点、16 张教师 GPU 与 48 张学生 GPU，约 3 天完成 52.6473B token 的训练暴露。
article.why_it_matters: 它表明开源的两阶段语音模型可以把语音理解、推理和工具调用放在同一个骨干上，并在 τ-Voice 上以 65.51% 的成功率和 1.91 秒延迟接近专有系统，同时语音合成可以独立更换。
article.limitations: 论文自述以英语语音理解与对话为主，多语言仅靠自动语音翻译评测，跨语种鲁棒性不均。内部与公开结果在提示、判分、推理预算和任务上限上不一致，聚合分数不构成配对显著性检验；合成数据与蒸馏可能传播错误目标，且没有对单项数据或监督选择做因果消融。冻结视觉塔也不保证图像推理不变——九项图像基准中三项高于 Gemma 基线、六项低于基线。
article.figure_caption_zh: 先学语音接口、再扩展任务能力：第一阶段冻结骨干只训投影器，第二阶段在语音任务、合成对话、工具交互与文本回放上同时更新投影器和骨干，并按来源施加交叉熵、前向 KL 或二者组合的监督。

email_papers.title: CausalWAM: Learning the Causes of Actions in World Action Models
email_papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) learn latent variables from observations and use these to both predict the evolution of the scene and to generate actions. The prediction has to be of the whole scene, whereas only a portion of the scene causes actions. WAMs fitted to demonstrations do not, in general, guarantee that they will generate actions solely from the latent causes of the demonstrated actions (the action-relevant latent variables), as the model could just as well learn to imitate in this way whilst entangling the action-relevant latent variables with the nuisance variables. We therefore separate out what causes action from what prediction depends on. We prove that under a sparsity constraint the latent variables used to generate actions are an invertible function of the action-relevant latent variables alone and the true structure is identified up to a permutation of the latent variables. This requires neither sufficient temporal dependence nor any assumptions on how the unobserved regimes evolve and holds even when the action-relevant latent variables are statistically dependent on the rest. We therefore propose CWAM (Causal WAM), which incorporates the constraint into a pretrained WAM by adding a sparse routing path to its action head, with the world modeling objective remaining unchanged. Experiments on both synthetic data and real-world robots validate the theory as well as showcase the improved efficiency in closed-loop success.

CausalWAM: Learning the Causes of Actions in World Action Models
Juntao Cheng
Affiliation:

Abstract
World action models (WAMs) learn latent variables from observations and use these to both predict the evolution of the scene and to generate actions. The prediction has to be of the whole scene, whereas only a portion of the scene causes actions. WAMs fitted to demonstrations do not, in general, guarantee that they will generate actions solely from the latent causes of the demonstrated actions (the action-relevant latent variables), as the model could just as well learn to imitate in this way whilst entangling the action-relevant latent variables with the nuisance variables. We therefore separate out what causes action from what prediction depends on. We prove that under a sparsity constraint the latent variables used to generate actions are an invertible function of the action-relevant latent variables alone and the true structure is identified up to a permutation of the latent variables. This requires neither sufficient temporal dependence nor any assumptions on how the unobserved regimes evolve and holds even when the action-relevant latent variables are statistically dependent on the rest. We therefore propose CWAM (Causal WAM), which incorporates the constraint into a pretrained WAM by adding a sparse routing path to its action head, with the world modeling objective remaining unchanged. Experiments on both synthetic data and real-world robots validate the theory as well as showcase the improved efficiency in closed-loop success.
1
Introduction
The action a robot performs when stacking a single block atop another depends on the position of both blocks and the fact that the gripper is currently holding the uppermost block. The camera image’s pixels will change significantly if the robot removes the tablecloth or clears away the clutter located behind the table; however, this will have no effect upon the motion itself. WAMs (World Action Models) like Fast-WAM
(
Yuan et al., 2026
)
, and Cosmos 3
(
NVIDIA, 2026
)
are able to extract latent variables from images and can be used to generate actions from those latent variables, while also being capable of generating images of potential subsequent frames. Since prediction has to account for the whole scene, these latent variables also describe the tablecloth and the clutter. We refer to the latent variables that cause the demonstrated actions as action-relevant latent variables, and to the others as nuisance variables.
Fitting the demonstrations well does not in itself guarantee that the WAM is acting from the action-relevant latent variables. For each step of the demonstration we could write

whilst their latent variables differ by an arbitrary invertible transformation. This transformation can mix the action-relevant latent variables with the nuisance ones, so a very flexible action head could generate actions from variables which also contain information about the tablecloth (which doesn’t in fact cause the motion) and still fit the demonstrations equally well.
To make latent variables identifiable, existing works in nonlinear independent component analysis (ICA) introduce auxiliary variables, such as domain or time indices, or exploit temporal dependence
(
Hyvärinen and Morioka, 2016
;
Hyvärinen and Morioka, 2017
;
Hyvärinen et al., 2019
;
Khemakhem et al., 2020
)
. For latent causal processes, identifiability has been established under sufficient temporal dependence
(
Yao et al., 2022
)
and conditions on the latent dynamics
(
Song et al., 2023
)
. Interventions with known targets have also been introduced to pin down the latents
(
Lippe et al., 2022
)
. Many of these assumptions might be violated for demonstrations in complex real-world scenarios such as robotics, where some time steps might be independent, the latent dynamics might not be Markov, and controlled interventions are either prohibitively expensive or simply impossible.
Another line of research constrains the generative process by restricting the function class or enforcing sparsity in the dependency structure
(
Kivva et al., 2022
;
Zheng et al., 2022
;
Lachapelle et al., 2022
)
. Most of these studies, similar to those previously discussed, aim to recover all latent variables, requiring their conditions to hold even for nuisance variables that a robot can disregard. In contrast, results on partial identifiability focus on a subset of latent variables, determined by side information accompanying the data, such as content shared across views
(
von Kügelgen et al., 2021
;
Yao et al., 2024
)
, components invariant across domains
(
Kong et al., 2022
)
, or elements relevant to specific tasks
(
Zheng et al., 2026
)
. For robots learning from demonstrations, the relevant subset consists of the latent causes underlying the demonstrated actions. Since no view, domain, or task label directly specifies this subset, the actions themselves must indicate which latent variables are pertinent. This raises the following question:
From demonstrations alone, can we separate what causes actions from what prediction needs?
In this work, we answer this question with a constraint on the action side that leaves prediction free to use every latent variable. Since each action is generated from only part of the latent state, constraining the number of dependencies between latent variables and action dimensions can separate that part from the rest. Specifically, we prove that, without such a constraint and under nondegeneracy conditions, fitting the demonstrations only ensures that each action dimension of the estimated mechanism depends on at least as many latent variables as the true one (Prop.
1
). We then incorporate a sparsity regularization on the dependency structure between latent state and action variables during estimation. Under the same conditions, the lower bound becomes an equality and the dependency structure is identified up to a permutation of the latent variables (Thm.
1
).
Moreover, we prove that the estimated action-relevant variables under the proposed constraint are an invertible function of the ground-truth latent variables causing the true action (Thm.
2
). The latent causes of the actions are thus identified as a block and are separated from the nuisance variables. The theoretical guarantee relies purely on observational demonstrations, without requiring any interventions, sufficient temporal dependence, or any assumptions about the latent dynamics. The framework also allows dependence between action-relevant latent variables and the nuisance variables (e.g., a tablecloth could be correlated with the positions of the cubes). According to the established theory, we propose CWAM (Causal WAM), which adds a sparse routing path from the visual and task tokens to the action head in Cosmos 3 and applies a token-level surrogate of the constraint to this path (Sec.
4
). In synthetic scenarios, we validate the identifiability claims shown by our theory. On RoboCasa365, LIBERO, and a real Franka R3 robot, the routing path improves aggregate closed-loop success over Cosmos 3 without it, and in most visualized frames its routing mass falls on the object being moved and its target (Sec.
5
).

6
Conclusion
We show how to learn causal actions in WAM from observational decomposition alone. Specifically, we prove that under non-degeneracy conditions and without a sparsity constraint, each action dimension of any mechanism estimated to fit the demonstrations can contain action-irrelevant latent variables. Sparsity regularisation enables identification of the true causes of the actions and the causal structure from latent variables to actions (up to a permutation). The latent variables used to generate the actions are then an invertible function of the latent causes of the actions alone, while the full estimated state continues to describe the entire scene for prediction. Neither of the identification results rely on interventions, temporal structure or supervision. Synthetic experiments are in agreement with the theory and CWAM does in fact assist with task completion in simulation as well as on a real robot. The main limitation is the lack of component-wise identifiability that would pin down the individual latents (which may not be required for separating actions but would be useful for precise interventions). There are many more open problems in WAMs that causality can help to address and this paper represents one of the first steps towards a causal understanding of actions.

article.headline: CWAM：用稀疏路由分离驱动动作的潜变量
article.lede: 世界动作模型要预测整幅场景，但只有一部分潜变量驱动动作。作者用稀疏约束识别这部分变量，并在 Cosmos 3 上验证。
article.problem: 世界动作模型（WAM）从观测中学习潜变量，既用来预测场景演化，也用来生成动作。预测必须覆盖整幅场景，而真正导致动作的只是其中一部分潜变量。仅拟合演示并不保证动作只来自这部分因果潜变量——模型完全可能把桌布、杂物等干扰因素混进动作路径。
article.method: 作者证明：在稀疏约束下，用于生成动作的潜变量是动作相关潜变量的可逆函数，状态到动作的依赖结构在潜变量置换意义下可识别，且不要求时间依赖或干预数据。据此提出 CWAM：保留 Cosmos 3 原有的联合整流流训练与世界建模目标不变，向动作头加一条稀疏路由路径，用 token 级稀疏损失把路由质量压到少量干净上下文 token 上。
article.results: 在 n=20 个潜变量、|I_A|=4 个驱动动作的合成设置中，CWAM 稀疏选块的相关 R² 为 0.9957±0.0014，干扰超额 Δ_nuis 为 0.039±0.093，接近零；RoboCasa365 的 17 个任务上宏观成功率从 0.24 升到 0.43（13 个任务提升），LIBERO 四个 suite 均优于匹配基线，真实 Franka 堆叠任务多数试验成功而基线不到一半。在成功率最高的 4 个 RoboCasa365 任务上，仅保留路由 token 平均成功率 60.3%，随机等量 token 只有 24.5%。
article.why_it_matters: 把“预测整幅场景所需的潜变量”与“真正驱动动作的潜变量”分开，意味着动作头可以更紧凑、更可审计，也更有希望在演示分布之外保持正确。论文为 WAM 的因果理解提供了一个可检验的理论起点。
article.limitations: 理论依赖非退化条件（每个动作维度的雅可比行需张成真实父坐标，并满足避免抵消的包含条件），且只给出块级可识别性，无法确定单个潜变量；实验上 RoboCasa365 有 4 个任务成功率下降或持平，部分帧的路由权重也分散到机械臂和墙壁。
article.figure_caption_zh: 动作只依赖潜状态中的一个块；CWAM 在 Cosmos 3 上把该块的估计经稀疏路由送到动作头，同时保留世界建模的稠密路径，即图中灰色虚线。

(a) In the world action process {eq:dgp} this block is $s_{t, }$, and the learner $( f, )$ estimates it from observations as the compact state $ $. (b) CWAM keeps the joint rectified-flow training of Cosmos~3 and adds a sparse router over clean context tokens, whose top-$k$ routed tokens form $ $. page_papers.title: When Steering Shifts Discourse: Identifying and Intervening on Discourse-Level Changes due to Activation Steering in LLMs
page_papers.abstract: Activation steering is an inference-time technique used to control or modify the behavior, tone, or safety properties of a large language model (LLM) without retraining the model's weights or editing its input prompt, but simply by adding a vector to its residual-stream activations. However, activation steering also changes the generated text in unintended ways, unrelated to intended behavior change, that are not well understood. Prior work has measured these changes only through coarse signals such as perplexity. In this work, we show that steering systematically produces significant changes in discourse dimensions of the generated text, such as its formality, use of evidence, and ambiguity. We present a way of countering this by adding a second, complementary vector that targets the affected discourse dimension. This intervention restores about 78% of the unintended discourse changes while preserving the intended steering behavior in about 93% of the generations.
page_papers.content:
When Steering Shifts Discourse: Identifying and Intervening on Discourse-Level Changes due to Activation Steering in LLMs
Shivam Adarsh   Hetianyu Huang   Lau Safin
Affiliation:
Maria Maistro   Christina Lioma
Affiliation:
University of Copenhagen
Affiliation:
{shad, mm, c.lioma}@di.ku.dk
Abstract
Activation steering is an inference-time technique used to control or modify the behavior, tone, or safety properties of a large language model (LLM) without retraining the model’s weights or editing its input prompt, but simply by adding a vector to its residual-stream activations. However, activation steering also changes the generated text in unintended ways, unrelated to intended behavior change, that are not well understood. Prior work has measured these changes only through coarse signals such as perplexity. In this work, we show that steering systematically produces significant changes in discourse dimensions of the generated text, such as its formality, use of evidence, and ambiguity. We present a way of countering this by adding a second, complementary vector that targets the affected discourse dimension. This intervention restores about
78
%
78\%
of the unintended discourse changes while preserving the intended steering behavior in about
93
%
93\%
of the generations
1
1
1
We will release our code upon acceptance.
.
1
Introduction
When using Large Language Models (LLMs), one may wish to control their behavior at inference time, e.g., to refuse unsafe requests, stay honest, or avoid sycophancy. Activation steering (AS) is a lightweight way to do this by adding a vector corresponding to the target behavior into the LLM’s activations (the residual stream)
2
2
2
In the rest of the paper, ‘residual stream’ refers to the activations after the MLP layer, unless stated otherwise.
without updating any weights
(
Rimsky et al., 2024
;
Turner et al., 2023
;
Subramani et al., 2022
)
.
However, AS can also introduce other changes in the output text, often called side-effects, such as reduced coherence or increased repetition
(
Herbster et al., 2026
;
Sprejer et al., 2026
;
Bhalla et al., 2024
;
Braun et al., 2026
)
. These unintended effects are generally detected through a single perplexity or coherence score
(
Herbster et al., 2026
;
Turner et al., 2023
)
, which reflects the drop in quality of the output but not the specific text aspects affected. Some methods exist for limiting these side-effects by keeping the steered output close to the unsteered model
(
Stickland et al., 2024
)
, calibrating or gating how much AS is applied
(
Vogels et al., 2026
;
Hedström et al., 2025
;
Lee et al., 2025
)
, or building the AS direction from sparser features
(
He et al., 2025
)
. However, these methods
tend to not identify the specific text properties affected by AS.
In this work, we explore key discourse changes that occur when AS is applied to an LLM, such as how formal the generated text is or how it is organized. We then test how these changes can be restored without losing the intended steering behavior (Fig.
1
). We contribute: (i) a fine-grained, human-validated categorisation of 15 discourse dimensions that change during AS; and (ii) a targeted intervention that restores an affected discourse dimension toward its unsteered level while preserving steerability.
Across 3 LLMs, 11 datasets, and 15 discourse dimensions, scored by an LLM judge and validated against a human annotator, we find a statistically significant discourse shift in the generated text under steering. Our intervention on 6 of the discourse dimensions affected by AS shows that we can restore about
78
%
78\%
of these unintended discourse shifts while preserving the intended steering behavior in roughly
93
%
93\%
of the generations.
Figure 1:
Example where steering changes the model’s behavior as intended, but causes an unintended loss of reasoning depth. Our intervention keeps the steered behavior while restoring reasoning depth (
green
).
2
Related Work
Activation Steering
can control the behavior of an LLM at inference time by adding a contrastive direction to its residual stream
(
Rimsky et al., 2024
;
Turner et al., 2023
;
Subramani et al., 2022
)
. However, the reliability of AS to change behavior varies widely across models, datasets, and inputs
(
Tan et al., 2024
)
, and its effect can be non-monotonic, with too little steering bringing no change in behavior and too much leading to degenerate outputs
(
Taimeskhanov et al., 2026
)
. Beyond the target behavior, steering can unintentionally degrade the coherence of the output
(
Herbster et al., 2026
;
Sprejer et al., 2026
;
Bhalla et al., 2024
)
, harm unrelated capabilities
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
and introduce repetition and hallucinations
(
Braun et al., 2026
)
. Prior work approximates the measurement of these issues in output quality through either perplexity
(
Turner et al., 2023
;
Vogels et al., 2026
)
or a coherence score
(
Herbster et al., 2026
;
Sprejer et al., 2026
;
Bhalla et al., 2024
)
. However, these scores register an overall drop in quality but do not reflect which linguistic dimensions of the text are affected. We do this by studying which discourse aspects of the generated output are affected by steering.
To reduce the unintended changes to output quality due to activation steering, prior works have adopted multiple strategies.
Stickland et al. (2024)
fine-tune the model so its steered and unsteered outputs stay close on benign inputs.
Vogels et al. (2026)
and
Hedström et al. (2025)
adapt the steering strength to the input, the latter abstaining when it cannot steer confidently.
Lee et al. (2025)
apply steering only to targeted prompts via a condition vector, and
He et al. (2025)
construct the steering direction from sparse features. However, these works do not pinpoint the individual dimension that steering changes. In this work, we identify several discourse dimensions that are unintentionally affected and show that intervening on them directly can restore them toward their unsteered levels without undoing the intended steering behavior.
Discourse aspects of text
, such as how formal or technical the wording is, how the text is organized, and how it conveys stance, have been studied in LLM output, but not by a very large body of work.
Nieth et al. (2026)
score LLM outputs on a fixed set of stylistic dimensions, and
Harel-Canada et al. (2024)
prompt a language model to rate outputs on fine-grained, human-interpretable dimensions such as psychological depth. In this work, we build discourse-based dimensions to study unintended effects of activation steering, and specifically the linguistic properties that change under steering regardless of the intended behavior change of the steering. We then restore such discourse dimensions without tampering with the steered behavior of the LLM.
3
Methodology
3.1
Activation Steering
To study how AS changes discourse, we use datasets from a text generation task for binary-choice questions, similarly to
Tan et al. (2024)
;
Rimsky et al. (2024)
;
Turner et al. (2023)

To compare how the generation from an LLM differs under AS, we return first an unsteered generation with no AS, and then steered generations for both options. We use Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA)
(

To construct the behavior vector, we run the LLM on each question concatenated with its positive and negative option separately, and extract the residual stream activations at the last prompt token. 3. Scaling Dimension Annotations:

Conclusion
We studied the unintended changes to the quality of the text generated by an LLM when applying activation steering to change the behavior of the LLM. While this drop in text quality under steering was observed before, ours is the first work to examine it’s key discourse aspects. Using an LLM judge and a human annotator, we detected 15 discourse dimensions that unintentionally change under steering, across models and datasets. Steered outputs become more ambiguous and contradictory, less formal, offer less evidence, and use less terminology. All of these effects are unintentional. To counter these effects, we intervened on 6 discourse dimensions by extracting a vector per dimension and adding/subtracting it alongside the behavior steering. Our intervention was experimentally found to be 78% successful, while preserving the intended steering behavior 93% of the time.
7
Limitations
We note several limitations of our study. First, we intervene only on samples where steering drives the dimension score from one extreme to the other. In practice these samples are not known in advance, so identifying where a correction is needed would require an additional detection step. Second, our intervention corrects a side-effect of steering by applying more steering, adding a second vector to the residual stream. It may therefore share some of the difficulties of steering itself, such as sensitivity to oversteering. Third, we restore one discourse dimension at a time. We find that correcting one dimension does not consistently disturb correlated ones, but we do not jointly restore multiple dimensions. Fourth, our study covers only contrastive activation steering, and our findings may not transfer to other steering variants. Finally, our analysis relies on an LLM judge to score discourse dimensions. Although we validate these scores against human annotations, the results still depend on the judgments of an LLM. Running it at scale carries a computational cost, though this cost is incurred once and the extracted vectors can be reused.
8
Ethical Considerations
This work is primarily aimed at understanding how activation steering changes the discourse dimensions of the generated text, and at restoring those dimensions while preserving the intended steering behavior. We do not foresee direct negative societal impacts from this study. However, the ability to control discourse dimensions is dual-use. It can be used to add qualities such as reasoning depth and evidence to a model’s outputs, but also to remove them. All datasets used are publicly available and do not contain personally identifiable information.

Dimension
Description
Alternative options
Offers a course of action different from the one requested or proposed.
Ambiguity
Can be read in more than one way, with no clear intended meaning.
Claim supported by evidence
Makes claims backed by facts, named sources, or external authority.
Contextualization
Guides the reader on how to interpret and situate what is being said.
Contradiction
Contains two or more propositions that cannot all be true at once.
Critical perspective
Raises a counter-position, limitation, or challenge, pushing back on the premise, its own claim, or a rival view.
Dialogic approach
Leaves room for other viewpoints rather than asserting a single right answer.
Emotional tone
Expresses feeling, such as joy, worry, frustration, enthusiasm, sympathy, or fear.
Ethical stance
Judges whether a claim or behavior is morally right or wrong; a higher score indicates a stronger stance.
Evaluative language
Judges something as good or bad rather than merely describing it, including intensifiers (
very
,
completely
,
never
,
always
,
slightly
) that scale the evaluation up or down.
Formality
Reads like professional writing rather than casual, everyday speech.
Hedging
Signals uncertainty about what is being said, through qualifying language or the acknowledgement of opposing views.
Hypothetical
Imagines a scenario not present in the prompt; a higher score reflects more or more detailed scenarios.
Informational density
Amount of information packed into the text, approximated by the proportion of content-bearing words.
Metaphors
Uses words in a non-literal, figurative sense.
Neutrality
Presents information without taking a side on the question posed; a higher score indicates no stance taken.
Personalisation
Addresses the reader as an individual, tailoring or referencing their situation.
Persuasion
Guides the reader toward a stance or action rather than merely informing them.
Prescriptiveness
Commands or instructs the reader on what to do or what the correct course of action is, rather than merely informing or guiding.
Presupposition
Treats propositions as already true and agreed upon without stating them outright, reflecting the text’s prior assumptions.
Prioritization
Degree to which ordering conveys emphasis, i.e. how much meaning or emphasis changes if the text is reordered.
Reasoning depth
Explains
why
, connecting a conclusion to its reasons through multiple inferential steps.
Repetition
Repeats the same wording or content without adding new information.
Self-referentiality
Refers to itself as a speaker or system, including its nature, capabilities, role, or limits.
Terminology use
Frequency of domain-specific or technical vocabulary.
Use of examples
Supplies concrete instances to illustrate what is meant.

Oversteering
: Once a generation reaches its unsteered score we stop increasing

k
for that generation, because pushing the correction further can overshoot the target and lower the score. Fig.

illustrates this on Qwen, using the same-layer (S) method in the add direction. Each panel is one intervened dimension, and at every correction strength

Beyond the point where a generation first reaches its target, however, further correction can push it past the target rather than holding it there, and some generations that had reached score 2 fall back to score 1. Correlations
. Since some dimensions, such as reasoning depth and contextualization, are implicitly related to the length of the output, we check whether the LLM-judge scores track word count. Fig.
11
reports the Kendall’s

correlation between word count and dimension score, per dimension and model. The correlations are moderate, reaching up to about 0.6, so length explains part but not all of the score. Because we intervene on one dimension at a time, we also check whether correcting one dimension moves other, correlated dimensions. Fig.
12
and Fig.

k

Discourse-Behavior Similarity
: To understand why steering changes these discourse dimensions, we measure how aligned the behavior vector and the discourse vectors are across layers. Fig.
14
shows the cosine similarity between the behavior vector and the discourse vectors at each layer, averaged across the discourse dimensions, with one line per behavior (corr. dataset). At the middle layers, where we apply our interventions, the similarity is close to zero, so the behavior and discourse directions are largely independent there and can be steered without strongly affecting one another. Toward the later layers, however, the similarity grows in magnitude, either positive or negative depending on the behavior, which entangles the discourse directions with the behavior direction. This growing alignment offers a partial explanation for why steering a behavior also shifts discourse dimensions.
