A calendar entry for an upcoming trip may prompt checking a database for needed supplies and a file for purchase authorization.
These facts can justify a reminder without permitting a purchase.
Retrieved evidence must guide the intervention’s timing, inform its content, and establish the authorized scope.
Benchmarks differ in how agents obtain evidence for proactive decisions.
Some provide user activity directly
(
Lu et al., 2024
;
Tang et al., 2026
)
.
Such observations may signal a need without establishing a remedy or permission to act.
PROBE supports SQL and semantic document retrieval
(
Pasternak et al., 2025
)
, while interactive benchmarks support additional tool use
(
Oh et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026
)
.
Evaluating these capabilities requires linking retrieved evidence to human verdicts on the resulting interventions.
Detecting a relevant need does not by itself make an intervention acceptable. An intervention may still fail because it is mistimed, insufficient, excessive, irrelevant, or unsupported by evidence. Existing benchmarks primarily rely on scalable automated metrics: ProAgentBench evaluates intervention prediction and response similarity
(
Tang et al., 2026
)
, while ProactiveBench uses a reward model trained on human acceptance labels
(
Lu et al., 2024
)
. Human studies have examined how users perceive proactive assistance
(
Oh et al., 2026
)
, but existing benchmarks provide limited human diagnosis of why individual model responses are accepted or rejected.

HALO combines structured database querying and unstructured file retrieval with fine-grained human evaluation.
HALO-Arena
models 4 proactive need types: Dependency, Blockage, Risk, and Opportunity.
It spans 10 everyday domains and 50 personal environments.
Operational applications expose evolving events, while separate databases and text files provide structured and unstructured evidence.
Addressing a need requires the agent to retrieve relevant evidence and then judge whether assistance is warranted, when to act, and how far to intervene.
At each evaluation checkpoint, agents receive an observed event prefix and may retrieve evidence over multiple rounds before returning 1 executable response or no action.
On HALO-Arena, we construct
HALO-8K
, comprising 8,000 responses from 10 models across 400 scenarios, annotated by 20 experts. Annotators assign action levels and acceptability verdicts, with human diagnosis of rejections covering timing, intensity, and other issues such as unsupported evidence, irrelevance, and factual contradiction. Verdicts on no-action responses distinguish erroneous Inaction from warranted restraint. Reasoning tokens and retrieval rounds quantify agent effort.
Our central finding is that
over-proactivity is the dominant observed failure mode
: Premature timing or Excessive intensity accounts for 61.20% of rejected responses. Proprietary and open-source models peak at 72.88% and 56.63% acceptability. Further analysis yields 3 complementary findings.
(1) Restraint contributes to acceptability:
gains in accepted action can be outweighed by losses in warranted restraint.
(2) Evidence acquisition accompanies better help:
among reminders, local content access is associated with higher acceptability and lower Insufficient diagnosis rates.
(3) Timing alone is not enough:
among well-timed rejections, reminders tend to be insufficient and executions excessive. These findings support granular evaluation of proactive assistance.
Our contributions are as follows:
•
We introduce
HALO-Arena
, an executable benchmark spanning 4 proactive need types and 10 everyday domains, with evidence retrieval informing proactive decisions.
•
We construct
HALO-8K
: 8,000 responses across 400 scenarios, annotated by experts for action level, verdicts, and human diagnosis.
•
We evaluate 10 models, revealing tradeoffs among intervention, restraint, timing, intensity, and retrieval effort.

HALO-Arena
3.1.1
Overview
Applications.
HALO-Arena combines email, calendar, chat, contacts, and wallet apps with SQLite databases and text files.
Agents use 29 interaction commands for evidence retrieval and 19 action commands for attention, preparation, and execution.
Appendix
B
lists the apps and commands by category.
Domains.
The 10 domains are education and learning, work and professional life, home and household management, family and caregiving, health and wellbeing, travel and mobility, personal finance and consumer life, community and civic life, social and cultural life, and recreation (sports and hobbies).
Each domain has 5 instances, each representing a different person, yielding 50 distinct personal environments.
Proactive needs.
We consider 4 need types.
Dependency
is a missing prerequisite for a future activity.
Blockage
occurs when an ongoing activity cannot continue.
Risk
is a possible adverse outcome that has not yet occurred.
Opportunity
is an optional benefit whose omission causes no failure or loss.
Each environment contains 2 scenarios per need type, yielding 8 scenarios.
As shown in Figure

, HALO-Arena provides executable environments for agent actions, with 400 designed scenarios.

3.2.2
Annotation Protocol
20 annotators provide 1 verdict per response, keeping each scenario’s annotator fixed across models.
Human verdicts and diagnosis use the event prefix, retrieved evidence, response, and execution result.
Appendix
E
describes annotator preparation.
Action levels.
Annotators confirm or correct the command-based action level pre-filled by the interface.
L0 Observation
observes or retrieves information without initiating an intervention.
L1 Attention
draws the user’s attention to relevant information or needs without carrying out the underlying task.
L2 Preparation
prepares an intervention or organizes internal information for later use without creating an external commitment.
L3 Execution
carries out an intervention that changes the user’s active commitments or creates external effects.
Higher levels do not imply better assistance.
Human Verdict and Diagnosis.
Annotators first give an acceptability verdict on whether a response provides grounded, useful help with appropriate timing and scope, accepting L0 when restraint is warranted.
Acceptability is the proportion of accepted responses. These automatically receive Appropriate timing and intensity.
Rejected L0 responses receive the human diagnosis
Inaction
for missing warranted help, without further diagnostic labels.
For rejected L1–L3 responses, separate questions assess timing and intensity.
Premature
and
Belated
indicate intervention before and after its useful window, respectively.
Insufficient
indicates inadequate help, while
Excessive
indicates intervention beyond supported scope or authority.
Appropriate denotes suitable timing or proportionate intensity.
Annotators may also flag Other Issues, detailed in Appendix
G
.
Resource Consumption.
For each annotated response, we sum reasoning tokens across retained calls and count completed retrieval rounds.

4.2
Main Results
4.2.1
Model Comparison
Table
1
compares acceptability, action levels, recorded consumption, and timing and intensity errors on the same 800 responses per model.
Acceptability.
Scores range from 30.38% for GPT-OSS-20B to 72.88% for Gemini3.8-Flash, a 42.50-point gap.
DeepSeekV4-Pro leads open-source models with 56.63% acceptability.
The score range reflects substantial variation in acceptability under the same annotation protocol, while even the strongest model leaves over 25% of responses unacceptable.
Proprietary models average 63.08%, versus 47.55% for open-source models, a 15.53-point gap.
These means also conceal uneven performance within each group.
The 3 strongest open-source models lie within 2.50 points of each other, whereas the full group spans 26.25 points.
Their lower mean thus reflects a weak tail as well as a gap at the top.
The groups overlap: DeepSeekV4-Pro exceeds both Gemini3.1-Pro and GPT5.6-Luna, so group membership provides an incomplete account of individual quality.
These scores cover completed, human-annotated responses under the recorded inference settings, excluding transport and parsing failures.
Action choices.
Attention (L1) is the most frequent level for every model, accounting for 69.20% of all responses.
L1 exceeds 50% of responses in 9 models and ranges from 48.00% for Claude-Opus5.5 to 87.00% for GPT5.6-Luna.
Preparation (L2) remains rare at 4.18%, while execution (L3) accounts for 16.09%.
This concentration makes the timing and usefulness of L1 responses central to the aggregate result.
At the group level, L3 shares are almost identical at about 16.1%, despite the 15.53-point acceptability gap.
The main observed policy difference lies in observation and attention: proprietary models choose L0 about 2 times as often, while open-source models choose L1 more often.
Execution frequency alone cannot explain the observed acceptability gap.
Resource Consumption.
Open-source models use fewer retrieval rounds at similar mean reasoning usage.
They average 4.77k reasoning tokens and 1.21 retrieval rounds per response, compared with 5.53k and 2.55 for proprietary models.
The reasoning-token means differ by about 14%, whereas open-source models use about 53% fewer retrieval rounds.
Lower recorded retrieval use accompanies lower acceptability, so resource savings should be assessed alongside the quality of the resulting responses.
Within the proprietary group, second-ranked Claude-Opus5.5 uses about 23% of the recorded reasoning tokens of the leading Gemini3.8-Flash.
Strong performance thus occurs at different levels of recorded consumption.
These profiles support comparing quality and resource use jointly under the recorded inference settings and provider accounting conventions.

4.2.3
Error Analysis
We identify over-proactivity as Premature timing or Excessive intensity, counting each response once when either diagnosis applies.
As shown in Figure
3
, it occurs in 2,188 of 3,575 rejected responses (61.20%).
Model-wise shares range from 44.23% to 79.66%, exceeding 50% of rejections in 6 of 10 models.
Across all responses, Premature timing is almost 3 times as common as Belated timing, while Excessive intensity is about 2 times as common as Insufficient.
These 2 asymmetries indicate more frequent early or excessive intervention.
This pattern holds across all 4 proactive need types and all 10 domains, with over-proactivity accounting for more than 50% of rejections in each category.
The 2 highest-acceptability models also have the lowest Premature and Excessive rates, associating stronger overall performance with fewer premature or excessive interventions.
Inaction alone gives a different picture: Qwen3.8-27B records 0% Inaction but reaches only 55.13% acceptability and chooses L0 on just 0.38% of responses.
Because Inaction applies only to rejected L0 responses and is reported over all responses, a policy that rarely chooses observation has few opportunities to incur this error.
Action-level shares therefore provide essential context for interpreting individual error rates.
Over-proactivity is the dominant failure mode of proactive agents.

Further Pattern Analysis
We examine action and restraint, need-dependent strategies, evidence acquisition, and residual failures despite appropriate timing.
5.1
Action and Restraint
We compare intervention choices and acceptability at shared checkpoints.
More frequent intervention can accompany lower acceptability when warranted restraint losses outweigh accepted action gains.
Figure 4:
Paired intervention rates and acceptability.
Figure
4
compares Qwen3.5-9B to Qwen3.8-27B at 201 shared checkpoints and Gemini3.8-Flash to Gemini3.1-Pro at 623.
Pairs match instance, scenario, event, and annotator without filtering verdicts.
Intervention frequency, the L1–L3 share, rises by 27.36 and 28.89 points, respectively, yet acceptability rises by 14.43 points for Qwen and falls by 14.77 for Gemini.
The Gemini loss combines a 5.94-point gain from accepted interventions with a 20.71-point decline from accepted L0.
Both changes use all matched responses as their denominator and sum to the acceptability change, so the intervention gain reflects a frequency change, not conditional success.
The error changes clarify the different outcomes: Qwen reduces Inaction-or-Insufficient by 17.91 points while increasing Premature-or-Excessive by 5.97, whereas Gemini increases the latter by 21.51.
Matching fixes the observed prefix and annotator, but configurations and retrieved evidence can differ, with Qwen’s version and parameter count changing together.
The comparisons therefore do not isolate the causal effect of intervening more.
Restraint can also follow substantial inspection: Flash’s 182 accepted L0 responses average 16.74 commands, versus 14.65 for 401 accepted interventions.
These groups cover different checkpoints, but show that L0 records final commitment rather than inspection effort.
5.2
Needs and Strategies
Similar acceptability across need types can mask different balances of accepted intervention and warranted restraint. Figure
5
contrasts Opportunity and Dependency. Despite similar acceptability (55.85% vs. 55.05%), models are more likely to refrain from intervention for Opportunity: L0 accounts for 13.60% of Opportunity responses, compared with 7.20% for Dependency. Accordingly, accepted L0 contributes 10.65 points to Opportunity acceptability and 5.25 points to Dependency acceptability, while accepted interventions contribute 45.20 and 49.80 points, respectively.
All 10 models choose L0 more often for Opportunity than Dependency, although the size of this difference varies substantially. Gemini3.8-Flash chooses L0 for 39.00% of Opportunity responses and 17.00% of Dependency responses, whereas Qwen3.8-27B chooses L0 for 0.50% and 0.00%, respectively. These differences do not imply fixed action requirements for each need type: need labels characterize entire scenarios, while the appropriate action depends on the checkpoint and its available evidence. Paired examples clarify the role of content and permission.
At a shared household checkpoint, Gemini3.8-Flash’s accepted L1 supplies the no-pry instruction and a concrete dispatch route.

6
Conclusion
HALO evaluates proactive assistance through executable environments, human verdicts, and human diagnosis.
HALO-8K contains 8,000 human-annotated responses from 10 models across 400 scenarios and 2,160 checkpoints.
Over-proactivity dominates the observed rejections.
Further analyses distinguish useful action from warranted restraint, relate evidence acquisition to acceptability, and identify contrasting intensity errors among well-timed rejections.
These patterns expose calibration problems obscured by aggregate acceptability.
HALO-Arena provides operational applications and separate structured and unstructured evidence stores.
Repeated retrieval lets an agent inspect relevant evidence before deciding whether to notify, prepare, execute, or remain silent.
Acceptability peaks at 72.88% for proprietary and 56.63% for open-source models.
HALO records retrieved evidence and executed commands, enabling comparison of human verdicts and diagnosis for responses produced at identical checkpoints.
The practical targets differ: timely reminders need enough grounded detail to be useful, while execution must respect the scope of available permission.
These results motivate better evidence gathering and response calibration. More frequent action or higher commitment alone does not establish better assistance.
Systems should be compared jointly on acceptable action, warranted restraint, residual intensity errors, and inspection effort.
Limitations
Real-world validity.
HALO uses constructed scenarios and simulated apps to study proactive decisions under controlled conditions.
Its designed need distribution does not estimate how often those needs or failure modes occur in everyday use.
Checkpoint evaluation also omits users’ responses and the cumulative effects of repeated interventions, so performance may not transfer directly to sustained deployment.
Human personalization.
Human verdicts depend on preferences for initiative, useful detail, and commitment.
Shared criteria ground judgments in personal context and authority, but borderline responses can be useful to some users and intrusive to others.
The annotators’ broadly similar backgrounds further limit the preferences represented, so aggregate acceptability should not be treated as a universal user preference.
Evaluation granularity.
Action levels group interventions by commitment, but actions at the same level can differ in reversibility and user burden.
Human verdicts and diagnostic labels identify acceptable help and common failures without ranking acceptable alternatives by usefulness.
Consequently, aggregate acceptability does not capture the full tradeoff between benefit, burden, and intervention risk.

Appendix I
Prompts
We provide prompt templates.
I.1
Agent Prompt
You are a proactive personal Agent in a simulated environment.
At this checkpoint, decide whether to keep observing, inspect local information,
or proactively help. Judge only the observed Event prefix; checkpoints are
independent, so no earlier Agent behavior is part of the state. Use only observed
Events and inspection results. Do not infer future Events or invent records.
Intervene only when it is useful now. Choose an intervention that is effective
for the current need, supported by the available evidence, and safe. This
judgment is internal and must not be described in the JSON.
Events may reveal the need without containing every fact required for a good
response. When a possible intervention depends on a qualification, prior
record, identifier, procedure, constraint, preference, inventory fact, or safe
next step, inspect the local SQLite database and/or TXT Files before responding.
Do not assume that communications and calendar entries are the complete source
of truth, and do not invent a missing detail instead of retrieving it.
Use assistant.notify_user when a grounded message to the Instance user would
provide useful help now. Explain the relevant finding or concrete next step;
merely restating Events or giving generic advice is insufficient. The message
does not obtain a user reply or approval, or carry out the operations it
suggests. Never claim to have completed an operation that was not performed.
The time field of the newest observed Event is the current simulation time. The
runner supplies operation timestamps for Action commands whose signatures omit
them. App record timestamps and Calendar business times do not replace the
Event time. Ignore the real wall-clock date and any model training date; an
Event is not "in the past" merely because its absolute date precedes the real
date outside this episode.
Return one compact JSON object in exactly one of these forms:
{
"decision": "inspect",
"content": [{"app":"...","function":"...","parameter":...}]
}
or
{
"decision": "final",
"content": null | {"app":"...","function":"...","parameter":...}
}
Rules:
- inspect: content must be one non-empty list of private information-gathering
commands from the Inspect commands below. The runner executes these commands
and returns their results at the next round. You may repeat retrieval as often
as the evidence requires; there is no fixed retrieval limit.
- final: content must be null for no action or exactly one intended command
from the Action commands below. The command is executed once at the isolated
checkpoint to verify its result. Never return multiple final
commands or a standalone text response.
- Null final content applies only to this checkpoint.
Instance context:
<<INSTANCE>>
Observed Events through the current checkpoint:
<<EVENTS>>
Inspection results from this checkpoint:
<<TOOL_RESULTS>>
Agent-facing App surface:
<<TOOLS>>

I.2.1
Instance Creator
You create base Instances for a proactive-agent benchmark.
Given a broad Domain, define one coherent person and a concrete part of that
person’s life. The Instance should be narrower than the Domain while supporting
eight meaningfully different Scenarios across several recurring activities.
Create stable background state, not a proactive need.
Keep the setting understandable to a general reader and valid throughout
calendar year <<BENCHMARK_YEAR>>. Make it materially different from existing
Instances in role, responsibilities, workflows, and record design.
Return raw JSON only, without Markdown or code fences. Return one JSON object
with exactly these fields:
1. instance_id: copy the assigned ID.
2. instance_description: roughly 100 words total, written as four concise,

article.headline: 主动智能体评测：过度主动是主要失败模式
article.lede: HALO 用可执行个人环境加 20 位专家标注的 8000 条响应评测主动智能体，发现被拒回答中 61.20% 源于过早
article.problem: 主动智能体要在没有明确请求时自行判断是否该帮、何时帮、帮到什么程度，但现有评测多依赖自动分数或二元判定，难以说明一条回答为何被接受或被拒。检测到需求并不等于干预可接受：回答可能因为时机不对、力度不足或过度、内容无关、缺乏证据支撑而失败，而这些维度此前没有被逐条做人工诊断。
article.method: 作者构建 HALO-Arena，覆盖 Dependency、Blockage、Risk、Opportunity 四类主动需求、10 个日常领域和 50 个个人环境，共 400 个可执行场景；智能体需先用 SQL 查询或文本文件检索证据，再决定是否行动以及行动层级（L0 观察、L1 提醒、L2 准备、L3 执行）。在此基础上构建 HALO-8K：从 10 个模型在 2160 个检查点上的回答中采样 8000 条，由 20 位标注者给出可接受性判定，并对被拒回答分别诊断时机（过早、过晚）与力度（不足、过度），同时记录推理 token 与检索轮数。
article.results: 可接受性从 GPT-OSS-20B 的 30.38% 到 Gemini3.8-Flash 的 72.88%，相差 42.50 个百分点；开源模型最高为 DeepSeekV4-Pro 的 56.63%，专有模型平均 63.08% 对开源 47.55%。核心发现是过度主动占主导：过早或过度合计占 3575 条被拒回答中的 2188 条（61.20%），10 个模型中的 6 个该比例超过 50%。检索轮数与可接受性正相关（r=0.885，ρ=0.830）；在 5536 条 L1 回答中，获取到本地内容的可接受性为 59.0%，未获取为 40.8%，不足率分别为 5.2% 和 15.5%。在时机正确的被拒干预中，623 条 L1 有 52.81% 属力度不足，312 条 L3 有 76.28% 属过度。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「帮不帮」的评测拆成可接受行动、合理克制、时机、力度与检索代价几个可分别观察的量，说明更频繁行动或更高承诺层级本身并不等于更好的帮助，为主动智能体的校准提供了可诊断的评测口径。
article.limitations: 场景与应用均为构造和模拟，设计的需求分布不能反映真实使用中各类需求与失败模式的出现频率；检查点式评测不包含用户回应与重复干预的累积效应，因此结论未必迁移到长期部署。人工判定依赖标注者的偏好，且标注者背景相近，聚合可接受性不应被视为普遍用户偏好；同一行动层级内不同动作的可逆性与用户负担差异也未被区分。
article.figure_caption_zh: HALO 总览：HALO-Arena 提供个人应用与本地证据，智能体检索证据后决定是否、何时以及多大程度介入，HALO-8K 记录人工判定、时机与力度诊断及资源消耗；圈出的选项示例一次过早且过度的 L3 干预。

figure.caption: Overview of HALO. HALO-Arena supplies personal apps and local evidence. Agents retrieve evidence and decide whether, when, and how far to intervene. HALO-8K records human verdicts, timing and intensity diagnosis, and resource consumption. The circled choices illustrate a premature and excessive L3 intervention.

page_papers.title: CaPtain: A Pipeline for Post-Training Code-as-Policy Robot Agents
page_papers.abstract: Across coding, web, and tool-use tasks, language-model agents are now routinely trained with the same recipe: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the interface, then multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) to master it. Code-as-policy (CaP) casts robot manipulation in the same form, as the policy writes code against robot APIs and reads back the results, so the same recipe should apply. Yet existing CaP agents sidestep training: they either prompt closed frontier models or delegate manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) and high-level skills, while small open vision-language models (VLMs) fail outright. We present CaPtain, an open post-training pipeline that turns a small open VLM into a capable CaP agent, with no VLA, frontier model, or privileged state at test time. CaPtain trains and deploys the policy inside CaPtain-Harness, which exposes low-level perception, geometry, and guarded-motion primitives across simulation and real hardware. We first align the base model via SFT on synthetic trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra, then apply multi-turn RL. Multi-turn RL must credit tens of agent requests, whose physical effects often surface turns later, from a single end-of-episode outcome. We therefore introduce a physical critic that reads privileged simulator state, never seen by the policy, and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success. Starting from Qwen3.5-4B (0% zero-shot), CaPtain-4B reaches 55.4% held-out LIBERO success after SFT and 73.8% after RL. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 78.5%, surpassing several frontier-model agents, and its RL gains persist across three perturbation suites (+17.6 to +21.2 points). Without target-domain training, it attains 83.3% on SimplerEnv WidowX, exceeds frontier models on CaP-Bench, and runs on a real robot after simulation-only adaptation. We release all code, data, and model weights.

Abstract
Across coding, web, and tool-use tasks, language-model agents are now routinely trained with the same recipe: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the interface, then multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) to master it.
Code-as-policy (CaP) puts robot manipulation in the same form, as the policy writes code against robot APIs and reads back the results, so the same recipe should apply.
Yet, existing CaP agents sidestep training: they either prompt closed frontier models or delegate manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) and high-level skills, while small open vision-language models (VLMs) fail outright.
We present CaPtain, an open post-training pipeline that brings this recipe to CaP and turns a small open VLM into a capable CaP agent, with no VLA, frontier model, or privileged state at test time.
CaPtain trains and deploys the policy inside CaPtain-Harness, which exposes low-level perception, geometry, and guarded-motion primitives across simulation and real hardware.
Within this harness, we first align the base model via SFT on synthetic trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra, and then apply multi-turn RL.
Multi-turn RL, however, must credit tens of requests from the agent, whose physical effects often surface several turns later, with a single outcome observed only at the end of the episode.
Since training runs in simulation, we introduce a physical critic that reads the privileged physical state in simulator, which the policy never sees, and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success.
Starting from Qwen3.5-4B (0% zero-shot), CaPtain-4B achieves 55.4% held-out LIBERO success after SFT and 73.8% after RL.
On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 78.5%, surpassing several frontier-model agents, and its RL gains persist across three perturbation suites (+17.6 to +21.2 points).
Without target-domain training, it attains 83.3% on SimplerEnv WidowX, exceeds frontier models on CaP-Bench, and runs on a real robot after simulation-only adaptation.
We release all code, data, and model weights.
1
Introduction
Language-model agents have improved rapidly in coding, web navigation, and tool use, and much of this progress follows a common recipe: the agent acts inside a fixed execution harness, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) teaches it the interface, and multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) refines its behavior from the outcomes of its own interactions

give robot manipulation the same form: the policy observes camera images, writes programs against perception and motion APIs, and reads back what happened.
Since the program is composed at test time, a CaP agent inherits much of the generalization of the language model that writes it, and frontier models have made this approach strikingly capable. Used directly as a robot policy, GPT-6 Astra ranks above every public entry on the RoboDojo leaderboard

This raises a natural question:
Can a small open model be trained into such a CaP agent with the same SFT-and-RL recipe, rather than relying on a frontier model at test time?
In practice, existing CaP agents sidestep training, and in doing so hand the manipulation itself to components the agent cannot learn to improve.
One line of work prompts closed frontier models without weight updates

Another line delegates manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) or high-level skills. PyRUA trains a 4B coder over a frozen VLA and a motion planner

67

In these systems, the code decides
which

how
to grasp, approach, and place. Therefore, the agent stays bounded by the data on which the skill was trained, and RL can at best learn to sequence it.
Small open vision-language models (VLMs), meanwhile, fail outright when asked to control a robot directly. Qwen3.5-4B solves none of the LIBERO episodes in our harness, and the few efforts that train such models rely mainly on SFT
[
45
]
or single-turn text-only RL
[
20

.
What is missing is a complete SFT-and-RL recipe that teaches a small open VLM to manipulate through low-level primitives, with every manipulation decision made by the policy itself.
Applying the recipe at this low level is harder than at the skill level, for a reason that does not arise for language agents.
Without semantic skills such as grasp and place, the policy must itself decide where to grasp, from which direction to approach, and when to close the gripper, and these decisions are spread over tens of requests per episode, most of which only perceive or verify.
Multi-turn RL must then credit these requests, whose physical effects often surface several turns later, with a single outcome observed only at the end of the episode.
Outcome-only RL assigns the same credit to every request, while a language-model critic would have to infer physical progress indirectly from text and images.
Robot learning, however, offers an asymmetry that language agents lack: training runs in simulation, where exact object poses, grasp states, and sub-goal progress are known, even though the deployed policy must act from its cameras alone.
A critic can thus read the physical state that the policy cannot see, and credit each request by how much it moves the task toward success, while the policy itself still acts from its cameras at test time.
We present
CaPtain
, an open post-training pipeline built on these two observations.
CaPtain trains and deploys the policy inside
CaPtain-Harness
, an execution environment that exposes 22 low-level perception, geometric measurement, and guarded-motion primitives and nothing higher. There are no grasp, place, or open-drawer skills and no VLA. Perception returns masks and points, and motion takes an explicit end-effector pose or gripper command.
Every call returns a structured text receipt reporting what physically happened, such as measured poses, contact forces, or why a motion stopped, and the policy-facing API is unchanged across LIBERO

We then run multi-turn RL with a simulator critic that reads privileged physical state hidden from the policy and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success, combining the streaming RL formulation of SAO

Transfer remains limited on RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo (22.6% and 0.8% success), which require dual-arm coordination and unfamiliar arm kinematics.
Together, these results suggest that robot manipulation over a low-level execution harness can be post-trained like any other language agent.

Context management.
A long episode does not fit in the context window of a small model, so the harness manages the history explicitly.
Tool outputs are truncated to a fixed token budget, at most 20 receipt lines are printed per cell, and only the 12 most recent images are kept.
When the history approaches the context limit, the harness compacts it turn by turn.
It keeps the initial task context and the most recent turns verbatim, and replaces the removed turns with a short notice that lists the commands they ran and warns that the scene may have changed since.
Because the agent’s variables live in the Python session rather than in the prompt, detections, poses and helper functions survive compaction.
Compaction behaves identically during RL rollouts and at test time, so the policy is trained on the inputs it will see.
A persistent Python session.
The only tool is
python
, a sandboxed Python session with a pre-imported
robot
module.
Variables persist across requests, so the agent can store detections, poses and its own helper functions and reuse them later.
Robot calls do not raise exceptions; each returns a structured result with a success flag, a failure category, a message and a value.
This lets the agent write ordinary control flow (
if
, loops, retries) around robot calls within a single request.

There are no grasp, place or open-drawer skills and no VLA.
The agent must decide where to grasp, from which direction to approach and when to close the jaw.
The harness turns each
move_to
into a straight Cartesian motion, solves inverse kinematics, checks self-collision and monitors force at every control substep, stopping at first contact unless the agent requests a manipulation mode that tolerates load.
Because every approach vector, grasp pose, and jaw command is written explicitly in Python, the full manipulation policy is exposed to language-model post-training.
Receipts.
After each robot call, the harness appends a short
receipt
to the cell output that reports what physically happened: for motions, the stop reason, the executed distance, the peak force and the jaw opening before and after; for perception, the detection identity, its metric position and its offset to the destination.
The agent can also attach up to four camera images per cell.
Receipts give the policy dense, grounded feedback in text that complements the images.
Self-verification and success.
A completion gate on the host checks the agent’s own recorded measurements and may reject
finish()
twice before accepting it.
Host success
is the benchmark’s goal predicate, evaluated by the environment host on the final state.
Strict success
additionally requires that the agent ended the episode with
finish()
, since a robot that does not declare completion cannot be deployed.
Portability.
The policy-facing API is unchanged across LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, RoboDojo, SimplerEnv, CaP-Bench and the real robot; backend adapters, some of which add benchmark-specific safeguards, are listed in Appendix

All evaluations run in

Cost.
A
CaPtain-4B
episode on LIBERO uses on average 32.6 requests (median 26), 16.6 physical actions and 7.3k output tokens, and takes 417 s of wall time on a GPU shared by eight episodes.
This amounts to about 52 GPU-seconds of policy compute, or an estimated $0.03–0.06 per episode at $2–4 per GPU-hour, excluding perception services.
Published code agents report $0.18–0.24 (SPARK, WAA, RACaP) to $8–22 (OpenRUA) per episode.

5
Limitations
•
Single-benchmark RL training and bimanual control.
Our RL stage is trained exclusively on the 40 LIBERO tasks with a single 7-DoF arm.
While
CaPtain-4B
transfers zero-shot to unseen single-arm tasks and embodiments, cross-benchmark performance remains below in-domain accuracy, and tasks requiring simultaneous bimanual coordination or tight kinematic reach on unfamiliar 6-DoF arms are not yet addressed (§
4.3
).
•
Privileged state during RL.
Training the simulator critic relies on exact simulator state.
In our offline sensitivity study, replacing ground-truth object poses with noisy estimates degrades correlation with the privileged
Δ
​
V
\Delta V
(0.49 under 2 cm pose noise, 0.36 under 5 cm, and 0.21 using the policy’s own perception), indicating that online RL directly on physical hardware would require an external state estimator.
•
Interface and SFT coverage.
The agent’s action space is bounded by the 22 capabilities of
CaPtain-Harness
and the behaviors demonstrated in the synthetic SFT trajectories (Appendix
C
).
Tasks that require continuous force-controlled compliance—such as Wipe on CaP-Bench, which demands sustained downward pressing—cannot be expressed by guarded Cartesian position primitives.
6
Conclusion
We presented
CaPtain
, an open post-training pipeline that turns a 4B vision-language model into a standalone code-as-policy robot agent operating directly over low-level perception and motion primitives.
By pairing a portable execution harness (
CaPtain-Harness
) with synthetic SFT trajectories and multi-turn RL guided by a privileged simulator critic,
CaPtain
converts sparse episode outcomes into dense per-request credit concentrated on physical manipulation decisions, while requiring no privileged information, demonstration-trained VLA skills, or frontier API calls at test time.
Across held-out LIBERO and three perturbation suites,
CaPtain-4B
improves substantially over SFT, matches or surpasses several frontier-model agents at a small fraction of their inference cost, transfers zero-shot to unseen benchmarks and embodiments, and deploys on a physical robot through simulated embodiment adaptation alone.
Extending the simulator critic to value termination decisions, bimanual coordination, and multi-embodiment workspaces offers a direct path toward closing the remaining gap to frontier systems.

An episode may use at most 60 requests, 1,080 s of wall time and 150 physical actions (120 during RL).

finish()

false finish

finish()
on a failed state.
Strict success is the deployable metric: a robot that never declares completion cannot be used.

Only assistant turns are supervised.
A text-hint mask replaces earlier

Training uses full fine-tuning of the language model with the vision tower frozen.

Appendix D
Diversity of tasks and layouts during post-training
Diversity of tasks and scene layouts in the post-training data is essential for keeping the visual grounding of the base model.
In an earlier version of our data, most episodes started from the official LIBERO initial states, in which each object occupies nearly the same position across episodes (per-object position standard deviation about 1.4 cm).
Models fine-tuned on these data learned to reproduce object positions from the task identity rather than reading them from the image: replacing the input image left the likelihood of the predicted pixel coordinates unchanged.
The policy had effectively memorized the layouts and lost the vision-language model’s ability to ground objects in new scenes.
We therefore collect SFT data on wide-layout starts, whose per-object position standard deviation is about 15 cm, mix all task suites, and randomize lighting, camera pose and materials during RL.
With this diversity, the model grounds every
mark_point
and
segment
call in the current image, which is also what allows it to transfer to the unseen objects and layouts of the real-robot tasks (§
4.4
).

Appendix F
RL infrastructure
Layout.
Rollout and training run on separate 8-GPU nodes.
The rollout node serves six vLLM policy replicas, SAM 3 and Molmo, and renders 64–80 concurrent MuJoCo episodes; the trainer uses FSDP2 on the other node.
Rollouts are streamed: the environment server keeps generating while the trainer updates, and a request may come from a policy that is at most two versions old.
New weights reach the rollout servers by NCCL in under one second, and checkpoints are written asynchronously, which reduces the blocking time of a checkpoint from about 500 s to 5–9 s.

Appendix G
Lessons from RL on a multi-turn agent
•
Measure the gradient noise before choosing the batch.
With two start states per optimizer step, the weight displacement from the SFT model grew as the square root of the number of steps and consecutive updates were nearly orthogonal: the policy performed a random walk.
The gradient-noise scale of outcome-only advantages is in the thousands of episodes (Appendix
H
), so we accumulate 1,024 episodes per optimizer step.
•
Start states must cover the whole task.
A curriculum that started episodes at intermediate states of successful demonstrations placed every start after the grasp, because a grasp does not change the distance of the object to its goal; the policy then learned only to place held objects.
We train from fresh initial states only.
•
Layout diversity keeps the model looking.
Without diverse layouts, the model memorizes object positions and stops grounding its calls in the image (Appendix
D
).
•
Keep the policy’s behavior out of the critic.
Counters of perception or failed calls act as proxies for elapsed time and move credit from grasps to perception (§
4.5
).
•
Termination needs its own signal.
A critic trained on task success values every post-success state near one, so the decision to stop receives no credit from the critic; post-success costs and a missed-finish return are needed to make the agent declare completion (Appendix
I
).

article.headline: 4B模型经SFT与多轮RL成为代码策略机器人智能体
article.lede: 开源SFT加多轮RL流水线，把4B小模型训练成代码即策略机器人智能体；LIBERO成功率从零样本0%升到73.8%。
article.problem: 现有代码即策略（CaP）机器人智能体大多绕开训练：要么在测试时调用闭源前沿模型，成本高、无法按新机器人微调、也上不了机载算力；要么把抓取、放置等操作委托给预训练的VLA或高层技能，RL至多学会调用顺序。小开源视觉语言模型直接上手则完全失败——Qwen3.5-4B在本文的执行环境下解不出一个LIBERO回合。缺的是一条直接教小模型在低层原语上做操作的完整SFT加RL配方。
article.method: 作者构建CaPtain-Harness，只暴露22个低层感知、几何测量与带保护的运动会原语，没有grasp/place宏，也没有VLA，每次调用返回结构化文本回执。训练分两步：先在GPT-6 Astra生成的合成轨迹上做SFT（遮蔽重复失败轮次、以0.2概率遮蔽历史像素坐标迫使模型看当前图像），再做多轮RL。RL的关键是一个模拟器critic：它读取策略看不到的36维特权物理状态，预测任务成功率，并在固定请求索引下取前后差值作为每个请求的信用，使只做感知或校验的请求几乎得不到信用；测试时critic被移除，策略仅凭相机图像与回执行动。
article.results: 从Qwen3.5-4B（零样本0%）出发，CaPtain-4B在留出LIBERO上经SFT达到55.4%、经RL达到73.8%（strict 52.1%→67.5%），虚假finish从7.1%降到2.1%，平均请求数从39.1降到32.6。LIBERO-PRO三套件59.5%→78.5%（四套件49.2%→68.6%，+19.4），LIBERO-Plus 48.6%→66.1%（+17.6，七个扰动维度全部在p<0.05下提升），LIBERO-MAX Dynamic +21.2、Base +18.8。零样本迁移：SimplerEnv WidowX 83.3%，CaP-Bench 75.0（SFT为55.0，未训练模型为5.0），但RoboTwin 2.0仅22.6%、RoboDojo仅0.8%（Score 1.7）。每回合平均32.6次请求、16.6个物理动作、约52 GPU秒，估算0.03–0.06美元。
article.why_it_matters: 它表明机器人操作只要跑在低层执行环境上，就能像其他语言智能体一样被后训练，一个4B开源模型在测试时不调用前沿API、不依赖VLA技能，就在多项基准上超过若干前沿模型智能体，并能在仅用粗模拟孪生适配后上真机。
article.limitations: RL只在40个LIBERO任务、单条7自由度臂上训练，双臂协调与陌生6自由度臂的可达性问题未解，跨基准迁移仍明显低于域内精度。critic依赖精确模拟器状态，离线敏感性实验显示2 cm位姿噪声下相关性降到0.49、5 cm降到0.36、改用策略自身感知仅0.21，因此真机在线RL需要外部状态估计器；此外22个原语无法表达持续力控任务（如CaP-Bench的Wipe）。

page_papers.title: SketchDirector: Complex Scene Sketching via Agentic Layout Reasoning and Detail Refinement
page_papers.abstract: Existing sketch generation methods often rely on image guidance and are largely limited to individual objects or simplified scenes, leaving text-guided complex scene sketching underexplored. We present SketchDirector, an agentic framework that mimics the human sketching workflow for automatic multi-concept scene sketching. Given a scene-level text prompt, SketchDirector first employs a large language model~(LLM) to decompose the scene into multiple draft assets, where each is represented by a set of Bézier curves. Then, an agentic reasoning loop iteratively plans and executes their spatial arrangement, guided by self-evolving memory. Finally, a detail refinement module leverages diffusion priors to enhance sketch quality while preserving geometric structure. To support future research and applications in multi-concept scene sketch generation, we further introduce the \textit{MCSketch8K} dataset, comprising editable vector assets, compositional layouts, and object-level manipulation annotations. Extensive experiments show that SketchDirector outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in semantic and compositional quality while effectively preserving overall contour organization during refinement. The project page is: \href{https://yiki77.github.io/SketchDirector/}{https://yiki77.github.io/SketchDirector/}.
page_papers.content:
SketchDirector: Complex Scene Sketching via Agentic Layout Reasoning and Detail Refinement
Yiqi Liang
Xiaodong Cun
\corresponding
Abstract
Existing sketch generation methods often rely on image guidance and are largely limited to individual objects or simplified scenes, leaving text-guided complex scene sketching underexplored.
We present SketchDirector, an agentic framework that mimics the human sketching workflow for automatic multi-concept scene sketching.
Given a scene-level text prompt, SketchDirector first employs a large language model (LLM) to decompose the scene into multiple draft assets, where each is represented by a set of Bézier curves. Then, an agentic reasoning loop iteratively plans and executes their spatial arrangement, guided by self-evolving memory. Finally, a detail refinement module leverages diffusion priors to enhance sketch quality while preserving geometric structure. To support future research and applications in multi-concept scene sketch generation, we further introduce the
MCSketch8K
dataset, comprising editable vector assets, compositional layouts, and object-level manipulation annotations. Extensive experiments show that SketchDirector outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in semantic and compositional quality while effectively preserving overall contour organization during refinement. The project page is:
https://yiki77.github.io/SketchDirector/
.
GVC Lab, Great Bay University
https://yiki77.github.io/SketchDirector/
Figure 1:
Visual results of SketchDirector
. The top row shows scene sketches depicting diverse concepts. The bottom-left row shows rich layout variations for the same prompt, highlighting the effectiveness of agentic reasoning for automatic scene composition. The bottom-right row shows the progressive sketch refinement process, which enhances sketch details while preserving sketch structure and spatial layout.
1
Introduction
Sketching is a concise visual representation that effectively captures the intentions of human beings.
As its scope expands from individual objects to multiple concepts, scene sketching has shown great potential in applications such as animation, proof of concept, and interactive design, as in Fig.
2
(A).
However, complex scene sketching requires more than depicting individual objects. It involves organizing multiple concepts, reasoning about their spatial relationships, and maintaining coherent details within a unified scene.
Therefore, generating semantically aligned scene sketches with reasonable layouts and coherent details remains a big challenge.
Previous automatic scene sketching generation methods
(
Li et al. 2019a
;
Li et al. 2019b
;
Chan et al. 2022
;
Vinker et al. 2023
;
Liang et al. 2025b
)
primarily operate at the holistic scene level, treating scene sketches as an indivisible entity without object representations, thereby hindering local editing and object reuse.
Recent studies
(
Wu et al. 2025
;
Zhang et al. 2026
;
Zhan et al. 2025
)
have explored object-aware generation, but objects are often treated as predefined components or auxiliary structures.
Consequently, these methods lack dynamic control, layout planning, and iterative optimization for individual objects, which limits their potential as visual components.
In contrast, real-world sketch creation is inherently iterative: artists continually revise, group, and rearrange individual elements to improve the overall composition and presentation. They also adapt the level of refinement to suit their creative goals, producing sketches that range from rough drafts to highly detailed renderings, as illustrated in Fig.
2
(B). Digital vector sketches are particularly well suited to such flexible and iterative workflows because they are naturally represented as collections of Bézier curves, enabling efficient programmatic manipulation.
We thus propose
SketchDirector
, an automatic agentic framework
(
Vinker et al. 2025
;
Du et al. 2026
;
Liu et al. 2025
;
Liang et al. 2025a
)
for text-guided multi-concept scene sketch generation by mimicking the pipeline of human creators.
Specifically,
given a textual description,
SketchDirector
first employs a Large Language Model (LLM) based method to decompose the scene and generate each individual object as draft asset, each represented as a set of Bézier curves.
To enable layout control between multiple asset, we introduce an operating action library comprising a set of executable operations,
e.g.,
move()
,
scale()
, to manipulate object attributes, enabling flexible adjustment of spatial relationships among objects.
Building upon this library, we propose an agentic reasoning loop, which formulates layout manipulation as an iterative operations and execution process.
To achieve reliable closed-loop reasoning, rather than predicting the entire scene layout at once,
SketchDirector
progressively organizes draft assets through an iterative
Plan–Execute–Verify–Correct
process.
At each step,
SketchDirector
generates and executes object-level operations, updates the scene representation, and evaluates the resulting composition through geometric checks and multimodal verification.
When the layout fails verification,
SketchDirector
revises its decisions and corrects the layout using a hierarchical self-evolving memory that leverages short-term failure reflections and accumulated long-term experiences.
After that, we introduce an additional detail refinement step to address the challenges of structural consistency in scene sketch distillation from the diffusion prior.
Unlike traditional methods that treat Bézier curves as unstructured point sets, we treat object curve segments as the optimization primitives.
Then, by jointly optimizing local objects and the global canvas using pre-scene distillation, our method is able to generate scene sketches with varying levels of object refinement while maintaining consistency with the textual description. Finally, with the lack of available object-aware and editable scene sketch datasets, we construct a multi-concept scene sketch dataset called
MCSketch8K
to facilitate future research and applications in scene sketch generation.
The dataset comprises 1,000 scene sketches with over 4,000 disentangled vector object assets across 800 object categories.
Each scene is annotated with compositional layouts and object-level manipulation operations, providing structured supervision for object decomposition, spatial arrangement reasoning, and controllable scene editing.
Our key contributions are summarized as:
•
We propose
SketchDirector
, an automatic framework for text-guided complex scene sketching with flexible object-level control and structure-preserving detail refinement.
•
SketchDirector
contains two key techniques to assist in scene sketch generation:
i) agentic reasoning
, which formulates generation as a closed-loop process;
ii) detail refinement
, which performs Bézier curve parametrization and progressively joint local-global vector optimization to refine scene sketches.
•
We construct
MCSketch8K
, a multi-concept scene sketch dataset comprising vector object assets, compositional scene layouts, and object-level manipulation annotations.
Figure 2:
Motivation of multi-concept scene sketch generation.
(A) Widely used in animation, concept art, and design. (B) Artists adjust sketch refinement from draft to detailed sketch preserving structure for different goals.
2
Related Work
Scene Sketch Generation.
Scene sketch generation aims to translate visual or textual descriptions into coherent sketches.
Early methods formulated this task as image-to-sketch translation
(
Li et al. 2019a
;
Li et al. 2019b
;
Chan et al. 2022
)
, converting photographs into rasterized contour drawings via supervised learning or adversarial training.
Later studies increasingly adopt vector representations for scalable and editable sketch generation.
Image-conditioned methods such as Clipascene
(
Vinker et al. 2023
)
and MROSS
(
Liang et al. 2025b
)
produce vector scene sketches from a reference image, while text-guided methods
(
Frans et al. 2022
;
Jain et al. 2023
;
Xing et al. 2023
;
Xing et al. 2024
;
Xing et al. 2025
)
further enable open-domain vector sketch generation from textual descriptions.
In particular, VectorFusion
(
Jain et al. 2023
)
distills text-to-image diffusion priors into SVGs through score distillation, DiffSketcher
(
Xing et al. 2023
)
directly optimizes Bézier curves with diffusion-based supervision, and SVGDreamer
(
Xing et al. 2024
)
improves text-to-SVG generation through semantic-driven vectorization and particle-based score distillation.
Despite these advances, existing methods optimize the scene holistically, leaving objects implicitly encoded and limiting editing to strokes rather than objects.
Multi-concept Sketch Generation.
Recent studies explore structured scene generation by introducing different forms of concept decomposition and controllability.
For instance, SketchTriplet
(
Wu et al. 2025
)
assembles individual objects to construct scene datasets, although the objects mainly serve as fixed composition units without supporting layout planning or per-concept editing.
SketchAny
(
Zhang et al. 2026
)
separates foreground and background to improve structural coherence, yet provides limited control over individual concept instances.
CoProSketch
(
Zhan et al. 2025
)
represents objects with unsigned distance fields to enable progressive scene generation and improved editability, while generation is still performed at the scene level rather than through independent concept generation.
Collectively, these methods highlight the value of concept-aware representations, yet objects remain passive elements rather than autonomous units for planning, interaction, and iterative refinement.
Agents for Sketch Generation.
The rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has introduced new opportunities for reasoning, planning, and iterative interaction into sketch generation.
For instance, SketchAgent
(
Vinker et al. 2025
)
introduces a language-driven sequential sketch generation framework, where an LLM-based agent can generate sequences of vector sketches and supports conversational sketch refinement.
Building upon this, Du et al.
(
Du et al. 2026
)
further explores controllable vector sketch generation by training a multimodal agent with part-level annotations and process-level feedback, enabling interpretable and locally editable sketch synthesis.
In addition, AutoSketch
(
Chin et al. 2025
)
investigates style-aware vector sketch completion, leveraging VLM-based iterative adjustment to preserve the abstraction level and stroke characteristics of input sketches during completion. Despite promising results, existing methods lack high-level scene reasoning and multi-object coordination. SketchDirector addresses this with an agentic framework for hierarchical planning, object-level control, and iterative refinement.
Figure 3:
SketchDirector
pipeline
. Given a scene description,
SketchDirector
first generates object-level draft assets. The agent then progressively composes the scene through executable operations from the action library, maintaining scene programs and spatial asset attributes. A closed-loop process iteratively adjusts the layout, supported by self-evolving memory that incorporates short-term failure feedback and long-term experiences. Finally, detail refinement employs curve contour resampling and progressive joint optimization to enhance sketch details while preserving the established scene layout and object structures.
Figure 4:
Example agentic reasoning trajectory in
SketchDirector
.
A real log illustrating how agents interleave layout planning, scene state updates, geometric-semantic verification, memory evolution, and correction.
Figure 5:
A success example of planning and execution in
SketchDirector
.
Each operation updates both the executable program and the represented scene state, yielding a traceable trajectory from the initial drafts to the final layout.
3
SketchDirector
The goal of
SketchDirector
is to generate editable multi-concept scene sketches from textual descriptions.
Each sketch is represented as a collection of SVG assets parameterized by black Bézier curves, enabling object-level editability and structural preservation.
Given a scene description, we first decompose it into individual concepts and generate corresponding vector draft assets (Sec.
3.1
).
To support executable scene composition, we define an operating action library consisting of primitive operations that manipulate object attributes and update the scene state (Sec.
3.2
).
Building upon these, an agentic layout reasoning step progressively composes the scene through a closed loop, where agents translate spatial intentions into executable editing programs and iteratively plan, execute, verify, and correct the scene composition (Sec.
3.3
).
Finally, a detail refinement step further enhances sketch details through Bézier curve contour resampling and progressive joint optimization, while preserving the structure of draft assets and spatial layout of the canvas (Sec.
3.4
).
A high-level illustration is shown in Fig.
3
.

Agentic Layout Reasoning
After generating draft assets, directly assembling drafts often produces implausible spatial relationships (

Plan–Execute–Verify–Correct
process to iteratively improve scene composition. At each iteration, the
agent plans object-level programs, executes them, evaluates the resulting layout, and revises its
decisions when necessary, as illustrated in Figs.

Planning and Execution.
Planning aims to translate high-level layout intentions into an executable program.
We encode layout decisions as a sequence of functional tools rather than directly predicting object attributes, including

The agent infers the grid location of each object, which is deterministically mapped back to the corresponding canvas position during execution.
The agent generates programs by jointly reasoning over geometric and visual clues, where object attributes, grid positions, and bounding boxes provide spatial constraints, while rendered canvases and layout histories provide global context.
The generated operations are sequentially executed to update object attributes and scene states, producing an explicit and traceable composition trajectory, as illustrated in Fig.

This traceability allows the agent to identify problematic operations during subsequent verification and correction.

Self-Evolving Correction.

(

The Short-Term Failure Memory.
The Short-Term Failure Memory maintains a trajectory-level record for each failed attempt. Each entry contains the generated program, intermediate rendering results, object-level attributes, verification feedback, and the corresponding failure category.
These records are discarded after successful correction and are only used within the current scene generation process.
The Long-Term Experience Memory.

Impact of Agentic Layout Reasoning.
Figure
10
and Table
3
show that removing any component leads to performance degradation, confirming that all modules in agentic reasoning are essential for high-quality scene sketch generation.
Removing planning (
w/o Plan
) leads to severe layout degradation.
Without executable scene programs, the model struggles to organize object attributes, resulting in frequent object overlaps, unreasonable spatial arrangements, and boundary violations.
These demonstrate that converting high-level semantic intentions into structured layout operations is essential for reliable scene composition.
Disabling geometric verification (
w/o Geo. Ver.
) mainly affects physical plausibility.
Although the generated objects remain semantically relevant, their positions and sizes may violate basic spatial constraints, such as objects extending beyond the canvas or unrealistic relative scales between objects.
This indicates that geometric constraints provide necessary low-level guidance for maintaining valid scene structures.
Without visual-semantic verification (
w/o Sem. Ver.
), the agent lacks high-level visual feedback during layout refinement.
Consequently, generated scenes may contain incorrect object relationships, missing semantic interactions, or unnatural occlusion orders.
The comparison highlights the importance of multimodal evaluation in aligning generated layouts with the intended scene description.
Furthermore, memory modules improve the agent’s ability to learn from previous reasoning trajectories.
Removing short-term memory (
w/o Short Mem.
) does not cause significant visual layout degradation, but leads to repeated exploration of similar unsuccessful layouts, increasing the number of reflection iterations.
Removing long-term memory (
w/o Long Mem.
) also preserves comparable visual structures in many cases, yet prevents the agent from retrieving reusable layout experiences from related scenes, resulting in less effective layout composition.
Overall, these qualitative examples verify that each component contributes complementary capabilities, enabling more reliable and controllable scene reasoning.
Impact of Detail Refinement.
Fig.
11
provides additional comparisons between point-based and curve-based sampling.
Point-based sampling uniformly samples sparse control points from object regions without considering the underlying contours.
During optimization, these points may drift independently, causing geometric distortions and loss of characteristic object shapes.
In contrast, our curve contour resampling method derives Bézier primitives directly from object contours.
By preserving the original contour topology, the curves provide a more stable optimization space.
Fig.
12
presents additional comparisons of different optimization strategies.
Removing local supervision (
w/o Local
) optimizes objects only according to global objectives, allowing unrelated semantic information to interfere with individual object.
This often results in distorted local structures.
Removing global supervision (
w/o Global
) focuses only on individual object while ignoring interactions among objects.
Although individual objects may remain recognizable, the resulting scenes exhibit weaker spatial coherence, such as unnatural object relationships.
Without progressive optimization (
w/o Progressive
), local and global objectives are optimized simultaneously from the beginning.
The strong coupling between object-level refinement and scene-level consistency introduces optimization conflicts, causing unstable updates and reduced object fidelity.
By progressively incorporating objects, our method enables stable local refinement first and gradually improves global scene integration.

4.4
Limitations.
Although
SketchDirector
generates multi-concept scene sketches, several limitations remain. First, it struggles with complex physical and semantic relations, such as interactions between a woman and a kettle or a castle located on a hill (Fig.
13
(A)). Stronger relational and interaction modeling may improve scene understanding. Second, refinement may hallucinate redundant instances, leading to object inconsistency, such as duplicating a sheep (Fig.
13
(B)). Instance-aware constraints could help preserve object identity and count. Third, multimodal verification and iterative optimization incur computational costs, particularly when multiple refinement rounds are required. Efficient verification and optimization strategies will be explored in future work.

5
Conclusion
We present
SketchDirector
, an agentic framework that emulates the human sketching workflow. Designed for complex scene sketch generation,
SketchDirector
converts textual descriptions into editable vector assets and executable layout operations. It consists of three stages: concept representation for generating object-level draft assets, agentic reasoning with iterative
Plan–Execute–Verify–Correct
and self-evolving memory for reliable spatial composition, and detail refinement for progressively optimizing Bézier-based vectors while preserving the original sketch structure. We further introduce
MCSketch8K
, a benchmark containing editable vector assets and composition annotations for multi-concept scene sketch generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that
SketchDirector
outperforms existing methods in semantic and compositional quality while effectively preserving structural integrity during refinement.

article.headline: 用智能体规划布局，把文本变成可编辑场景草图
article.lede: SketchDirector 让 LLM 拆解概念、智能体闭环摆放草稿、扩散先验补细节，输出可编辑的矢量场景草图。
article.problem: 现有草图生成方法多依赖图像引导，适用范围基本停留在单个物体或简化场景，文本引导的复杂场景草图仍少有人做。早期方法把整幅场景当成不可分的实体整体优化，物体被隐式编码，无法单独编辑或复用；近期的物体感知方法又把物体当作预设组件或辅助结构，缺少对单个物体的布局规划与迭代优化。
article.method: 给定场景级文本，LLM 先把场景拆成若干可独立绘制的概念，每个概念由 SketchAgent 生成采样点并用最小二乘拟合成三次 Bézier 曲线草稿，同时给出深度序。随后智能体在 move/scale/rotate/layer/delete/modify 六个原子操作组成的动作库上，以 Plan–Execute–Verify–Correct 闭环迭代布置：几何检查边界与缩放范围 [0.1,1.5]，VLM 从语义、构图、完整度、尺寸、美观五维加权打分，失败轨迹写入短期失败记忆、成功布局以 Jaccard 相似度检索进长期经验记忆。最后做曲线轮廓重采样（de Casteljau 细分，保持原拓扑）与渐进式局部-全局 RFDS 联合优化，只更新控制点、固定曲线顺序以保住结构。
article.results: 在从 MCSketch8K 采样的 30 条多概念提示上，由 Qwen3.7-Plus、Claude-Opus-4-7、Gemini3.1-Pro、GPT-5.5 四个 VLM 评判，SketchDirector 五项指标为语义 0.916、构图 0.772、完整度 0.821、美观 0.836、尺寸 0.821，加细节精炼后升至 0.923/0.788/0.843/0.869/0.842，均高于五个基线；对照的 GPT-5.5 为 0.911/0.730/0.811/0.813/0.820，SVGDreamer 为 0.690/0.546/0.620/0.650/0.695，VectorFusion 仅 0.466/0.252/0.338/0.417/0.412。耗时上 SketchDirector 约 6 分钟、加精炼约 21 分钟，GPT-5.5 与 SketchAgent 约 20 秒，SVGDreamer 约 24 分钟。消融显示去掉规划后语义降至 0.676、构图 0.503，去掉语义验证语义降至 0.603，去掉短期记忆迭代次数从 1.375 升到 2.875；完整模型验证通过率 0.873。用户研究招募 68 人、15 条提示，每项标准收集 5100 份回答，各基线对比中参与者均更偏好本方法。作者同时发布 MCSketch8K，含 1,000 幅场景草图、4,000 余个解耦矢量物体资产、覆盖 800 个物体类别。
article.why_it_matters: 它把场景草图从“整图优化”改成“物体级程序化编排”，输出的 SVG 资产和布局可单独移动、缩放、替换，对动画、概念设计和交互设计这类需要反复改稿的流程更直接可用，MCSketch8K 也为物体级场景草图提供了带布局与操作标注的训练/评测基础。
article.limitations: 论文自陈三类问题：难以建模复杂物理与语义关系（如人与水壶的交互、山丘上的城堡），精炼阶段会幻觉出多余实例（例如重复画出一只羊），以及多模态验证与迭代优化带来的计算开销。此外，不加精炼时语义分 0.916 仅比 GPT-5.5 的 0.911 高 0.005，而耗时约 6 分钟对约 20 秒，优势主要体现在构图（0.772 对 0.730）上；评测仅用 30 条提示、且由 VLM 打分，规模与评判独立性都值得进一步检验。
article.figure_caption_zh: SketchDirector 中的一段真实智能体推理日志，展示智能体如何交替进行布局规划、场景状态更新、几何-语义验证、记忆演化与纠错。

figure.caption: {Example agentic reasoning trajectory in {SketchDirector}.} A real log illustrating how agents interleave layout planning, scene state updates, geometric-semantic verification, memory evolution, and correction.

page_papers.title: Does Scaling Toward AGI Depend on What System-1 Lets System-2 Execute?
page_papers.abstract: Progress toward artificial general intelligence (AGI) has largely relied on scaling a resource-intensive executive, System-2, through larger models, more data and compute, longer reasoning, and more agents. We ask whether the next stage may come instead from co-designing it with System-1, a lightweight, semantically aware predictor that evaluates candidate interactions before execution, so that System-2 acts only on those worth their cost. Our answer is a qualified yes. We study conditional interaction, a predict--gate--execute--update loop: System-1 estimates each candidate's utility, System-2 executes those admitted by an adaptive threshold, and the outcomes update System-1. The loop spans training, test-time reasoning, adaptive decision-making, and agentic tool use, with utility and cost defined by the application. Under ideal screening and equal execution costs, execution compute falls by a factor approaching 1/ρ_u, where ρ_u is the density of utility-relevant interactions (cost-weighted when costs differ); prediction errors, exploration, and distribution shift reduce the saving. We bound selection regret by predictor error and the utility margin. These results motivate our central hypothesis: ρ_u is a measurable coordinate of scaling efficiency and makes informative compute a better description of scaling than total compute.
page_papers.content:
Abstract
Progress toward artificial general intelligence (AGI) has largely relied on scaling a resource-intensive executive, System-2, through larger models, more data and compute, longer reasoning, and more agents. We ask whether the next stage may come instead from co-designing it with System-1, a lightweight, semantically aware predictor that evaluates candidate interactions before execution, so that System-2 acts only on those worth their cost. Our answer is a qualified yes.

Section
4.1
states the core formal results: what prediction buys, in time and memory, and the regret a cheap predictor risks. The remaining subsections ask why a cheap System-1 can make a useful prediction about an expensive interaction at all, from three complementary views. These connections are interpretive rather than separate contributions; each supplies insight and, under its own assumptions, a guarantee, but none is a derivation of the framework.

article.headline: 别只堆算力：让 System-1 先筛一遍
article.lede: 论文主张：通往 AGI 的扩展不只在放大 System-2，还需轻量 System-1 预筛候选交互再执行。
article.problem: 当前通往 AGI 的进展主要靠把执行器 System-2 做大：更大模型、更多数据与算力、更长推理链、更多智能体，成本随规模同步膨胀。论文追问，下一阶段是否应改为与 System-1 协同设计——一个轻量、具备语义感知的预测器，在交互真正执行前先评估候选是否值得其代价。
article.method: 作者给出一个形式化框架：System-1 用廉价特征与历史为每个候选嵌入并打分，门控只放行分数超过阈值 τ_t 的候选，控制器调节阈值以维持目标放行率 π*（阈值更新式）；被抑制的候选只需付出 c_pred，另留一小部分审计样本强制执行以检测预测漏判。执行结果被记录并回流重训 System-1，System-2 也从同一批结果中学习。论文另从信息论与具身（域随机化、尾部风险）等视角解释廉价预测为何可能对昂贵交互有效。
article.results: 论文在第 4.1 节给出核心形式化结论：预测在时间与内存上带来什么收益（Eq. (12)、Proposition 7），以及廉价预测器带来的 regret 风险；信息论视角对应 Proposition 14，效用相关交互的密度定义见 Eq. (14)。论文未给出具体数字：全文没有实验或基准结果，GRESO、MoPPS、GPS、MPTS 等被引工作只作例证而非验证。
article.why_it_matters: 若这一框架成立，扩展 AGI 的杠杆可能从“更大的执行器”转向“更准的预筛器”，这直接对应推理时算力分配、rollout 分配与智能体强化学习的成本结构。它也把“何时不值得执行”变成一个可以被学习和被控制的目标放行率问题。
article.limitations: 作者自承三条理论线索是“解释性而非独立贡献”，没有一条是该框架的推导，相关实证工作是“例证而非验证”，全文亦无实验支撑。阈值调节、regret 界与目标放行率在真实负载与非平稳分布下是否仍成立，仍属存疑。

figure.caption: {Architectural realization: represent, predict, gate, learn.} Every candidate is embedded {1} and scored cheaply by System~1 {2}. The gate {3} admits only candidates whose score clears the threshold $ _t$, which a controller adjusts to hold a target admission rate $ ^*$ (Eq.~( {eq:threshold-update})). Admitted candidates are executed by System~2; suppressed ones cost only $c_{ {pred}}$, and a small audit sample of them is executed anyway so that the predictor's misses can be detected. Executed outcomes are logged and refit System~1 {4}, while System~2 learns from the same outcomes. Dotted arcs mark the two other interfaces of co-design: what is distilled from System~2 into System~1, and which of System~2's representations System~1 may access.

page_papers.title: Apriel Voice 27B Preview: An Open Model for Speech, Reasoning, and Tool Use
page_papers.abstract: A capable voice assistant must do more than recognize words; it must understand requests, reason over context, sustain conversations, and act through tools. We present Apriel Voice 27B Preview, an open speech-language model that unifies these capabilities within a shared reasoning backbone while retaining text and image input modalities. Built on the post-trained Gemma 4 26B-A4B checkpoint, Apriel Voice directly processes speech and generates both responses and tool calls without requiring a separate dialogue model. We introduce a two-stage training procedure to adapt the model to speech. The first stage establishes the speech interface, while the second jointly adapts the projector and backbone through supervised fine-tuning, text replay, and source-dependent cross-entropy and forward Kullback--Leibler divergence supervision. Automatically constructed speech-conditioned dialogues provide conversational training data, while local teacher serving, overlapping teacher and student computation, and fused full-vocabulary losses enable efficient online distillation. In thinking mode, Apriel Voice achieves a score of 98.90 on Big Bench Audio, 81.13 on Speech-BFCL, and a task success rate of 65.51% on τ-Voice, with a mean latency of 1.91 seconds. It also achieves 51.27% English EVA accuracy and 74.13% experience pass@1. Finally, we deploy Apriel Voice 27B Preview on a custom serving platform to support interactive voice interactions.

Apriel Voice 27B Preview: An Open Model for Speech, Reasoning, and Tool Use
Abstract
A capable voice assistant must do more than recognize words: it must understand a request, reason over context, sustain a conversation, and act through tools. We present Apriel Voice 27B Preview, an open speech-language model that unifies these abilities into a shared reasoning backbone while retaining text and image input modalities. Built on the post-trained Gemma 4 26B-A4B checkpoint, Apriel Voice processes speech directly and generates both responses and tool calls without requiring a separate dialogue model. A two-stage training procedure adapts the model to speech. Stage 1 establishes the speech interface. Stage 2 jointly adapts the projector and backbone using supervised fine-tuning, text replay, and source-dependent cross-entropy and forward Kullback–Leibler divergence supervision. Automatically constructed speech-conditioned dialogues provide conversational training data. Local teacher serving, overlapping teacher and student computation, and fused full-vocabulary losses enable effective online distillation. In thinking mode, Apriel Voice scores 98.90 on Big Bench Audio, 81.13 on Speech-BFCL, and 65.51% task success on
τ

-Voice, with a mean latency of 1.91 seconds. English EVA accuracy and experience pass@1 reach 51.27% and 74.13%. We serve Apriel Voice 27B Preview through a custom platform to enable interactive voice interactions.
Figure 1:
One reasoning backbone across speech, text, and images.
Apriel Voice receives speech through an encoder and projector, retains the original text and image interfaces, and generates both responses and tool calls. Application components execute tools, return their results to the conversation, and stream response text to a replaceable synthesizer. The frozen teacher is used only during training.
1
Introduction
An employee reporting a locked account may describe the problem aloud, share a screenshot, correct an identifier, and ask an assistant to open a ticket. The useful outcome is a resolved request: the assistant must connect the evidence, follow the conversation, choose an appropriate action, and interpret the result. Supporting such interactions requires speech understanding alongside the reasoning and tool use of a large language model (LLM).
Recognition accuracy is necessary but insufficient for voice agent success. A model may transcribe a request correctly yet lack the ability to follow constraints or invoke the necessary tools to complete the associated task. Likewise, strong text performance does not establish that the same model can reason reliably when the request arrives as audio. We therefore evaluate speech as an interface to general capability, covering reasoning, instruction following, conversation, and task completion alongside recognition and translation
[
23
,
4
,
39
]
.
Voice systems connect these capabilities in several ways. A conventional
3-stage
cascade combines automatic speech recognition (ASR), an LLM, and text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis, passing a transcript to the reasoner. Speech-conditioned models instead expose the reasoner to learned acoustic features
[
28
,
45
,
43
,
11
]
; native speech-generating models also integrate the output audio pathway
[
8
,
51
]
. Another deployment pattern separates the spoken conversation from a backend model responsible for reasoning and tools
[
34
]
. These designs allocate speech understanding, reasoning, synthesis, and interaction control to different components.
We present
Apriel Voice 27B Preview
, or
Apriel Voice
in short, an open speech-language model built on the post-trained Gemma 4 26B-A4B checkpoint
[
14
,
15
]
. Apriel Voice uses the same reasoning backbone to understand speech, respond in conversation, and decide when and how to call tools. Text, images, and returned tool results remain part of its context (
Figure
1
). Speech synthesis is independently replaceable, allowing voices and deployment choices to change without retraining the reasoner.
We release
Apriel Live
, an interactive interface enabling practitioners to experience Apriel Voice in real conversations.
The training problem is to extend an already capable decoder with a speech interface while preserving the behavior that makes it useful. We address it in two stages. Multilingual transcription, translation, and continuation first train a speech projector with the backbone frozen. Broad supervised fine-tuning (SFT) then updates the projector and backbone using speech tasks, internally generated conversations, tool interactions, and text replay. Source-dependent cross-entropy (CE) and forward Kullback–Leibler divergence (FKL) combine task targets with online supervision from a frozen copy of the original backbone. The teacher supports learning during adaptation and is absent at inference.
Contributions.
This report brings together four contributions:
1.
Broad speech-conditioned agentic capability.
A shared model handles spoken reasoning, instruction following, conversation, and tool-call generation while retaining text and image processing capabilities.
2.
A staged adaptation recipe.
Speech interface learning with automatically constructed speech-conditioned dialogues and source-dependent CE/FKL supervision connects task acquisition with capability retention.
3.
An efficient online-supervision implementation.
Local teacher serving, overlap with student computation, fused full-vocabulary losses, and coordinated checkpointing support the combined training workload.
4.
Evaluation and interactive deployment.
Detailed results span speech, text, images, multilingual translation, service interactions, and enterprise workflows; Apriel Live demonstrates the corresponding application interface.

5
Data Construction
5.1
Constructing speech-conditioned conversations
Our custom task and conversation data are generated synthetically in-house. We first construct text interactions containing user requests, assistant responses, and, where relevant, tool calls and returned results. This representation makes the intended task, role structure, and target behavior explicit. An automated conversion pipeline then renders selected user content as audio through reference-conditioned TTS and voice cloning.
Spoken requests can refer to material best retained as text, such as a code fragment, table, formula, or case-sensitive identifier. The conversion therefore supports both whole-turn speech and mixed text/audio turns. System instructions, assistant targets, and tool messages remain text, preserving the supervision for conversation and action.

Efficient Training with an Online Teacher
Online full-vocabulary distillation adds a teacher forward pass and distribution transfer to the student’s training workload. The implementation distributes teacher inference across local workers, overlaps it with student computation, and reduces temporary storage for loss evaluation.
7.1
Local teacher workers and sharded students
Teacher inference and student training have different resource requirements. The teacher performs forward computation; the student also stores optimizer state and executes backward computation. We assign them separate workers and use FSDP to shard student state

Student workers send teacher contexts and position information to assigned teacher workers through GPU point-to-point communication. The full-vocabulary path returns teacher logits in bfloat16 (BF16) format. This traffic stays within a node, while student workers use distributed collectives across their own process group. The same local allocation can therefore be repeated across nodes.

Evaluation Design
8.1
Questions and coverage
We structure our evaluation around three major research questions to establish whether a unified speech-language backbone trained with our two-stage recipe can achieve competitive performance compared to leading open-source and proprietary systems across reasoning, end-to-end task completion, and multimodal capability retention.
RQ1: Whether Apriel Voice supports audio reasoning, instruction following, and tool use beyond foundational speech capabilities.
One of the core contributions of speech-language models lies in their ability to process spoken instructions, reason over problems, and generate tool calls, not merely perform foundational speech recognition and translation. Therefore, we target evaluations across different foundational tasks (speech recognition, speech translation) and audio reasoning tasks, including instruction following (MT-Bench
