10
Discussion
10.1
Speech capability across tasks
Apriel Voice can reason over spoken requests, follow instructions, produce tool calls, and participate in task-oriented conversations, while continuing to process text and images.
The benchmarks measure complementary capabilities. BBA and IFEval characterize different reasoning demands; BFCL tests structured calls; EVA combines service outcomes with conversational experience; and
τ
\tau
-Voice tests completion through speech. Thinking improves several reasoning and workflow scores, while some recognition and function-calling tasks score higher in non-thinking mode. Reasoning-mode selection therefore depends on the task.
10.2
Training and supervision
Interface training learns a projector that connects the frozen speech encoder to the fixed decoder. Task SFT then adapts the projector and backbone for conversation and tool use. Source-dependent teacher supervision supports adaptation on selected speech examples and retention on text replay. Paired text/audio dialogues provide corresponding speech and text contexts for training.
The systems implementation addresses the resulting cost: local teacher workers separate inference from student state, lookahead overlaps teacher and student computation, and fused losses reduce temporary probability storage. Together, these mechanisms support full-vocabulary online supervision at the training scale described in
Tab.
2
. The evaluations assess the combined method; component effects require controlled ablations.
10.3
Optimization behavior
The combined stage-two objective decreases over training (
Figures
8
and
9
). CE and FKL need not move together: CE measures fit to target responses, whereas FKL measures divergence from the frozen teacher on selected contexts. Source composition and supervision weights also affect the aggregate.

11
Conclusion
Apriel Voice 27B Preview extends a text-and-image backbone to speech, using the same model for reasoning, conversation, and tool-call decisions. Evaluations demonstrate these capabilities through spoken reasoning, instruction following, multilingual translation, service interactions, and complete workflows.
The recipe combines interface learning, broad task SFT, synthetic speech-conditioned dialogues, and source-dependent CE/FKL supervision. Local teacher serving, lookahead, and fused losses support online distillation. A shared real-time API enables deployment and supports integration with voice benchmarks through WebSocket communication.
Limitations
Multilinguality.
Apriel Voice 27B Preview prioritizes English speech understanding, reasoning, and instruction following for real-world English conversational-agent settings.
Multilingual capabilities and evaluations remain limited, with primary assessment through automatic speech translation. English performance does not imply comparable quality across languages; multilingual robustness is uneven and can represent a clear limitation. Enhancing multilingual speech understanding and conversational robustness across diverse language families is a priority for future versions.
Evaluation and comparison.
Internal and public results differ in prompting, language coverage, output modality, reasoning budgets, judging, and task limits. Aggregate scores do not establish paired significance, non-inferiority to the starting backbone, or a controlled ranking against every frontier system. Recognition means describe the evaluated language subsets; public and internal scoring can differ even when the language selection is shared.
Data and attribution.
Synthetic generation and distillation can propagate incorrect targets or teacher predictions. Conversion-fidelity checks can miss errors and do not establish coverage of natural speech variation. The evaluations characterize the combined recipe, with no causal attribution to individual data or supervision choices. Frozen visual components also do not guarantee unchanged image reasoning through an updated decoder. Transfer to other backbone families remains untested.

Appendix A
Synthetic Data Construction Details
The pipeline converts selected user content to speech while preserving the dialogue structure and assistant targets. Each converted dialogue retains a corresponding text version (
Figure
3
).
Selection strategies.
Whole-turn selection synthesizes the complete user message. Instruction-only selection does the same for generative requests without reference material. Question-only selection leaves reference material in text and speaks the question. Content-focused selection speaks material requested for reading or recitation. Multi-span selection speaks several disjoint intervals while retaining intervening text. A configurable override adds whole-turn examples. Extraction validates selected source substrings before constructing the interleaved representation. Malformed selections are retried and rejected if the retry budget is exhausted.
Voice assignment and chunking.
A reference utterance is assigned once per conversation and reused across its turns and chunks. Spoken-form conversion expands written expressions into pronounceable text. Sentence-based chunking respects a duration limit. Contiguous chunks may be joined; disjoint spans retain their position among text. Speaker-aware scheduling and resumable processing preserve the reference assignment during generation.
Conversion fidelity.
Spoken-form judging compares normalized content with its source. Recognition-based judging compares a synthesized chunk’s transcript with the intended speech. Optional turn-level faithfulness checks assess consistency across the complete converted turn.

article.headline: Apriel Voice 27B：语音推理与工具调
article.lede: Apriel Voice 27B 预览版以 Gemma 4 26B-A4B 为骨干，两阶段适配语音接口，用同一模型完成语
article.problem: 语音助手不能只做识别：它要理解请求、对上下文推理、维持多轮对话，并通过工具真正把事办完。传统三级级联把 ASR、LLM 与 TTS 拆成不同组件，语音条件模型则把声学特征直接送进推理器。难点在于给一个已经后训练好的多模态解码器加语音入口，同时不丢掉原有的文本与图像能力。
article.method: 两阶段训练：第一阶段冻结骨干，只训练约 4770 万参数的语音投影器，把 Whisper large-v3-turbo 编码器的 1280 维特征经 8 帧堆叠和 SwiGLU 映射进解码器空间，用多语言转写、翻译与续写建立语音接口。第二阶段联合更新投影器与语言骨干（含 MoE 路由），数据混合语音任务、内部合成的语音条件对话、工具交互与文本回放，每个来源独立选择交叉熵、前向 KL 或二者加权；冻结的原始骨干作在线教师，配合本地教师 worker、单批前瞻与融合全词表损失完成蒸馏。推理时教师被移除，语音合成器可独立替换。
article.results: 在 thinking 模式下，模型在 Big Bench Audio 得 98.90、BFCL 得 81.13，τ-Voice 平均任务成功率 65.51%，平均延迟 1.91 秒；EVA 的 EVA-A 与 EVA-X 分别为 51.27% 和 74.13%。识别上 LibriSpeech test-clean/test-other 的 WER 为 2.23 和 5.15，全部识别基准平均 WER 12.61；德、法、西译英平均 BLEU 42.87。第二阶段用 8 个节点、16 张教师 GPU 与 48 张学生 GPU，约 3 天完成 52.6473B token 的训练暴露。
article.why_it_matters: 它表明开源的两阶段语音模型可以把语音理解、推理和工具调用放在同一个骨干上，并在 τ-Voice 上以 65.51% 的成功率和 1.91 秒延迟接近专有系统，同时语音合成可以独立更换。
article.limitations: 论文自述以英语语音理解与对话为主，多语言仅靠自动语音翻译评测，跨语种鲁棒性不均。内部与公开结果在提示、判分、推理预算和任务上限上不一致，聚合分数不构成配对显著性检验；合成数据与蒸馏可能传播错误目标，且没有对单项数据或监督选择做因果消融。冻结视觉塔也不保证图像推理不变——九项图像基准中三项高于 Gemma 基线、六项低于基线。
article.figure_caption_zh: 先学语音接口、再扩展任务能力：第一阶段冻结骨干只训投影器，第二阶段在语音任务、合成对话、工具交互与文本回放上同时更新投影器和骨干，并按来源施加交叉熵、前向 KL 或二者组合的监督。

page_papers.title: CausalWAM: Learning the Causes of Actions in World Action Models
page_papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) learn latent variables from observations and use these to both predict the evolution of the scene and to generate actions. The prediction has to be of the whole scene, whereas only a portion of the scene causes actions. WAMs fitted to demonstrations do not, in general, guarantee that they will generate actions solely from the latent causes of the demonstrated actions (the action-relevant latent variables), as the model could just as well learn to imitate in this way whilst entangling the action-relevant latent variables with the nuisance variables. We therefore separate out what causes action from what prediction depends on. We prove that under a sparsity constraint the latent variables used to generate actions are an invertible function of the action-relevant latent variables alone and the true structure is identified up to a permutation of the latent variables. This requires neither sufficient temporal dependence nor any assumptions on how the unobserved regimes evolve and holds even when the action-relevant latent variables are statistically dependent on the rest. We therefore propose CWAM (Causal WAM), which incorporates the constraint into a pretrained WAM by adding a sparse routing path to its action head, with the world modeling objective remaining unchanged. Experiments on both synthetic data and real-world robots validate the theory as well as showcase the improved efficiency in closed-loop success.

Abstract
World action models (WAMs) learn latent variables from observations and use these to both predict the evolution of the scene and to generate actions. The prediction has to be of the whole scene, whereas only a portion of the scene causes actions. WAMs fitted to demonstrations do not, in general, guarantee that they will generate actions solely from the latent causes of the demonstrated actions (the action-relevant latent variables), as the model could just as well learn to imitate in this way whilst entangling the action-relevant latent variables with the nuisance variables. We therefore separate out what causes action from what prediction depends on. We prove that under a sparsity constraint the latent variables used to generate actions are an invertible function of the action-relevant latent variables alone and the true structure is identified up to a permutation of the latent variables. This requires neither sufficient temporal dependence nor any assumptions on how the unobserved regimes evolve and holds even when the action-relevant latent variables are statistically dependent on the rest. We therefore propose CWAM (Causal WAM), which incorporates the constraint into a pretrained WAM by adding a sparse routing path to its action head, with the world modeling objective remaining unchanged. Experiments on both synthetic data and real-world robots validate the theory as well as showcase the improved efficiency in closed-loop success.
1
Introduction
The action a robot performs when stacking a single block atop another depends on the position of both blocks and the fact that the gripper is currently holding the uppermost block. The camera image’s pixels will change significantly if the robot removes the tablecloth or clears away the clutter located behind the table; however, this will have no effect upon the motion itself. WAMs (World Action Models) like Fast-WAM
(
Yuan et al., 2026
)
, and Cosmos 3
(
NVIDIA, 2026
)
are able to extract latent variables from images and can be used to generate actions from those latent variables, while also being capable of generating images of potential subsequent frames. Since prediction has to account for the whole scene, these latent variables also describe the tablecloth and the clutter. We refer to the latent variables that cause the demonstrated actions as action-relevant latent variables, and to the others as nuisance variables.
Fitting the demonstrations well does not in itself guarantee that the WAM is acting from the action-relevant latent variables. For each step of the demonstration we could write

Separating action from prediction is then about recovering (up to certain indeterminacies) the action-relevant latent variables and which of those variables cause each action dimension. Without further assumptions, the latent causal variables cannot be identified from their observations
(
Hyvärinen and Pajunen, 1999
;

)
. Observing the actions as well doesn’t help with this ambiguity, as two models can give rise to the same distribution of

whilst their latent variables differ by an arbitrary invertible transformation. This transformation can mix the action-relevant latent variables with the nuisance ones, so a very flexible action head could generate actions from variables which also contain information about the tablecloth (which doesn’t in fact cause the motion) and still fit the demonstrations equally well.
To make latent variables identifiable, existing works in nonlinear independent component analysis (ICA) introduce auxiliary variables, such as domain or time indices, or exploit temporal dependence
(
Hyvärinen and Morioka, 2016
;
Hyvärinen and Morioka, 2017
;
Hyvärinen et al., 2019
;
Khemakhem et al., 2020
)
. For latent causal processes, identifiability has been established under sufficient temporal dependence
(
Yao et al., 2022
)
and conditions on the latent dynamics
(
Song et al., 2023
)
. Interventions with known targets have also been introduced to pin down the latents
(
Lippe et al., 2022
)
. Many of these assumptions might be violated for demonstrations in complex real-world scenarios such as robotics, where some time steps might be independent, the latent dynamics might not be Markov, and controlled interventions are either prohibitively expensive or simply impossible.
Another line of research constrains the generative process by restricting the function class or enforcing sparsity in the dependency structure
(
Kivva et al., 2022
;
Zheng et al., 2022
;
Lachapelle et al., 2022
)
. Most of these studies, similar to those previously discussed, aim to recover all latent variables, requiring their conditions to hold even for nuisance variables that a robot can disregard. In contrast, results on partial identifiability focus on a subset of latent variables, determined by side information accompanying the data, such as content shared across views
(
von Kügelgen et al., 2021
;
Yao et al., 2024
)
, components invariant across domains
(
Kong et al., 2022
)
, or elements relevant to specific tasks
(
Zheng et al., 2026
)
. For robots learning from demonstrations, the relevant subset consists of the latent causes underlying the demonstrated actions. Since no view, domain, or task label directly specifies this subset, the actions themselves must indicate which latent variables are pertinent. This raises the following question:
From demonstrations alone, can we separate what causes actions from what prediction needs?
In this work, we answer this question with a constraint on the action side that leaves prediction free to use every latent variable. Since each action is generated from only part of the latent state, constraining the number of dependencies between latent variables and action dimensions can separate that part from the rest. Specifically, we prove that, without such a constraint and under nondegeneracy conditions, fitting the demonstrations only ensures that each action dimension of the estimated mechanism depends on at least as many latent variables as the true one (Prop.
1
). We then incorporate a sparsity regularization on the dependency structure between latent state and action variables during estimation. Under the same conditions, the lower bound becomes an equality and the dependency structure is identified up to a permutation of the latent variables (Thm.
1
).
Moreover, we prove that the estimated action-relevant variables under the proposed constraint are an invertible function of the ground-truth latent variables causing the true action (Thm.
2
). The latent causes of the actions are thus identified as a block and are separated from the nuisance variables. The theoretical guarantee relies purely on observational demonstrations, without requiring any interventions, sufficient temporal dependence, or any assumptions about the latent dynamics. The framework also allows dependence between action-relevant latent variables and the nuisance variables (e.g., a tablecloth could be correlated with the positions of the cubes). According to the established theory, we propose CWAM (Causal WAM), which adds a sparse routing path from the visual and task tokens to the action head in Cosmos 3 and applies a token-level surrogate of the constraint to this path (Sec.
4
). In synthetic scenarios, we validate the identifiability claims shown by our theory. On RoboCasa365, LIBERO, and a real Franka R3 robot, the routing path improves aggregate closed-loop success over Cosmos 3 without it, and in most visualized frames its routing mass falls on the object being moved and its target (Sec.
5
).

6
Conclusion
We show how to learn causal actions in WAM from observational decomposition alone. Specifically, we prove that under non-degeneracy conditions and without a sparsity constraint, each action dimension of any mechanism estimated to fit the demonstrations can contain action-irrelevant latent variables. Sparsity regularisation enables identification of the true causes of the actions and the causal structure from latent variables to actions (up to a permutation). The latent variables used to generate the actions are then an invertible function of the latent causes of the actions alone, while the full estimated state continues to describe the entire scene for prediction. Neither of the identification results rely on interventions, temporal structure or supervision. Synthetic experiments are in agreement with the theory and CWAM does in fact assist with task completion in simulation as well as on a real robot. The main limitation is the lack of component-wise identifiability that would pin down the individual latents (which may not be required for separating actions but would be useful for precise interventions). There are many more open problems in WAMs that causality can help to address and this paper represents one of the first steps towards a causal understanding of actions.

article.headline: CWAM：用稀疏路由分离驱动动作的潜变量
article.lede: 世界动作模型要预测整幅场景，但只有一部分潜变量驱动动作。作者用稀疏约束识别这部分变量，并在 Cosmos 3 上验证。
article.problem: 世界动作模型（WAM）从观测中学习潜变量，既用来预测场景演化，也用来生成动作。预测必须覆盖整幅场景，而真正导致动作的只是其中一部分潜变量。仅拟合演示并不保证动作只来自这部分因果潜变量——模型完全可能把桌布、杂物等干扰因素混进动作路径。
article.method: 作者证明：在稀疏约束下，用于生成动作的潜变量是动作相关潜变量的可逆函数，状态到动作的依赖结构在潜变量置换意义下可识别，且不要求时间依赖或干预数据。据此提出 CWAM：保留 Cosmos 3 原有的联合整流流训练与世界建模目标不变，向动作头加一条稀疏路由路径，用 token 级稀疏损失把路由质量压到少量干净上下文 token 上。
article.results: 在 n=20 个潜变量、|I_A|=4 个驱动动作的合成设置中，CWAM 稀疏选块的相关 R² 为 0.9957±0.0014，干扰超额 Δ_nuis 为 0.039±0.093，接近零；RoboCasa365 的 17 个任务上宏观成功率从 0.24 升到 0.43（13 个任务提升），LIBERO 四个 suite 均优于匹配基线，真实 Franka 堆叠任务多数试验成功而基线不到一半。在成功率最高的 4 个 RoboCasa365 任务上，仅保留路由 token 平均成功率 60.3%，随机等量 token 只有 24.5%。
article.why_it_matters: 把“预测整幅场景所需的潜变量”与“真正驱动动作的潜变量”分开，意味着动作头可以更紧凑、更可审计，也更有希望在演示分布之外保持正确。论文为 WAM 的因果理解提供了一个可检验的理论起点。
article.limitations: 理论依赖非退化条件（每个动作维度的雅可比行需张成真实父坐标，并满足避免抵消的包含条件），且只给出块级可识别性，无法确定单个潜变量；实验上 RoboCasa365 有 4 个任务成功率下降或持平，部分帧的路由权重也分散到机械臂和墙壁。
article.figure_caption_zh: 动作只依赖潜状态中的一个块；CWAM 在 Cosmos 3 上把该块的估计经稀疏路由送到动作头，同时保留世界建模的稠密路径，即图中灰色虚线。

page_papers.title: On the Origin and Evolution of Training-Inference Mismatch in LLM Reinforcement Learning
page_papers.abstract: On-policy reinforcement learning for large language models assumes that training responses are sampled from the current policy. In practice, an inference engine samples the responses and a separate trainer computes the gradients, and the training-inference mismatch between the two makes the training data off-policy. The mismatch has two sources, the numerics of the engine and the stale weights of asynchronous sampling, and a correction that stabilizes training under one source can fail under the other. We ask which property of a mismatch source decides the correction it needs. Evaluating the trainer at the sampler's weights splits each sampled-token error exactly into a numerical discrepancy of the engine and a policy lag of the trainer, and we follow both through training. The numerical discrepancy stays approximately constant, so it biases the updates by a nearly fixed amount, and centering the score at each prefix removes its leading bias. The policy lag is produced by the trainer's own updates: the bias it leaves enters the next update, which enlarges the next lag and closes a feedback loop. Importance weighting cuts this loop only while the lag ratio stays concentrated, and on Qwen3-1.7B it fails at the step where the effective sample size of the ratio falls below one half. From this account we derive the discrepancy-lag correction (DLC), which centers the numerical discrepancy, clips the lag ratio against the sampler's weights and resynchronizes the sampler when this effective sample size falls below one half. Under a stale sampler, DLC keeps the KL divergence from on-policy training within twice the KL between two independent on-policy trainings on Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B, and its resynchronization prevents collapses that the per-token corrections leave and that a KL measured on the sampler's prefixes does not detect.

Origin and Evolution of Training-Inference Mismatch
On the Origin and Evolution of Training-Inference Mismatch in LLM Reinforcement Learning
Yu Li
Yufa Zhou
Tian Lan
Abstract
On-policy reinforcement learning for large language models assumes that training responses are sampled from the current policy.
In practice, an inference engine samples the responses and a separate trainer computes the gradients, and the
training-inference mismatch
between the two makes the training data off-policy. The mismatch has two sources, the numerics of the engine and the stale weights of asynchronous sampling, and a correction that stabilizes training under one source can fail under the other.
We ask which property of a mismatch source decides the correction it needs.
Evaluating the trainer at the sampler’s weights splits each sampled-token error exactly into a
numerical discrepancy
of the engine and a
policy lag
of the trainer, and we follow both through training. The numerical discrepancy stays approximately constant, so it biases the updates by a nearly fixed amount, and centering the score at each prefix removes its leading bias. The policy lag is produced by the trainer’s own updates: the bias it leaves enters the next update, which enlarges the next lag and closes a feedback loop. Importance weighting cuts this loop only while the lag ratio stays concentrated, and on Qwen3-1.7B it fails at the step where the effective sample size of the ratio falls below one half. From this account we derive the
discrepancy-lag correction
(DLC), which centers the numerical discrepancy, clips the lag ratio against the sampler’s weights and resynchronizes the sampler when this effective sample size falls below one half. Under a stale sampler, DLC keeps the KL divergence from on-policy training within twice the KL between two independent on-policy trainings on Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B, and its resynchronization prevents collapses that the per-token corrections leave and that a KL measured on the sampler’s prefixes does not detect.

1
Introduction
Reinforcement learning for language models
(
Shao et al., 2024
;
Li et al., 2026a
;
Zhou et al., 2026a
)
typically runs two systems on the same weights. Inference engines such as vLLM
(
Kwon et al., 2023
;
Zheng et al., 2024
;
Li et al., 2026b
)
sample the responses, and a trainer computes the policy gradient on them. The engine computes token probabilities with its own kernels and precision, so its distribution
q
q
differs from the trainer’s distribution
p
p
even at identical weights
(
Yao et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2025a
)
, and low-precision samplers widen the gap. Asynchronous systems such as AReaL
(
Fu et al., 2025
)
and PipelineRL
(
Piché et al., 2025
)
add a second source, since the sampler keeps the weights of the last synchronization while the trainer moves on. Training on samples from
q
q
with gradients of
p
p
is therefore off-policy. We call the whole gap between
q
q
and
p
p
, from both sources, the
training-inference mismatch
. Prior work addresses this mismatch with three corrections
(
Yao et al., 2025
;
Marek and Ryabinin, 2026
;
Schulman et al., 2017
)
: (1) truncated importance sampling weights each sampled token by the truncated ratio
p
/
q
p/q
; (2) score centering subtracts the sampler’s mean score at each prefix and thereby removes the drift, the part of the update that depends on the advantages only through their mean; (3) PPO clips the ratio of the trainer to a reference policy at each token.
The outcome of these corrections depends on the source of the mismatch. Score centering keeps training stable with a quantized sampler and falls behind importance sampling with a stale one, while PPO trains under staleness and fails under quantization
(
Marek and Ryabinin, 2026
)
. Under staleness alone the collapse of asynchronous GRPO scales with the product of staleness and learning rate
(
Song et al., 2026
)
, and importance-weighted asynchronous training loses its effective sample size before it diverges
(
Huang et al., 2026
)
. The behavior of a correction therefore depends jointly on the estimator and on the process that produces the mismatch. At a single prefix, however, the untruncated ratio and centering both remove the drift, so the source must act through what each correction leaves after the drift and through how that remainder evolves during training. The question is which property of a mismatch source decides the correction it needs.
We trace the mismatch to its origin in the two layers of the system and follow its evolution during training. The infrastructure decides how far the sampler departs from the trainer, and the algorithm corrects what reaches the gradient. Once the infrastructure aligns sampling, reporting and token sequences, the mismatch reaches the algorithm as a numerical discrepancy and a policy lag, and the trainer’s log-probability at the sampler’s weights splits the sampled-token error exactly into these two terms, as
Figure
1
illustrates. The numerical discrepancy originates in the engine and stays approximately fixed during training. The policy lag originates in the trainer’s own updates, the residual bias it leaves enters the next update, and the next update sets the next lag. Corrections of the policy lag therefore have to keep this loop from amplifying the update. Our contributions follow this account.
❶
Following the factorization of the importance ratio at the sampler’s weights
(
Guan et al., 2026
)
, we split the sampled-token error exactly into the numerical discrepancy and the policy lag. After centering removes the drift, the remaining bias consists of a prefix, a continuation, a token and a tail term, which keep a fixed size for the numerical discrepancy and grow with the accumulated update for the policy lag.
❷
For the policy lag, the token and prefix terms enter the next update and close a loop, which locates the part of the known staleness bias
(
Song et al., 2026
;
Xu et al., 2026
)
that survives centering. As a consequence, the excess update norm of score centering over importance sampling has a positive quadratic term in the product
η
​
k
\eta k
of learning rate and step count. Ratio weighting removes the token term within its validity range, which ends where the effective sample size of the lag ratio falls below one half. On Qwen3-1.7B the heavy tail of the ratio brings this crossing to step 11, three steps before the Gaussian prediction, and importance sampling leaves the noise floor at that step.
❸
The discrepancy-lag correction (DLC) centers the numerical discrepancy, clips the lag ratio against the sampler’s weights
(
Chang et al., 2026a
)
and resynchronizes the sampler at the end of the validity range. Under a stale sampler DLC keeps the deviation from on-policy training within twice the noise floor on Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B, and on Qwen3-1.7B the resynchronization prevents the collapses that the clip alone leaves.

Background
2.1
Training-inference mismatch
Table
1
lists the mismatch by the layer that corrects it. Once the infrastructure aligns sampling, reporting and token sequences, only the weight version and the engine numerics reach the algorithm, and only the weight version changes with the update.
The other three rows of the infrastructure layer concern what the sampler reports and what the trainer receives. Top-p sampling and processed log-probabilities make the reported
q
q
differ from the distribution that drew the token, so the sampler has to report the drawn distribution. Retokenization of the decoded text can change the token sequence, and passing token ids to the trainer keeps the sequence identical on both sides. Filtering responses by their reward and deferring long responses in partial rollouts make the composition of the batch depend on the outcome, and outcome-independent batching keeps the batch a sample of
q
q
. These three mismatches vanish under the configuration of
Section
3
, so the weight version and the engine numerics remain as the two sources that the algorithm has to correct. In the algorithm layer, the weight version gives the policy lag, which grows with the update, and decoupled PPO and M2PO weight the ratio of the trainer to the sampler’s weights, while VCPO scales the learning rate by the effective sample size. The engine numerics give the numerical discrepancy, which stays approximately fixed in training, and truncated importance sampling and score centering correct it at each sampled token.

Our account places the sampler inside a training loop, since the sampler is a biased copy of the trainer that synchronizes back to it.

Section

2.2
Off-policy correction and staleness
Truncated and clipped importance weights have a long history in off-policy reinforcement learning
(
Ionides, 2008
;
Munos et al., 2016
;
Espeholt et al., 2018

(

;

;

)

(

(

)
.

(

(

)

8
Conclusion
Training-inference mismatch reaches the gradient as two components with different dynamics. The numerical discrepancy of the engine stays approximately fixed during training, so removing its drift suffices. The policy lag comes from the trainer’s own updates and feeds back through the residual bias of centering into later updates, and ratio weighting cuts this loop only until the effective sample size of the lag ratio falls below one half. DLC follows this account: it centers the discrepancy, clips the lag ratio and resynchronizes the sampler at that crossing, which keeps a stale sampler within twice the noise floor and prevents the collapses that the off-support share of the trainer’s own responses reveals.

Appendix C
Step Cost, a Larger Model and Continuous Asynchrony
Table
7
splits the wall-clock time of a training step on Qwen3-1.7B under a stale sampler into generation, the forward pass at the sampler’s weights and the parameter update, averaged over the three runs of each correction. DLC adds two costs to the step. The sampler reports its top-128 head, which doubles the generation time as it does for score centering, and the trainer computes the head log-probabilities at the sampler’s weights in a forward pass that PPO with the sampler’s weights as reference also needs. In our implementation about 19 of the 54 seconds of this forward come from a second reference forward on the KL path of verl, whose output does not enter the loss at a zero KL coefficient. The resynchronization copies the trainer’s weights to the sampler once per run in 40 steps and takes at most 1.5 seconds per copy, against about 4500 seconds of training per run. On-policy training copies the weights after each step and spends 1.2 seconds per step on the copy.

In continuous asynchronous training the sampler receives the trainer’s weights after each step, so each token carries the version that generated it. With a maximum version gap of four on Qwen3-1.7B, the sampled tokens lag the trainer by 2.85 versions on average, and DLC clips the ratio against the generating version of each token. The admission variant defers a response whose effective sample size of the lag ratio falls below one half and regenerates it with the newer weights.

article.headline: 拆解训练-推理不匹配：DLC修正策略滞后
article.lede: 论文将LLM RL的训练-推理不匹配拆为数值差异与策略滞后，提出DLC分别中心化、裁剪并重同步。
article.problem: LLM的on-policy强化学习实际由推理引擎采样、独立训练器算梯度，引擎数值差异和异步采样的陈旧权重使训练数据变成off-policy。已有重要性采样、score centering和PPO等修正对不匹配来源敏感：同一方法在量化采样器下稳定，在陈旧采样器下可能失效，反之亦然。论文追问：不匹配来源的哪个性质决定了它需要哪种修正。
article.method: 作者在采样器权重处让训练器做一次前向，把每个采样token的误差精确分解为数值差异和策略滞后。数值差异来自引擎且近似恒定，策略滞后由训练器自身更新产生并通过残差偏置进入下一轮更新，形成反馈环。据此提出DLC：中心化数值差异、用PPO clip裁剪滞后比，并在滞后比的有效样本量低于1/2时把训练器权重同步给采样器。
article.results: 在Qwen3-0.6B的陈旧采样器下，DLC第40步偏离为噪声底的1.9倍，importance sampling with centering为2.1倍，score centering为31.7倍且测试准确率仅12.2%；DLC准确率31.7%，on-policy为46.5%。Qwen3-1.7B陈旧采样器下DLC至第40步保持在噪声底1.2倍以内、结束时0.6，测试准确率51.9%，on-policy为57.6%；importance sampling在第11步有效样本量跌破1/2，偏离到第30步达噪声底152倍。Qwen3-8B上DLC偏离3.1倍、准确率49.6%，on-policy为55.3%；连续异步下DLC为1.2倍和55.9%。
article.why_it_matters: 把不匹配拆成固定的数值差异与自诱导的策略滞后，能解释为何同一修正对量化与异步一个有效、一个失效。DLC用有效样本量给出明确的重同步判据，对LLM RL训练系统的稳定性有直接工程意义。
article.limitations: 实验限于Countdown任务和40步短训练：Qwen3-0.6B/1.7B每个配置三次，Qwen3-8B与连续异步每组仅一次，长期大规模行为尚未验证。DLC每步需在采样器权重处额外前向，Qwen3-1.7B陈旧采样器下步时约113.2秒，而on-policy为50.4秒；重同步阈值1/2和clip 0.2等超参也仍是设定值。

page_papers.title: An ODE-based Sampler for Discrete Diffusion Models
page_papers.abstract: The marginals of a continuous diffusion model can be reproduced by a deterministic ordinary differential equation (ODE), known as the probability flow ODE, which provides a foundation for accelerated sampling and consistency distillation. In this paper we address the question whether an analogous formulation exists for discrete diffusion models and answer it affirmatively by introducing exponential residual flows (ERFs). Our framework augments the discrete state with a continuous residual variable for each token and position. These residuals evolve deterministically according to piecewise-defined ODEs whose vector fields depend on the current discrete state and the forward and backward rate matrices of the prescribed diffusion model. The discrete state changes whenever a residual reaches zero. We prove that this construction preserves the marginals of the original diffusion. We derive a practical discretization of our sampler and specialize it to masked and uniform diffusion. The deterministic trajectories of ERFs support consistency distillation and yield empirical improvements over previous approaches across a variety of benchmarks including code and text generation tasks.
page_papers.content: The marginals of a continuous diffusion model can be reproduced by a deterministic ordinary differential equation (ODE), known as the probability flow ODE, which provides a foundation for accelerated sampling and consistency distillation. In this paper we address the question whether an analogous formulation exists for discrete diffusion models and answer it affirmatively by introducing exponential residual flows (ERFs). Our framework augments the discrete state with a continuous residual variable for each token and position. These residuals evolve deterministically according to piecewise-defined ODEs whose vector fields depend on the current discrete state and the forward and backward rate matrices of the prescribed diffusion model. The discrete state changes whenever a residual reaches zero. We prove that this construction preserves the marginals of the original diffusion. We derive a practical discretization of our sampler and specialize it to masked and uniform diffusion. The deterministic trajectories of ERFs support consistency distillation and yield empirical improvements over previous approaches across a variety of benchmarks including code and text generation tasks.

article.headline: 为离散扩散模型构造概率流ODE采样器
article.lede: 论文提出指数残差流ERF，为离散扩散模型给出确定性ODE采样，并证明其保持原扩散模型的边缘分布。
article.problem: 连续扩散模型的边缘分布可由概率流ODE确定性复现，这为加速采样和一致性蒸馏提供了基础。但离散扩散模型是否存在对应的ODE形式，此前没有得到明确回答。
article.method: 作者为每个token和位置的离散状态增加一个连续残差变量，残差按分段定义的ODE确定性演化，其向量场依赖当前离散状态以及给定扩散模型的前向、后向速率矩阵。当某个残差归零时离散状态发生跳变，作者证明该构造保持原扩散模型的边缘分布，并给出可实现的离散化方案，分别针对masked扩散与uniform扩散做了特化。
article.results: 论文摘要声称，ERF在代码与文本生成等多项基准上优于此前方法，但摘要未给出具体数字。图注显示对比对象为ERF、ancestral sampling、Euler与categorical τ-leaping：上排是GSM8K在不同采样温度下的准确率（附逐点95% bootstrap置信区间），下排是OpenWebText上的熵与GPT-2 Large生成困惑度，困惑度轴取对数并反向。
article.why_it_matters: 若确定性轨迹确实成立，离散扩散就能像连续扩散一样借用ODE求解器加速采样，并支持一致性蒸馏这类少步生成技术。这把连续扩散的工具链迁移到了文本、代码等离散序列领域。
article.limitations: 离散状态在残差归零时跳变、向量场分段定义，实际采样精度会受步长与离散化方式影响，温度敏感性也需要在图示范围之外进一步检验。摘要只给出定性结论，并未报告采样步数、加速比以及与一致性蒸馏结合后的具体收益数字。

page_papers.title: Drift, Then Spread: Learning One-Step Generative Policies for Online Reinforcement Learning
page_papers.abstract: Generative policies offer expressive action distributions for online reinforcement learning (RL), but many diffusion- and flow-based policies require costly iterative sampling. We propose DriftSpread, a one-step generative policy based on Drifting for online maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL. To incorporate entropy without a tractable policy density, we build on an energy-based view of Drifting and derive critic-guided Drift and entropy-induced Spread from the negative MaxEnt objective. Our method learns these updates sequentially in the same actor, using action regression for value improvement and distribution matching to capture the effect of entropy. The actor updates require neither direct samples from the critic-defined Boltzmann target nor policy-density or score estimation. Under exact fitting with a fixed critic, we prove convergence to the Boltzmann target in the small-step limit followed by the long-time limit. On MuJoCo, DriftSpread achieves the highest aggregate normalized return among all evaluated methods, while outperforming the diffusion- and flow-based baselines in both training and inference efficiency.

Drift, Then Spread: Learning One-Step Generative Policies for Online Reinforcement Learning
Chunyu Luo
Hongyu Zhao
Guangyi Ni
Yue Song
Lingkai Kong
The University of Hong Kong  Beihang University

Abstract
Generative policies offer expressive action distributions
for online reinforcement learning (RL), but many diffusion-
and flow-based policies require costly iterative sampling.
We propose
DriftSpread
, a one-step generative policy based on
Drifting for online maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL.
To incorporate entropy without a tractable policy density,
we build on an energy-based view of Drifting and derive
critic-guided Drift and entropy-induced Spread from the
negative MaxEnt objective.
Our method learns these updates sequentially in the same
actor, using action regression for value improvement and
distribution matching to capture the effect of entropy.
The actor updates require neither direct samples from
the critic-defined Boltzmann target nor policy-density
or score estimation.
Under exact fitting with a fixed critic, we prove
convergence to the Boltzmann target in the small-step
limit followed by the long-time limit.
On MuJoCo,
DriftSpread
achieves the highest aggregate
normalized return among all evaluated methods,
while outperforming the diffusion- and flow-based
baselines in both training and inference efficiency.

Generative policies offer expressive action distributions
for online reinforcement learning (RL).
Diffusion- and flow-based policies can capture multimodal
distributions that are difficult to represent with a single
Gaussian
(
Dong et al., 2025
;
Celik et al., 2025
)
.
However, many of these approaches generate actions through
iterative sampling, requiring repeated network evaluations
during training and inference.
Recent MeanFlow-based methods reduce this cost through
few-step or one-step action generation
(
Dong et al., 2026
;
Chen et al., 2025
;
Kim et al., 2026
)
.
Drifting offers a different way to train one-step
generators
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
.
At each training iteration, it uses target data to
move generated samples toward the desired distribution,
then trains the generator to reproduce the moved
samples from the same inputs.
Through these repeated updates, the generator learns
to produce samples from the target distribution in
a single forward pass at inference.
This approach has shown better performance than
MeanFlow variants in one-step image generation on
ImageNet
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
.
These results motivate exploring Drifting for online
RL, where its use remains less studied.
We consider the maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL objective,
which balances expected return with policy entropy
to encourage exploration
(
Haarnoja et al., 2018
)
.
The critic defines a Boltzmann target distribution
for policy improvement, but does not directly provide
samples from it
(
Li et al., 2026
)
.
We therefore adopt an energy-based view of Drifting
(
Gretton et al., 2026
;
Han et al., 2026
)
,
using the negative MaxEnt policy-improvement objective
as the energy.
This energy guides updates to actions generated by
the current policy.
For the value term, critic gradients tell us how to
move actions toward higher values.
The entropy term is harder to use: an implicit actor
generates actions but does not provide a tractable
density for computing their distribution’s entropy.
We therefore need training targets that capture
the effect of entropy without explicitly computing it.
We propose
DriftSpread
, a one-step generative policy in the
Drifting model family for online MaxEnt RL.
Our key idea is to derive two updates from this energy
and fit them sequentially to the same actor through
repeated Drift–Spread cycles.
In each cycle, Drift uses critic gradients to move
generated actions toward higher values.
The actor then learns to reproduce these updated
actions from the same inputs through regression.
Spread captures the entropy contribution through
diffusion of the action distribution.
We approximate this diffusion by adding appropriately
scaled independent noise to actions from the updated
actor, then train the actor to match the resulting
distribution.
This allows the actor to learn the effect of entropy
without explicitly computing it.
For a fixed critic, we prove
that the learned policy converges to the Boltzmann
target distribution in the small-step, long-time limit.
Our main contributions are:
(1) We introduce
DriftSpread
, a Drifting model for online
MaxEnt RL with expressive policies and one-step action
generation.
(2) We develop sequential Drift–Spread training through
critic-guided regression and entropy regularization to
address the challenge of entropy computation for implicit
policies.
(3) On MuJoCo,
DriftSpread
outperforms 13 baselines
in aggregate normalized return, with lower training
costs than the diffusion, flow, and MeanFlow baselines
(Figure
1
).
2
Related Work
Generative policies for online RL.
Diffusion and flow models provide expressive action
distributions for online RL.
One line of work optimizes policies by backpropagating
critic gradients through diffusion or flow sampling
(
Wang et al., 2024
;
Lyu et al., 2025
)
.
DIME also differentiates through diffusion sampling
while optimizing a variational lower bound on the
MaxEnt objective
(
Celik et al., 2025
)
.
Another line of work constructs training targets
for learning critic-defined Boltzmann distributions.
DQS uses weighted averages of critic gradients
to construct score targets
(
Jain et al., 2025
)
.
SDAC and MaxEntDP instead use critic values to weight
denoising supervision and noise estimates, respectively
(
Ma et al., 2025
;
Dong et al., 2025
)
.
Reverse flow matching unifies these gradient-expectation
and noise-expectation formulations through posterior-mean
estimation
(
Li et al., 2026
)
.
These approaches use iterative action sampling,
motivating few-step and one-step policies for online RL.
MeanFlow was introduced for one-step generative modeling
and learns average velocities
(
Geng et al., 2025
)
.
Recent online RL methods use this formulation
to learn policies with fewer generation steps.
FPMD trains rectified-flow and MeanFlow policies
through policy mirror descent, with both variants
supporting one-step inference
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
.
MFPO trains few-step MeanFlow policies using velocity
estimates for critic-defined Boltzmann targets
(
Dong et al., 2026
)
, while SOM constructs velocity
targets from critic-based score estimates to train
one-step MeanFlow policies
(
Kim et al., 2026
)
.
Drifting models and policy learning.
Drifting learns one-step generators by repeatedly
moving generated samples and training the generator
to reproduce their updated positions.
This approach has achieved state-of-the-art performance
in one-step image generation on ImageNet
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
.
Subsequent work relates specific Drifting fields
to Wasserstein gradient flows
(
Gretton et al., 2026
)
and uses
optimal-transport couplings to construct sample
updates
(
He et al., 2026
)
.
W-Flow derives sample movements from an objective
over distributions and trains a one-step generator
on the resulting samples
(
Han et al., 2026
)
.
Drifting has also been applied to policy learning.
For offline RL, DriftQL combines critic-guided
policy improvement with a Drifting regularizer
based on the behavior distribution
(
Houssaini et al., 2026
)
.
For offline-to-online RL, Drifting Field Policy
derives a KL-regularized policy update through
Wasserstein gradient flow and constructs training
targets from actions ranked by the critic
(
Koo et al., 2026
)
.
Our work focuses on online MaxEnt RL from scratch.

Conclusion and Limitations
We introduced
DriftSpread
, a Drifting-based approach to
learning expressive one-step policies for online RL.
Building on an energy-based view of Drifting, we derive
critic-guided Drift and entropy-induced Spread from
the MaxEnt objective.
The two updates are learned sequentially by the same
actor: Drift moves actions toward higher values,
while Spread matches a broader distribution constructed
from the updated actor.
This design incorporates the effect of entropy without
estimating policy densities or scores, while allowing
each action sample to be generated in one forward pass.
Under exact fitting, our analysis establishes convergence
to the fixed-critic Boltzmann target in the small-step,
long-time limit.
MuJoCo experiments show that
DriftSpread
combines strong
control performance with efficient training and inference,
supporting Drifting as a practical approach to
generative policy learning.
Our work leaves two directions for future research.
First, our evaluation is limited to simulation
environments.
Testing on real-world control tasks would help
assess robustness to observation noise and changes
in system dynamics.
Second, we use a fixed spreading-noise distribution
and scale during training.
Adapting the spreading strength as learning progresses
may better balance exploration and value improvement.

E.3
Evaluation and runtime measurements
Control performance.
The main MuJoCo learning curves report evaluation
returns averaged over five seeds, with sample standard
deviations shown as shaded bands.
For
DriftSpread
and MFPO, evaluation generates ten
candidate actions and executes the action with the
highest critic value.
Other methods use the action-selection rules of
their reference implementations.
Aggregate normalized return.
For each task and seed, we average the final ten
evaluation returns.
We divide each result by the corresponding task’s
mean return for
DriftSpread
, averaged over its seeds.
We then average the normalized results across
seeds and tasks, giving each task equal weight.
Thus a normalized return of one corresponds to
the
DriftSpread
reference level.
The aggregate error bars are 95% bootstrap intervals
obtained by resampling seed results while keeping
the task-specific normalization constants fixed.
Training and inference time.
The methods included in the efficiency comparison
are timed using JAX implementations on the same
NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU.
We exclude one-time compilation and warm-up from
both training and inference measurements.
Training measurements also exclude evaluation
and experiment-management overhead.
Average training time is the total GPU time for
one seed on all five tasks, each with
10
6
10^{6}
interactions, divided by five.
Inference time is measured per selected action and
averaged across tasks.
It includes candidate generation, critic scoring,
and final selection when these steps are used.
For
DriftSpread
and MFPO, this includes all ten evaluation
candidates.
Each candidate requires one generation step for

article.headline: DriftSpread：在线RL的一步生成策略
article.lede: 提出一步生成策略 DriftSpread：评论家引导的 Drift 更新价值，熵诱导的 Spread 扩展分布。
article.problem: 扩散与流策略能表达多峰动作分布，但通常需要迭代采样，训练和推理成本高。最大熵 RL 需要利用熵项，而隐式 actor 不提供可处理的密度或 score，难以直接计算熵。
article.method: 方法基于 Drifting 的能量视角，从负最大熵目标推导出评论家引导的 Drift 与熵诱导的 Spread。每个周期先让动作沿 critic 梯度移动并用回归拟合，再向更新后 actor 的动作加噪、用 MMD/特征函数匹配其分布，从而在同一个 actor 上顺序学习。推理时只需一次前向。
article.results: 在五个 MuJoCo-v3 任务、每任务 10^6 次交互和 5 个随机种子下，DriftSpread 在 13 个基线中取得最高聚合归一化回报；单动作推理耗时 0.15 ms，低于 DIME 的 1.24 ms 和两步 MFPO 的 0.36 ms。玩具高斯实验中，顺序拟合的 KL 为 0.000422，联合拟合为 0.512165；步长从 0.01 降到 0.000625 时，顺序拟合 KL 从 0.001788 降到 6.29×10^-6，联合拟合仍约 0.51。
article.why_it_matters: 若能在保持表达力的同时把动作生成压到一次前向，生成式策略在在线 RL 中的训练与部署成本会更可接受，也为免密度/score 的最大熵策略学习提供了一条路径。
article.limitations: 评估仅限 MuJoCo 仿真，尚未验证真实控制中的观测噪声与动力学变化；扩散噪声分布和尺度在训练中固定，收敛保证也只覆盖固定 critic、精确拟合及小步长/长时间极限。
article.figure_caption_zh: DriftSpread 概览：(a) critic 学习与顺序 Drift–Spread actor 更新交替，Drift 用动作回归、Spread 用分布匹配；(b) 示意负最大熵目标下 Drift 将动作推向更高价值、Spread 扩展分布以体现熵。

figure.caption: {Overview of {}.} (a) Training alternates between critic learning and sequential Drift--Spread actor updates, using action regression for Drift and distribution matching for Spread. The maps $f_ $ represent the same actor at different training stages, each generating an action sample from reference noise in one forward pass. (b) The surface schematically represents the negative MaxEnt objective over policy distributions. The samples below illustrate how Drift moves actions toward higher critic values and Spread then broadens the post-Drift distribution to capture the effect of entropy.

page_papers.title: ReLift: Dense 3D Tracking as Lifted Trajectory Repair
page_papers.abstract: Dense 3D tracking from monocular video requires establishing point correspondences over time, estimating their depth, and inferring their trajectories during occlusion. Existing methods typically learn these tasks jointly, a demanding objective given the scarcity of 4D supervision. We show that strong pretrained 2D trackers and 3D geometry models provide an effective foundation: lifted trajectories, with occluded segments simply interpolated, already rival dedicated 3D trackers using the same geometry. However, lifted trajectories inherit correspondence and depth errors, and under occlusion, their depth comes from the occluder rather than the tracked point. We introduce ReLift, an efficient feed-forward framework that recasts dense 3D tracking as geometric trajectory repair and completion. At its core, a trajectory corrector alternates attention along and across trajectories to preserve reliable observations, repair corrupted positions, and complete missing motion. Using only geometric inputs allows us to train directly on 3D trajectories with simulated lifting errors, decoupling training from images and from any specific tracker or geometry model. Concentrating 4D supervision on trajectory refinement yields a reusable model that consistently improves lifted trajectories across trackers and geometry providers without retraining, so it benefits directly from future advances in either component. On WorldTrack, ReLift achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy, improving on the strongest baselines by 2.1 APD on all points and 3.0 on dynamic points, with faster configurations remaining competitive with leading 3D trackers while running faster than 4RC. Visit our supplementry page for more examples and code.
page_papers.content:
ReLift: Dense 3D Tracking as Lifted
Trajectory Repair
Assaf Singer
1∗
Maroun Khriesh
1∗
Noam Rotstein
1,2
Yoni Kasten
1,2
Or Litany
1,2
1
Technion – Israel Institute of Technology
2
NVIDIA
*
Equal contribution
Abstract
Dense 3D tracking from monocular video requires establishing point correspondences over time, estimating their depth, and inferring their trajectories during occlusion.
Existing methods typically learn these tasks jointly, a demanding objective given the scarcity of 4D supervision.
We show that strong pretrained 2D trackers and 3D geometry models provide an effective foundation: lifted trajectories, with occluded segments simply interpolated, already rival dedicated 3D trackers using the same geometry.
However, lifted trajectories inherit correspondence and depth errors, and under occlusion, their depth comes from the occluder rather than the tracked point.
We introduce ReLift, an efficient feed-forward framework that recasts dense 3D tracking as geometric trajectory repair and completion. At its core, a trajectory corrector alternates attention along and across trajectories to preserve reliable observations, repair corrupted positions, and complete missing motion. Using only geometric inputs allows us to train directly on 3D trajectories with simulated lifting errors, decoupling training from images and from any specific tracker or geometry model.
Concentrating 4D supervision on trajectory refinement yields a reusable model that consistently improves lifted trajectories across trackers and geometry providers without retraining, so it benefits directly from future advances in either component. On WorldTrack, ReLift achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy, improving on the strongest baselines by 2.1 APD on all points and 3.0 on dynamic points, with faster configurations remaining competitive with leading 3D trackers while running
2.7
–
4.4
×
2.7\text{--}4.4\times
faster than 4RC.
Visit our
project page
for more examples and code.
Figure 1:
ReLift combines pretrained 2D tracking and 3D geometry
with learned trajectory repair and completion, achieving state-of-the-art
dense 3D tracking accuracy on WorldTrack and a strong speed–accuracy trade-off.
Left:
Long-range 3D trajectories recovered from a real-world video.
Right:
WorldTrack accuracy versus full-pipeline FPS
(see Appendix
D.4
for details).
1
Introduction
Dense 3D point trajectories describe how scene content moves through space over
time, and are key in downstream tasks such as manipulation policy learning,
dynamic scene reconstruction, sensor simulation, and motion-controlled video
generation
(
Chen et al., 2025
;
Bharadhwaj et al., 2024
;
Lu et al., 2024
;
Geng et al., 2025
;
Borreda et al., 2026
;
Singer et al., 2026
)
.
Recovering them from monocular video is usually posed as a single learning
problem: one feed-forward network is trained end to end to output 3D tracks.
Such a network has to learn three things at once: finding correspondence across
frames, recovering the geometry of the scene, and inferring motion behind
occlusions. However, pretrained models already excel at two of these tasks.
Dedicated 2D trackers establish strong
correspondences
(
Harley et al., 2025
;
Lai et al., 2026
)
and can exceed
the image-plane accuracy of projected 3D predictions (Appendix
C.4
),
while geometry models provide depth and cameras learned from scalable geometric
supervision without requiring annotated dynamic 4D
trajectories
(
Lin et al., 2025
;
Wang et al., 2026
)
.
This motivates focusing the scarce 4D supervision on what remains: repairing
errors in the combined estimates and completing occluded motion.
We therefore introduce ReLift, which combines strong 2D correspondences and
pretrained scene geometry for dense 3D tracking.
We take the viewing ray of each point from a 2D tracker and its
range along that ray from a depth model, and lift the two into a 3D trajectory
we call the lift.
Since occluded tracks sample the occluder’s depth, we discard predictions flagged as occluded and initialize missing positions by interpolation.
Even before learned correction, these initialized lifts can match or exceed the mean accuracy of
learned 3D trackers using the same geometry (Tables
1
and
2
).
However, these lifts still lack observations during occlusion and suffer from jumps at depth
boundaries and jitter from per-frame depth fluctuations. These failures can produce severe
trajectory discontinuities and leave hidden motion unresolved.
We recast dense 3D tracking as geometric trajectory repair and completion.
A compact learned corrector preserves reliable observations while repairing corrupted positions and
recovering missing motion. Alternating attention along and across tracks shares temporal and spatial
evidence, while processing track groups independently keeps dense feed-forward correction efficient.
A natural training strategy is to run pretrained tracking and geometry models on synthetic videos
with ground-truth 3D trajectories, then train the corrector to recover those trajectories from the
resulting lifts. However, this ties the training inputs to the errors of the chosen estimators.
We avoid this by training without ever running a tracker, a depth model, or a
renderer. We model the geometric effects of lifting failures directly as
randomized corruptions of clean 3D trajectories from
PointOdyssey
(
Zheng et al., 2023
)
, producing
simulated lifts
from which
we train a network to recover the clean trajectories.
Training uses geometric annotations without images or provider predictions,
concentrating supervision on learning motion priors for trajectory repair and
completion (Sec.
3.4
).
Our ablation supports this choice: training on simulated lifts improves accuracy over
training on lifts generated by AllTracker and Depth Anything 3 (Sec.
4.4
).
Training on simulated lifts supports transfer across providers. We evaluate the same ReLift corrector without retraining with AllTracker
(
Harley et al., 2025
)
or
CoWTracker
(
Lai et al., 2026
)
, each paired with depth and camera estimates from
Depth Anything 3
(
Lin et al., 2025
)
, VGGT-
Ω
\Omega
(
Wang et al., 2026
)
, or 4RC
(
Luo et al., 2026
)
.
Correction improves all six lifts (Fig.
3
).
Moreover, using the same depth and camera estimates as 4RC, our 2D tracking and correction pipeline
achieves higher mean tracking accuracy than 4RC’s trajectory predictions (Table
1
).
Our contributions can be summarized as follows:
•
A strong lifting baseline.
We show that pretrained 2D tracks lifted with
estimated geometry and simple gap initialization can match or exceed dedicated 3D trackers
using the same geometry.
•
ReLift,
an efficient feed-forward framework for dense monocular 3D tracking that
combines pretrained 2D motion and 3D geometry through learned trajectory repair and completion.
•
A provider-agnostic training strategy based on randomized geometric corruptions of synthetic trajectories,
without running tracking or geometry models during training. The same weights transfer
across evaluated providers without retraining, allowing the framework to incorporate future advances in
either component.
•
Our framework achieves state-of-the-art mean dense 3D tracking accuracy on WorldTrack, with faster
configurations retaining competitive accuracy at substantially lower runtime than comparably
accurate 3D trackers.
2
Related Work
Dynamic 3D reconstruction from monocular video.
Classical non-rigid structure-from-motion methods recover time-varying 3D
structure from image correspondences using local rigidity and low-rank
constraints to reduce monocular ambiguity
(
Bregler et al., 2000
;
Akhter et al., 2008
;
Taylor et al., 2010
;
Dai et al., 2014
)
.
Modern per-video optimization methods combine image evidence with depth,
tracking, and deformation priors
(
Zhang et al., 2022
;
Liu et al., 2023
)
.
Shape of Motion
(
Wang et al., 2025b
)
and MoSca
(
Lei et al., 2024
)
combine pretrained depth and tracking cues with structured motion
representations for reconstruction and rendering.
These cues provide the initialization that rendering-based optimization needs, since
photometric gradients vanish when rendered and observed content do not
overlap
(
Cohen Rimon et al., 2026
)
.
Uni4D
(
Yao et al., 2025
)
and TrackingWorld
(
Lu et al., 2025
)
optimize camera poses and
dense 3D trajectories from pretrained depth, tracking and segmentation models, or from densified
2D tracks. These methods demonstrate the strength
of combining 2D motion with 3D geometry, but require lengthy per-scene optimization;
we pursue this combination with a feed-forward model.
Feed-forward 3D geometry models.
DUSt3R and MASt3R predict geometry and correspondences from image
pairs
(
Wang et al., 2024
;
Leroy et al., 2024
)
, while VGGT, VGGT-
Ω
\Omega
, and
Depth Anything 3 extend geometry estimation to multiple
views
(
Wang et al., 2025a
;
Wang et al., 2026
;
Lin et al., 2025
)
.
MonST3R adapts point-map prediction to dynamic scenes and aligns predictions across a
video
(
Zhang et al., 2025b
)
; St4RTrack and Dynamic
Point Maps also represent motion and correspondences
(
Feng et al., 2025
;
Sucar et al., 2025
)
,
with V-DPM extending pairwise dynamic point maps to video
(
Sucar et al., 2026
)
.
Geometry and tracking capabilities thus overlap. In our pipeline, frozen geometry models
supply depth and cameras, while 2D trackers establish point identities across frames.
2D tracking.
2D tracking follows the image projections of scene points over time.
CoTracker jointly tracks multiple points
(
Karaev et al., 2024
)
, while AllTracker and
CoWTracker extend tracking to every reference-frame pixel
(
Harley et al., 2025
;
Lai et al., 2026
)
.
Per-video self-supervision also yields strong correspondences without ground-truth annotations
for the input video:
DINO-Tracker adapts pretrained image features
(
Tumanyan et al., 2024
)
, while OmniMotion
optimizes globally consistent tracks
(
Wang et al., 2023
)
.
These approaches show that correspondence estimation can exploit real-video evidence without
annotated 3D motion, motivating its use as a separate component.
Our comparison supports reusing
strong 2D correspondences: native CoWTracker surpasses the evaluated 3D methods in image-space
accuracy (Appendix
C.4
).
Established tracks also provide a useful representation for recovering dynamic 3D structure.
TracksTo4D reconstructs geometry and motion from 2D tracks using a feed-forward, low-rank
formulation without 3D supervision
(
Kasten et al., 2024
)
. Seurat learns depth changes from
2D trajectories and combines them with pretrained depth estimates
(
Cho et al., 2025
)
.
Building on these precedents, ReLift starts from tracks already lifted with pretrained depth and
cameras, and learns 3D residuals to repair corrupted observations and complete missing motion.
Dense feed-forward 3D tracking.
Feed-forward 3D trackers estimate trajectories from video, either jointly predicting geometry and
motion or conditioning on externally supplied depth.
DELTA and DELTAv2 predict dense long-range 3D tracks using video and depth
inputs
(
Ngo et al., 2025b
;
Ngo et al., 2025a
)
, while SpatialTrackerV2 jointly
estimates geometry, camera motion, and point motion
(
Xiao et al., 2025
)
.
Trace Anything, Track4World, and 4RC predict dense trajectories or queryable
geometry and motion
(
Liu et al., 2026
;
Lu et al., 2026
;
Luo et al., 2026
)
.
TrackCraft3R repurposes pretrained video-diffusion models for dense 3D
tracking
(
Nam et al., 2026
)
; MotionCrafter uses video generative
priors for geometry and scene flow
(
Zhu et al., 2026
)
.
Available 3D motion supervision includes complete synthetic trajectories from
PointOdyssey
(
Zheng et al., 2023
)
and trajectories reconstructed from real stereo videos
in Stereo4D
(
Jin et al., 2025
)
. We use PointOdyssey to learn repair and completion of
lifted trajectories. Under matched geometry, these lifts already rival dedicated 3D trackers,
and correction further improves them
(Sec.
4.2
).
3
Method
Given a monocular video, we recover dense 3D trajectories in the camera coordinates of the reference frame
I

I_{0}

Frozen pretrained models supply 2D tracks, depth and camera estimates, which we combine into
lifted trajectories (Sec.
3.1

The lift is accurate where tracking and depth are reliable.
We use predicted visibility to mask observations, leaving gaps to complete. Retained observations
may still be corrupted by missed occlusions, depth errors or tracking drift, and therefore require repair.
Our corrector model uses positions, viewing rays and availability masks (Sec.
3.2

We hypothesize that temporal inconsistencies and disagreements between tracks provide cues for repair, while observations before and after gaps, together with related motion, can guide completion.
We therefore use alternating attention along and across tracks to aggregate these cues and predict 3D residual corrections (Sec.

Temporal chunking and batched track groups enable efficient

2
).
Because the corrector uses only geometry, we train it on simulated lifts
constructed directly from clean 3D trajectory annotations, without rendering
images or running providers (Sec.
3.4

Conclusion
We showed that pretrained 2D tracks lifted with estimated geometry and simple gap initialization
already rival dedicated 3D trackers using the same geometry. Building on this observation,
ReLift combines these providers with efficient feed-forward trajectory repair and completion
for dense monocular 3D tracking. Training on simulated lifting errors enables one corrector to
improve all evaluated tracker–geometry combinations without retraining, with the largest gains
on occluded points. Our framework achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy on WorldTrack, while
faster configurations retain competitive accuracy at substantially lower runtime than comparably
accurate 3D trackers. Performance remains sensitive to input geometry (Appendix
C.1
),
motivating future work on robustness to geometric and persistent correspondence errors.

Evaluation protocol.
We project 3D predictions through their associated cameras without ground-truth alignment.
Projections are mapped to original image coordinates, accounting for resizing and crop offsets,
before the common rescaling. Point–frames behind the ground-truth camera are excluded;
predictions behind their camera or with non-finite projections count as misses at every threshold.
Native AllTracker and CoWTracker predictions are scored directly in 2D at the same queries,
with the same scaling and ground-truth masks.
Track4World and DELTAv2 use inputs capped to our grid, with ADT uncapped
(Appendix
B.2
). PS has identical All and Dyn scores because all its queries
meet the dynamic-track criterion.

Results.
Native CoWTracker achieves the highest APD2D in every reported column, outperforming projected
3D trajectories and motivating our use of strong pretrained 2D correspondences
(Sec.
4.2
).
Our CoWTracker variant with 4RC geometry leads mean All APD2D among 3D methods and ranks second
on Dyn, behind Track4World. Switching from AllTracker to CoWTracker improves every dataset and
geometry pairing, adding 1.86–1.92 points to mean All and 2.32–2.36 to mean Dyn. For either
tracker, the means vary across geometry providers by only 0.15 (All) and at most 0.57 (Dyn) points.
Tracker choice therefore has a larger effect on APD2D here.
Relation to 3D accuracy.
All six of our configurations remain below their native tracker in both means.
With CoWTracker and 4RC geometry, the gaps are 1.48 points
on All and 3.82 on Dyn. This comparison evaluates the complete pipeline; it neither isolates
the corrector’s effect nor separates visible and occluded points.
APD2D evaluates trajectories together with their projection cameras, including any camera recovery.
It cannot measure range errors along a valid viewing ray: lifting and reprojecting through the
same camera returns the input pixel. The small variation across geometry providers therefore
does not imply similar 3D accuracy. The APD3D gains over initialized lifts in Fig.
3
provide complementary evidence of improved 3D estimation.

article.headline: ReLift：把稠密 3D 跟踪变为轨迹修复
article.lede: 冻结的 2D 跟踪器与深度模型把像素提升成 3D 轨迹，小型校正器负责修补缺口与错误——ReLift 在 WorldTr
article.problem: 稠密单目 3D 跟踪要同时解决跨帧对应、深度估计和遮挡下的运动推断。现有方法通常用一个网络端到端联合学习这三件事，但 4D 监督数据稀缺，训练目标负担很重。论文则主张把前两项交给预训练的 2D 跟踪器与几何模型。
article.method: ReLift 用 2D 跟踪器给出的像素轨迹确定视线方向、用深度模型给出沿视线的距离，把两者合成 3D 提升轨迹；被标记为遮挡的观测被丢弃，缺口用插值初始化。校正器对每条轨迹的 token 交替做时间注意力和跨轨迹注意力，输出逐帧 XYZ 残差并加回初始化轨迹。训练时直接在 PointOdyssey 的干净 3D 轨迹上注入随机的射线、距离和可见性误差，不运行跟踪器、深度模型或渲染器。
article.results: 在 WorldTrack 上，CoWTracker + 4RC 几何的平均 APD3D 达到 89.01（全部点）和 86.95（动态点），比全部点最强基线 4RC 高 2.1 点、比动态点最强基线 V-DPM 高 3.0 点。校正相对初始化提升平均增加 1.6–3.6 点，CoWTracker + VGGT-Ω 的全部点 APD3D 从 84.9 升到 87.5。VGGT-Ω 配置完整流水线耗时 7.3–11.7 秒，比 4RC 的 31.8 秒快 2.7–4.4 倍。
article.why_it_matters: 把稀缺的 4D 监督集中在轨迹修复上，使同一组权重能跨不同跟踪器和几何提供方迁移，未来任一组件进步都可直接转化为收益。
article.limitations: 性能仍受输入几何质量制约——Kubric 上使用 DA3/VGGT-Ω 几何时全点 APD3D 为 67.29/66.57，明显低于 4RC 的 85.33，且训练未显式模拟相机位姿误差与持续的身份切换；校正器按轨迹组处理，预测也可能受同组其他轨迹影响。
article.figure_caption_zh: ReLift 推理流程：冻结的 2D 跟踪器与几何模型把视频观测提升为含噪、带缺口的 3D 轨迹，校正器再预测逐帧 XYZ 残差得到最终轨迹。

The corrector adds residuals to initialized XYZ coordinates to produce the final trajectories (d--e). Below: ray--point tokens $ _{ti}$ are grouped into $C$-frame tracklets and embedded as tokens $ h_{ni}$, then processed by alternating temporal and across-track attention. page_papers.title: HiFOR: Hierarchical Foresight with Action-Guided World Grounding for Vision-Language-Action Model
page_papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated promising capabilities in robotic manipulation by integrating visual perception, language understanding, and action generation. Recent advances have further incorporated future prediction to enhance the understanding of environmental dynamics and task progression. However, existing methods often model short-term dynamics and long-term task objectives separately, while directly incorporating predicted futures into action policies without sufficiently considering their relevance to current action requirements. To address these limitations, we propose HiFOR, a hierarchical foresight framework with action-guided world retrieval. Specifically, Hierarchical Foresight Prediction jointly predicts short-term state evolution, semantic milestones, and final goal states through a Hierarchical Dependency Mask (HDM), establishing dependencies across temporal horizons. Building upon these predictions, Structure-Aware Latent World Modeling organizes future latent representations along the horizon, view, and spatial dimensions to facilitate fine-grained retrieval. Furthermore, Action-Guided Factorized World Retrieval adaptively retrieves relevant future information from the structured latent world based on evolving action representations during denoising, providing targeted guidance for action generation. Extensive experiments on two simulation benchmarks and six real-world robotic manipulation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.
