Abstract
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated promising capabilities in robotic manipulation by integrating visual perception, language understanding, and action generation. Recent advances have further incorporated future prediction to enhance the understanding of environmental dynamics and task progression. However, existing methods often model short-term dynamics and long-term task objectives separately, while directly incorporating predicted futures into action policies without sufficiently considering their relevance to current action requirements. To address these limitations, we propose
HiFOR
, a hierarchical foresight framework with action-guided world retrieval. Specifically,
Hierarchical Foresight Prediction
jointly predicts short-term state evolution, semantic milestones, and final goal states through a Hierarchical Dependency Mask (HDM), establishing dependencies across temporal horizons. Building upon these predictions,
Structure-Aware Latent World Modeling
organizes future latent representations along the horizon, view, and spatial dimensions to facilitate fine-grained retrieval. Furthermore,
Action-Guided Factorized World Retrieval
adaptively retrieves relevant future information from the structured latent world based on evolving action representations during denoising, providing targeted guidance for action generation. Extensive experiments on two simulation benchmarks and six real-world robotic manipulation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.
1
Introduction
Figure 1
:
Comparison of Foresight VLA Models.
(a) Existing methods typically adopt single-horizon foresight and directly feed predictions into VLA models without selective utilization. (b) In contrast, HiFOR combines multi-horizon foresight with action-guided retrieval of relevant future information.
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models
[
19
,
16
,
46
,
56
,
34
,
29
,
59
,
26
]
have achieved remarkable progress in robotic manipulation by integrating visual perception, language understanding, and action generation within a unified end-to-end framework. Benefiting from advances in large-scale vision-language models and the growing availability of diverse robotic demonstrations, recent VLA models have demonstrated promising capabilities across a wide range of manipulation tasks. As robotic manipulation tasks become increasingly complex, anticipating future environmental changes and task evolution becomes essential for effective action generation. To this end, recent studies have explored incorporating foresight capabilities into VLA models to enhance their understanding of environmental dynamics and task progression
[
27
,
18
,
43
]
. Existing approaches primarily predict future states or latent representations to model environmental dynamics
[
27
,
30
,
52
,
57
,
15
]
, or generate future images and videos to anticipate visual scene evolution
[
53
,
18
,
43
,
33
,
6
]
, thereby providing additional foresight information for action generation.
Despite these advances, effectively translating future predictions into actionable guidance for complex robotic manipulation remains challenging. First,
modeling short-term world dynamics or long-term task objectives in isolation limits hierarchical coordination across temporal horizons.
As illustrated in Fig.
1
(a), many existing foresight-based VLA methods primarily focus on a single prediction horizon. Short-term prediction methods
[
58
,
8
,
47
,
21
]
emphasize near-future environmental changes and local motion dynamics, capturing fine-grained state evolution but often lacking explicit connections to subsequent task stages and ultimate goals. In contrast, long-term prediction methods
[
53
,
9
,
54
,
36
,
28
]
provide intermediate task guidance through semantic subtask planning or visual subgoal prediction, enabling the policy to anticipate key future task states. However, these methods often lack sufficient modeling of the continuous state transitions and motion dynamics required to achieve such objectives. Although both forms of foresight provide valuable information, modeling them independently makes it difficult to establish explicit dependencies among local state evolution, key semantic milestones, and final task objectives, thereby limiting the policy’s coherent understanding of task progression across temporal horizons.
More importantly,
directly incorporating predicted future information into action generation often overlooks its varying relevance to current action requirements.
As illustrated in Fig.
1
(a), many existing approaches
[
58
,
8
,
47
,
53
,
9
,
54
,
38
]
directly incorporate predicted future images or latent representations into action policies as additional conditioning signals, without sufficiently distinguishing the relevance of different predictions to current actions. However, future information across different prediction horizons, camera views, and spatial regions contributes differently to action generation, and its relevance dynamically evolves throughout task execution and the action generation process. Therefore, even with rich and complementary future predictions, selectively retrieving and utilizing information relevant to current action requirements remains essential for fully exploiting the decision-making potential of foresight. These observations motivate a unified framework that establishes hierarchical dependencies across temporal horizons and adaptively retrieves and leverages relevant future information according to current action requirements.
To address these challenges, we propose
HiFOR
, a hierarchical foresight framework with action-guided world retrieval for robotic manipulation. As illustrated in Fig.
1
(b), HiFOR integrates multi-horizon foresight prediction with action-guided selective retrieval, enabling future information across different temporal horizons to provide targeted guidance according to evolving action requirements. Specifically, ❶ we first introduce
Hierarchical Foresight Prediction
, which jointly predicts short-term state evolution, key semantic milestones, and final goal states. By incorporating a Hierarchical Dependency Mask (HDM), the prediction module establishes asymmetric dependencies across temporal horizons, connecting local motion dynamics with intermediate task progression and long-term objectives. ❷ Building upon these predictions, we propose
Structure-Aware Latent World Modeling
, which organizes predicted future latent representations along the horizon, view, and spatial dimensions to construct a structured latent world while preserving fine-grained structural information for subsequent selective retrieval. ❸ Furthermore, we develop
Action-Guided Factorized World Retrieval
, which leverages evolving action representations during denoising to perform factorized attention over the structured latent world. By adaptively evaluating the relevance of different prediction horizons, camera views, and spatial regions to current actions, the retrieved future information provides targeted guidance for action generation. Through these designs, HiFOR effectively integrates hierarchical future modeling with action-guided information retrieval, enabling foresight predictions to better support robotic manipulation.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:
First,
we propose a
hierarchical foresight prediction mechanism
that jointly models short-term state evolution, key semantic milestones, and final goal states through hierarchical dependency modeling, establishing explicit connections between local world dynamics and long-term task objectives.
Second,
we develop an
action-guided structured world retrieval mechanism
that adaptively retrieves future information relevant to current action requirements from a structured latent world organized along the horizon, view, and spatial dimensions through denoising-aware factorized attention.
Third,
we conduct extensive experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and six real-world robotic manipulation tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of HiFOR and further validating the contributions of its key components through comprehensive ablation studies.
2
Related Works
2.1
Vision-Language-Action Model
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models aim to integrate visual perception,
language understanding, and action generation to develop general-purpose
robotic policies capable of executing complex manipulation tasks.
Based on their action representations and generation mechanisms,
existing VLA models can be broadly categorized into two paradigms:
discrete and continuous action generation.
Discrete action generation methods
[
4
,
3
,
19
,
48
,
54
,
31
,
44
,
23
,
45
]
convert continuous actions into discrete tokens or textual sequences,
enabling autoregressive action prediction.
In contrast, continuous action generation methods
[
17
,
2
,
16
,
22
,
13
]
typically employ specialized action prediction modules to directly
generate continuous control signals, mainly adopting regression-based,
diffusion-based, or flow-matching-based approaches.
Specifically, regression-based methods
[
17
,
42
]
directly learn mappings from observations to actions,
while diffusion-based methods
[
25
,
41
,
12
,
40
]
generate action sequences through iterative denoising.
Flow-matching-based methods
[
2
,
16
,
32
,
60
,
37
,
35
]
learn a continuous vector field to transform samples from a noise distribution into the target action distribution. Although these approaches have improved the action generation and generalization capabilities of VLA models, they primarily focus on action prediction itself, whereas accurate local action predictions do not necessarily guarantee successful completion of complex manipulation tasks.
2.2
Foresight Predication in VLA
To overcome the limitations of local action prediction, recent studies have incorporated foresight prediction into VLA to anticipate future environmental changes and task progression, thereby guiding action generation. Based on how future information is represented, existing methods can be categorized into implicit and explicit foresight prediction. Implicit methods
[
27
,
30
,
52
,
57
,
15
,
49
]
model environmental dynamics in state or latent feature spaces, leveraging predicted future representations to facilitate policy learning and action generation. In contrast, explicit methods
[
53
,
18
,
43
,
33
,
6
,
7
]
generate future images or videos to anticipate visual scene evolution and potential action outcomes, supporting robotic planning and decision-making.
Despite these advances, existing methods still face limitations in modeling and utilizing future information.
First
, predicting short-term dynamics and long-term task objectives in isolation overlooks dependencies across temporal horizons, limiting coherent modeling of task progression.
Second
, existing methods often directly incorporate predicted future information into action policies as additional conditioning signals, without adequately considering its varying relevance to current action requirements.

5
Conclusion
In this paper, we propose HiFOR, a hierarchical foresight-guided framework for vision-language-action robotic manipulation. HiFOR employs Hierarchical Foresight Prediction to jointly predict short-term dynamics, intermediate semantic milestones, and final goal states, capturing dependencies across different prediction horizons. Structure-Aware Latent World Modeling further organizes these predictions along the horizon, view, and spatial dimensions to construct a structured latent world. Action-Guided Factorized World Retrieval then adaptively retrieves action-relevant future information to guide subsequent action generation. Extensive experiments on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0, together with real-world evaluations, demonstrate the effectiveness of HiFOR in improving robotic manipulation performance.

article.headline: 分层预见加动作引导检索，VLA操作成功率提升
article.lede: HiFOR让VLA同时预测短期动态、语义里程碑与最终目标，并按当前动作需求检索未来信息。
article.problem: 现有带未来预测的VLA方法大多只做单一时间尺度的预见：短期预测擅长刻画局部运动却与任务目标脱节，长期预测给出子目标却缺少连续状态建模，两者割裂导致跨时间尺度的依赖关系难以建立。更关键的是，预测出的未来图像或隐表示通常被直接当作额外条件塞进策略，没有区分不同时间尺度、相机视角和空间区域对当前动作的相关性差异。
article.method: 作者提出分层预见预测，用分层依赖掩码让短期、里程碑、最终目标三组可学习查询在共享预测模块中按 s≺m≺g 的顺序逐步扩展注意力可见性，并以冻结DINOv2 ViT-L/14的多视角4×4 patch特征作为视觉监督、以未来机器人状态序列辅助短期预测。随后结构感知潜世界建模把预测表示沿时间尺度、视角、空间三个维度组织成结构化潜世界，并额外聚合出尺度级和视角级特征。动作引导因子化世界检索则在去噪每一步用动作专家的隐表示构造查询，沿这三个维度做因子化注意力，动态挑选与当前动作最相关的未来信息注入动作生成。
article.results: 在LIBERO上平均成功率98.3%，高于π0.5的96.9%，其中LIBERO-Long从92.4%提升到95.8%（增益3.4个百分点），Spatial达99.4%。在RoboTwin 2.0的Hard设置下20个任务平均成功率49.40%，比π0.5的40.35%高9.05个百分点。真实世界6个任务平均成功率81.7%，比π0.5高11.0个百分点，叠块任务提升16.0个百分点。消融显示短期预见把RoboTwin平均从40.35%提到44.15%，加入里程碑和目标预测后达45.60%和46.95%，再加动作引导检索升至49.40%（额外2.45%）。短时预测步长取5步时LIBERO-Long为95.8%、平均98.3%，优于RGB像素预测的94.2%和97.7%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「预测未来」从单一尺度的辅助条件改造成可按动作需求检索的结构化信息源，为长程操作任务中如何组织和调用预见信息提供了一个可复用的设计范式。
article.limitations: 真实世界验证仅限AgileX Piper单臂平台上的6个任务、每任务50次 rollout，规模有限；短时预见的最优步长（5步）与LIBERO的策略更新间隔对齐，这种依赖在更新频率不同的平台上是否成立论文未给出具体数字。此外里程碑标注依赖规划代理自动定位并需人工复核低置信度样本，且消融中单独加入目标预测的增益相对较小。
article.figure_caption_zh: HiFOR总览：VLA在动作生成中接入分层预见预测与动作引导的世界检索，其中(b)按分层依赖预测短期、里程碑与目标未来，(c)沿尺度、视角、空间组织未来潜表示，(d)用去噪感知的因子化注意力检索与动作相关的未来信息。

figure.caption: {The overview of HIFOR.} (a) We augment the VLA with hierarchical foresight prediction and action-guided world retrieval, enabling the Action Expert to leverage future information during action generation. (b) Hierarchical Foresight Prediction ( {sec::Foresight Prediction}) predicts short-term, milestone, and goal futures through hierarchical dependency modeling. (c) Structure-Aware Latent World Modeling ( {sec::Latent World}) organizes future latent representations along the horizon, view, and spatial dimensions. (d) Action-Guided Factorized World Retrieval ( {sec::World Retrieval}) selectively retrieves action-relevant future information through denoising-aware factorized attention to guide action generation.

page_papers.title: WeFair: Fidelity-Aware Alignment from Human Feedback for Personalized Query Rewriting in Short-Video Search
page_papers.abstract: Short-video search needs compact query rewriters that recover users' personalized intent from ambiguous queries under strict latency constraints. Existing LLM-based methods have improved rewriting by using synthetic reasoning and subsequent consumption-behavioral feedback. However, overemphasizing subsequent consumption can favor engaging content over the user's immediate need, causing intent drift even when rewritten queries are grounded in behavioral history. We propose WeFair, Fidelity-Aware Alignment from Human Feedback for Personalized Query Rewriting in WeChat short-video search. WeFair uses human feedback according to how directly it reflects personalized intent, assigning feedback fidelity to a progression from demonstration to preference to verification. We first mine actual queries and user reformulations from search sessions, and then screen them for contextual support. In the demonstration stage, a supervised fine-tuning curriculum progresses from large-scale context-to-query learning to reasoning and direct prediction on human reformulation and preservation. In the preference stage, direct preference optimization learns relative preferences from subsequent consumption feedback. In the verification stage, group relative policy optimization rewards exact agreement with reformulation or preservation targets to constrain intent drift. Abstract.
Short-video search needs compact query rewriters that recover users’ personalized intent from ambiguous queries under strict latency constraints. Existing LLM-based methods have improved rewriting by using synthetic reasoning and subsequent consumption-behavioral feedback. However, overemphasizing subsequent consumption can favor engaging content over the user’s immediate need, causing intent drift even when rewritten queries are grounded in behavioral history.
We propose WeFair,
F
idelity-
A
ware Al
i
gnment from Human Feedback for Pe
r
sonalized Query Rewriting in
We
Chat short-video search. WeFair uses human feedback according to how directly it reflects personalized intent, assigning feedback fidelity to a progression from demonstration to preference to verification. We first mine actual queries and user reformulations from search sessions, and then screen them for contextual support. In the demonstration stage, a supervised fine-tuning curriculum progresses from large-scale context-to-query learning to reasoning and direct prediction on human reformulation and preservation. In the preference stage, direct preference optimization learns relative preferences from subsequent consumption feedback. In the verification stage, group relative policy optimization rewards exact agreement with reformulation or preservation targets to constrain intent drift. Further analysis shows that broad supervision benefits the full curriculum supervised training, while strict verification achieves better performance than the tested auxiliary rewards. In offline experiments, the compact WeFair-2B model outperforms strong rewriting baselines in overall accuracy and intent preservation. Furthermore, a 10-day online A/B test shows relative increases of 2.951% in click-through rate and 2.593% in effective video-view rate, alongside a 2.350% relative reduction in query reformulation rate. WeFair-2B has been deployed in the WeChat short-video search system, which serves over 100 million queries per day.
Keywords:
Personalized query rewriting, Short-video search, Reinforcement learning, Intent drift mitigation
1.
Introduction
Figure 1.
Overview of intent drift in WeChat short-video search. The original query “crepe cake” is redirected toward recipes instead of the intended eating videos. WeFair uses fidelity-aware human feedback through demonstration, preference, and verification to mitigate intent drift.
Overview of intent drift in WeChat short-video search. The original query ``crepe cake'' is redirected toward recipes instead of the intended eating videos. WeFair uses fidelity-aware human feedback through demonstration, preference, and verification to mitigate intent drift.
Personalized query rewriting is essential when an ambiguous search query does not fully express the user’s immediate information need. In short-video search, the intended meaning may depend on recent searches, viewed content, or other context available when the query is issued. Rewriting can expose this information to retrieval by producing a more informative expression, but it must also satisfy strict latency constraints
(
Gong et al., 2026
;
Chu et al., 2026
)
. Therefore, the practical objective is training a compact rewrite model that can resolve ambiguity without replacing the user’s current intent and needs. Furthermore, the rewrite pipeline also needs to accurately decide when to rewrite or preserve the original query.
Although general large-size large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong reasoning capabilities, they fail to accurately understand diverse user intents and incur excessive per-inference latency, which is unacceptable for real-time search.
To address these limitations, some approaches use synthetic Chain-of-Thought(CoT) traces to distill reasoning capabilities from large teacher LLMs into smaller rewrite models, and then use large-scale subsequent consumption feedback to align them with platform-specific user preferences.
Figure 2.
WeFair training and serving. (a) Search sessions yield screened reformulation and preservation targets. (b) Progressive training aligns the model through demonstration, preference, and verification stages. (c) Rewrites expand the candidate pool through cache lookup and search while also informing online ranking.
WeFair training and serving. (a) Search sessions yield screened reformulation and preservation targets. (b) Curriculum SFT builds rewriting capabilities, DPO learns preferences from reformulations and consumption feedback, and GRPO applies strict target verification to constrain intent drift. (c) Rewrites expand retrieval through cache lookup and search, while the original query remains a retrieval and ranking anchor.
However, consumption-oriented alignment does not necessarily reflect the user’s immediate information need. When insufficiently constrained by direct evidence of user intent, a rewriter may favor queries that retrieve engaging content while redirecting the original search intent, resulting in intent drift. Figure
1
shows an example of intent drift.
To better capture personalized intent, recent methods incorporate actual user reformulations, which provide more direct evidence of how users clarify their information needs. PicQue
(
Chu et al., 2026
)
uses historical reformulations as context for generating training examples that subsequently undergo manual verification, while WeWrite
(
Cheng et al., 2026
)
directly uses mined reformulations for supervised fine-tuning and reward construction in GRPO. While these advances demonstrate the value of real user reformulations, the subsequent consumption feedback differs in how directly they reflect personalized intent, and its fine-grained use across training stages remains underexplored.
To bridge the gap, we propose WeFair, a fidelity-aware alignment framework for training a compact personalized query rewriter model in WeChat short-video search. Its central idea is to match supervision fidelity to the requirements of each training stage, improving how human feedback guides a small model toward faithful and efficient rewriting. This progression can enable a compact model to acquire personalized query rewriting capabilities while mitigating intent drift.
WeFair combines automated data construction with three complementary training stages. We mine actual reformulations from search sessions and apply LLM screening and contextual verification to retain demonstrations grounded in user intent. Training then proceeds through three stages, each with a distinct purpose. In the demonstration stage, a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) curriculum progresses from context-to-query prediction to context-conditioned reasoning and finally direct query rewriting, building solid intent understanding capability. The broad coverage of human demonstrations prepares the compact policy model to generate useful candidates for later optimization. In the preference stage, direct preference optimization (DPO) learns from candidate pairs distinguished by subsequent consumption outcomes, increasing the probability of rewrites associated with better personalized user intent. Finally, group relative policy optimization (GRPO) applies a strict verification reward based on exact match with actual human reformulations or preservation. This final stage anchors policy updates to observed human expressions without adding graded similarity, retrieval, or other judge rewards. At inference time, the rewrite model directly outputs a short rewrite or a preservation decision, avoiding additional CoT generation latency. Figure
2
shows the overview of the proposed WeFair.
Our further analysis suggests that the three training stages differ in their tolerance for supervision with varying intent fidelity. SFT can tolerate lower-fidelity supervision to acquire broad rewriting capabilities, while DPO can incorporate preferences inferred from subsequent consumption to refine candidate selection. In contrast, final GRPO optimization requires strict fidelity to the intended target. Auxiliary rewards may involve more fine-grained supervision but reduce rewriting accuracy. Offline and online experiments demonstrate WeFair’s effectiveness in personalized rewriting. WeFair-2B rewrite model has been
deployed in the online WeChat short-video search system, serving over 100 million queries per day.
Our main contributions can be summarized as follows:
(1)
We examine the role of supervision fidelity in personalized rewriting post-training. Demonstrate that extensive broad lower-fidelity supervision benefits curriculum SFT, while strict verification better supports on-policy alignment.
(2)
We propose WeFair, a fidelity-aware framework that matches human feedback to demonstration, preference, and verification stages, enabling compact models to capture personalized needs while mitigating intent drift.
(3)
Offline and online experiments demonstrate that WeFair achieves strong rewriting performance with compact models and significant improvements in online WeChat short-video search.
2.
Related Work
2.1.
Personalized Query Rewriting
LLM-based query rewriting improves retrieval by enriching query representations and adapting to search domains. Query2doc generates pseudo-documents, while CardRewriter incorporates platform knowledge through knowledge cards
(
Wang et al., 2023
;
Gong et al., 2026
)
. Domain adaptation further aligns query expressions with retrieval requirements. BEQUE combines supervised rewriting with retrieval feedback
(
Peng et al., 2024
)
, and negation-aware rewriting preserves explicit constraints
(
Guo et al., 2025b
)
. MAAQR and QP-OneModel extend this direction through adaptive refinement and unified query understanding
(
Zheng et al., 2025
;
Huang et al., 2026
)
. Beyond representation enrichment, IterQR and Think-Then-Rewrite incorporate reasoning into retrieval-oriented training
(
Chen et al., 2025
;
Li et al., 2026a
)
. MiniELM combines lightweight distillation with simulated feedback
(
Nguyen et al., 2025
)
. For personalized search, user context and observed behavior provide evidence of the user’s current information need, helping resolve ambiguity and determine when to rewrite. PicQue combines hybrid reasoning supervision with GRPO to address over-rewriting
(
Chu et al., 2026
)
, while Think-to-Personalize uses purchase history to support personalized retrieval
(
Jiang et al., 2026
)
. WeWrite mines actual user reformulations and trains with SFT and GRPO using lexical similarity and conditional query-volume rewards
(
Cheng et al., 2026
)
.
Furthermore, OneBar emphasizes content-grounded recommendations, while short-video and conversational query suggestion address consumption utility and intent coverage
(
Tang et al., 2026
;
Tian et al., 2026
;
Liu et al., 2026
)
. DVCQR aligns separate rewrites with sparse and dense retrieval
(
Li et al., 2026b
)
. These studies demonstrate the value of contextual and behavioral signals for query rewriting, while highlighting distinct objectives such as retrieval relevance, consumption utility, and personalized intent.
2.2.
LLM Post-Training and Feedback Alignment
Post-training methods provide different mechanisms for learning from demonstrations, preference pairs, and verified rewards. SFT learns demonstrated responses, whereas DPO optimizes chosen–rejected preferences without separately training a reward model, and GRPO estimates advantages within sampled groups
(
Guo et al., 2025a
;
Ren et al., 2026
;
Rafailov et al., 2023
;
Ouyang et al., 2022
)
. Beyond algorithm selection, recent work examines which supervision is useful at different learning stages. Stage-specific data selection distinguishes capability acquisition from reinforcement
(
He et al., 2026
)
. SmartSearch uses a process-reward-guided curriculum
(
Wen et al., 2026a
)
. Hindsight self-distillation further derives corrections and preferences from follow-up user interactions
(
Kleine Buening et al., 2026
)
. This work motivates matching supervision to both the policy’s capabilities and the evidence available from users.
In search applications, AWHCP combines SFT, DPO, and GRPO with quality, format, and recall rewards
(
Ou et al., 2026
)
, while CoRe uses deployed relevance feedback
(
Wen et al., 2026b
)
. Such signals align generation with search outcomes, but provide different evidence about intended reformulations. Comparisons under compute constraints further show that on-policy rewriting need not outperform prompted alternatives
(
Xu et al., 2026
)
, motivating examination of the optimization signals alongside the algorithms.
On-policy optimization consequently requires considering the reliability of candidate-level feedback. TTRL shows that noisy pseudo-labels can still yield reliable rewards
(
Zuo et al., 2025
)
. This motivates prioritizing reward purity in on-policy preference alignment.

4.2.
Overall Offline Performance
We present the offline performances in Table
1
. WeFair achieves the best overall performance. The WeFair-4B model reaches 73.48% overall accuracy, exceeding the strongest large-size baselines Gemini3.1 and DeepSeek4.1. WeFair-2B achieves 72.81% and the highest consistent Recall of 83.95%. Its EM also exceeded the other two adaptive rewrite baselines. Gemini 3.1 retained the highest EM and the lowest Hallucination and Intent Drift Rates, while achieving much lower rewrite recall. This suggests that large-size models with CoT can substantially reduce hallucination and intent drift, but yield more incorrect preservation. WeFair’s advantage lies in the balance of successful rewriting and preservation. Notably, our small-size WeFair-2B achieves significantly lower hallucination and intent drift rates than other comparable rewriting methods (with its intent drift rate reduced to about one-third), validating the effectiveness of our fidelity-aware training approach.
Intent fidelity.
WeFair achieves lower hallucination and intent drift rates than WeWrite and AWHCP, while more reliably preserving queries that did not require rewriting. Both baselines tended to favor rewriting, particularly AWHCP. Even the smallest WeFair-0.8B surpasses AWHCP-8B in preservation. The large-size LLMs generally had lower intent drift rates than WeFair but also lower successful-rewrite recall. These trends support the value of fidelity-aware alignment with human feedback in mitigating intent drift while maintaining effective personalized rewriting.
Gains from model scaling.
WeFair’s overall accuracy increased by 5.91 percentage points from 0.8B to 2B, but only 0.67 points from 2B to 4B, while consistent recall remained nearly unchanged. These results indicate diminishing gains over the backbone sizes, with most of the observed gain already attained at 2B.
Inference mode.
Direct WeFair exceeds WeFair-CoT in overall accuracy at both 2B and 4B, and also achieves lower intent drift. CoT variants yield higher EM and PD Recall, but these gains did not translate into better overall performance, indicating explicit reasoning is unnecessary for the strongest results in these comparisons. For general large-size LLMs, we observe that Qwen3.8-27B with CoT achieves much better performance than direct prediction. These results suggest that our fidelity-aware training enables the rewriter to perform more effective implicit reasoning than explicit CoT. We further analyze the corresponding decode tokens and inference latency in Section
4.5
.

Ablation Study
4.3.1.
Ablation Study of Curriculum SFT
To examine the role of curriculum learning in the SFT stage, we ablate the C2Q and CoT phases before direct human-target adaptation (HR). All four variants use the same number of human reformulation examples, but C2Q adds context-to-query samples in
C
C
. The results in Table
3
show that this broader, lower-fidelity demonstration supervision is most beneficial when combined with the subsequent human-target learning phases. Specifically, C2Q
→
\to
HR improves consistent recall over HR Only but reduces preservation recall, producing little overall gain. CoT
→
\to
HR achieves higher preservation recall and decision accuracy than both variants, supporting the contribution of reasoning supervision to rewrite-or-preserve decisions. Full Curriculum further improves rewrite consistency and decision accuracy, achieving the highest overall accuracy. These findings suggest that the broad and lower-fidelity C2Q and CoT supervision can aid capability acquisition in our curriculum SFT.
4.3.2.
Ablation Study of Progressive Alignment.
To assess the contribution of each stage in our progressive alignment framework, we compared four training configurations on the 2B model: SFT Only, SFT
→
\to
DPO, SFT
→
\to
GRPO, and the full training sequence (WeFair). All configurations use the same total amount of training data. Results are shown in Table
3
.
Demonstration builds the rewriting foundation.
Our curriculum SFT already surpasses all evaluated adaptive baseline variants in consistent recall. This supports the effectiveness of demonstration-based learning in establishing rewriting capabilities in compact models. However, its low PD recall reveals a strong tendency to rewrite queries even when preservation is appropriate. Demonstration learning provides a capable starting point but remains insufficient for reliable rewrite-or-preserve decisions.
Consumption preference alignment further improves rewriting.
The subsequent consumption-guided DPO yields modest improvements in consistent recall and precision, further strengthening successful rewriting. However, PD Recall decreases slightly, also indicating an increased tendency to rewrite preservation-required queries. This imbalance limits the improvement in overall accuracy, suggesting that consumption-based preference alignment refines rewriting capabilities but cannot reduce over-writing.
Verification delivers the largest benefits.
Adding strict-verification GRPO produces the largest improvement in overall accuracy, substantially improving preservation while maintaining high rewrite-decision recall. Importantly, the full sequence achieves higher consistent recall and precision than SFT
→
\rightarrow
GRPO. These gaps even exceed the corresponding gains from adding DPO to SFT alone, suggesting that the value of preference alignment extends beyond its immediate improvements. Although SFT
→
\rightarrow
GRPO achieves slightly higher PD recall, the full sequence delivers the best overall performance by combining successful rewriting with effective preservation.
All these ablation results support the complementary roles of demonstration, preference, and verification. Their progressive combination achieves the strongest overall performance.

4.5.
Offline Efficiency Analysis
To examine the effects of model size and inference mode, we measure the mean number of decoded tokens and per-sample inference latency with the same computing resource. The DeepSeek and Gemini baselines use the API call and only report the mean number of decoded tokens. The other methods are deployed on an Nvidia H20 GPU with the same settings. Decoded tokens include reasoning when CoT is enabled. All the results are reported in Table

General-purpose LLMs achieve competitive rewriting performance without task-specific fine-tuning, but their full-CoT configurations incur substantial decoding overhead. The CoT–Direct comparison for Qwen3.8-27B illustrates this trade-off. Explicit reasoning improves rewriting quality but sharply increases inference time, making full-CoT inference impractical in real-time search systems.
In contrast, WeFair achieves low latency while retaining strong rewrite quality. WeFair-2B required only 7.60 decoded tokens and 0.316 s per sample, compared with 26.65 tokens and 0.795 s for WeFair-CoT-2B. At 4B size, direct WeFair used 72.66% fewer tokens and achieved a
2.32

1
). Relative to WeWrite at matched sizes, WeFair delivered higher overall accuracy and slightly lower mean latency.
For the three direct WeFair variants, WeFair-2B retained nearly the latency of WeFair-0.8B while improving overall accuracy. Increasing the size to 4B significantly raises inference time with only a slight accuracy gain. Accordingly, we select WeFair-2B for both online A/B testing and production deployment.

We measured click-through rate (CTR), effective video-view rate (VV>10s), and query reformulation rate (QRR). We also measured P95 model inference latency (81 ms) and the end-to-end search latency increase (+16 ms).
As shown in Table

WeFair with only cache retrieval also achieves improvement against the control method. Additional lightweight vector retrieval further reduces the query reformulation rate. Together with the online gains, these examples support WeFair’s effectiveness in translating contextual clues into rewrites that better serve personalized information needs.
5.
Conclusion
We presented WeFair, a fidelity-aware alignment framework for training compact personalized query rewriters that mitigate intent drift. The framework matches human feedback to three complementary roles: demonstration through curriculum SFT, preference learning through DPO, and verification through GRPO. Offline experiments showed that WeFair achieves the best overall accuracy and reduced intent drift while maintaining low inference latency. A 10-day online A/B test further showed significant gains in engagement and fewer query reformulations. Furthermore, our analyses revealed that broad, lower-fidelity context-to-query supervision benefited the complete SFT curriculum, while consumption-based preference learning complemented subsequent verification. In GRPO, strict agreement with human targets yielded higher overall accuracy than the tested auxiliary rewards. These findings support matching supervision fidelity to the role of each training stage. Our method has been deployed in WeChat short-video search, demonstrating the practical value of proposed fidelity-aware alignment for effective personalization under production latency constraints.

article.headline: 腾讯WeFair按反馈保真度分阶段训练2B改写模型
article.lede: 腾讯WeFair按反馈保真度分阶段训练2B改写模型，离线总体准确率72.81%，线上CTR相对提升2.951%。
article.problem: 短视频搜索中的查询往往含义模糊，需要小型改写模型在严格延迟限制下从上下文恢复用户的即时意图，并判断该改写还是该保留原查询。已有的LLM蒸馏方法依赖合成推理轨迹和后续消费行为对齐，而过度强调消费容易把改写引向更吸引点击的内容，偏离用户当下的真实需求，形成意图漂移。
article.method: 作者把人工反馈按「多直接反映个性化意图」分为演示、偏好、验证三级，并从搜索会话中挖掘真实查询与用户改写，先经规则过滤再交由三个大模型多数投票筛选上下文支撑。训练分三阶段递进：课程式SFT从上下文到查询预测、带推理的改写、直接改写逐步收敛；DPO用后续消费结果构造偏好对；GRPO只对与人工改写或保留标记完全一致的回答给予奖励。推理时模型直接输出改写或保留标记，不生成思维链。
article.results: 离线测试中WeFair-2B总体准确率72.81%、一致召回83.95%（均为表中最高），4B版本达73.48%，高于Gemini-3.1-Pro的64.42%与DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash的62.55%；2B的意图漂移率为5.36%，低于WeWrite-2B的16.45%与AWHCP-8B的13.34%。从0.8B到2B总体准确率提升5.91个百分点，2B到4B仅提升0.67个百分点。推理时2B模型平均解码7.60个token、单样本0.316秒，而WeFair-CoT-2B为26.65个token、0.795秒。10天线上A/B测试（对照为WeWrite）显示CTR相对提升2.951%、有效播放率提升2.593%、查询改写率下降2.350%（P<0.01），P95推理延迟81毫秒，端到端搜索延迟增加16毫秒；系统日均服务超过1亿次查询。消融显示SFT单独总体准确率55.48%，加DPO为56.54%，加GRPO为70.35%，三阶段完整为72.81%。
article.why_it_matters: 它给出一个可操作的工程结论：训练信号的「保真度」应当与训练阶段匹配，宽松的上下文监督适合打基础，而最终的在策略优化必须锚定高保真的人工目标。对需要在线上毫秒级预算内做个性化改写的搜索系统，2B级别的直接输出模型已可与大模型CoT方案在总体准确率上竞争。
article.limitations: 离线评价高度依赖一个LLM裁判（作者报告其与人工判断一致率96.6%、Cohen's Kappa为0.919），严格精确匹配奖励的负向纯度低于RM增强方案，说明它会把一些可接受的替代表达判为负例；线上收益只来自单一平台10天的A/B测试，案例分析中亦有一例因改写丢失「XX市」而退化。此外，保留标记比正确改写更易生成，存在策略偏向保留的奖励攻击风险，论文只称通过数据配比与奖励设置缓解，未给出定量上界。
article.figure_caption_zh: 图1：微信短视频搜索中的意图漂移示例——原查询「可丽饼」被导向食谱而非用户想看的吃播视频，WeFair用演示、偏好、验证三级的保真度反馈来抑制这种偏移。

page_papers.title: FrameForge: Harnessing Priors of Video Foundation Models for Unified Image Generation
page_papers.abstract: Unified conditional image generation requires a single model to preserve different aspects of a visual input while producing a target image that follows textual guidance. Pretrained video models provide a promising foundation by encoding visual transformations across time, yet existing approaches typically assign the condition and target to fixed temporal positions. We observe that condition-target relationships vary substantially across generation tasks, while video models naturally encode visual transformations at different temporal scales. This motivates us to model conditional generation through input-adaptive virtual temporal relations. We propose FrameForge, which captures two complementary aspects of such relations. Mixture of Temporal Experts (MoTE) models how far the target lies from the condition by dynamically selecting temporal RoPE experts with different virtual intervals. Chain of Temporal Reasoning (CoTR) models how the condition is transformed into the target through a latent intermediate state, with a reasoning-bottleneck attention mask encouraging information propagation through this pathway. Experiments on DreamBench, COCO2017, and GEdit-Bench show that FrameForge achieves superior performance in subject-driven generation, canny-to-image generation, and image editing among the compared methods.

Introduction
With recent advances in generative modeling

, text, reference images, and structural maps) that impose constraints at different semantic and spatial levels. Modeling these heterogeneous condition-target relations within a unified framework remains challenging.
Figure 1:
Motivation of FrameForge.
Top: The LPIPS distances between frame pairs sampled from natural videos at different temporal intervals. Bottom: The condition-to-target LPIPS distances for image editing, subject-driven generation, and canny-to-image generation, where the dashed lines denote the median distance of each task.
Existing approaches to heterogeneous conditional image generation are predominantly image-centric. Some train unified models on large-scale multi-task datasets
[
42
,
2
,
46
,
9
,

,

,

, while others extend pretrained generators with control branches or lightweight adapters
[
63

,

,
65
]
. These approaches typically inject conditions as auxiliary spatial or semantic signals without explicitly modeling how strongly the condition and target differ or how one should be transformed into the other. This can make it difficult for a shared model to accommodate substantially different generation behaviors.
Pretrained video generation models provide a natural alternative by learning visual transformations across time. Recent studies exploit these priors by arranging the condition and target as different frames
[
54
,
27
,
31
,
6
]
. However, existing approaches typically assign the condition and target to fixed temporal positions, resulting in an invariant temporal positional relation across different tasks and samples. Such a fixed offset overlooks the variation in condition-target relations and may limit a single shared adapter.
Our key observation is that heterogeneous condition-target relations can be interpreted through a
virtual temporal interval
. In natural videos, frames separated by different temporal intervals exhibit different degrees of visual variation. A similar phenomenon arises in conditional image generation: image editing typically requires relatively small changes while preserving most source content, whereas subject-driven and canny-to-image generation often involve larger variations in appearance, structure, or scene composition. As shown in
Fig.
1
, these tasks exhibit clearly different condition-target LPIPS distributions, while their variation ranges substantially overlap with those observed in natural video transitions. This suggests that different conditional generation tasks may correspond to different regions of the temporal transformation prior learned by a video model. The broad distributions within individual tasks further suggest that a task label alone cannot specify the required transformation magnitude. An input-dependent relation can account for both differences across tasks and variations among samples within the same task. Therefore, instead of assigning all condition-target pairs a fixed temporal offset, we model their relation with an input-adaptive virtual temporal interval.
This perspective reveals two complementary aspects of conditional generation:
how far
the target lies from the condition under the learned temporal prior, and
how
the condition should be transformed into the target. An adaptive interval addresses the former but does not uniquely determine the transformation. Modeling the latter requires a latent mechanism that learns condition-to-target transformations without explicit intermediate-frame supervision.
To this end, we propose
FrameForge
, a unified conditional image generation framework built upon a pretrained video foundation model. To model
how far
the target lies from the condition,
Mixture of Temporal Experts (MoTE)
selects among temporal RoPE experts with different virtual intervals using the joint textual and visual context. To model
how
the condition evolves into the target,
Chain of Temporal Reasoning (CoTR)
inserts a noise-initialized latent to form a condition-reasoning-target chain. The latent is progressively contextualized through attention with textual and visual tokens. During an intermediate training stage, a
reasoning-bottleneck attention mask
prevents target tokens from directly accessing text or condition tokens, encouraging information propagation through the reasoning latent. The MoTE router and a single shared LoRA are jointly optimized across all tasks, while the pretrained video backbone remains frozen. This design enables heterogeneous conditional generation without task-specific adapters.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:
Conceptual contribution.
We formulate heterogeneous conditional image generation from the perspective of input-adaptive virtual temporal relations in pretrained video models. Our analysis shows that different generation tasks exhibit distinct condition-target transformation magnitudes, motivating adaptive temporal relation modeling.
Technical contribution.
We propose FrameForge, a unified adaptation framework that jointly models two complementary aspects of conditional generation. MoTE adaptively determines
how far
the target lies from the condition through input-dependent temporal positional priors, while CoTR provides a latent pathway to model
how
the condition is transformed into the target without explicit intermediate supervision. The entire framework is jointly trained across tasks with a single shared LoRA.
Experimental contribution.
We conduct extensive experiments on subject-driven generation, canny-to-image generation, and instruction-guided image editing. Results on DreamBench, COCO2017, and GEdit demonstrate that a single unified FrameForge model achieves superior performance across all three tasks compared with task-specific and unified baselines. Comprehensive ablations further validate the effectiveness of the proposed MoTE and CoTR modules.

3.5
Training Strategy
We freeze the pretrained video-backbone weights and the VAE encoder, and insert a single LoRA adapter
[
20
]
into the attention and feed-forward projections of the MM-DiT.
Three-stage optimization.
In the first stage, we optimize only the MoTE router with the condition-target formulation, keeping the LoRA parameters fixed and omitting the reasoning latent. This stage learns temporal routing before introducing the additional intermediate pathway. In the second stage, we add the reasoning latent, jointly optimize the router and LoRA, and apply the stochastic mask in
Eq.
11
. In the final stage, we retain both modules and continue joint optimization with full attention. The final stage matches the attention configuration used at inference, where the router selects a temporal expert at each denoising step. Furthermore, the shared adapter is used for every task.

MoTE Routing Analysis
Fig.
6
reports expert selection ratios over 50 denoising steps, averaged over 500 cases. The MoTE router exhibits distinct task-dependent and timestep-dependent preferences.
Figure 6:
Visualization of MoTE routing behavior for editing, subject-driven generation, and canny-to-image. Gate 0, Gate 1, and Gate 2 denote the short-, medium-, and long-interval temporal RoPE experts, respectively. Each curve reports the average expert usage ratio over 500 cases at each denoising step.
Canny-to-image generation, which has the largest condition-target distance, predominantly selects the long-interval expert, particularly during early denoising. Subject-driven generation and editing initially favor the medium-interval expert while target latents remain dominated by noise, with a higher selection ratio for subject-driven generation. As target content emerges, both shift toward the short-interval expert. Editing makes this transition earlier and more strongly, consistent with greater source-content preservation. These within-task shifts suggest that expert selection responds to the evolving target representation, rather than assigning each task a fixed temporal interval. These results complement the dataset-level analysis in
Fig.
1
, showing that MoTE dynamically adapts the virtual temporal relation to both the task and denoising stage.

When combined, the full model achieves the best overall performance, with the highest scores on subject-driven generation and editing and the lowest FID on canny-to-image generation. Conclusion
In this work, we presented FrameForge, a unified adaptation framework that leverages the temporal priors of pretrained video foundation models for heterogeneous conditional image generation. Rather than assigning a fixed temporal relation to all condition-target pairs, we introduced an input-adaptive virtual temporal relation perspective. Based on this formulation, MoTE selects an appropriate temporal positional prior from multiple interval experts according to the textual and visual context. CoTR introduces an unsupervised reasoning latent and a reasoning-bottleneck attention mask to model the unobserved condition-to-target transformation. The proposed framework enables joint adaptation across subject-driven generation, canny-to-image generation, and image editing while keeping the video foundation model frozen. Experiments on DreamBench, COCO2017, and GEdit demonstrate strong performance across all three tasks, and the ablation studies verify the effectiveness of both adaptive temporal relation modeling and implicit temporal reasoning.

article.headline: 用视频模型的时间先验统一条件图像生成
article.lede: FrameForge 冻结视频扩散骨干，按输入选择虚拟时间间隔并插入无监督推理隐变量，统一三类条件图像生成任务。
article.problem: 统一条件图像生成要求同一个模型在遵循文本指令的同时，保住参考主体的身份、结构图的几何或编辑中不该改动的内容，但不同任务对「条件和目标差多远」的要求差别很大。现有做法要么把条件和目标放在固定的时间位置上，要么用控制分支、轻量适配器把条件当作辅助信号注入，都没有显式建模条件与目标的差异强度以及条件如何转变成目标。作者观察到，编辑、主体驱动生成、canny-to-image 三类任务的条件-目标 LPIPS 分布明显不同，却又与自然视频中不同时间间隔帧对的分布范围大幅重叠，这提示可以用视频模型的时间变换先验来解释这些关系。
article.method: FrameForge 以 HunyuanVideo1.5 的首阶段视频扩散模型为骨干，冻结骨干与 VAE，只插入一个在所有任务间共享的 LoRA，并把条件图像生成表述为「目标帧预测」。Mixture of Temporal Experts（MoTE）构造多个对应不同虚拟间隔的时间 RoPE 专家（默认等效视频帧跨度为 17、69、121，对应隐空间跨度 5、18、31），用轻量 router 根据文本、条件与噪声目标表示做样本级 Top-1 路由，并以直通估计器端到端训练、加上负载均衡损失防止路由塌缩。Chain of Temporal Reasoning（CoTR）在条件与目标之间插入一个高斯噪声初始化、无显式监督的推理隐变量，在中间训练阶段以概率 0.5 施加推理瓶颈注意力掩码，切断目标 token 与文本/条件 token 的直接注意力，迫使信息经由该隐变量传递。
article.results: 在 DreamBench 主体驱动生成上，FrameForge 的总体分 O 为 0.739（SC 0.739、PQ 0.783），论文称比 ChronoEdit 的 0.729 提升 1.37%，但主体一致性一项排第二。COCO2017 canny-to-image 上 SSIM 为 0.447，比次优的 EasyControl（0.417）相对提升 7.2%，CLIP-T 为 0.323，FID 为 23.47。GEdit-Bench 上总体 G-O 为 6.12（ChronoEdit 5.08），Motion Change 的 G-O 为 6.84（ChronoEdit 5.76），但两项仍低于 GPT-4o 的 8.01 和 7.81。训练使用每任务 170K、共 510K 样本，分辨率 512×512，可训练参数 182M（LoRA rank 与 alpha 均为 32），在两张 A800 上训练 12,000 步、约 6 天。换到 HunyuanVideo1.0 骨干后，主体驱动分从 0.699 升到 0.736，编辑分从 4.38 升到 5.00，canny FID 从 24.52 降到 23.07。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「条件到目标差多远」变成一个可按样本、按去噪步连续选择的时间位置先验，为统一条件生成提供了一条不需要任务专用适配器的参数高效路线。这也给出了一个可检验的观点：视频模型学到的时间变换先验，可以按输入重新组合，而不只是一个固定偏移。
article.limitations: canny-to-image 的 FID 23.47 仍差于 ControlNet 的 20.42，作者自己也承认 FID 与人类判断存在分歧；实验只在 512×512、三个基准上做，DreamBench 仅 30 个主体，GEdit 英文子集 606 条，且评分依赖 GPT-4o/4.1 打分。消融显示，不添加模块的共享 LoRA 会让编辑分从任务专用的 5.99 掉到 4.94，说明任务干扰只是被缓解而非消除；专家数增到 5 或 7 时，其他任务指标反而下降。
article.figure_caption_zh: FrameForge 总览：异质条件图像生成被表述为预训练视频扩散模型的目标帧预测，MM-DiT 骨干处理文本、条件、推理与噪声目标 token，MoTE 在每步去噪选择不同虚拟间隔的时间 RoPE 配置，CoTR 通过注意力更新噪声初始化的中间隐变量，中间训练阶段用随机注意力掩码阻断文本/条件与目标的直接注意力。

figure.caption: Overview of FrameForge. Heterogeneous conditional image generation is formulated as target-frame prediction with a pretrained video diffusion model. The MM-DiT backbone processes text, condition, reasoning, and noisy target tokens to predict the target velocity. Mixture of Temporal Experts (MoTE) selects a temporal RoPE configuration at each denoising step, adapting the virtual interval between the condition and target. Chain of Temporal Reasoning (CoTR) adds a noise-initialized intermediate latent whose hidden representation is updated through attention. During the intermediate training stage, a stochastic attention mask blocks direct text/condition-target attention to encourage use of this intermediate pathway.

page_papers.title: Value as Memory: Online Value-Guided Post-training for General Robot Policies
page_papers.abstract: Real-world post-training of generalist robot policies faces two challenges: partial observability makes action selection ambiguous, while offline post-training methods delay feedback from deployment experience. We present Value as Memory (VaM), a framework that addresses these challenges through value caching and online real-world reinforcement learning (RL). Value caching conditions actions on recent value predictions as task-progress memory, while online updates enable timely policy improvement by combining offline demonstrations, off-policy interventions, and on-policy rollouts for sample-efficient adaptation. As a result, VaM transitions from offline RL warmup to online autonomous learning with sparse rewards. Across long-horizon tasks involving deformable objects and contact-rich manipulation, VaM yields a mean absolute success-rate gain of $29.4\%$ with value caching, while achieving a $32.8\%$ gain with online autonomous learning over matched offline training. The evaluated online schedule performs $8\times$ as many policy iterations under the same gradient-step budget, with more than $2\times$ lower recorded time per gradient step with concurrent data collection and training.

1
Introduction
Real-world reinforcement learning (RL) enables generalist robot policies to learn from physical interaction and improve on deployment tasks
(
Chen et al., 2025b
;
Physical Intelligence et al., 2025
)
.
Initialized from offline expert demonstrations, a policy aims to maximize cumulative task rewards
(
Luo et al., 2024
;
Frans et al., 2025
)
and optionally learns from human-intervention data during deployment
(
Luo et al., 2025a
;
Wang et al., 2026
)
.
However, current real-world RL methods face limitations in data reuse and policy-update frequency.
On-policy updates primarily use fresh rollouts, limiting the reuse of historical experience
(
Chen et al., 2025a
)
.
Iterated offline RL separates data collection from optimization, delaying feedback from newly encountered states
(
Physical Intelligence et al., 2025
)
.
Besides, partial observability poses another challenge.
With limited observation histories, visually similar states may require different actions.
Meanwhile, value functions provide compact task-progress estimates, but typically serve as filtering scores or optimization weights
(
Physical Intelligence et al., 2025
;
Frans et al., 2025
)
.
We therefore ask whether value estimates on observation histories can augment policy inputs to mitigate partial observability, and how an online RL system can exploit a learned value function to incorporate offline demonstrations, off-policy data, and on-policy rollouts for joint adaptation of the policy and value functions with high sample efficiency and rapid closed-loop feedback.
To this end, we introduce
Value as Memory (VaM)
, an offline-to-online RL system with two key features.
First
, we propose value caching, which extends value predictions beyond training supervision by supplying their recent history as an additional policy input.
Alongside visual and proprioceptive histories, this cache indicates whether estimated progress improves, stalls, or declines, helping distinguish states requiring different actions.
Second
, VaM uses a hybrid training data scheme that combines offline demonstrations, off-policy trajectories, and current on-policy rollouts for sample-efficient joint adaptation of policy and value models.
Our training regime progresses from offline RL warmup through human-assisted collection to autonomous learning with sparse rewards.
Across real-world tasks involving deformable objects and contact-rich manipulations, VaM improves mean absolute success rate by
29.4
%
29.4\%
over its variant without value caching.
It gains
32.8
%
32.8\%
in mean absolute success rate over its offline RL counterpart under matched training budgets.
The evaluated online schedule performs
8
×
8\times
as many policy iterations under the same gradient-step budget, with more than
2
×
2\times
lower recorded time per gradient step with concurrent data collection and training.
These results support value caching for mitigating partial observability and our online RL system with a hybrid training data scheme for improving sample efficiency and policy iteration frequency.
Our contributions are twofold:
1.
We propose value caching to condition policies on recent task-progress estimates, with theoretical analysis and real-world ablations supporting its role in mitigating action ambiguity under partial observability.
2.
We develop an online RL framework that reuses offline demonstrations, off-policy trajectories, and current on-policy rollouts for joint policy and value adaptation, improving sample efficiency and policy iteration frequency.

3.1
Method Overview
VaM uses a distributional value expert to supply recent progress predictions to the action expert through a value cache and advantage labels for policy post-training.
Training proceeds through four stages: offline demonstration initialization, offline RL warmup, Online DAgger, and Learn from Experience (LfE).
The value and action experts are updated in parallel during online RL.

5
Related Work
5.1
Post-training of Generalist Robot Policies
Policy-centric post-training adapts generalist robot policies through residual updates or RL objectives tailored to consistency, diffusion, and flow-based policies
(
Xiao et al., 2026
;
Chen et al., 2025b
;
Li et al., 2026
;
Chen et al., 2025a
)
.
Likelihood-based, hierarchical, and latent-space formulations support optimization of generative policies
(
Ren et al., 2025
;
Lei et al., 2026
;
Wagenmaker et al., 2025
;
Li et al., 2025
;
Chen et al., 2025a
)
, while world models reduce physical interaction by providing imagined or synthetic experience
(
Yang et al., 2026
;
Zhu et al., 2026
;
GigaBrain Team et al., 2026
)
.
To learn from a robot’s own experience, some prior methods learn an additional value function to filter out suboptimal segments.
General-purpose reward and critic models learn transferable evaluations from robot trajectories or vision-language supervision
(
Liang et al., 2026
;
Tan et al., 2026
;
Zhai et al., 2026
)
, while advantage-oriented methods derive relative progress from temporal relations in demonstrations and trajectories
(
Liu et al., 2026
;
Yu et al., 2026a
;
Zhang et al., 2025
)
.
RECAP combines demonstrations, policy rollouts, and human interventions to estimate value and annotate data for advantage-conditioned policy extraction through CFGRL
(
Physical Intelligence et al., 2025
;
Frans et al., 2025
)
.
However, learning value estimates from fixed or periodically refreshed datasets can leave the critic stale as the deployment distribution changes between updates.
In addition, when value predictions serve only as rewards, filtering scores, annotations, or optimization weights, the deployed policy does not receive them as inputs.
Without this explicit task-progress information, visually similar observations can obscure different stages of execution, leaving the policy with partial observability of task progress.
VaM instead continually updates value from online rollouts and human interventions and uses its predictions both as policy-learning supervision and an explicit policy input.
5.2
Human-in-the-loop Online Adaptation
Human operators intervene during deployment to correct uncertain or failing policy behavior
(
Luo et al., 2025b
;
Deng et al., 2026
;
Hu et al., 2026
)
.
Methods such as HG-DAgger and Sirius use interventions as corrective demonstrations for policy improvement
(
Kelly et al., 2019
;
Liu et al., 2023
)
.
Fleet-DAgger, SiriusFleet, and ARMADA scale intervention collection by allocating operators or requesting assistance only when necessary
(
Hoque et al., 2023
;
Liu et al., 2025
;
Yu et al., 2026b
)
, while recent fleet-scale systems combine online robot rollouts with human corrections across multiple robots and tasks
(
Pan et al., 2026
;
Wang et al., 2026
)
.
VaM further uses intervention trajectories to update a value model that guides policy learning and conditions the policy input.
5.3
Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning
Offline-to-online RL stabilizes policy improvement by retaining or replaying offline data during online training
(
Ball et al., 2023
;
Peng et al., 2019
;
Nair et al., 2020
;
Li et al., 2025
)
.
RLPD mixes offline and online samples, Cal-QL calibrates an offline value function for online fine-tuning, and Warm-Start RL initializes online learning with replay data that preserves pretrained behavior
(
Ball et al., 2023
;
Nakamoto et al., 2023
;
Zhou et al., 2025
)
.
In real-world robotics, SERL and HIL-SERL combine behavior-cloning initialization with off-policy learning for physical manipulation
(
Luo et al., 2024
;
Luo et al., 2025a
)
.
VaM combines offline demonstrations, historical off-policy intervention data, and current on-policy experience for sample-efficient online adaptation.
6
Discussions and Conclusions
Though VaM demonstrates improvement over prior methods in sample efficiency and mitigates partial observability in generalist robot policies, it has several limitations that suggest directions for future work.
First, value caching depends on a value function that closely tracks actual task progress, making offline RL warmup necessary for stable online training.
The cached history consists of the value expert’s own predictions, so its usefulness as task-progress memory depends on the quality of those predictions.
Second, our real-world RL framework is currently limited to a single robot.
Our experiments do not establish how the framework scales when multiple robots contribute data.
Scaling VaM to robot fleets with shared experience is a promising direction for further improving sample efficiency.
In conclusion, we presented VaM, a framework that uses recent value predictions as task-progress memory and combines offline demonstrations, off-policy trajectories, and on-policy rollouts for online policy and value adaptation.
Value caching addresses action ambiguity under partial observability, while the offline-to-online RL pipeline supports continued learning from deployment experience.
Together, these components offer a practical approach to post-training generalist robot policies.

Appendix A
Experimental Setup
Figure
8
summarizes the real-robot platforms and task workspaces, while Table
3
reports the episode counts used for offline demonstrations, offline RL warmup, and each Online RL collection round.
A.1
Task Procedures
Box Assembly
.
A cardboard box is placed in a random pose on the table.
The robot grasps one of its front flaps to bring the box upright.
The other arm then slowly folds a side flap inward and clamps it in place.
Finally, the robot lays the box flat and repeats the inward fold-and-clamp operation on the opposite side.
We evaluate the task on four tablecloths that differ in both texture and appearance.
The task is successful if, within the 120 s time limit, both side flaps are fully locked in place and the box lies horizontally on the table.
Laundry Folding
.
A crumpled garment is randomly arranged at a corner of the table.
The robot first moves it into its workspace.
It repeatedly locates the garment seams and progressively spreads the garment flat.
If necessary, the robot rotates the garment to a horizontal orientation.
It folds both sleeves inward, rotates the garment back to a vertical orientation, and folds it in half.
It then pushes the folded garment to the table corner.
The task is successful if the robot completes the procedure within 240 s and pushes the garment to the table corner while keeping it folded.
Magnetic Bus Assembly
.
The robot starts with six magnetic blocks scattered across the workspace and first identifies the three base blocks of the bus.
It sequentially aligns and magnetically joins their narrow side edges to form a horizontal base.
The robot then identifies the three body blocks labeled “V”, “A”, and “M” and attaches them magnetically to the base in that order, placing each block flush against its neighboring body block.
The task is successful if, within 300 s, all six blocks form the bus, with a connected horizontal base and tightly adjoining body blocks spelling “VAM”.

article.headline: VaM：值缓存与在线RL后训练机器人策略
article.lede: VaM 将近期值预测缓存为策略输入，结合离线演示与在线真实世界 RL 联合更新；三类操作任务平均绝对成功率提升 29.4
article.problem: 真实世界后训练通用机器人策略面临两个问题：部分可观测使视觉相似状态需要不同动作，离线后训练又延迟部署反馈。现有值函数多用于过滤或加权，很少直接作为策略输入，且在线更新频率受数据复用限制。
article.method: VaM 用分布值专家预测近期任务进展并缓存为动作专家的额外输入，同时在四阶段流程中从离线演示、离线 RL 预热推进到 Online DAgger 和 LfE。在线阶段混合离线演示、off-policy 干预轨迹与当前 on-policy rollout，联合更新策略和值函数，并用稀疏结果奖励继续学习。
article.results: 在 Box Assembly、Laundry Folding、Magnetic Bus Assembly 上，value caching 相对无缓存变体在最终三个 checkpoint 取得 29.4% 平均绝对成功率增益（全部 LfE checkpoint 为 31.3%），成功率分别为 96.7%/88.9%/76.7% 对 81.7%/48.9%/43.3%。在线自主学习相对匹配离线 RL 平均增益 32.8%；相同梯度步预算下在线调度完成 8× 策略迭代，每梯度步记录时间平均降低 57.8%（Box Assembly 为 16 次对 2 次）。
article.why_it_matters: 把值预测同时用作监督信号和策略输入，为缓解长时程操作中的部分可观测提供了一条直接路径；在线闭环与混合数据复用也提升了真实机器人后训练的样本效率和迭代频率。
article.limitations: 值缓存依赖值函数紧跟任务进展，因此离线 RL 预热对稳定在线训练必要，缓存质量受值预测质量限制。实验目前仅限单机器人，尚未验证多机器人共享数据时的扩展性。
article.figure_caption_zh: VaM 的四阶段离线到在线训练流程，以及分布值专家如何把历史值预测转成值缓存来条件化动作专家。

The bottom panel shows how the distributional value expert turns previously computed value predictions into the value cache that conditions the action expert.

page_papers.title: WorldBridge: Bridging Video and Action for Task Generalization in World Action Models
page_papers.abstract: Achieving the broad task generalization of embodied models in physical environments remains a central challenge in robot learning. We study this challenge in World Action Models (WAMs) through two complementary capabilities: video generalization, which predicts the visual evolution of new tasks, and action generalization, which translates these predictions into executable behavior through a video-to-action bridge. By varying video and action supervision for tasks outside an initial training set, we examine their respective contributions to task transfer. On RoboTwin 2.0, using only in-distribution video-action supervision yields a 25.07% success rate on out-of-distribution tasks. Introducing videos of these tasks without their action labels raises success to 55.90%, while adding just one action-labeled demonstration per task further improves it to 70.70%. These findings suggest that broader video coverage enables task transfer by leveraging existing inverse-dynamics capabilities, while even sparse action supervision further strengthens those capabilities. Guided by this perspective, we introduce WorldBridge, a WAM with separate video and action experts connected through structured attention and trained with joint flow matching. WorldBridge incorporates visual memory at two temporal scales and action forcing, alongside a unified data processing pipeline that standardizes and filters heterogeneous robot trajectories and egocentric hand-derived supervision. Across multiple manipulation benchmarks, WorldBridge achieves state-of-the-art performance among the compared methods, including 96.23% on RoboTwin 2.0 full data setting and 80.9% on clean to random setting, 82.8% on RoboCasa GR1 TableTop, and 57.6% on DOMINO Level-1. Our study highlights the complementary roles of video prediction and action grounding in developing robots that generalize across tasks.
page_papers.content:
WorldBridge: Bridging Video and Action for Task Generalization in World Action Models
WorldBridge Team
Joy Future Academy
Abstract
Achieving the broad task generalization of embodied models in physical environments remains a central challenge in robot learning.
We study this challenge in World Action Models (WAMs) through two complementary capabilities: video generalization, which predicts the visual evolution of new tasks, and action generalization, which translates these predictions into executable behavior through a video-to-action bridge.
By varying video and action supervision for tasks outside an initial training set, we examine their respective contributions to task transfer.
On RoboTwin 2.0, using only in-distribution video-action supervision yields a 25.07% success rate on out-of-distribution tasks.
Introducing videos of these tasks without their action labels raises success to 55.90%, while adding just one action-labeled demonstration per task further improves it to 70.70%.
These findings suggest that broader video coverage enables task transfer by leveraging existing inverse-dynamics capabilities, while even sparse action supervision further strengthens those capabilities.
Guided by this perspective, we introduce
WorldBridge
, a WAM with separate video and action experts connected through structured attention and trained with joint flow matching.
WorldBridge incorporates visual memory at two temporal scales and action forcing, alongside a unified data processing pipeline that standardizes and filters heterogeneous robot trajectories and egocentric hand-derived supervision.
Across multiple manipulation benchmarks, WorldBridge achieves state-of-the-art performance among the compared methods, including 96.23% on RoboTwin 2.0 full data setting and 80.9% on clean to random setting, 82.8% on RoboCasa GR1 TableTop, and 57.6% on DOMINO Level-1.
Our study highlights the complementary roles of video prediction and action grounding in developing robots that generalize across tasks.
Project page:
https://worldbridge-jd.github.io/
1
Introduction
Task generalization marks a fundamental shift from earlier pretrained NLP models, such as BERT
[
16
]
, to modern large language models (LLMs)
[
6
,
63
,
15
]
.
Whereas earlier models typically require task-specific fine-tuning, a single LLM can perform diverse tasks specified through natural-language instructions or a few in-context examples, without updating its parameters for each new task.
This capability has motivated the pursuit of generalist embodied agents that can translate human instructions into a broad repertoire of physical behaviors.
Vision-language-action (VLA) models represent an important step toward this goal, transferring knowledge from large-scale vision-language pretraining into robot control
[
5
,
47
]
.
However, understanding an instruction does not automatically provide the physical competence needed to execute it.
Bringing task generalization into robotics requires connecting semantic knowledge to the visual dynamics and motor behaviors of physical interaction.
Despite substantial progress, a prominent focus of embodied generalization research remains robustness to changes in the conditions under which a task is performed, including object arrangements, camera viewpoints, lighting, and visual appearance.
Benchmarks such as LIBERO-Plus systematically evaluate these variations, exposing the brittleness of otherwise successful policies
[
19
]
.
Task generalization introduces an additional challenge: a robot must execute behaviors beyond those covered by its original training tasks.
Achieving this capability requires understanding how a newly requested task should unfold and producing the actions that realize it, even when corresponding robot demonstrations are scarce or unavailable.
Figure 1
:
Overview of our WorldBridge, a foundational WAM for task generalization.
WorldBridge utilizes heterogeneous data sources and is trained with a simple but effective model architecture in two stages. The bottom panels report task-generalization results under different video and action supervision settings, benchmark performance, and real-world deployment results.
World Action Models (WAMs) provide a promising foundation for addressing this challenge by coupling visual prediction with action generation.
Video offers dense supervision of physical interactions, allowing models to learn how scenes evolve beyond the coverage of action-labeled robot data.
DreamZero demonstrates that video priors can support unseen-task execution and transfer from video-only demonstrations
[
68
]
, while Zero-WAM explores task generalization through in-context human video guidance
[
75
]
.
Recent advances in native video-action pretraining
[
72
]
, systematic WAM pretraining
[
58
]
, and temporal context
[
24
]
further strengthen this paradigm.
These developments motivate a more specific question:
how do broader video coverage and additional action supervision contribute to task generalization, and when does the connection between them become the limiting factor?
In this work, we investigate task generalization in WAMs through two complementary capabilities: video generalization and action generalization.
Video generalization enables a model to predict the visual evolution required by tasks beyond its initial training distribution.
Action generalization refers to the ability to translate those visual predictions into executable actions beyond the tasks that supplied action supervision.
This translation forms a
video-to-action bridge
, serving the role of an inverse dynamics model (IDM).
A model may predict an appropriate visual future yet lack the action grounding needed to realize it.
Conversely, a transferable bridge can allow knowledge acquired from additional videos to improve task execution without corresponding action labels, which motivates studying the availability of video and action supervision separately.
Figure 2
:
Task generalization under progressively expanded supervision.
Compared with in-domain (ID) video-action training alone (25.07% OOD success rate), adding out-of-distribution (OOD) videos increases success to 55.90%, while adding a few paired OOD video-action examples further improves it to 70.70%.
Figure
2
illustrates this progression, which we examine by varying supervision for tasks outside an initial in-distribution (ID) training set.
With only ID video-action pairs, the model achieves nontrivial but limited generalization, obtaining a 25.07% success rate on out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks.
Adding videos of those OOD tasks while keeping action supervision restricted to the ID set increases OOD success to 55.90%.
This improvement suggests that expanded video coverage can support new task execution through a bridge learned from ID action supervision.
Keeping the video set fixed, adding only one action-labeled demonstration per OOD task further raises success to 70.70%.
These rapid gains are consistent with sparse paired examples strengthening the bridge for visual transitions that are already covered by the video data.
Together, these observations support a complementary account of task generalization: video supervision expands the range of task evolutions a WAM can model, while action supervision improves its ability to turn that knowledge into reliable control.
Guided by this perspective, we introduce
WorldBridge
, a WAM that couples video prediction and action generation through a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture
[
35
]
.
WorldBridge maintains separate video and action experts trained with a joint flow-matching objective.
A structured attention mask establishes a directional information path from observed context to future video representations and then to action predictions, making predicted visual dynamics an explicit source of conditioning for control.
Short-term and long-term visual memories provide information about local motion and task progression.
We additionally employ action forcing, assigning independent noise levels to actions within a chunk during training so that the action expert learns to predict actions using temporal context at varying levels of corruption.
To support learning across heterogeneous sources, we develop a unified pretraining data pipeline for robot trajectories and egocentric human demonstrations.
The pipeline standardizes control semantics and maps available robot controls and human hand-derived targets into a shared 46-dimensional action representation.
Dimension-wise validity masks preserve partial supervision across embodiments with different control interfaces.
Robot trajectories undergo kinematic and temporal consistency checks, while egocentric hand trajectories are standardized in a common reference frame and filtered using geometric and motion constraints.
This processing supports broader visual coverage together with usable action supervision, providing a common interface for learning the video-to-action bridge across diverse data sources.
Our evaluations demonstrate strong performance across a range of manipulation tasks.
WorldBridge achieves state-of-the-art results among the compared methods on multiple benchmarks, with average success rates of 96.23% on RoboTwin 2.0, 80.9% in the RoboTwin 2.0 C2R setting, 82.8% on RoboCasa GR1 TableTop, and 57.6% on DOMINO Level-1.
On RMBench, it matches the best result in our comparison, with an 83.0% success rate.
We further conduct real-world evaluations on the Agibot-G2 and AC-1 platforms, covering long-horizon execution, memory-dependent tasks, spatial localization, and bimanual coordination.
Together with our task-generalization study, these results support the value of jointly developing video prediction and action grounding.
Our contributions are threefold:
•
We study task generalization in WAMs through the complementary roles of video generalization and action generalization, quantifying the gains from additional task videos and sparse action supervision.
•
We introduce WorldBridge and a unified data processing pipeline that connect visual dynamics to executable control across heterogeneous robot and egocentric demonstrations.
•
We evaluate WorldBridge across RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa GR1 TableTop, RMBench, DOMINO Level-1, SimplerEnv-WidowX, and RoboDojo, covering diverse manipulation demands and distribution shifts. We further deploy it on AgiBot G2 and ARX AC-1, fine-tuning the same jointly pretrained checkpoint for each platform and evaluating long-horizon execution, memory-dependent interaction, spatial alignment, and bimanual coordination.
Figure 3
:
Overview of the WorldBridge model architecture.

2.1.1

The two experts maintain modality-specific parameters and exchange information through joint self-attention, enabling coupled modeling of future visual observations and robot actions. Each expert contains its own feed-forward networks and output decoder, while the video expert additionally incorporates language features through cross-attention
[
