2.1.4
Attention Mask
Figure 4
:
Attention mask design.
(a) Attention mask for pretraining. (b) Attention mask for post-training.
We adopt stage-specific attention masks to control information exchange
between video and action tokens within each MoT block.
As illustrated in Figure
4
, the joint sequence
comprises four groups: memory tokens, current frame tokens, future frame tokens, and action tokens. We use a densely connected video mask during pretraining and introduce
more structured dependencies during post-training.
We use stage-specific attention masks to balance flexible multimodal learning during pretraining with an explicit video-to-action pathway during post-training. During pretraining, video tokens attend to all video tokens but not to action tokens, preserving action-independent video generation. Action tokens attend to both video and action tokens, allowing the action expert to learn from the full visual and action context. During post-training, memory and current-frame tokens attend to one another; future-video tokens attend to the current-frame and future-video tokens, and action tokens attend to future-video and action tokens. This structure routes information from memory and current observations through predicted future features to action predictions, encouraging actions to be grounded in the modeled visual evolution. For tasks with strong memory demands, we use the pretraining mask instead, allowing action tokens to access memory tokens directly.
2.2
Data Processing
2.2.1
Robot Data Processing
We curate heterogeneous robot demonstrations through a unified pipeline comprising semantic auditing, representation standardization, and trajectory filtering. We first map source-specific state and action fields into a shared representation with explicit validity masks. We then trim stationary episode boundaries, remove short trajectories, and apply kinematic and temporal consistency checks. Processing rules are configured for each source and embodiment to accommodate differences in annotation availability, control semantics, and signal characteristics.
Semantic Auditing and Representation Standardization.
We first check what each source field represents, including joint order, EEF coordinates and rotations, gripper opening direction, and the meaning of recorded actions. State and action are mapped separately because a measured state and a control target are not interchangeable. Available values are placed in the shared 46-dimensional layout described in Section
2.3.2
. Separate state and action masks identify which entries are available; missing or non-finite values are set to zero and masked out.
EEF rotations are converted to unit quaternions in

Depending on the robot, we reorder the original channels, combine coupled finger joints, or map a shared hand-closure signal to the corresponding finger-bending slots. These slots therefore do not always represent independently measured finger joints. Unsupported hand motions remain masked. Four additional slots store supported waist and torso signals, such as waist pitch and torso lift, with a mapping specified for each robot; unused slots remain masked. Signal Anomaly and State–Action Consistency Filtering.
We apply three complementary signal checks and reject episodes that fail an applicable criterion.
Sudden-change detection.
We estimate a smooth trajectory using median and Savitzky–Golay filtering, then evaluate the residual together with second- and third-order temporal differences. A sample is flagged when an excessive residual coincides with an excessive higher-order difference. Robust, channel-specific thresholds distinguish abrupt anomalies from ordinary motion. Quaternion signs are aligned temporarily during detection to avoid artificial discontinuities between equivalent rotations. The smoothing and sign alignment are used for detection and do not replace the stored signals.
State–action consistency.
For comparable joint dimensions with sufficient motion, we compare the directions of changes in smoothed state and action signals. We search offsets within

Extreme-value detection.
We estimate the 1st and 99th percentiles from valid samples within each repository. The admissible interval extends beyond these quantiles by the larger of five times their span and a channel-specific minimum margin. Episodes containing out-of-range or non-finite active values are rejected. Quaternion, gripper, and dexterous-hand channels are exempt from this range test. Source-specific configurations determine the applicable checks and exemptions.

Hand-to-Action Mapping.
We derive a canonical wrist pose from each transformed hand.
The wrist keypoint defines its position, while the wrist and
metacarpophalangeal joints define its orientation. Specifically,
the forward axis points from the wrist toward the centroid
of the four finger bases, and a least-squares palm plane
provides the palm normal. A handedness correction gives the
left and right hands consistent axis semantics.
We additionally extract a continuous gripper-openness target
from the distance between the thumb tip and a virtual opposing
finger formed from the index and middle fingertips.
Normalizing this distance by palm width reduces dependence
on hand size. For dexterous-hand supervision, finger bending
and thumb opposition are mapped to six bounded joint-position
targets per hand.
Quality Filtering and Validity Masks.
We assess hand annotations using biomechanical plausibility,
coordinate bounds, bone lengths, and temporal motion
statistics, including velocity, acceleration, and jerk.
Motion derivatives are computed using actual timestamps
and world-coordinate hand trajectories. Camera rotations
are checked for orthogonality and determinant consistency.
Dataset-specific thresholds accommodate differences in
motion statistics across sources.
Quality annotations are consumed at the sampled action
timesteps. Targets associated with rejected frames are
masked, while windows with more than 20% rejected action
timesteps are discarded. An invalid reference camera pose
invalidates the corresponding action chunk. During action
construction, non-finite coordinates, padded frames, and
degenerate hand geometry are further excluded through
validity masks. Missing observations of one hand do not
automatically invalidate the other. This preserves usable
visual context and partial hand supervision without treating
unavailable action dimensions as valid zero-valued targets.

2.4
Efficiency Implementation
Inference acceleration.
We accelerate inference by decoupling video and action denoising. At deployment, a naive implementation performs
N
N
denoising steps in both the video and action branches, typically with
N
=
10
N=10
. Multi-step denoising in the computationally intensive video branch substantially increases inference cost. For acceleration, we perform
n
n
synchronized denoising steps that update both branches and construct per-layer video key–value features; the remaining
N
−
n
N-n
action denoising steps reuse the features from the final synchronized step. The directional attention mask permits this reuse without feedback from action tokens to video tokens, although freezing early video features approximates joint denoising. Visual features are refreshed for every observation, and future-video RGB decoding is omitted. Action chunks, comprising 48 steps in the paper setting, amortize observation encoding across the predicted sequence.
We further accelerate action inference through operator fusion and CUDA Graph replay. The action denoising computation is compiled with
torch.compile
into optimized GPU kernels, fusing compatible operations to reduce intermediate memory traffic and kernel launches. CUDA Graphs capture the resulting GPU execution sequence and replay it during subsequent denoising steps, reducing Python dispatch and CPU-side kernel-launch overhead. The policy runs in BF16 under inference mode. We also reuse language context, scheduler metadata, and timestep-dependent AdaLN tensors, and evaluate QKV projection, KV-buffer, and fixed-shape attention optimizations. Compilation and graph capture are completed during warmup.
Asynchronous execution.
To maintain smooth robot motion despite model inference latency, we decouple policy inference from action execution in real-world experiments. The server computes the next action chunk on the GPU while the client continues executing the current chunk. The client prefetches new predictions based on the remaining execution time of its current plan, with at most one outstanding request to avoid accumulating stale observations. Each predicted chunk is timestamped relative to its input observation. Upon receipt, expired actions are discarded, while the remaining actions retain their original execution times. The client resamples the chunk once onto the 100 Hz servo grid, and the C++ controller handles trajectory splicing and final amplitude limiting.
3
Experiments
3.1
Task Generalization
We investigate how video and action supervision contribute to task generalization in WAMs.
Table
2
compares different supervision settings on RoboTwin 2.0.
Across all settings, we keep the ID video and action data fixed, while varying the availability of OOD videos and action labels.
Here, ID and OOD refer to a fixed task partition defined before introducing additional supervision.
Generalization from ID supervision alone.
When trained with only ID video-action supervision, the model achieves a high ID success rate of 91.85%, but its OOD success rate is limited to 25.07%.
The nonzero OOD performance indicates that the model can transfer some capabilities beyond the tasks providing supervision.
However, the substantial gap between ID and OOD performance shows that this transfer alone is insufficient for reliable execution across the OOD task set.
Additional videos enable transfer without OOD action labels.
Introducing OOD videos while retaining action supervision exclusively from ID tasks raises OOD success from 25.07% to 55.90%, an absolute improvement of 30.83 percentage points.
Meanwhile, ID performance remains nearly unchanged at 91.96%.
The resulting overall success rate increases from 71.81% to 81.14%.
This improvement demonstrates that additional task knowledge supplied through videos can translate into better robot execution without corresponding OOD action labels.
It is consistent with the perspective illustrated in Figure
2
: broader video coverage supports task transfer through a video-to-action bridge whose action supervision comes from ID tasks.
Nevertheless, the remaining gap between ID and OOD success suggests that video supervision alone does not fully resolve the challenges of executing these tasks.
Sparse action supervision strengthens task-specific grounding.
Keeping the video data fixed, adding only one action-labeled demonstration per OOD task increases OOD success from 55.90% to 70.70%.
With five demonstrations per task, success further rises to 84.67%, yielding a 28.77-point improvement over the setting with OOD videos but no OOD action labels.
These gains are consistent with sparse paired supervision strengthening the inverse-dynamics capability that connects visual task evolution to executable actions.
In this regime, the additional demonstrations provide action grounding for tasks already covered by the video data.
Increasing the action budget to 20 demonstrations per task yields 90.03% OOD success, only 2.80 points below the 550-demonstration setting while using approximately 3.6% of its OOD action-label budget.
With 100 demonstrations, OOD success reaches 93.17%; increasing the budget to 550 produces a comparable result of 92.83%, suggesting diminishing returns at higher supervision levels.

Scaling videos yields further gains with limited action supervision.
Experiments 5–9 further illustrate the complementary roles of video and action supervision.
With 100 action-labeled demonstrations per OOD task, increasing OOD videos from 100 to 550 raises OOD success from 88.83% to 93.17%, a gain of 4.34 percentage points.
In contrast, with 550 OOD videos fixed, increasing the action budget from 100 to 550 demonstrations yields no improvement, from 93.17% to 92.83%.
Moreover, the setting with 550 videos and 20 action-labeled demonstrations (Exp. 5) outperforms that with 100 videos and 100 demonstrations (Exp.8), despite using one-fifth as many action labels.
These results suggest that a relatively small amount of paired supervision may suffice to learn an effective video-to-action bridge, or inverse dynamics model.
Once this action grounding is established, additional videos can further improve OOD task execution, whereas increasing action supervision offers limited additional gains in this regime.

RoboTwin 2.0.
We evaluate on 50 language-conditioned manipulation tasks using the ALOHA-AgileX bimanual robot in RoboTwin 2.0
[

We consider two settings: Full RoboTwin uses 50 Clean and 500 Randomized demonstrations per task, while Clean2Random uses only the 50 Clean demonstrations to assess generalization to randomized scenes of the same tasks. The policy conditions on head and wrist RGB observations, language instructions, and proprioception, and incorporates short- and long-term visual memory to predict joint-position and gripper commands. We train for 60,000 steps on the combined Clean and Randomized data in Full RoboTwin, and for 20,000 steps on Clean data alone in Clean2Random. Under Clean2Random, it achieves 88.3% on Clean and 73.4% on Randomized scenes, averaging 80.9%. These results demonstrate reliable execution across diverse manipulation tasks and robustness to scene variations, including transfer to randomized environments when downstream training uses only Clean demonstrations.

Tasks and evaluation procedure.
We evaluate WorldBridge on six complementary manipulation tasks across AgiBot G2 and ARX AC-1, covering long-horizon execution, precise manipulation, spatial alignment, bimanual coordination, and memory-dependent interaction.
Figure
6
presents representative executions, with annotations highlighting the operations associated with these capability requirements.
On G2,
arranging flowers
requires relocating vases, successively grasping and inserting two slender flowers, and placing the completed arrangement.
It tests long-horizon sequencing together with precision insertion, since the robot must preserve task progress while repeatedly aligning a thin stem with a vase opening.
Scanning drinks
interleaves sequential manipulation with human-induced scene changes, testing whether the robot can maintain task continuity and the required processing order using visual memory.
Hanging cups
requires grasping two mugs and placing their handles onto rack hooks at different heights.
It tests spatial understanding and orientation-sensitive placement, coupling grasp selection with alignment of the handle and hook.
On AC-1,
separating LEGO bricks
requires repeated bimanual disassembly of connected bricks followed by sorting into bins by color.
It tests long-horizon coordination, stable grasping during separation, and classification-guided placement as the assembly changes throughout execution.
Sorting screws
requires grasping small screws and nuts, placing them into their designated compartments, and closing the box.
It combines fine-grained object discrimination with precise grasping and placement, requiring correct part selection and accurate manipulation within a single sequence.
Packing books
requires opening a schoolbag, inserting a book while maintaining access to the opening, and final closing the bag.
It tests long-horizon manipulation of a deformable container: the robot must coordinate bag opening with subsequent insertion despite changes in the bag’s shape and accessible geometry.

Cross-embodiment experiments.
Cross-embodiment adaptation follows our unified 46-dimensional action representation, which maps robot-specific control variables into fixed semantic slots and uses dimension-wise validity masks to exclude unavailable components from pretraining supervision.
This common interface allows the action expert to learn from heterogeneous control data while preserving the semantics of the available controls.
For the real-robot experiments, we fine-tune the same jointly pretrained checkpoint separately for G2 and AC-1, transferring the shared video and action experts and adapting the state and action interfaces to each platform.
G2 uses 16-dimensional native commands comprising seven joints per arm and two grippers, whereas AC-1 uses 14-dimensional commands comprising six joints per arm and two grippers.
Platform-specific input and output adapters connect the common pretrained experts to these native interfaces.

Pretraining improves all six tasks.

On G2, the gains are 15 percentage points for arranging flowers, 20 for hanging cups, and 15 for scanning drinks.
The improvements therefore span precise small-object handling, spatial alignment, coordinated manipulation, and memory-dependent execution.
In particular, the substantial gains on the AC-1 tasks support the value of joint pretraining for downstream adaptation under the available task demonstrations.
Memory-dependent drink scanning.
In this task, the robot must grasp a scanner, scan the original drinks in order, and finally scan an additional drink introduced by a human during execution.
Correct execution requires three aspects of memory.
First, the robot must remember each drink’s placement destination after scanning, preserving the spatial association across grasping, scanning, and placement.
Second, it must track which drinks have already been scanned to select the next drink without repeating or omitting a scan.
Third, it must identify the newly introduced drink and defer its scan until the original drinks have been processed, preserving the order of task events despite the scene change.
The drink-scanning row in Fig.
6
visualizes these dependencies through placement markers, highlighted scanned drinks, and the human introduction of a drink designated for the final scan.
A drink’s current pose does not necessarily reveal its scanning status or when it entered the scene; visually similar observations can therefore demand different next actions depending on the execution history.
WorldBridge conditions action prediction on short- and long-term visual history, providing context for recent manipulation transitions and earlier task events.

5
Conclusion
We presented WorldBridge, a World Action Model that connects visual dynamics to executable control for task generalization.
Our study highlights the complementary roles of video coverage and action grounding: additional task videos enable transfer beyond the tasks providing action supervision, while even a single action-labeled demonstration per new task substantially improves execution.
Guided by these findings, WorldBridge couples video and action experts through structured attention and joint flow matching, incorporating temporal memory, action forcing, and unified pre-training on heterogeneous robot and egocentric demonstrations.
Experiments across simulation benchmarks and two real-robot platforms demonstrate strong manipulation performance and the benefits of joint video–action pretraining.
These results suggest that advancing task generalization requires both broader visual experience and a transferable video-to-action bridge.
Extending this bridge to more diverse tasks with less action supervision remains an important direction for future work.

article.headline: WorldBridge：视频拓宽机器人任务泛化
article.lede: 论文量化视频覆盖与动作监督对分布外任务的各自贡献，并提出世界动作模型 WorldBridge。
article.problem: 机器人需要在训练任务之外执行新任务，但现有 VLA 研究多集中在物体摆放、视角、光照等执行条件鲁棒性上，而非任务本身的泛化。世界动作模型（WAM）同时做视觉预测与动作生成，被视为通向任务泛化的路径；但视频泛化与动作泛化各贡献多少、二者之间的「视频到动作桥」何时成为瓶颈，此前缺少拆分测量。
article.method: WorldBridge 采用 Mixture-of-Transformers，视频专家与动作专家各自持有参数，通过联合自注意力交换信息；结构化注意力掩码把信息流从历史观测与当前帧导向预测的未来视频，再导向动作。训练使用联合 flow matching，并加入短、长两个时间尺度的视觉记忆和 action forcing（同一动作块内不同 token 赋不同噪声等级）。数据侧搭建统一管线，把异构机器人轨迹与第一人称人手演示映射到 46 维动作表示，用维度有效性掩码保留部分监督。
article.results: 在 RoboTwin 2.0 上，仅用分布内视频-动作监督时 ID 成功率 91.85%、OOD 仅 25.07%；加入 OOD 视频但动作标签仍限于 ID 后 OOD 升至 55.90%，每任务再加 1 条动作演示达 70.70%，5 条 84.67%，20 条 90.03%。全量数据下平均 96.23%（Clean 96.16%、Randomized 96.30%），Clean2Random 80.9%，RoboCasa GR1 TableTop 82.8%，DOMINO Level-1 为 57.6% SR / 64.6 MS，RMBench 83.0%，SimplerEnv-WidowX 84.4%，RoboDojo 平均 26.03 分 / 19.15% SR；真机六任务平均 72.5%，对比 π0.5 的 57.5%。
article.why_it_matters: 它拆分并量化了「多拍视频」与「少量动作标注」对任务泛化的边际收益，给出了可操作的数据配比结论：视频扩展覆盖范围，稀疏动作补足视觉到动作的接地。
article.limitations: 任务泛化的定量结论只在 RoboTwin 2.0 单一基准和固定 ID/OOD 划分上得到，且无 OOD 动作标签时 55.90% 仍远低于 ID 的 91.96%，说明桥接并不完整。真机每任务仅 20 次试验、螺丝分拣成功率 55%，而推理加速中复用早期视频特征只是对联合去噪的近似。
article.figure_caption_zh: WorldBridge 总览：融合异构数据源、两阶段训练，底部给出不同视频与动作监督下的任务泛化结果、基准成绩及真机部署表现。

figure.caption: {Overview of our WorldBridge, a foundational WAM for task generalization.} WorldBridge utilizes heterogeneous data sources and is trained with a simple but effective model architecture in two stages. The bottom panels report task-generalization results under different video and action supervision settings, benchmark performance, and real-world deployment results.

page_papers.title: Disentangling Dual Image References in Frequency Aware Diffusion Models for Personalized Generation
page_papers.abstract: Personalized image generation aims to synthesize text-driven images conditioned on reference images, while mainly casting the generation as image customization for foreground and style transfer for background. Previous arts of diffusion models suffers from the text misalignment with background for image customization and foreground for style transfer during the denoising process. Such facts, as we observed, rooted from the entanglement among hybrid frequency bands during the denoising process. To address such salient limitation, in this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle these Dual image references within Frequency-aware Diffusion Models, dubbed Dual-FDM, to simultaneously tackle two crucial personalized image generation tasks: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. For customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference. For color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference. Both the substituted frequency bands are used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image.Extensive experiments validate the superiority of Dual-FDM over the state-of-the-art diffusion models for personalized image generation. Our code can be accessed from https://github.com/htyjers/Dual-FDM.
page_papers.content:
Disentangling Dual Image References in Frequency Aware Diffusion Models for Personalized Generation
Haipeng Liu
Yang Wang
†
†
thanks:
Yang Wang is the corresponding author
Meng Wang
Affiliation:
School of Computer Science and Information Engineering
Affiliation:
Hefei University of Technology, China
Email:
hpliu_hfut@hotmail.com
yangwang@hfut.edu.cn
eric.mengwang@gmail.com
Abstract
Personalized image generation aims to synthesize text-driven images conditioned on reference images, while mainly casting the generation as image customization for foreground and style transfer for background. Previous arts of diffusion models suffers from the text misalignment with background for image customization and foreground for style transfer during the denoising process. Such facts, as we observed, rooted from the entanglement among hybrid frequency bands during the denoising process. In particular, the low-frequency band primarily captures color information, mid-frequency band encodes global structure, while high-frequency band corresponds to local texture.
Besides, the early (high-noise) denoising stage mainly focuses on the low-and-mid frequency bands, while the late (low-noise) denoising stage progressively exhibits the high-frequency band, resulting in the dominance of low-and-mid over high frequency bands, especially when entangled within a single image reference, tends to reinforce each other at the early stage, hence the pitfall of overwhelming suppression of text prompt guidance. To address such salient limitation, in this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle these
Dual
image references within
F
requency-aware
D
iffusion
M
odels, dubbed
Dual-FDM
, to simultaneously tackle two crucial personalized image generation tasks: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. For customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference. For color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference. Both the substituted frequency bands are used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image.
We further compute the ratio of information entropy of the substituted frequency bands to adaptively modulate the denoising timesteps between the early and late stages. Extensive experiments validate the superiority of
Dual-FDM
over the state-of-the-art diffusion models for personalized image generation. Our code can be accessed from
https://github.com/htyjers/Dual-FDM
.

:
Personalized images generated by our
Dual-FDM
. (a) The generated examples of

for customized references (left) and style references (above); (b) The generated examples of

for color references (left) and style references (above).
1
Introduction
Figure 2
:
(a) Comparison of the generated results, as well as the attention score map of text prompts and image references, between IP-Adapter
Ye et al. (2023)
and MS-Diffusion
Wang et al. (2025)
for image customization. (b) Comparison of the generated results between InstantStyle
Wang et al. (2024a)
and StyleStudio
Lei et al. (2025)
for style transfer. (c) Comparison of generated results guided by different frequency band of the image reference.
Personalized image generation focuses on synthesizing text-driven images conditioned on reference images, which enjoys remarkable progress, benefiting from the powerful denosing capabilities of Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs)
Ho et al. (2020)
;
Liu et al. (2024)
;
Liu et al. (2025a)
,
e.g.
, Stable Diffusion
Rombach et al. (2022)
;
Esser et al. (2024)
;
Podell et al. (2023)
;
Qian et al. (2022)
;
Qian et al. (2023)
;
Wang et al. (2024c)
. Typically, the personalized image generation involves two key subtasks,
i.e.
,
image customization
and
style transfer
. Given text prompts, image customization
Xiao et al. (2025)
;
Zeng et al. (2024)
;
Pang et al. (2024)
;
Gal et al. (2022)
;
Ruiz et al. (2023)
;
Kumari et al. (2023)
;
Liu et al. (2025b)
;
Ma et al. (2024)
;
Li et al. (2024)
;
Li et al. (2023)
;
Liu et al. (2022)
;
Cao et al. (2026)
;
Jiang et al. (2026)
aims to generate images by substituting the foreground semantics in the text prompts with the foreground extracted from the reference images, while preserving the background of the text prompts. In contrast, style transfer
Qin et al. (2025)
;
Rout et al. (2025)
;
Liu et al. (2023)
;
Sohn et al. (2023)
;
Zhu et al. (2025)
;
Qi et al. (2024)
;
Hertz et al. (2024)
;
Lei et al. (2025)
;
Gao et al. (2024)
;
Xing et al. (2024)
;
Wang et al. (2024b)
;
Wang et al. (2024a)
;
Jeong et al. (2024)
;
Wang et al. (2022)
focuses on disentangling style (
background
) from reference images and aligning the foreground with the text prompt. However, prior arts have struggled to align the generated image with the text prompts within each individual subtask.
Figure 3
:
Illustration of our proposed
Dual-FDM
pipeline (a); For customization style transfer (b), we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference, named
Dual-FDM
cust
(Sec.
2.3
). For the color style transfer (c), we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference, named
Dual-FDM
cost
(Sec.
2.4
). Each of the two personalized image generation tasks are conducted in the early and late stage of the whole denoising process guided by text prompts as illustrated in Eq. (
1
).
For image customization, substantial efforts
Ye et al. (2023)
;
Aiello et al. (2025)
;
Huang et al. (2025b)
aim to
emphasize dense image references of the foreground while overwhelming sparse text prompts of the background, especially for complex ones
,
e.g.
, a degraded “
flower wreath
” and the missing “
coffee
” in the IP-Adapter
Ye et al. (2023)
of Fig.
2
(a). Building on this, layout-based methods
Wang et al. (2025)
;
Huang et al. (2025b)
;
Zhang et al. (2024)
exploit spatial layouts to explicitly constrain reference concepts to the foreground, while assigning background regions to text prompts.
This preserves the foreground identity, but the explicit separation of foreground and background in the layout disrupts overall consistency, leading to the misalignment with (complex / long) text prompts.
As illustrated in the MS-Diffusion
Wang et al. (2025)
of Fig.
2
(a), the generated spatial arrangement of “
flower wreath
” and “
coffee
” diverges from the prompt and instead resembles
“A flower wreath around a dog near a coffee”
.
When coming to style transfer, during the early stage of the denoising process with high-level noise, the foreground is reconstructed from sparse text prompts,
the dense style information intended for the background often leaks into the foreground, resulting in misalignment with the text prompts
,
e.g.
, the incorrect number of “
woman
" in the InstantStyle
Wang et al. (2024a)
of Fig.
2
(b). To resolve such issue, StyleStudio
Lei et al. (2025)
applies style via instance normalization
Huang and Belongie (2017)
in the cross-attention layers and leverages layout to preserve foreground in the self-attention layers. Nevertheless, self-attention score maps highlight only the most salient regions, implying that the extracted layout can align only with simple text prompts (
i.e.
, “
a dog
") rather than the multi-objects (“
two pillows and one lemon
" in the StyleStudio
Lei et al. (2025)
of Fig.
2
(b)) text prompts, thereby
preventing it from handling the complex text prompts
.
So far, neither image customization nor style transfer achieves satisfactory alignment between the generated image and the text prompt for diffusion models. Such facts, as we observed, rooted from the entanglement among hybrid frequency bands. Intuitively, as shown in Fig.
2
(c), the low-frequency and mid-frequency bands capture color and global structure, while high-frequency band focuses on local texture, where different frequency bands are mainly denoised during
different
stages of the denoising process. As we observed, the early (high-noise) denoising stage mainly focuses on the low-and-mid frequency bands, while the late (low-noise) denoising stage progressively exhibits the high-frequency band (See Sec.
A
of the Appendix), the dominance of low-and-mid over high frequency bands, especially when entangled within a single image reference, suggesting reinforce each other at the early stages, resulting in an overwhelming suppression of text prompt guidance.
To resolve the text misalignment for personalization generation, we propose to solve the problem upon dual references and develop a paradigm to disentangle these
Dual
image references within
F
requency-aware
D
iffusion
M
odels, dubbed
Dual-FDM
, for two classical personalized image generation tasks in a row: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. Specifically:
•
We propose to map the foreground or background of image references into the frequency domain via Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT), where a mask is applied from left to right to progressively disentangle the low-, mid-, and high-frequency bands. Notably, for customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference, named
Dual-FDM
cust
(Fig.
1
(a)). The style reference with the mid-frequency band substituted is used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image in the decoupled cross-attention layer. For the color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference, named
Dual-FDM
cost
(Fig.
1
(b)). The style reference with the substituted low-frequency band is further utilized as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image in the decoupled cross-attention layer.
•
To pop up the foreground or background of the image reference, we utilize the key projection matrices in the decoupled cross-attention layer to represent the foreground, which are then reformulated through singular value decomposition (SVD) to derive the corresponding
background matrix
for the background.
•
For each task, we further compute the ratio of information entropy of the substituted frequency bands to adaptively modulate the denoising timesteps between the early and late stages, so as to achieve a well-balanced performance between text alignment and dual-image similarity.
Extensive experiments validate the superiority of Dual-FDM over the state-of-the-art diffusion models for personalized image generation.
2
Methodology
Central to our proposed Dual-FDM cover the following aspects: 1) how to pop up the background of the image references (Sec.
2.2
); 2) how to disentangle the mid-frequency band in customization style transfer (Sec.
2.3
); 3) how to disentangle the low-frequency band in color style transfer (Sec.
2.4
); 4) how to adaptively modulate the timesteps within the denoising process between early and late stages (Sec.
2.5
). Before shedding light on Dual-FDM, we elaborate the preliminary regarding decoupled cross-attention mechanism, which plays a pivotal role of personalized image generation.

Text and Image Alignment
via
CLIP
1
1
1
Since CLIP is trained on real image–text (T) pairs, it is particularly sensitive to image style, which may distort text–image similarity. To alleviate this, we propose CLIP-TS by measuring similarity with style reference (S), thereby reducing the style influence . In addition, the generated background aligned with text prompts can interfere with the customized reference (C); hence we propose CLIP-TC, which incorporates text prompts to suppress such interference. We also provide CLIP-T (image–text similarity) and CLIP-CS (image–image reference similarity) for comparison.

4
Conclusion
In this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle dual image references within frequency-aware diffusion models, dubbed
Dual-FDM
, for two classical personalized image generation tasks in a row: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. Extensive experiments validate
the superiority of
Dual-FDM
over the state-of-the-art diffusion models.

Appendix C
The algorithm of customization style transfer and color style transfer
Due to the page limitation, we summarize the process of customization style transfer in Algorithm
1
and color style transfer in Algorithm
2
.
To tackle the text-alignment issue in personalized image generation, in this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color and style reference - and propose a paradigm to disentangle these
Dual
image references within
F
requency-aware
D
iffusion
M
odels, dubbed
Dual-FDM
, for two classical personalized image generation tasks in a row: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy within frequency domain. For customization style transfer, we replace the mid-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from the foreground of the customized reference. For color style transfer, we substitute the low-frequency band of the background in the style reference with that from both the foreground and background of the color reference. Both the substituted frequency bands are used as the key and value to reconstruct the query foreground and background of the denoised personalized image.
For each task, we further compute the ratio of information entropy of the substituted frequency bands to adaptively modulate the denoising timesteps between the early and late stages.

Appendix D
More details about the implementation details
As mentioned in Sec.3.1 of the mainbody, due to page limitation, we further provide more details about the implementation details as follows:
Datasets.
We evaluate
Dual-FDM
on combined datasets covering image customization, style transfer, and text-to-image (T2I) generation:
•
Image Customization
: 1)
DreamBench
Ruiz et al. (2023)
+
TI benchmark
Gal et al. (2022)
: a well-known single-object personalized image generation dataset comprising 38 subjects, covering unique objects and pets such as backpacks, stuffed animals, dogs, cats, sunglasses, and cartoons, with each subject associated with 25 prompts; 2)
DreamBench++
Peng et al. (2025)
: the latest human-aligned personalized image generation benchmark, comprising 65 object classes, 20 human classes, and 45 animal classes. For each image, 9 text prompts are generated by GPT-4o to span a range of difficulty levels.
•
Style Transfer
: 1)
IS-Plus benchmark
Wang et al. (2024b)
: a style evaluation benchmark containing 104 images across diverse styles; 2)
StyleBench
Gao et al. (2024)
: a style evaluation benchmark covering 73 distinct styles, ranging from paintings, flat illustrations, and 3D rendering to sculptures with varying materials. For each style, 5–7 distinct images with variations are collected. In total, StyleBench contains 490 images across diverse styles.
•
T2I generation
:
T2I-CompBench++
Huang et al. (2025a)
: an enhanced benchmark for compositional text-to-image generation. T2I-CompBench++ comprises 8,000 compositional text prompts categorized into four primary groups: attribute binding, object relationships, generative numeracy, and complex compositions. These are further divided into eight sub-categories.
Based on the above, we construct several combined datasets for different joint tasks: 1) for customization style transfer (small-scale), we concatenate
DreamBench
and
TI benchmark
as the customization references, and use
IS-Plus benchmark
as the style references; 2) for customization style transfer (large-scale), we take
DreamBench++
as the customization references and
StyleBench
as the style references; 3) for color style transfer, we combine
InstantStyle-Plus
and
StyleBench
as the color and style references, while text prompts are provided by
T2I-CompBench++
for stylized image generation.
Metrics.
We consider 9 evaluation metrics from three aspects to evaluate our
Dual-FDM
:
•
Text and Image Reference Alignment
: we follow previous methods and adopt two representative models,
CLIP
2
2
2
Since CLIP is trained on real image–text (T) pairs, it is particularly sensitive to image style, which may distort text–image similarity. To alleviate this, we propose CLIP-TS by measuring similarity with style reference (S), thereby reducing the style influence . In addition, the generated background aligned with text prompts can interfere with the customized reference (C); hence we propose CLIP-TC, which incorporates text prompts to suppress such interference. We also provide CLIP-T (image–text similarity) and CLIP-CS (image–image reference similarity) for comparison.
and
DINO
Caron et al. (2021)
, for evaluation. Specifically,
CLIP-T
measures the similarity between generated images and the given text prompts;
CLIP-TC
and
CLIP-TS
evaluate the similarity between generated images and customized (or style) reference images while jointly considering the text prompts; finally,
CLIP-CS
assesses the similarity between generated images and dual-reference images.
•
Image Generation Quality
: we employ Image Reward (
IR
)
Xu et al. (2023)
to model human preferences for image quality and
HPS V2
Wu et al. (2023)
that combines perceptual studies with deep learning for comprehensive visual and semantic assessment. Both metrics measure the semantics consistency of the high-quality image generation aligned with human standards;
•
Time Complexity
: We employ the inference time (
Times
) and Video Random Access Memory (
VRAM
) consumption to evaluate the computational efficiency and memory footprint of different methods during image generation.
Model Configuration.
Our main experiments are conducted on the pre-trained IP-Adapter-Plus
Ye et al. (2023)
with SDXL
Podell et al. (2023)
model as the text-to-image diffusion model, configured with 30 sampling steps and and a fixed random seed of 42, to ensure high-quality outputs. We use the recommended hyper-parameters for each method across all images to ensure fair comparison. All experiments are implemented in PyTorch and conducted on a NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU.

article.headline: 频域解耦双参考改善个性化生成文本对齐
article.lede: 论文提出Dual-FDM，用DCT掩码在频域分离定制/颜色参考与风格参考，缓解双参考频带纠缠造成的文本提示压制。
article.problem: 个性化图像生成需同时保持文本对齐与参考相似，但图像定制常使背景文本提示被密集参考压制，风格迁移又会让风格信息泄漏到前景。作者将成因归为去噪过程中低、中、高频段的纠缠：早期高噪声阶段低中频占主导并压制文本引导。
article.method: Dual-FDM把参考前景/背景经DCT变换后用掩码分离低中高频。定制风格迁移用定制参考前景的中频替换风格参考背景的中频，颜色风格迁移用颜色参考前景与背景的低频替换风格参考背景的低频。替换后的频带作为解耦交叉注意力的key/value重建查询，并用信息熵比自适应划分早晚去噪阶段。
article.results: 表1中Dual-FDM_cust的CLIP-T为0.3194、CLIP-TC为0.5031、HPS×10为2.6007，均高于表中对比方法；表2颜色类CLIP-TS为0.5015、CLIP-S为0.7178、DINO-S为0.4970。推理时间10.26s、显存12.48GB。消融显示自适应时间步结果落在0.4与0.5固定比例之间。
article.why_it_matters: 把双参考生成中的频带纠缠显式拆开，为「定制+风格」和「颜色+风格」两类任务提供统一的频域替换框架。
article.limitations: 作者指出，当风格参考包含极稀疏的线条图案时，中频定制线索可能衰减高频风格细节，导致风格信息不完整；论文也未报告误差棒或统计显著性检验（检查表填 N/A）。

Abstract
Pixel-space diffusion models have recently re-emerged as a compelling alternative to latent diffusion, avoiding the lossy latent bottleneck and separately trained autoencoder. JiT shows that a vanilla diffusion transformer can generate directly in pixel space by replacing the commonly used velocity prediction (

In addition, we find that vanilla pixel diffusion transformers, irrespective of parameterization, retain a persistent high-frequency deficit relative to real images. To address this, we introduce

Introduction
Diffusion and flow-based models have become a leading paradigm for visual generation in recent years.
Modern versions of these models predominantly operate in the latent space, obtained from compressing the pixel-space data with a separately-trained autoencoder.
However, latent diffusion models (LDMs) (

Recent works (
Li and He (2026)
;
Chen et al. (2026b)
;

;

aforementioned drawbacks in LDMs.

Prediction parameterization alone does not resolve all limitations of
vanilla pixel diffusion transformers. Irrespective of the parameterization,
we find that JiT-family models exhibit a persistent high-frequency deficit
relative to real images. This suggests a limitation
of the minimalist large-patch design, where patch tokens are projected
directly back to pixels using
MLP
-layers without an explicit local refinement pathway. We
introduce
ConvRefiner
, a lightweight residual convolutional
module trained post hoc with perceptual and adversarial supervision while
keeping the diffusion backbone frozen. With only 5% post-hoc training,
ConvRefiner
brings the generated high-frequency spectrum closer to that of
real images while preserving FID.
Overall, this work presents adaptive prediction parameterization and fine-scale signal modeling
as complementary directions for improving vanilla pixel diffusion transformers.
To summarize, the key contributions are:
•
We introduce
MFlow
, a framework of continuous, direction-adaptive prediction
parameterization whose gains are learned jointly with the generator
under a standard velocity-space flow-matching objective. We show
MFlow
is a general framework and can be used for diverse domains like pixel-space video generation, high-dimensional latents (like RAEv2) in addition to pixel-space image generation.
•
We identify a high-frequency deficit in vanilla
JiT-style models and introduce
ConvRefiner
, a lightweight post-hoc
module that restores high-frequency details while preserving fidelity matching the frequency spectrum of real images.

4.2
ConvRefiner: A simple post-hoc fix
Based on our analysis we suspect that this high-frequency deficit might be specific to the JiT-based pixel diffusion architecture. However, as seen in the previous section, convolutional VAE decoders are able to recover high-frequency.
Chen et al. (2025a)
note that only finetuning the last few layers of a pretrained VAE with an adversarial loss can improve local details at a reduced training cost.
Motivated by this, we add a few lightweight convolutional blocks and post-hoc train only these blocks using an additional GAN loss apart from flow-matchting losses (Fig

Conclusion
We revisit two design questions in vanilla pixel diffusion transformers: how their prediction parameterization should adapt to the data, and whether their minimalist architecture captures high-frequency. We introduce
MFlow
, a direction-adaptive parameterization that learns a continuous interpolation between clean-data and velocity prediction across principal data directions, avoiding the need for manual subspace selection, saving parameterization search cycles.
Our analysis of the learned M-curves further shows that the preferred parameterization changes systematically with both data statistics and model capacity.
Beyond parameterization, we identify a persistent high-frequency deficit in JiT-style models and address it with
ConvRefiner
, a lightweight post-hoc convolutional module that restores high-frequency statistics while preserving generative quality. Together, these results suggest that both adaptive prediction targets and explicit treatment of fine-scale signal structure are important ingredients for scaling simple pixel-space diffusion transformers.
AI use statement
In this work, we used AI tools only in supporting non-research roles under author supervision. Specifically, we used it to correct grammatical errors and improve the clarity of author-written text, and to assist with software tooling. In particular, we used it for plotting and visualization code used to produce some of the figures in this paper. We did not use AI tools for research ideations, for deriving results, for designing experiments, or for generating any scientific claims. We have reviewed all the AI-assisted text and figures for correctness.
Reproducibility statement
We provide the
MFlow
’s closed-form velocity-recovery rule in Sec.
3.2
and Python-like pseudocode in Sec.
A.2
. The post-hoc
ConvRefiner
is specified as an architecture figure in Fig.
7
, and its training objective is provided in Section
4
and Appendix
A.7
. Full training and sampling configurations like optimizer, learning-rate schedule, batch size, EMA, noise schedule, and the guidance interval, guidance scale, and number of sampling steps used at evaluation, are tabulated per model in Appendix
A.1
. Radially-averaged power spectrum (RAPS) evaluation protocol are described in Appendix
A.6
. All reported metrics (FID, FVD, RAPS, GenEval, DPG, Prism) are computed with standard public implementations we cite.

article.headline: 像素扩散Transformer：自适应预测目标
article.lede: MFlow 沿数据主方向连续插值 x0 与速度预测，免去手工选秩；ConvRefiner 事后补回高频。
article.problem: JiT 证明朴素扩散 Transformer 可以在像素空间直接生成，其做法是把常用的速度预测换成干净图像（x0）预测；但采样时仍需把 x0 转成速度，在低噪声端这一步病态。AsymFlow 用固定秩 r 的硬截断缓解该问题，可秩要按数据集手工扫，论文称其调一个秩就需要 6 次训练。此外，作者发现 JiT 家族模型无论用哪种参数化，生成图像在 0.5–0.7 径向频率段都相对真实图像存在高频缺失。
article.method: MFlow 把二值投影算子换成对称的加性算子 M = U diag(m1…mD) Uᵀ（U 为 patch-PCA 基），每个主方向的增益 mi∈[0,1] 由 sigmoid(φi) 参数化、与生成器联合训练，回归目标为 uG = x0 − Mε；由于相应线性系统行列式恒为负，速度可以被精确恢复，因此训练仍用标准的速度空间 flow-matching 损失。ConvRefiner 是一个轻量残差卷积模块，在冻结扩散主干的前提下事后训练，用感知损失与对抗损失（PatchGAN，仅作用于近干净样本）修正 x0 预测。
article.results: ImageNet 256×256 的 B 级模型上，不加 LPIPS 时 MFlow 的 FID 为 3.74，反而不及 JiT 的 3.70 与 AsymFlow 的 3.59；加上 LPIPS 后 MFlow 降到 3.33，优于 JiT 的 3.42 和 AsymFlow 的 3.40。H 级（953M 参数、363 GFLOPs）上 JiT、AsymFlow、MFlow 分别为 1.82、1.79、1.81。UCF-101 视频 B 级 FVD 为 122（JiT 152、AsymFlow 126、Wan2.1 latent 169），L 级为 97，再加事后 Framewise-LPIPS 后为 94。文生图方面，1.1B 的 MFlow-L 在 GenEval、DPG、PRISM 上分别为 0.8843、84.70、73.9，13B-MoE（2.9B 激活）的 XXL 模型为 0.8898、86.10、75.2。高频缺口方面，JiT-H 的平均径向功率亏损为 −6.69 dB、MFlow-H 为 −6.63 dB，加上 ConvRefiner 后收紧到 −1.29 dB，同时 FID 保持 1.81 不变；该模块仅在已训练 600 epoch 的冻结模型上再训 30 epoch（约 5%）。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「用 x0 还是用速度」从一次性超参选择变成可端到端学习的逐方向连续权重，省掉参数化搜索，并给出了可解释的 M-curve 观察：模型容量越大、越多方向偏向速度预测，而数据表征与目标决定这些方向如何分配。同时它指出高频缺失是 JiT 式大 patch 主干的结构性问题，可以用一个事后的小卷积模块与参数化改进互补地修补。

Abstract
While current Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) provide robust control priors for humanoids, they only execute pre-defined reference motions. As a result, they are vulnerable to environmental shifts and incapable of reactive whole-body coordination.
Naively cascading them with generative motion planners fails to achieve true reactivity, as inevitable tracking discrepancies induce fatal cumulative exposure bias.
To bridge this gap, we propose
ReactiveBFM
, a real-time closed-loop planning-control framework.
At its core, we effectively mitigate exposure bias via a scheduled prefix sampling curriculum, forcing the generative planner to actively learn error-recovery behaviors from imperfect physical states rather than ground-truth trajectories.
Systematically, to reconcile the severe latency mismatch between auto-regressive planning and high-frequency tracking, we introduce an asynchronous replanning mechanism. Combined with trajectory chunking to temporally ensemble spatial references, our system guarantees spatio-temporally fluid execution without physical jitter.
Deployed on the Unitree G1 humanoid, ReactiveBFM demonstrates unprecedented physical agility across a vast repertoire of text-conditioned closed-loop motions. Notably, ReactiveBFM achieves zero-shot moving target reaching, showcasing intricate whole-body coordination and on-the-fly replanning.
In sim-to-sim benchmarking under severe perturbations, ReactiveBFM achieves a 93.1% success rate, significantly outperforming cascaded open-loop baselines by 28.6%.
Our code is available at
https://github.com/zjwzcx/ReactiveBFM
.

1
Introduction
Developing general-purpose humanoid robots demands the mastery of a vast repertoire of diverse motor skills while navigating unpredictable real-world dynamics. When deployed in unstructured environments, humanoids are inevitably subjected to unforeseen physical interactions and evolving task constraints. Thus, a robust autonomous system must consequently function as a reactive planner capable of continuously generating and adapting context-aware whole-body trajectories on the fly.
While recent advancements in universal trackers
[
45
,
47
,
25
]
and Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs)
[
48
,
20
]
provide robust low-level control priors, they strictly demand precise trajectory inputs. Simply cascading them with existing motion generators fails to achieve true reactivity. Current generators predominantly perform offline synthesis
[
41
,
18
,
17
]
or sparse keyframe in-betweening
[
19
,
25
]
, rigidly enforcing an open-loop paradigm. Completely blind to real-time environmental shifts and state transitions, these approaches cause the robot to rapidly accumulate severe physical drift.
To achieve genuine reactivity, the generative planner must operate in an online, closed-loop manner.
However, this architectural shift fatally collides with cumulative exposure bias. Typical planners
[
3
,
52
,
37
]
, accustomed to perfect historical inputs via teacher-forcing, are completely unequipped to handle inevitable tracking discrepancies. Once pushed out of their training distribution, they fail to recover, causing execution errors to compound recursively.
To bridge these critical gaps, we propose
ReactiveBFM
, a closed-loop planning-control framework that fundamentally resolves
cumulative exposure bias
in reactive humanoid control.
Our core solution is a scheduled prefix sampling curriculum for planner training. Instead of relying on perfect ground-truth prefixes, the model actively learns error-recovery behaviors to survive imperfect physical states.
Second, a reactive system must seamlessly handle mid-execution command shifts. We integrate condition dropout and temporal regularization to prevent jerky transitions, ensuring spatio-temporal smoothness during runtime instruction updates.
Finally, redundant kinematic features inherently accelerate physical drift. We strip away this over-parameterization, utilizing a compact representation to strictly bound the error space.
Beyond algorithmic robustness, real-world deployment faces a strict
latency bottleneck
, as auto-regressive generation inherently operates at a lower frequency than motion tracking.
We resolve this frequency mismatch via asynchronous replanning.
To eliminate the physical jitter caused by overlapping asynchronous predictions, we apply trajectory chunking
[
53
,
8
]
to temporally ensemble the spatial references, ensuring fluid hardware execution.
We extensively validate ReactiveBFM through rigorous sim-to-sim benchmarking and real-world deployments on the Unitree G1 humanoid.
ReactiveBFM achieves a 90% success rate and sustains over 40 seconds of continuous execution in zero-shot dynamic target reaching, successfully generalizing without any dynamic-target training data.
Furthermore, our robust streaming interactive control enables seamless transitions between long-horizon maneuvers under continuous text commands.
Sim-to-sim benchmarking reveals our closed-loop architecture achieves a 93.1% task success rate and reduces the fall rate to merely 2.0% under severe perturbations. It significantly outperforms cascaded open-loop baselines, such as TextOp
[
44
]
combined with SONIC
[
25
]
, by 28.6%.

Recent efforts further push motion generators towards autoregressive streaming, real-time interaction, and scaled-up training

However, without rigorous physical constraints, these datasets frequently exhibit physically implausible artifacts, such as foot sliding and self-penetration. Directly injecting these uncorrected priors into a closed-loop framework inevitably triggers severe sim-to-real gaps.

Despite their impressive tracking fidelity, integrating these models into autonomous systems exposes a critical architectural flaw: the reliance on open-loop execution. Frameworks like Mimic2DM

Even when utilizing text-conditioned planners like TextOp

More restrictively, SONIC

25

Similarly, VisualMimic

3
ReactiveBFM: A Closed-Loop Planning-Control System
In this section, we present our closed-loop planning-control framework ReactiveBFM, as illustrated in Fig.
2
. We first detail the training strategies of the reactive whole-body motion planner in Sec.
3.1
. Next, Sec.
3.2
elaborates on our closed-loop architecture and real-world deployment. Finally, we provide an overview of the key implementation details of our BFM in Sec.
3.3
.
3.1
Reactive Whole-Body Motion Planner
We introduce an auto-regressive (AR) motion diffusion model as a reactive, closed-loop planner.
The primary bottleneck in deploying AR planners is
cumulative exposure bias
.
The execution errors compound recursively, shifting the model out of its training distribution.
To break this cycle and ensure robust execution, we propose the following designs.

,

,
3
]
.
Conditioned on language instructions, target positions, and historical proprioception, our AR model synthesizes feasible reference trajectories on the fly in real time.
Traditional representations

Scheduled Auto-Regressive Prefix Sampling.
A fundamental challenge in deploying generative planners within a closed-loop paradigm is mitigating the compounding errors caused by open-world disturbances and imperfect downstream tracking. Traditional kinematic motion generators
[
38
,
37
]
heavily rely on teacher forcing during training, conditioning exclusively on perfect ground-truth prefix trajectories. However, this creates a severe exposure bias. When deployed, any minor discrepancy between the generated reference and the controller’s actual execution forces the planner out of its training distribution, often leading to cascading failures.
To ensure robust closed-loop execution, we propose a curriculum learning paradigm. During the initial training phase, we employ teacher forcing to rapidly warm up the diffusion model. As training progresses, we introduce scheduled sampling by linearly decaying the probability of using ground-truth prefixes. Instead, the model transitions into a
self-rollout
mode, where it autoregressively conditions on its own previously generated predictions over an extended horizon. To further close the sim-to-real gap, we inject Gaussian noise into the prefix representations as domain randomization. This forces the generative planner to learn error-recovery behaviors, ensuring it can stably output physically plausible trajectories even when the current robot state diverges from ideal conditions.
Replanning Smoothness and Condition Adherence.
Beyond prefix stability, a practical closed-loop system must maintain spatiotemporal smoothness and dynamically respond to streaming multi-modal instructions.
First, standard MDMs typically optimize a point-wise MSE loss, which is agnostic to temporal dynamics. This often yields jerky motions that fail to smoothly connect with the robot’s current state. To explicitly enforce kinematic consistency, we augment the training objective with a temporal consistency loss, including first-order (velocity) and second-order (acceleration). The temporal regularization penalizes non-smooth transitions, ensuring holistic trajectory smoothness and zero-order continuity at the prefix-generation boundary.
Second, to prevent the planner from collapsing into a single conditioning modality, we apply independent dropout to the text instructions and target positions during training. As a result, our planner captures unconditioned motion prior.
Also, we simulate cross-motion transitions to handle streaming interactive control where users may issue new commands mid-execution.
Consequently, when reacting to unpredictable conditional shifts, the model relies on this generalized prior to synthesize stable transitions. This fundamentally prevents out-of-distribution tracking errors from escalating into cumulative exposure bias.
High-Quality Data Curation.
Raw kinematic datasets often contain physically infeasible artifacts, such as foot sliding and self-penetration, which rapidly destabilize closed-loop systems through error accumulation. To prevent our planner from proposing unreachable states, we process diverse text-motion corpora including 100STYLE
[
27
]
, AMASS
[
26
]
-HumanML3D
[
9
]
) and Kungfu
[
21
]
through a rigorous physical curation pipeline. First, we enforce kinematic canonicalization and explicit physical corrections via simulation
[
6
]
to strictly eliminate dynamically invalid motions.
In addition, we synthesize 10,000 goal-conditioned reaching trajectories using a pre-trained PhysHSI
[
40
]
policy.
Together, these two data streams yield 37.14 hours of dynamically verified motion data. Ultimately, this corpus equips the planner to translate high-level text intents and dynamic spatial targets into safe, hardware-executable trajectories.
Planner Architecture.
To ensure the real-time inference frequency, our planner adopts a lightweight architecture employing an 8-layer transformer decoder
[
39
]
, following
[
37
,
3
]
. Our transformer-based planner is optimized via a standard diffusion objective
[
11
]
.
Planner Optimization.
To ensure physical continuity between past and future states, we formulate the trajectory generation as a conditional motion inpainting task
[
23
,
14
]
. Specifically, the primary motion stream takes the temporal concatenation of the observed motion prefix and the noisy future motion, processing them jointly through bidirectional self-attention to capture full sequence context. Concurrently, the diffusion time step embedding, and the text instruction tokens are concatenated to form a unified memory stream. This conditioning sequence is subsequently injected into the motion stream via cross-attention layers, allowing the denoising process of the future frames to dynamically query both the semantic intent and the temporal diffusion schedule.
3.2
Closed-Loop System & Real-World Deployment
While our planner provides robust priors, a naive planner-controller cascade often fails under real-world physical disturbances. To enable robust deployment, our closed-loop system resolves three critical challenges: inference latency, replanning consistency, and stable-to-dynamic generalization.
Asynchronous Replanning and Acceleration.
To prevent the planner from blocking the 50 Hz control loop, we implement an event-driven asynchronous execution mechanism. Whenever the unexecuted reference frames in the control buffer drop below a safe margin
N
b
​

frames, the system asynchronously extracts the latest historical proprioception and triggers a non-blocking planner thread.
To minimize the inherent inference and communication latency, we aggressively optimize both networks using TensorRT compilation, reducing the planner’s latency to 19.3 ms and the controller’s to 5.9 ms. Crucially, we strictly isolate the controller process with real-time CPU scheduling priority during deployment. This ensures the 50 Hz control loop is never preempted by the planner’s inference, maintaining stringent real-time responsiveness without compute starvation.
Temporal Ensembling and Spatial Alignment.
Asynchronous replanning inherently generates overlapping reference trajectories, which can induce high-frequency oscillations during deployment. To mitigate this, we employ temporal ensembling
[
53
,
8
]
via trajectory chunking. By blending the overlapping positional and rotational references, we enforce strict spatio-temporal consistency, thereby eliminating inference-induced jittering and ensuring seamless transitions between continuous replanning cycles.
A fundamental prerequisite for stable closed-loop operation is a strictly unified spatial reference. Through data canonicalization during planner training and hardware calibration at controller initialization, both modules are guaranteed to operate within a globally unified world coordinate system, anchored at the robot’s initial footprint.
Figure 3:
(a) ReactiveBFM enables long-horizon zero-shot deployment of reaching a moving target. (b) The recorded actual robot-target trajectories show the effectiveness. (c) The curve illustrates that our system reactively plans coordinated whole-body motion and always reaches the moving global localizer.
Zero-Shot Dynamic Target Reaching via Ego-Centric Reset.
To validate the system’s dynamic replanning agility in the real world, we design an autonomous task to reach moving targets.
The core challenge is a severe distribution shift. Our generative planner was trained exclusively on a limited corpus of static reaching data
[
40
]
.
To resolve this, we propose a continuous ego-centric alignment strategy. At each replanning step, we reset the robot’s instantaneous root pose as the new global origin and transform the target’s position into this egocentric frame. This effectively decomposes continuous dynamic tracking into a sequence of static-reaching sub-tasks, perfectly aligning on-the-fly observations with the static training prior. Meanwhile, physical momentum is seamlessly preserved by conditioning our AR planner on historical proprioception. Consequently, the system achieves robust, zero-shot generalization to long-horizon dynamic target reaching.
3.3
Behavior Foundation Model
We employ ScaleBFM
[
49
]
as our low-level controller. ScaleBFM is a large-scale, pretrained humanoid behavior foundation model capable of robust and versatile whole-body control across diverse behavioral specifications. By formulating whole-body motion tracking as a unified proxy task, ScaleBFM is pretrained via PPO
[
34
]
on a corpus exceeding 100 million retargeted human motion frames. Built upon an expressive and scalable architecture known as the Humanoid Transformer, the model naturally induces structured latent representations of behavioral intentions. Through a carefully designed scaling recipe, ScaleBFM achieves superior control accuracy, robustness, and generalization across diverse scenarios, making it an ideal backbone for our system.
Specifically, we integrate the Whole-Body and Global control modes of ScaleBFM, with root localization provided by an HTC Vive Ultimate Tracker. This configuration enables accurate global motion tracking while maintaining strong resilience to out-of-distribution state deviations, thereby seamlessly complementing our closed-loop planning and control framework.

Deployment.
All real-world experiments are conducted on a Unitree G1, driven by an off-board workstation with an RTX 4090 GPU. During deployment, the moving target’s global pose is captured via an HTC Vive Ultimate Tracker as shown in Fig.
7
and continuously streamed to the planner via Wi-Fi broadcast.
A 50 Hz low-level controller tracks motions generated by an asynchronous planner, which autoregressively predicts 40-frame chunks from the latest 20-frame observation history.
More deployment, training, and evaluation details are provided in the appendix.
4.2
Real-World Deployment
Zero-Shot Dynamic Target Reaching.
Continuous moving targets introduce severe sim-to-real gaps, as varying physical momentum and execution delays easily break open-loop plans. ReactiveBFM solves this by aggressively replanning in the robot’s instantaneous local frame while preserving the autoregressive action prefix to maintain momentum. As shown in Fig.
3
, our closed-loop system achieves zero-shot dynamic target reaching, sustaining continuous execution for over 40 seconds. Across 10 real-world trials, the system maintains a robust 90% success rate without any dynamic-target training data. Ultimately, this demonstrates that our closed-loop architecture can efficiently reuse limited static priors to solve harder, online control problems on physical hardware.
Streaming Interactive Control and Task Switching.
Streaming continuous, text-conditioned behaviors introduces a critical challenge: open-loop generation creates discontinuous joint references when new commands arrive.
As shown in Fig.
4
(e-f), in real-world deployment, ReactiveBFM supports seamless transitions across long-horizon locomotion, expressive upper-body motions, and highly dynamic whole-body maneuvers. The planner conditions on the latest proprioceptive prefix and the current textual instruction, allowing new commands to overwrite the previous intent without resetting the robot. These results validate that our training strategy for condition switching and proprioceptive grounding translates into practical interactive control on hardware.
Robustness Under Physical Disturbances.
We finally evaluate system recovery from external physical perturbations. When pushed outside the intended motion manifold, open-loop baselines fail by rigidly tracking obsolete references. In contrast, during real-world deployments (Fig.
5
), ReactiveBFM recovers by dynamically conditioning future planning windows on the forcefully altered physical state. To further quantify this capability, we benchmark the survival time, fall rate, and tracking error in Table
4
. The results consistently demonstrate superior recovery over open-loop variants. Crucially, this confirms that physical robustness is not merely inherited from the low-level tracking controller, but actively emerges from continuously closing the loop at the planning level.

5
Conclusion & Limitations
We presented ReactiveBFM, a closed-loop planning-control framework for reactive humanoid control in real-world deployment. We solve cumulative exposure bias through scheduled prefix sampling, reduce physical drift via compact state conditioning, and resolve execution latency by asynchronous replanning with trajectory chunking, while also enabling smoother command transitions via condition dropout and temporal regularization.
On Unitree G1, our approach achieves 90% success in zero-shot dynamic goal reaching and sustains over 40 seconds of continuous execution. In sim-to-sim benchmarking under severe perturbations, it attains 93.1% task success with a 2.0% fall rate, surpassing cascaded open-loop baselines by 28.6%.
These results highlight the effectiveness of closed-loop generative planning for robust humanoid autonomy.
Limitations.
Despite strong real-world robustness and scalability, ReactiveBFM relies on two simplifying assumptions.
First, it does not explicitly model precise whole-body humanoid-object interaction, and may therefore fail in contact-rich tasks requiring loco-manipulation.
Second, the online planner is conditioned only on compact target positions, text commands, and kinematic states, which may be insufficient for tasks requiring high-dimensional vision or tactile feedback. Extending the framework to HOI and richer sensory modalities is an important direction for future work.

In the dynamic target reaching experiments, we employ a control paradigm that combines an online planner with global tracking. This requires precise, real-time global localization for both the robot and the handheld moving target. We utilize HTC VIVE Ultimate Trackers as shown in Fig.

as our underlying localization hardware. Prior to deployment, we perform a global mapping of the workspace and calibrate the origin of the world coordinate system. Subsequently, one tracker is rigidly mounted to the rear of the robot’s pelvis using a custom connector to capture the global base state of the humanoid. Concurrently, a second tracker is securely strapped to the human operator’s hand to track the spatial trajectory of the moving target. During online execution, a dedicated Windows laptop receives and processes the global localization data. This node then streams the coordinate information to the primary deployment host via TCP over a local area network (LAN) at 100 Hz, ensuring high-bandwidth and low-latency responses for the real-time control loop.
We note that external localization is task-dependent rather than required by the low-level policy. Our framework is fully flexible to modes including local (w/o global localization) and global tracking.

All real-world experiments are conducted on a Unitree G1 humanoid. The low-level controller runs at 50 Hz, while the motion planner asynchronously generates whenever the execution buffer approaches depletion. At each execution, the motion planner synthesizes 40-frame reference chunks conditioned on the latest 20-frame actual robot trajectories.
The planner is trained on a single RTX 4090 within 48 hours. The BFM is pretrained on 64 GPUs for about 10 days using over 102 million frames in 50 FPS of diverse motion data, delivering unprecedented global tracking precision and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer capabilities.
The deployment computer is equipped with an Intel i9-13900K CPU and an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU.

On the motion side, we perform kinematic canonicalization and explicitly conduct physical corrections within the PyBullet simulator. article.headline: 人形机器人闭环规划，扰动下成功率93.1%
article.lede: 港中文等提出ReactiveBFM，让Unitree G1边执行边重规划，扰动下仿真成功率93.1%。
article.problem: 现有的行为基础模型（BFM）只执行预先给定的参考动作，一旦环境变化或受到外力就无法应对。把生成式运动规划器直接接在它前面也不行：控制器跟踪必然有误差，规划器训练时只见过完美前缀，误差会递归累积，形成致命的暴露偏差（exposure bias）。
article.method: 作者用一个自回归运动扩散模型做闭环规划器，输入文本、目标位置和历史本体感受，输出36维的紧凑轨迹表示（根位置3维、四元数4维、29个关节）。训练上用计划性前缀采样课程：先用teacher forcing预热，再线性降低使用真值前缀的概率，转入self-rollout，并向前缀注入高斯噪声，迫使模型学会从错误状态恢复；同时加入速度、加速度的时间一致性损失和条件dropout。部署时采用事件驱动异步重规划，配合轨迹分块的时间集成来消除重叠预测造成的抖动。
article.results: 在带100N外力的sim-to-sim测试中，ReactiveBFM取得93.1%任务成功率、2.0%跌倒率、根相对MPJPE为34.6mm、重规划平滑度为96.9mm，比TextOp+SONIC（76.4%）高28.6%。时长匹配对照显示，开环ReactiveBFM从1×延长到5×时长成功率由75.2%降到62.3%，而同一5×时长下闭环提升到93.1%（+30.8%）。在Unitree G1真机上，零样本移动目标到达10次试验成功率90%，连续执行超过40秒；TensorRT加速后规划器延迟19.3ms、控制器5.9ms，控制环保持50Hz。规划器训练数据共37.14小时。
article.why_it_matters: 它把“高层生成+低层跟踪”的松耦合级联改成了真正的闭环，说明鲁棒性可以从规划层持续闭环中生长出来，而不只是低层控制器给的，这为通用人形全身控制走向自主提供了可复制的工程路径。
article.limitations: 作者承认两点：系统不显式建模精确的全身物体交互，接触密集的loco-manipulation任务可能失效；在线规划器只以紧凑目标位置、文本和运动学状态为条件，缺少视觉和触觉，难以支撑高维感知任务。此外，真机实验依赖HTC Vive外部定位，附录指出失败主要来自跟踪器离开15m×15m测绘区域后的定位丢失，长时（≥45秒）多次技能切换后也会退化为中性姿态。
article.figure_caption_zh: ReactiveBFM总览：异步闭环推理经轨迹分块与本体感受反馈接入通用控制器，规划器从多模态流式条件生成平滑轨迹，并以计划性前缀采样课程和条件遵循训练缓解暴露偏差。

(b) Architecture of our reactive motion planner. It generates smooth robot trajectories from multi-modal streaming conditions. (c) Core training strategies including a scheduled prefix sampling curriculum and condition adherence to mitigate exposure bias.

*
Corresponding author
Abstract.
KV cache reuse accelerates LLM serving,
but existing systems manage host DRAM and NVMe SSD as a tiered hierarchy
where DRAM acts as an intermediate cache.
Production LLM workloads break both premises of this hierarchy.
First, bimodal reuse defeats DRAM temporal filtering,
since workloads are dominated either by one-shot blocks with long reuse distances
or by multi-gigabyte agentic sessions that exceed DRAM capacity,
putting SSD on the critical read path.
Second, DRAM staging and eviction-ordered layout bottleneck SSD restoration.
Holding host staging buffers for in-flight prefixes causes contention under load
that aborts prefetches, while incremental eviction scatters a session’s blocks
across the SSD and prevents large sequential reads.
We present
FlatCake
, a
flat
KV storage architecture that exposes host DRAM and NVMe SSD
as peer media in a unified 64-bit address space.
Exploiting the fact that KV blocks are write-once, immutable, and reused at session scope,
FlatCake
places each block directly onto its target medium in session-contiguous, layer-major order
at creation time and never migrates it.
FlatCake
streams coalesced SSD reads directly into a bounded GPU window via GPUDirect Storage
and decouples DRAM and SSD request queues to prevent head-of-line blocking.
On a production Claude Code trace with DeepSeek-V4-Flash,
FlatCake
sustains a 94% cache hit rate as load increases (versus 64% for Mooncake),
eliminates Mooncake’s
6.5
×
6.5\times
–
6.7
×
6.7\times
SSD read amplification,
and reduces peak-load mean TTFT by
1.6
×
1.6\times
while improving total token throughput by
1.6
×
1.6\times
.
Across 8K–128K contexts on Llama-3.1-70B,
FlatCake
further reduces mean TTFT by up to
2.4
