Keywords:
LLM serving, KV cache management, memory tiering,
flat KV storage, GPUDirect Storage
1.
Introduction
Prefix caching is now standard in large language model (LLM) serving,
allowing requests that share a prefix to reuse previously computed key-value (KV) tensors
and avoid redundant prefill computation
(
Kwon et al., 2023
;
Zheng et al., 2024
;
Qin et al., 2025
)
.
As LLM workloads evolve from short, globally shared system prompts
(
Wang et al., 2025
)
to multi-turn conversations
(
Hu et al., 2026
)
and long-context agentic coding sessions
that append tool outputs and retrieved files on every turn (averaging 219K input tokens
per request in a production Claude Code trace
(
SemiAnalysis, 2026
)
),
active KV working sets routinely reach tens of gigabytes per session and span hours.
Because these working sets far exceed GPU HBM and host DRAM capacity,
while recomputing evicted history consumes up to 93% of prefill compute
(
Hu et al., 2026
)
,
NVMe SSDs must serve as a primary KV cache medium on the critical path
(
Qiu et al., 2025a
)
.
Figure 1
.
Tiered and flat KV cache storage. (a) Tiering ranks DRAM above SSD,
so a block reaches SSD only when LRU evicts it.
(b)
FlatCake
places both media at one level behind a unified address space and
writes each block straight to its target, so nothing migrates.
Two KV cache storage organizations side by side, each serving
the same prefill and decode GPUs through GPU HBM. On the left, tiering ranks
host DRAM as L2 above NVMe SSD as L3, joined by a red arrow labelled LRU
evict. On the right, \sysninterposes
a flat interface over a unified address space, from which two arrows fan out
to host DRAM and NVMe SSD, both labelled L2 and drawn at the same level with
no arrow between them.
Existing systems such as Mooncake
(
Qin et al., 2025
)
, LMCache
(
Cheng and others, 2025
)
,
and SGLang HiCache
(
Xie and SGLang Team, 2025
)
manage GPU HBM, host DRAM, and NVMe SSD
as a classical
tiered hierarchy
(Figure
1
(a)),
placing host DRAM in front of SSD as an intermediate L2 cache and staging layer.
Borrowed from general-purpose memory and storage systems,
this hierarchical design relies on two foundational premises:
(1)
temporal filtering
, namely that recency-based caching in DRAM can capture
the active working set so the slower SSD serves only cold misses off the critical path; and
(2)
staging and coalescing
, namely that because incremental eviction scrambles
on-disk layout relative to read order, staging SSD accesses through host DRAM buffers
is an effective way to reassemble scattered reads and hide device latency.
Profiling eight production traces from Mooncake, Qwen Bailian, and Claude Code (§
2.2
)
reveals that LLM KV cache workloads violate both premises simultaneously.
First, bimodal reuse defeats DRAM temporal filtering,
putting SSD on the critical read path.
Across production traces, KV reuse falls into two regimes, and neither fits a DRAM cache filter.
In conversational and API workloads (seven traces), 53–94% of KV blocks are accessed only once,
while reusable prefixes span long reuse distances of hundreds to thousands of intervening requests;
admitting every request into DRAM pollutes it with one-shot blocks
that flush reusable prefixes to SSD before their next turn arrives.
Conversely, in agentic coding (Claude Code), 83.4% of blocks are reused (98.3% ideal hit rate)
with immediate turn-to-turn locality,
but multi-gigabyte session footprints quickly exceed host DRAM capacity across concurrent sessions.
In both regimes, most cache hits must be served from NVMe SSD,
so migrating blocks between DRAM and SSD adds data movement without keeping hot data in DRAM.
Second, DRAM staging and eviction-ordered layout turn SSD restoration
into a concurrency and I/O bottleneck.
When SSD must serve the bulk of hits, the tiered mechanisms meant to smooth SSD access
become the bottleneck itself.
Restoring a long-context prefix through host DRAM requires holding host staging buffers
for the entire in-flight hit, scaling memory demand with context length and concurrency.
Even when SSD-to-DRAM and DRAM-to-GPU transfers are pipelined,
concurrent restores contend for bounded staging memory,
delaying or aborting prefetches under load and turning blocks already stored on SSD into recomputed misses.
Worse, even when bypassing host DRAM via batched GPUDirect Storage (GDS),
tiered storage populates and reclaims SSD space in eviction or FIFO-bucket order rather than session order.
As a result, a session’s blocks are scattered across non-contiguous SSD offsets
and coarse bucket reclamation invalidates active prefixes across sessions,
forcing
O
⁡
(
layers
×
blocks
)
O(\text{layers}\times\text{blocks})
fragmented reads that underutilize sequential NVMe bandwidth.
Why does tiered storage fall into this trap?
Tiering is designed for mutable pages whose future access patterns and spatial grouping
are unknown when written.
Our key insight is that LLM KV cache blocks are write-once, immutable,
and reused together at the granularity of a session scope.
Because a block is never modified in place, there is no dirty state to write back;
because blocks generated in a turn belong to a known session prefix
and are always restored together across layers on subsequent turns,
their ideal on-disk spatial grouping is already known at creation time.
Consequently, if blocks are placed directly onto their target medium
in session-contiguous, layer-major order at write time and never migrated,
SSD restores become naturally sequential and no longer need host DRAM for either caching or reassembly.
Based on this insight, we propose
FlatCake
, a
flat KV storage architecture
that replaces the migratory hierarchy with peer storage media (§
3
).
As shown in Figure
1
(b),
FlatCake
exposes host DRAM and NVMe SSD
at the same level behind a unified 64-bit Global Virtual Address (GVA) space,
placing each KV block once at write time without cross-tier migration.
FlatCake
realizes this architecture through three coordinated components:
•
FC-GVA: Global Virtual Address Manager
(§
3.2
).
FC-GVA decouples KV placement from eviction by binding each block to DRAM or SSD once at creation
within a session-contiguous scope and encoding its medium, node, and offset in an immutable 64-bit GVA.
This eliminates cross-tier migration, enables
O
⁡
(
1
)
O(1)
media-aware routing without tier-by-tier lookup,
and supports zero-writeback, session-granularity SSD reclamation.
•
FC-MAS: Medium-Aware Request Scheduler
(§
3.3
).
Using the media semantics embedded in each GVA,
FC-MAS isolates fast DRAM-ready requests from long-latency SSD-preparing requests without DRAM pre-staging,
schedules background SSD prefetches by size-aware response ratio,
and re-admits prefetched requests by original arrival time to prevent both head-of-line blocking and starvation.
•
FC-CIO: Coalescing Direct I/O Engine
(§
3.4
).
FC-CIO co-designs write-time layer-major scope layout with read-time request coalescing
to collapse
O
⁡
(

×
blocks
)

scattered page reads into

sequential GPUDirect Storage transfers, streaming them through a bounded GPU HBM window
overlapped with layer-wise computation to eliminate host staging contention.
We implement
FlatCake
in SGLang and evaluate it with DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B hybrid MoE) on NVIDIA B200 GPUs
and Llama-3.1-70B (dense GQA) on NVIDIA A100 GPUs (§
5

Replaying a production Claude Code trace across increasing arrival rates,
FlatCake
sustains a 94.2–94.6% delivered cache hit rate,
staying within 0.6 percentage points of the trace’s 94.7% prefix-reuse ceiling,
whereas Mooncake’s hit rate drops from 87.9% at low load to 64.3% under staging contention.

Background and Motivation
2.1.
KV Cache Reuse and Tiered Storage
Once generated during prefill, KV cache
(
Vaswani et al., 2017
)
blocks are write-once and immutable,
and their reuse across requests follows three primary patterns
determined by how the shared prefix is formed.
Prefix caching
(
Zheng and others, 2024
)
reuses KV blocks
across
requests that share a static prefix, such as a system prompt or few-shot template,
so only the uncached suffix requires prefill computation.
Multi-turn conversations
reuse KV blocks
within
a user session,
where each turn appends a new prompt and model response to the accumulated history of prior turns.
Agentic workloads
also accumulate state within a session,
but append tool invocations, retrieved files, and command outputs on every turn
while spawning sub-agents that replay the shared session prefix in parallel.
As a result, per-turn context grows by tens of thousands of tokens,
and a single session’s KV footprint can reach tens of gigabytes.
To accommodate working sets that exceed GPU HBM, existing systems such as
Mooncake
(
Qin et al., 2025
)
, LMCache
(
Cheng and others, 2025
)
, and SGLang HiCache
(
Xie and SGLang Team, 2025
)
organize GPU HBM, host DRAM, and NVMe SSD as a three-level
tiered hierarchy
(Figure
1
(a)).
In this design, newly generated KV blocks are admitted into host DRAM first,
evicted incrementally to NVMe SSD under LRU or FIFO policies when DRAM fills,
and staged back through host DRAM buffers when restored to the GPU.
This architecture relies on two premises:
first, that host DRAM acts as an effective
temporal filter
that keeps the active working set in memory;
and second, that
staging and coalescing
SSD reads in host DRAM hides on-disk fragmentation and device latency.

2.2.
Why Tiered Storage Fails on LLM Workloads
Characterizing eight production traces from three providers (Table
1
,
evaluated at each trace’s native block size of 512, 16, and 64 tokens for Mooncake, Qwen Bailian, and Claude Code,
with reuse distance measured in intervening requests)
shows that LLM KV workloads break both premises of tiered storage.
Observation 1: Bimodal reuse defeats DRAM temporal filtering, putting SSD on the critical read path.
Table
1
shows that ideal hit rates under an infinite-capacity cache
span 36.6% to 98.3% across the eight traces.
The traces fall into two distinct reuse regimes,
and in neither regime can recency-based DRAM caching retain the active working set.
Across the seven prefix-caching and conversation traces, 53.2–94.0% of blocks
are accessed only once, peaking at 94.0% in Qwen to-B API and 78.5% in Mooncake ToolAgent.
While the top 10% of blocks account for 34–65% of all accesses (Figure
2
(a)),
reuse distances exhibit heavy tails, reaching a mean of 2,550 intervening requests
and a P99 of 54,728 in Qwen to-B API (489 and 4,085 in Mooncake ToolAgent).
When every newly generated block is admitted into host DRAM first,
one-shot blocks continually flush reusable session prefixes to SSD before their next turn arrives.
Consequently, replacing the DRAM eviction policy yields little benefit:
even when the fast tier holds 40.1% of total blocks in multi-turn serving,
LRU, FIFO, and queue-enhanced policies all achieve DRAM hit rates near 20%
(
Hu et al., 2026
)
.
The agentic coding trace (Claude Code) exhibits the opposite reuse pattern
but reaches the same storage outcome.
Because each turn extends and replays the session prefix and sub-agent fan-out
reuses prefixes almost immediately (mean reuse distance of 0.85 requests, P99 of 14),
only 16.6% of blocks are one-shot and the infinite-capacity hit rate reaches 98.31%.
However, each request spans an average of 3,421 blocks (218,922 tokens),
compared with 23 blocks in Mooncake Conversation.
Even under DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s compressed FP8 representation (Figure
2
(b)),
a single request requires a median of 0.52 GiB and a mean of 0.80 GiB of history KV state
per GPU rank (4.1 GiB median and 6.4 GiB mean across eight ranks, reaching 16.0 GiB at P90).
Across concurrent multi-turn sessions, the active working set rapidly exceeds host DRAM capacity.
Thus, whether reuse is sparse with long reuse distances or dense across multi-gigabyte contexts,
most cache hits must be served from NVMe SSD,
making cross-tier migration between DRAM and SSD unproductive.
Observation 2: DRAM staging and eviction-ordered layout bottleneck SSD restoration.
Because most cache hits must be served from SSD (Observation
2.2
),
end-to-end prefill performance is governed by the SSD restoration path.
Although storage I/O accounts for 51–98% of TTFT
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
,
raw NVMe bandwidth is not the primary limit:
even when the SSD is emulated in DRAM at 16.9 GiB/s,
KV offloading achieves only 2.0 GiB/s
(
Ren et al., 2025
)
.
Instead, when SSD serves the bulk of hits, the tiered mechanisms meant to smooth SSD access
become the bottleneck itself.

In a tiered hierarchy, restoring an SSD-resident prefix copies KV blocks from SSD
into host staging buffers before transferring them layer-by-layer to GPU HBM,
while background promotion separately populates the DRAM cache.

Takeaway.
Tiered storage falls into this trap because it is designed for mutable pages
whose future access patterns and spatial grouping are unknown when written.
In contrast, LLM KV cache blocks are
write-once, immutable,
and reused together at the granularity of a session scope

Because a block is never modified in place and its session-prefix grouping is known upon creation,
placing blocks directly onto their target medium in session-contiguous, layer-major order at write time
makes SSD restores naturally sequential and eliminates the need for host DRAM caching or reassembly.

Even when blocks are contiguous on disk, the inference engine’s radix tree queries prefixes at page granularity,
handing the storage backend hundreds of thousands of block descriptors that may span multiple turns or scopes
and arrive out of offset order.
To recover contiguous LBA ranges before issuing GDS calls,
FC-CIO performs a lightweight sort-merge pass at the submission layer (Figure
5
(b)).
It first sorts block descriptors by
(gpu_file_id, offset)
to place physically adjacent blocks next to one another,
and then scans linearly to coalesce adjacent ranges into single large read descriptors.
When partial prefix hits or sub-block alignments leave small unrequested gaps between adjacent ranges,
FC-CIO bridges gaps smaller than a configurable byte threshold (

trading a bounded amount of extra sequential bytes to eliminate NVMe command split overhead.
Merged descriptors are striped round-robin across worker threads,

4.
Implementation
We implement
FlatCake
in approximately 8.8K lines of C++17/CUDA and 7.1K lines of Python,
integrating it into SGLang
(
Zheng et al., 2024
)
behind the standard
HiCacheStorage
interface (
exists
,
get
,
put
)
without modifying model runner or attention kernels.
Pinned DRAM pool and hugepage allocation.
At engine initialization, the local DRAM backend pre-allocates the host KV pool using
mmap
with
MAP_POPULATE
and 2 MB hugepages (
MAP_HUGETLB
),
and registers the arena once with
cudaHostRegister
.
Pre-faulting and pinning hugepages at startup eliminates page-fault traps, TLB thrashing,
and per-transfer pinning overhead on the
cudaMemcpyAsync
path.
Pre-allocated NVMe file pool and GDS alignment.
To prevent filesystem metadata allocation and extent fragmentation on the write path,
FC-CIO pre-allocates a pool of fixed-size single-extent files on the XFS/RAID-0 array at startup using
fallocate
and opens each file with
O_DIRECT
and
cuFileHandleRegister
.
All logical block offsets within a GPU File and all GPU staging buffer slices are aligned to 4 KiB boundaries,
satisfying
libcufile
DMA alignment requirements and preventing driver-internal bounce buffering.
Double-buffered GPU staging and page scatter.
Because calling
cuFileBufRegister
dynamically on per-request GPU buffers incurs millisecond-scale
BAR1 and IOMMU mapping overhead, FC-CIO allocates and registers a fixed per-GPU HBM staging window once at initialization.
Restores pipeline GDS reads across two ping-pong layer buffers within this registered window;
as soon as a coalesced layer read completes on the I/O CUDA stream,
a lightweight CUDA scatter kernel copies each 256-token page from the contiguous staging buffer
into its non-contiguous destination slot in SGLang’s paged KV pool,
synchronizing with the model compute stream via
cudaEventRecord
and
cudaStreamWaitEvent
.
Lock-free Level-1 GVA index.
The Level 1 block-key-to-GVA index is implemented as a concurrent open-addressed hash table
using 64-bit atomic compare-and-swap (
CAS
) operations.
Because GVAs are immutable once published and session reclamation frees entire scopes asynchronously,
scheduler threads querying prefix hits execute wait-free reads without contending with background write-completion workers.

Experimental Setup
Testbed.
Our primary evaluation runs on an 8-GPU NVIDIA B200 server with 3 TB of host DRAM
and an 8-drive Samsung PM9A3 NVMe SSD RAID 0 array (Table
3
).
Every evaluated system is provisioned with an identical KV cache budget of 1 TiB host DRAM and 4 TiB NVMe SSD.
We build on SGLang v0.5.19, Mooncake v0.3.13, CUDA 13.1, and NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage (GDS) 1.16.1 (
libcufile
).
To evaluate generality across model architectures and GPU generations, we also run a context-length sensitivity sweep
with Llama-3.1-70B (TP4) on a 4-GPU NVIDIA A100 server (§
5.4
).
Model and workload.
We serve DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731
(
DeepSeek-AI, 2026
)
, a 284B-parameter MoE model
with 43 hybrid multi-head latent attention (MLA) layers and a 1M-token context window.
The model uses an
fp8_e4m3
KV cache with 256-token pages and a per-rank footprint of 7.5 KiB/token.
We replay the production
claude-code-weka-0621
agentic coding trace
(
SemiAnalysis, 2026
)
,
comprising 98,827 requests and 21.6B input tokens across 393 multi-turn sessions (Table
1
).
Requests are replayed in recorded arrival order across arrival rates from 0.1 to 1.0 QPS without cache warm-up,
following the SGLang HiCache benchmark methodology
(
Xie and SGLang Team, 2025
)
.
Baselines and metrics.
We compare three systems under identical engine and storage budgets:
•
+L2 Host DRAM
(
Xie and SGLang Team, 2025
)
: SGLang HiCache’s two-tier HBM–DRAM LRU cache without SSD offloading.
•
+L3 Mooncake
(
Qin et al., 2025
)
: A three-tier HBM–DRAM–SSD hierarchy where SSD-resident KV blocks are staged through host DRAM buffers before H2D transfer and promoted into the DRAM tier.
•
FlatCake
: Our flat peer storage architecture combining FC-GVA, FC-MAS, and FC-CIO.
In the Llama-3.1-70B context-length sweep, we additionally compare against
Recompute-only
(no KV offloading beyond GPU HBM)
and
Mooncake-GDS
(which replaces Mooncake’s host-staged SSD read path with GPUDirect Storage while retaining tiered eviction-ordered SSD placement).
We report mean and median (P50) Time-to-First-Token (TTFT), total token throughput (tokens/s),
delivered cache hit rate (counting only blocks transferred to GPU HBM before prefill),
SSD read bandwidth, SSD prefetch latency, and normalized SSD read/write amplification.

Why Tiered Storage Degrades: Delivered Cache Hit Rate.
Figure
6
(d) reveals the root cause of the latency and throughput gap.
Across all arrival rates,
FlatCake
sustains a delivered cache hit rate of 94.16–94.57%,
staying within 0.6 percentage points of the trace’s 94.72% prefix-reuse ceiling.
In contrast, +L2 Host DRAM plateaus at 53.30% across all rates because multi-gigabyte agentic sessions
exceed host DRAM capacity (Observation
2.2
).
More importantly, while +L3 Mooncake achieves an 87.9% hit rate at low load (0.1 QPS),
its delivered hit rate drops to 64.26% at 0.5 QPS and above, recovering only 11 percentage points over DRAM-only caching
despite having 4 TiB of NVMe SSD capacity.
This hit-rate collapse under +L3 Mooncake stems primarily from host staging contention (Observation
2.2
)
and coarse bucket reclamation (§
3.2
).
Because a tiered restore must stage an entire in-flight prefix in host DRAM buffers before H2D transfer completes,
concurrent long-context restores exhaust the engine’s bounded in-flight staging budget as QPS rises.
When staging memory saturates, SGLang revokes the blocked prefetch and falls back to recomputing the prefix on the GPU,
turning cached SSD blocks into expensive compute misses.
In contrast,
FlatCake
streams coalesced SSD reads directly into a fixed-size GPU HBM staging window (§
3.4
);
when the window is fully occupied under high load, incoming restores wait briefly on stream synchronization
rather than aborting prefetches, preserving a 94.16% hit rate at peak load.

In contrast,

Direct Storage I/O and Request Scheduling.
Several systems accelerate the SSD-to-GPU read path using GPUDirect Storage
(
Bergman et al., 2017
;
Bae et al., 2021
;
Qureshi et al., 2023
;
Qiu et al., 2025b
;
Li et al., 2025
)
,
pre-registered GPU buffers with parallel disk workers (LMCache
(
Cheng and others, 2025
)
),
GPU-initiated
io_uring
queues (Tutti
(
Qiu et al., 2025a
)
),
or storage-near execution
(
Pan et al., 2025
;
Luo and Shen, 2026
)
.
However, optimizing the transport primitive alone does not resolve on-disk fragmentation:
when SSD space is populated in LRU eviction order, a session’s prefix remains scattered across non-contiguous LBAs,
preventing NVMe controllers from coalescing reads into single DMA transfers (Observation
2.2

FlatCake
co-designs write-time layer-major scope layout within pre-allocated
GPU File

and read-time sort-merge coalescing (FC-CIO) so that standard GDS transfers read sequential per-layer extents.
Furthermore, unlike device-level I/O schedulers
(
Woo et al., 2021
)
,
FC-MAS uses the media identity encoded in each 64-bit GVA to decouple DRAM-ready and SSD-preparing queues
while preserving arrival-order fairness across media.
7.
Conclusion
We presented
FlatCake
, a flat KV storage architecture that replaces the migratory DRAM–SSD hierarchy
with peer storage media behind a unified 64-bit address space.

FlatCake
combines FC-GVA, FC-MAS, and FC-CIO to eliminate cross-tier migration and host staging contention.

article.headline: KV 缓存不再分层：DRAM 与 SSD 平级
article.lede: FlatCake 把主机 DRAM 与 SSD 放进统一地址空间，KV 块写入即定址、不再迁移，命中率稳定在 94%。
article.problem: 现有 Mooncake、LMCache、SGLang HiCache 把主机 DRAM 当作 SSD 之前的 L2 缓存层，依赖两个前提：DRAM 的时序过滤能留住活跃工作集，以及用 DRAM 暂存来重组 SSD 的碎片读。论文对 8 条生产轨迹的刻画显示，LLM 的 KV 复用呈双峰分布，在对话、API 类轨迹中，53.2%–94.0% 的块只被访问一次，且复用距离很长；而 Claude Code 这类 agentic 轨迹虽然 98.31% 的块会被复用，但单请求平均 3,421 个块（218,922 token），单卡历史 KV 中位数 0.52 GiB、P90 达 16.0 GiB，都会直接超出主机 DRAM 容量。两种情况下，多数命中都必须由 SSD 提供，跨层迁移只是在搬运数据；同时，按逐出顺序写入磁盘会让一个 session 的块散落在非连续 LBA 上，恢复时退化为 O(layers×blocks) 次小读。
article.method: 作者提出 FlatCake，把 DRAM 与 NVMe SSD 视为同一层级的对等介质，放在统一的 64 位全局虚拟地址（GVA）空间之后，并在写入时按 session 连续、layer-major 的顺序把每个 KV 块直接写入目标介质，此后永不迁移。FC-GVA 在创建时依据 radix 树引用计数、session 轮次、回复长度等写入时可观测信号，决定该块进入 DRAM 还是 SSD，并把介质、节点、偏移编码进 64 位 GVA，实现 O(1) 路由和以 session 为粒度的无回写回收；FC-MAS 用双队列隔离 DRAM-ready 与 SSD-preparing 请求，SSD 预取按“等待时间/KV 大小”的 size-aware HRRN 排序，并按原始到达时间重新入队以防饿死；FC-CIO 通过读时排序归并，把散块请求合并，再经 GPUDirect Storage 直接流式写入一个双缓冲、仅容纳两层规模的 GPU HBM 窗口，并与逐层计算重叠。
article.results: 在 8×B200 上回放生产 Claude Code 轨迹（98,827 请求、21.6B 输入 token），服务 DeepSeek-V4-Flash：FlatCake 的交付缓存命中率维持在 94.16%–94.57%，距轨迹 94.72% 的复用上限不足 0.6 个百分点；Mooncake 则从 0.1 QPS 的 87.9% 跌至 0.5 QPS 以上的 64.26%。在 1.0 QPS 峰值负载下，FlatCake 平均 TTFT 为 7.57 s，相比 Mooncake 的 12.24 s、L2 Host DRAM 的 17.51 s 分别降低 1.6 倍、2.3 倍；P50 TTFT 为 6.26 s（对比 11.45 s、18.39 s，降低 1.8 倍、2.9 倍）；总吞吐为 98.3K token/s，相比 61.6K、43.2K 提升 1.6 倍、2.3 倍。SSD 读带宽为 5.03 GB/s（Mooncake 2.69 GB/s，1.9 倍），预取延迟为 1.64 s（Mooncake 9.50 s，5.8 倍），并消除了 Mooncake 6.51 倍–6.72 倍的读放大；写放大方面，FlatCake 为 1.000 倍，Mooncake 为 1.007 倍–1.018 倍。消融实验中，去掉 FC-MAS 后，平均 TTFT 增加 10%–11%、P99 增加 27%、吞吐下降 12%。在 Llama-3.1-70B（TP4，A100）8K–128K 上下文上，平均 TTFT 相比 Recompute-only 降低 2.3 倍–4.9 倍，相比 Mooncake 降低 1.5 倍–2.4 倍，相比 Mooncake-GDS 最高降低 1.8 倍（64K 时分别为 3.74 s 与 6.60 s）。
article.why_it_matters: KV 复用已经是 LLM 服务的标准优化，FlatCake 用生产轨迹说明，“DRAM 做缓存层”这一来自通用存储的直觉在 agentic 负载下不再成立，并给出了一种以“写入时一次性定址 + session 连续布局”换取 SSD 顺序读的替代范式。它也提醒做前缀缓存和 offloading 的系统：GDS 这类传输原语本身不能解决磁盘碎片问题，必须与写入布局协同设计。
article.limitations: 主要结论来自单条生产 Claude Code 轨迹的回放，且遵循 HiCache 方法不做缓存预热，DRAM/SSD 配额固定为 1 TiB 与 4 TiB，其他 7 条轨迹只用于动机刻画，没有做端到端实验；FC-GVA 的介质判定依赖回复长度阈值 τ 与 session 上下文阈值 L_agent 等启发式参数，论文正文未给出具体数字，也未给出这些参数的敏感性分析，同时实现强依赖 GDS/cuFile、预分配 XFS/RAID-0 文件池与 4 KiB 对齐等部署条件。
article.figure_caption_zh: FlatCake 架构图：(a) 控制路径由 FC-GVA 把 block key 映射为 64 位 GVA，并在写入时一次性定址，FC-MAS 分离 DRAM-ready 与 SSD-preparing 两条队列；(b) 数据路径中，DRAM 命中走 cudaMemcpyAsync，SSD 读经 GDS 合并后流入有限的 GPU 暂存窗口。

figure.caption: architecture. (a)~Control path: maps block keys to 64-bit GVAs with write-once placement~( {182}), and separates DRAM-ready and SSD-preparing queues~( {183}). (b)~Data path: DRAM hits use {cudaMemcpyAsync}, while streams coalesced SSD reads via GDS~( {184}) into a bounded GPU staging window.

page_papers.content:
{surveycover}
Video Generation Meets Agent Harness
Agentic Video Generation, Agentic World Modeling and Recursive Self-Improvement
Liaoyuan Fan
∗
Yuhao Zheng
∗
Dongxing Mao
∗
Hangyu Ran
∗
Siyuan Hu
∗
Weijia Mao  Rui Zhao
Weijia Wu  Guian Fang  Yanzhe Chen  Zeyu Zhu  Yuxin Jiang  Yiren Song  Yuchao Gu  Junchao Yi  Qi Hu
Dan Kong  Alex Jinpeng Wang  Kevin Qinghong Lin
🖂
{}^{\text{\Letter}}
Mike Zheng Shou
🖂
{}^{\text{\Letter}}
Wei Liu
🖂
{}^{\text{\Letter}}
Video Rebirth National University of Singapore Nanyang Technological University Hong Kong University of Science and Technology University of Science and Technology of China Central South University University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
Abstract
Abstract:
Video generation is evolving from end-to-end synthesis toward agentic generation, in which planning, tool use, and feedback produce coherent multi-shot videos with greater control. Meanwhile, video world models provide action-conditioned observations and predicted futures and can serve as interactive environments for agents. We study this intersection through the
agent harness
: the executable runtime that constructs an agent’s context, exposes tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and enforces budgets around models such as video generators. The report is organized around three directions.
First, we study agentic video generation, where harnesses coordinate script and shot planning, asset management, shot production, and editing, and we discuss what the evaluation of such systems must separate. Second, we examine agentic world modeling, where harnesses mediate observation, control, execution, and state, including designs in which a game engine or a program written by a coding agent holds the world state while the video model renders it, and where agents and world models test and improve one another. Third, we examine recursive self-improvement (RSI) for video model development: we separate revisions of a current output from updates to harness state, generator parameters, and evaluators, and from changes to the procedure that produces later updates, and we identify the channels through which an improvement could re-enter development.
Across these directions, we analyze the agent capabilities that video imposes, from audiovisual perception, long-horizon planning, and memory to interaction through code and computer use, feedback-guided control, skill reuse, and multi-agent organization.
We conclude with open challenges, including autonomous video production, lifelong memory, programmable hybrid control, autonomous model development, provenance and cost accounting, and evaluation that links video quality and task performance to sustained improvement of models and harnesses.
Keywords
: Video Generation, Agent, Harness Engineering, World Models, Recursive Self-Improvement
Webpage
:
https://agentic-videogen.github.io/
GitHub
:
https://github.com/agentic-videogen/awesome-agentic-videogen
Figure 1:
Video generation meets agent harness.
This report explores how agent harnesses revolutionize video generation across key areas: agentic video generation, agentic world modeling, and recursive self-improvement.
Contents
1
Introduction
1.1
Motivation
1.2
Contributions and Positioning
1
Introduction
1.1
Motivation
Video generators produce increasingly realistic, controllable, and temporally
coherent clips
[
kong2024hunyuanvideo
]
. A generator alone, however, does
not organize the decisions needed to complete a video task. A creative brief
must become coherent shots;
references must persist across scenes; takes must be inspected; edits must
preserve what is correct
[
huang2026vimax
,
vista2025
]
. Interactive
video must also support continuing actions grounded in observations, not
just a finished clip
[
gao2026lingbotworld2
]
.
These requirements motivate a transition from video generation
to agentic video generation: a goal-directed process in which generated results
inform subsequent decisions. An agent can revise a plan, retrieve a reference,
select a tool, or localize a failure in response to actual outcomes
[
li2026videogenagent
]
.
Agentic video generation denotes a system-level perspective, not a new generator
architecture: the video model provides synthesis or predicted transitions,
while the agent makes consequential choices around those capabilities.
Video couples these choices over time. References affect later shots
[
chen2026cinecrew
]
,
actions change subsequent observations, and local repairs can disrupt
temporal consistency elsewhere. Plausible footage may still violate a
narrative requirement or fail to realize an intended action, so a quality
score alone rarely specifies what to do next
[
liu2024videogenerationevaluation
,
ding2026playworld
]
. Effective control
requires connecting observations to localized decisions while maintaining
project or interaction state and accounting for generation cost.
The development from large language models (LLMs) to agents offers a
foundation for this control. Rather than only generating a response, an
LLM can operate within a cycle of reasoning, tool use, and observation,
as demonstrated by ReAct
[
yao2023react
]
. Planning and memory extend
this cycle to tasks requiring multiple decisions
[
weng2023agents
]
.
Making these capabilities operational requires an agent harness:
the executable runtime around the model that constructs its context,
exposes tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and enforces permissions
and budgets
[
weng2026harness
,
ning2026code
]
(Section
).
For video generation, the harness is where a creative brief or an
interactive goal becomes executable operations on generators, editors,
and world models. The central question shifts from generating a good
clip to reliably completing a video
task through feedback. Agentic video generation and video world-model interaction are two
concrete settings. A further question is whether experience from these tasks
can improve the system that will perform future tasks.
Figure 2:
Agent involvement across three directions of video generation.
Representative works branch from a shared video generation foundation into
agentic world modeling, agentic video generation, and development toward
recursive self-improvement (RSI). These directions connect video models to
sustained world interaction, coordinated production, and the improvement of
models and the agent harness. Vertical position reflects increasing agent
involvement, from No Agent through Agent Assistance and Agent Guided
Improvement to Self Improvement.
Feedback changes different objects at different timescales. Prompt revision
or take replacement targets the current artifact
[
vista2025
]
;
retaining a skill targets subsequent tasks
[
wei2026videoweaver
]
;
updating a dataset, critic, or generator targets later model
versions
[
liu2025videoalign
]
. These outcomes
should not be conflated: effective repair of a current video does not by
itself establish improvement in future capability.
Beyond repairing individual outputs, context engineering considers
how instructions, retrieved evidence, memory, and execution records are
selected and organized for subsequent decisions
[
weng2026harness
]
.
Agentic Context Engineering (ACE), for example, accumulates and revises a
structured context from execution feedback rather than updating model
weights
[
zhang2025ace
]
. Such work shifts attention from a current
response toward reusable knowledge, while leaving open whether the
mechanisms that construct and update that knowledge can themselves improve.
Recent work on automated research extends these ideas to model
development. The AI Scientist links idea generation, coding, experiments,
and reporting
[
lu2024aiscientist
]
;
autoresearch
runs a bounded
loop of training code modification, experimentation, and validation-based
acceptance
[
karpathy2026autoresearch
]
. These workflows connect proposals
to empirical feedback, but automating a fixed experiment loop is not the
same as improving the loop itself. Research on self-improving agents,
exemplified by the Darwin Gödel Machine and Regularized Recursive
Self-Improvement (RRSI), explores changes to the
agent’s own code or harness
[
zhang2025dgm
,
xia2026rrsi
]
.
Such work motivates examining the processes that generate and validate
subsequent improvements.
Recursive self-improvement (RSI) asks whether a system can improve
the procedures that produce further improvements
[
chen2026surveyr04
,
duan2026surveyn21
]
.
Video-specific targets include failure diagnosis, data collection,
supervision construction, update
selection, and candidate validation. Repeating a fixed collection-and-training
pipeline is iterative improvement. The recursive direction additionally
allows evidence to revise that pipeline, changing how a later round discovers
and addresses weaknesses.
An agent harness provides an executable surface for this direction.
Its context construction, tool orchestration, memory, testing
workflow, and update-selection rules can be inspected and, where authorized,
revised
[
weng2026harness
]
. This does not make every harness
self-improving: a revision must be retained and independently evaluated on
later tasks or improvement rounds under stated resource constraints
[
xia2026rrsi
]
.
Existing video research supplies parts of this connection: feedback can
revise reusable production skills
[
wei2026videoweaver
]
, uncertainty can
guide data acquisition for adaptation
[
savov2025autoexplore
]
, and
validation can govern critic renewal for later training
[
yang2026dualipo
]
. These are
building blocks rather than evidence that one system has completed the full
RSI loop. Our survey therefore connects three questions: how harnesses
organize agentic video generation, how they support video world-model interaction,
and how they may drive video-generation development toward RSI. The first
two establish task execution and sources of experience; the third examines
persistent capability and the procedures used to improve it.
Figure
2
maps representative work from a shared video
generation foundation into the three directions corresponding to the questions
below.
1.2
Contributions and Positioning
The survey addresses three questions about the influence of the agent harness
on video generation (Figure
1
), each corresponding to
one core chapter.
How does the agent harness enable agentic video generation?
Agentic Video Generation (Section
) studies
how harnesses coordinate planning, execution, tool use, memory, editing, and
watermarking around shared project state, and what the evaluation of such
systems must separate. We examine how feedback changes
generation and editing decisions and how those changes affect video quality, consistency,
and efficiency.
How can the agent harness be integrated into video
world models?
Agentic World Modeling
(Section
) locates where a harness can intervene in
observation, control, execution, event organization, and state management,
and examines designs in which an engine holds the world state
while the video model renders it.
We examine how these interventions support sustained interaction, control
fidelity, state continuity, and agent-driven evaluation. The focus of this
question is how a harness enables reliable interaction with a video world
model.
How can video generation systems move toward recursive self-improvement?
Toward RSI in Video Generation
(Section
) examines how advances in video
generators and the agent harness can feed back into the process that produces
subsequent model improvements. We review foundation model improvement,
agent harness improvement, and evaluation, and identify the channels through
which gains in these components can strengthen failure diagnosis, data
curation, training, and validation in later development rounds. The goal is to identify mechanisms
and evidence needed for recursively improving development processes that
can support next-generation video generation models.
These questions connect through feedback: agentic video generation and world interaction
can expose failures, while development can turn selected evidence into
changes deployed in later tasks. Section
compares the shared
agent capabilities that support all three settings.
Differentiating Our Work from Existing Surveys
Existing surveys provide complementary accounts of video generation.
Work on spatiotemporal consistency examines generation models,
representations, training strategies, and evaluation, emphasizing the
mechanisms that maintain coherent video sequences
[
yin2025spatiotemporal
]
.
Post-training and alignment surveys organize methods for adapting video
generators to human intent, including supervised fine-tuning, distillation,
preference optimization, and inference-time adaptation
[
li2026videoposttraining
]
.
Evaluation surveys examine perceptual quality, semantic fidelity, and
alignment with user instructions
[
liu2024videogenerationevaluation
]
.
Together, these accounts explain how video models are built, improved,
and assessed.
More directly related to our system perspective, agentic visual generation
surveys organize the conditioning, execution, and adaptation decisions
available to a controller across visual modalities
[
huang2026agenticvisual
]
,
or study autonomous multimodal content creation and the construction of
stateful artifacts
[
xu2026ags
,
wang2026artifactcreation
]
. Wu et al. place agentic generation and world-modeling generation on a single
capability ladder of visual generation
[
wu2026visualnewera
]
.
World model surveys characterize predictive and simulation capabilities
across domains, focus on action conditioning, memory, and responsiveness
in sustained interaction
[
chu2026agenticworldmodel
,
liu2026interactiveworldmodel
]
,
or treat world models as interactive proxies that supply feedback to
continually improving agents
[
yang2026quovadis
]
.
Harness surveys analyze the execution layer around text and coding
agents
[
ning2026code
,
guo2026harnessdesign
]
.
Surveys of self-evolving agents and RSI examine evolutionary targets,
adaptation stages, and feedback loops across general AI
systems
[
gao2025surveyr02
,
chen2026surveyr04
,
wu2026rsisurvey
]
.
These perspectives share concepts such as feedback, memory, and agent
control, but none of them takes the harness around a video generator as the
unit of analysis across production, interaction, and model development.
Table
1.2
compares related surveys and
adjacent studies by scope, thematic coverage (including RSI), and agent design.
Our survey complements these perspectives with a framework centered on
video generation that covers three settings in which a harness meets a video
model: as a synthesizer in production, as an interactive environment, and as
the object of development. The settings are linked through the harness:
agents organize generation and refinement, while video models provide
interactive experience that can inform agent decisions and further model
development. Where capability ladders treat agentic
generation and world modeling as successive stages of the
generator
[
wu2026visualnewera
]
, we take the agent harness around the
generator as the unit of analysis, so that one framework covers production,
interaction, and development.
Our contributions are threefold.
•
A harness-centered framework. We define a common agent–harness
execution loop (Section
) and apply it to
production, organized by workflow function
(Section
), and to world-model interaction,
organized by the interfaces through which a harness intervenes,
including designs in which an engine or a program holds the world
state (Section
).
•
An account of improvement. We separate revisions of the current
output from updates to harness state, generator parameters, and
evaluators, and from changes to the development procedure. We identify four channels
through which an improvement could re-enter video development.
No surveyed system yet revises the procedure that trains and
validates the generator (Section
).
•
Evaluation requirements and open problems. We state how the agent harness
supports active testing and reciprocal evaluation of agents and
world models (Section
), what the
evaluation of agentic production must separate
(Section
),
which capabilities video imposes on agents
(Section
), and which challenges remain
(Section
).

and video model development toward Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI)
through a unified agent-harness framework.

article.headline: 综述:视频生成与智能体执行框架的交汇
article.lede: 一篇综述以 agent harness 为分析单元,串联智能体视频生成、视频世界模型交互与递归自我改进三条路线。
article.problem: 视频生成器能产出越来越逼真、可控且时间连贯的片段,但单个生成器并不负责组织完成一个视频任务所需的决策:创意简报要拆成连贯镜头,参考要在场景间保持,失败的镜头要被检视和局部修补。交互式视频还要求动作能基于观测持续进行,而不是只交付一段成品片段。作者认为,评价分数本身很少能说明下一步该做什么,控制需要把观测连到局部决策,同时维护项目或交互状态并核算生成成本。
article.method: 作者把 agent harness 定义为围绕模型的可执行运行时,负责构建上下文、暴露工具、维护状态、路由反馈并约束权限与预算,并以它作为统一的分析单元组织文献。综述按三条路线展开:智能体视频生成(协调剧本与分镜规划、素材管理、镜头生产与剪辑)、智能体世界建模(由游戏引擎或编码智能体写的程序持有世界状态、视频模型负责渲染),以及视频模型开发中的递归自我改进。在第三条路线中,作者明确区分当前输出的修订、harness 状态与生成器参数及评估器的更新,以及产生后续更新的流程本身的改动。
article.results: 这是综述而非实验论文,定量性能指标论文未给出具体数字。结构化结论为:综述围绕三条路线与三个核心问题展开,提出一个以 harness 为中心的框架,并识别出四条改进可以回流到视频开发流程的渠道;作者同时给出判断——在被调研的系统里,尚无一个系统修订了训练与验证生成器的那套流程。
article.why_it_matters: 把 harness 而非生成器当作分析单元,使视频生产、世界模型交互与模型开发三个场景被同一个框架覆盖,也把评估要求摆到台面上:必须把「修好当前这条视频」与「提升未来能力」分开衡量。对做视频生成与智能体的研究者来说,这提供了一个比对系统设计与评测口径的坐标系。
article.limitations: 综述不提供新实验或统一基准上的量化对比,其分类与「四条渠道」属于概念性梳理,组件图是示意性的——作者自己说明具体系统不必实现图中每个组件,场景缩略图也不是实验结果。关于递归自我改进,作者承认现有视频研究只提供了零散积木(如反馈修订可复用技能、不确定性引导数据获取),没有任何系统完成完整闭环,因此相关前景仍属推测。
article.figure_caption_zh: 图1展示从视频生成走向由 harness 中介的世界交互:条件生成仍是共同内核,harness 围绕它完成观测、决策、控制转译、生成调度,并纳入返回的反馈与相关历史。

figure.caption: {From video generation to harness-mediated world interaction.} Conditional visual generation remains the shared core. In a video world model, one-shot conditioning becomes sustained control, temporal context must support continuing state, and output frames become observations for the next decision. Around this core, the harness observes, decides, translates controls, schedules generation, and incorporates returned feedback and relevant history. The central interfaces translate controls, coordinate execution, and interpret returned observations. External memory and tracking are distinct from model-side state or context. The diagram summarizes shared, adapted, and added components; a particular system need not implement every component. Scene thumbnails illustrate visual observations; they are not experimental results.
